It invokes the STB's statutory duty to consider 'enhancing competition and safety' under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 but does not clarify or challenge the Board's interpretation of that standard. The filing is primarily a policy advocacy statement from an individual, not a legal brief. However, it is part of the public record and may be cited by the STB in its decision to demonstrate that small business shippers have concerns about merger impacts, though the STB will likely give it limited weight absent specific operational data or industry consensus.
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is a comment filing; no formal response deadline applies to DeCock. However, the applicants and other parties may address small business concerns in their briefs.

docket_entries.title: Charlie Buckels - Small Business Owner Opposition to UP-NS Merger

He contends that 'when businesses can't absorb these costs – and most small businesses cannot, they eventually get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for the essential goods and products they need.' Buckels also asserts that reduced competition leads to 'less innovation of services tailored to small business.' His opposition is fundamentally ideological—grounded in a general belief that competition is essential to the American economy and that railroad industry consolidation threatens small business viability. He does not propose specific remedial conditions beyond general aspirations that any approved merger 'meet the standards for enhancing competition and safety.' No settlement signals present.

Reduced competition results in less service innovation tailored to small business needs
Competition is foundational to long-term business viability, employee success, and consumer welfare
Small businesses suffer first when competition is reduced or unavailable
The proposed merger presents 'great amount of uncertainty and a likely increase in transportation cost'

Unfortunately, when businesses can't absorb these costs – and most small businesses cannot, they eventually get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for the essential goods and products they need.'
'Competition drives long-term viability and lower costs. The success of businesses, employees and customers across Louisiana depend on a strong rail system.'
'when competition is reduced or unavailable small business is the first to suffer'

docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Minimal legal significance. This is an individual consumer/small business perspective that illustrates the public interest dimension of the merger review but does not introduce new legal theories, statutory interpretations, or evidentiary frameworks. It does not affect the scope or burden of proof in the proceeding. The filing may be grouped with other retail customer comments expressing general opposition to consolidation.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing; no response deadline applies to applicants

docket_entries.title: Small Business Owner Adan Flores Opposes UP-NS Merger as Detrimental to Competition and Small Business Viability
docket_entries.entry_summary: Adan Flores, a small business owner in Texas selling heavy machinery and infrastructure equipment, opposes the UP-NS merger on the grounds that it would create 'a near duopoly' detrimental to competition. He argues from personal experience that 'poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain,' and that 'less competition in rail service leads to higher costs across the board.' Flores contends that when businesses cannot absorb increased costs, they pass them to consumers. He emphasizes that small businesses ('mom-and-pop stores') are 'impacted the most' by consolidations and that 'competition drives long-term viability and lower costs.' His opposition is grounded in general competitive principles and past industry experience rather than transaction-specific harms to his business.
key_arguments: The merger would form 'a near duopoly' in U.S. rail service, which is 'detrimental to competition.'
Poorly executed rail mergers 'slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers.'
Reduced rail competition 'leads to higher costs across the board,' which are eventually 'passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for essential goods and products.'
Small businesses ('mom-and-pop stores') are disproportionately 'impacted the most' by rail consolidations.
Competition is essential to 'long-term viability and lower costs' for businesses, employees, and customers.
key_excerpts: If the merger is approved, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would form a near duopoly. This would be detrimental to competition.
Poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers – and it's the mom-and-pop stores who are impacted the most.

Less competition in rail service leads to higher costs across the board. Unfortunately, when businesses can't absorb these costs, they eventually get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for the essential goods and products they need.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Denial of the merger. Flores does not request conditional approval but rather asks that 'the Surface Transportation Board considers the impact on local businesses and ensures the tenets of the merger meet the standards for enhancing competition and safety.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low significance for regulatory analysis. This is a lay comment expressing general competitive concerns without specific evidence, service data, rate impacts, or operational details. It does not introduce novel legal issues, challenge regulatory methodology, or propose concrete remedies. It illustrates public/small business sentiment but does not substantively advance the evidentiary record on transaction effects.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing (no direct response deadline)

docket_entries.title: Richard Diek (Walker, LA Resident) - Comment Opposing UP-NS Merger on Consumer Price Grounds
docket_entries.entry_summary: Richard Diek, a 20-year Walker, Louisiana resident, opposes the UP-NS merger on the ground that railroad consolidation reduces competition and raises consumer prices. He argues: 'Mergers are known to result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and these expenses don't stop at the rail yard. They trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.' Diek does not demand outright denial but requests that 'the Surface Transportation Board certifies that the tenets of the merger and conditions imposed on the transaction meet the standards for enhancing competition in the market.' This framing suggests he would accept approval if conditions adequately protect competition and prevent consumer price increases. He emphasizes protecting small-town Louisiana communities dependent on rail-delivered goods and affordable pricing.
key_arguments: Rail industry consolidation reduces competition, which drives higher freight costs that are passed through to consumer prices on groceries and everyday goods
Small communities like Walker, Louisiana depend on freight rail access to affordable nationwide goods, and consolidation threatens this access
Merger approval without 'appropriate protections for competition' poses unacceptable risk to consumers and community economic welfare
key_excerpts: Mergers are known to result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and these expenses don't stop at the rail yard. They trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.
We need to protect consumers and prevent rail industry consolidation from leading to higher costs and weaker service.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Either deny the merger, or if approved, impose conditions that 'enhance competition in the market' and 'protect consumers and prevent rail industry consolidation from leading to higher costs and weaker service.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low. This is an unrepresented consumer comment that does not raise novel legal or regulatory issues or provide evidentiary support for competition harm claims. However, it demonstrates that the STB is receiving public interest opposition framed around consumer price impacts—a statutory factor under 49 U.S.C. § 11324(b). Individual consumer opposition may support arguments from more sophisticated intervenors (shippers, labor, competitors) who make quantified competition claims. The comment confirms that consumer welfare concerns are part of the public record and may require applicants to address consumer cost arguments in their filings.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No deadline applies; this is a comment filed during the comment period. No response required from applicants or other parties.

docket_entries.title: Andy Hedge - Small Business Owner Opposition to UP-NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: Andy Hedge, a small business owner in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, opposes the UP-NS merger on the grounds that railroad consolidation historically leads to service delays, congestion, and cost increases that disproportionately harm small shippers. He argues that combined UP-NS control of 'most of the rail network' eliminates competition, allowing the merged entity to raise shipping costs that 'trickle down to customers.' He expresses concern that consolidations prioritize 'shareholder' returns over 'competition, safety, and service' but does not propose specific conditions or remedies. His opposition is rooted in general principles about the harms of reduced competition rather than analysis specific to this transaction.
key_arguments: Big railroad mergers historically result in 'delays pile up, congestion gets worse, and small businesses like mine end up stuck waiting and paying more to keep things moving.'

UP-NS combined control would eliminate competition: 'If this merger goes through, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would control most of the rail network. That kind of dominance leaves very little room for competition, and when competition drops, costs go up.'
Merger benefits accrue to shareholders, not service quality or competition: 'Any merger should have clear benefits for competition, safety, and service — not just for shareholders.'
Small businesses depend on 'dependable rail service to get the supplies we need and to ship our products out on time' and will suffer if service reliability declines post-merger.
key_excerpts: 'When big companies merge, it doesn't always mean better service — in fact, it often means the opposite. I've seen what happens when these large consolidations go through: delays pile up, congestion gets worse, and small businesses like mine end up stuck waiting and paying more to keep things moving.'

'If this merger goes through, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would control most of the rail network. That kind of dominance leaves very little room for competition, and when competition drops, costs go up.'
docket_entries.relief_requested: Requests that the Surface Transportation Board 'take a close look at how this merger could impact small businesses, local economies, and the people who depend on affordable, efficient shipping' and ensure 'any merger should have clear benefits for competition, safety, and service — not just for shareholders.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing carries minimal legal significance. It does not advance novel competitive theory, cite specific STB precedent, or propose legally enforceable remedies. It does contribute to the public record demonstrating small business concerns about consolidation, which the STB must consider under 49 U.S.C. § 11324(b) (public interest standard includes 'effect on ... shipper and consumer interests'), but it does not materially alter the evidentiary burden or scope of review.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment filing; no response deadline

docket_entries.title: Individual Farmer Opposition to UP-NS Merger - Rural Missouri Perspective
docket_entries.entry_summary: Mike Beardslee, a Missouri grain farmer, opposes the UP-NS merger based on concern that consolidation will harm agricultural shippers by reducing competitive alternatives and increasing freight rates. His core argument: 'Fewer railroads mean fewer options. And when there's less competition, there's less incentive for service to improve or prices to stay reasonable.' He emphasizes that timing is critical during harvest season—'When harvest hits, timing is everything. We've got combines running sunup to sundown, and trucks lined up to get grain to the elevator to market. Without dependable rail service, things back up fast. Delays cost money, and when freight rates climb, it eats into already thin margins.' Beardslee frames the issue as a rural community concern affecting not just farmers but 'grain elevators, truckers, fertilizer suppliers, seed dealers' and appeals to the STB to 'listen to the people in the heartland who will feel the impact.' He offers no settlement conditions or alternative proposals—his position is that the merger should be denied to preserve competitive rail service for agriculture.
key_arguments: Consolidation from multiple railroads to fewer competitors reduces shipper choice and competitive pressure on pricing and service quality: 'Fewer railroads mean fewer options. And when there's less competition, there's less incentive for service to improve or prices to stay reasonable.'

Agricultural operations face acute vulnerability to service disruptions and rate increases because harvest timing is inflexible and perishable commodity windows create bottleneck risk: 'When harvest hits, timing is everything...Without dependable rail service, things back up fast. Delays cost money, and when freight rates climb, it eats into already thin margins.'

The merger's impact extends beyond individual farmers to the entire rural agricultural supply chain—'grain elevators, truckers, fertilizer suppliers, seed dealers'—creating regional economic concentration risk
Regulatory review should prioritize rural stakeholder testimony over corporate arguments: 'Don't just listen to the big companies, listen to the people in the heartland who will feel the impact.'
key_excerpts: Fewer railroads mean fewer options. And when there's less competition, there's less incentive for service to improve or prices to stay reasonable.

When harvest hits, timing is everything. We've got combines running sunup to sundown, and trucks lined up to get grain to the elevator to market. Without dependable rail service, things back up fast. Delays cost money, and when freight rates climb, it eats into already thin margins.
Farmers and rural communities depend on fair, competitive rail service.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the merger. Beardslee requests that the STB 'take a hard look at this proposal' and specifically warns against allowing consolidation that reduces railroad options available to agricultural shippers.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing, though from an individual, creates an evidentiary record of direct end-user concerns about competitive effects in the agricultural sector. Under 49 U.S.C. § 11324(b), the STB must consider whether the proposed transaction 'is consistent with the public interest,' which includes consideration of effects on shippers and rural communities. Individual farmer testimony, when aggregated with similar submissions, can support findings that consolidation will reduce competitive alternatives in specific geographic/commodity markets. The filing also signals to the STB that agricultural interests are actively monitoring the proceeding and expect the Board to weigh their concerns—potentially affecting the Board's narrative framing of 'affected parties' in any eventual order.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Public comment filing; no response deadline for applicants

These changes can be the difference between a profitable season or closing the doors on a farm that has sustained the community for generations.
Agriculture needs a competitive rail system to survive, and we cannot afford changes that would weaken that system further.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Kucera requests that the STB 'keep farmers and ranchers in mind when these companies formally file' and preserve a 'competitive rail system' to ensure agriculture survival.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Minimal direct legal significance. Pre-filing comment expressing stakeholder concern about competitive consolidation in rail sector. Does not advance new legal theories or raise procedural issues. Represents agricultural shipper constituency but lacks operational specificity or evidentiary support that would shape STB's antitrust analysis. May be part of broader shipper coalition effort if similar comments are coordinated.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Pre-filing comment; no formal deadline or response required at this stage

docket_entries.title: Justin Hollis (Agua Clara Ranch) - Opposes UP-NS Merger as Threat to Agricultural Shipping Competition
docket_entries.entry_summary: Justin Hollis, a multi-generational Texas rancher, opposes the UP-NS merger on competition grounds. Hollis argues that the freight rail industry is 'already dominated by a small number of players' and that approval would 'create a near duopoly,' leaving farmers 'with fewer options and higher costs at a time when margins are already razor thin.' He does not propose settlement conditions but frames the issue as existential: 'These changes can be the difference between a profitable season or closing the doors on a farm that has sustained the community for generations.' Hollis appeals directly to the STB to prioritize agricultural interests, stating 'Agriculture needs a competitive rail system to survive, and we cannot afford changes that would weaken that system further.' This is a straightforward outright opposition grounded in market concentration risk, with no indication of conditional support.
key_arguments: The freight rail industry is already concentrated among a small number of carriers; UP-NS merger would create a near-duopoly that further reduces competition
Merger would leave agricultural shippers with fewer rail options and higher freight rates, threatening farm profitability at a time of already razor-thin margins
Rail service changes—higher rates, reduced options, or poorly executed mergers—create cascading supply chain disruptions that can determine whether a generational farming operation survives or fails
A competitive rail system is essential to agriculture's ability to survive and compete globally
key_excerpts: If this merger is approved, the two companies would create a near duopoly, further reducing competition and leaving farmers with fewer options and higher costs at a time when margins are already razor thin.
Agriculture needs a competitive rail system to survive, and we cannot afford changes that would weaken that system further.

When rail service falters — whether through higher rates, reduced options, or poorly executed mergers — it creates ripple effects across the entire supply chain. These changes can be the difference between a profitable season or closing the doors on a farm that has sustained the community for generations.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the proposed UP-NS merger. Hollis does not propose conditions; instead appeals to the STB to 'keep farmers and ranchers in mind' and protect competitive rail system 'we cannot afford [to weaken] further.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing, though from an individual customer rather than a major shipper organization, establishes that STB's competitive analysis under 49 U.S.C. § 11324(c) must account for effects on agricultural shippers—a politically and economically significant customer class. It may signal that agricultural groups will organize formal intervention, potentially leading to coordinated shipper testimony at hearing. The filing underscores that duopoly concerns will be a central theme in competition analysis, not just bilateral effects on specific routes.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Pre-filing comment; no formal response deadline, but filer will be on service list if formal merger application is filed.

docket_entries.title: COOMI Express Owner Daniel Lee: Opposition to UP-NS Merger on Competition and Small Business Impact Grounds
docket_entries.entry_summary: Daniel Lee, owner of COOMI Express (Dallas-based shipping business), opposes the UP-NS merger on grounds that it would create a 'near duopoly' harmful to competition and small businesses. Lee argues that 'poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers – and it's the mom-and-pop stores who are impacted the most.' He contends that 'less competition in rail service leads to higher costs across the board' and that cost increases get passed to consumers purchasing 'essential goods and products.' Lee frames the merger as fundamentally incompatible with competition standards: 'Competition drives long-term viability and lower costs. The success of businesses, employees and customers across Texas depend on a strong rail system.' He urges the STB to deny approval or at minimum ensure the merger 'meet[s] the standards for enhancing competition and safety.' This is a retail-customer-level opposition focused on competitive harm but lacking specific service metrics, rate data, or remedial conditions.
key_arguments: The merger would create a 'near duopoly' that is 'detrimental to competition' and reduce competitive alternatives available to small shippers like COOMI Express.

Poorly executed rail mergers historically 'slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers,' with disproportionate impact on small businesses.
Reduced rail competition directly causes 'higher costs across the board,' which small businesses cannot absorb and must pass on to consumers as price increases for essential goods.
The merger fails to meet statutory standards for 'enhancing competition and safety' and should be denied on that basis.
key_excerpts: If the merger is approved, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would form a near duopoly. This would be detrimental to competition.
Poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers – and it's the mom-and-pop stores who are impacted the most.

I've consistently seen how less competition in rail service leads to higher costs across the board. Unfortunately, when businesses can't absorb these costs, they eventually get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for the essential goods and products they need.
Competition drives long-term viability and lower costs. The success of businesses, employees and customers across Texas depend on a strong rail system.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the proposed merger. Lee requests that the STB 'consider the impact on local businesses and ensures the tenets of the merger meet the standards for enhancing competition and safety' and does not request conditional approval under any remedial framework.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing is of limited legal significance for case outcome but may be cited in STB's public interest analysis and competitive impact section. It represents the small business customer perspective on competition concerns and illustrates the 'shipper impact narrative' that may feature in the Board's statutory analysis under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 (merger approval standards requiring Board to consider effect on competition, shipper interests, and public interest). However, it provides no new legal arguments, regulatory precedent, or specific factual evidence requiring Board response. It may be aggregated with similar small business submissions in the proceeding record.
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is a comment filing with no response deadline. It appears to be submitted during the pre-filing phase before formal application.

docket_entries.title: Mayor of Greenville, Ohio - Opposition to UP-NS Merger on Competitive and Economic Grounds
docket_entries.filer_name: Mayor Jeff Whitaker (City of Greenville, Ohio)
docket_entries.entry_summary: Mayor Whitaker opposes the proposed UP-NS merger based on its threat to competition and service reliability in Western Ohio communities like Greenville. He argues: 'Freight rail sustains local employers, supports manufacturing and agriculture, and connects small towns like Greenville to national markets that keep our economy strong.' The core concern is competitive erosion: 'When competition declines, it can result in slower service, supply chain congestion, and higher transportation costs. Those costs do not remain confined to the rail industry; they ultimately reach our residents through higher prices on essential goods and services.' Whitaker frames the issue as essential to 'preserving that momentum' of small business growth and regional economic health. However, his framing suggests conditional opposition—he does not demand absolute denial but rather calls for 'safeguards that preserve competition, service quality, and safety' before approval, indicating he would accept the merger if conditions adequately address competitive and service concerns.
key_arguments: Merger will reduce competition, resulting in slower service, supply chain congestion, and higher transportation costs for shippers and consumers
Reduced rail competition directly harms small manufacturing and agricultural communities dependent on freight rail access to national markets
Cost increases in freight transportation are passed through to residents in higher prices on essential goods and services
Loss of competitive options will weaken Greenville's ability to attract investment and support small business growth
Service quality and reliability will diminish without competitive pressure between carriers
key_excerpts: When competition declines, it can result in slower service, supply chain congestion, and higher transportation costs. Those costs do not remain confined to the rail industry; they ultimately reach our residents through higher prices on essential goods and services.

A balanced, competitive rail network is essential to preserving that momentum. Any consolidation that limits options for shippers or weakens service quality would have tangible effects on our region's economic health and long-term stability.
Safeguards that preserve competition, service quality, and safety are vital to protecting local economies throughout Ohio and across the Midwest.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Urges STB to 'carefully evaluate this proposed merger to ensure that it does not harm communities like ours.' Requests that 'Safeguards that preserve competition, service quality, and safety' be maintained as conditions of any approval.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Represents the geographic broadening of opposition to include small municipalities and communities outside major shipper/competitor classes. Invokes consumer welfare and regional economic development as additional STB review factors beyond traditional competitive carrier analysis. Signals potential for broader Midwest regional intervention if merger proceeds without addressing competitive concerns in secondary markets.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing; no response deadline specified

docket_entries.title: Georgia House Majority Caucus Chair opposes UP-NS merger on competition grounds; flags local economic impacts
docket_entries.entry_summary: Rep. Williamson, Georgia House Majority Caucus Chair, opposes the UP-NS merger on competition and economic grounds, framing his opposition as defense of 'private-sector investment and innovation' and 'fair competition.' He argues the combined entity would control 'nearly 45 percent of U.S. rail tonnage and hold dominant market share' across six key industries (chemicals, metals, lumber, motor vehicles, crushed stone, food products), creating 'captive customers facing higher costs, service disruptions, and diminished access to markets'—particularly in 'smaller communities' lacking rail alternatives. He emphasizes Georgia-specific impact: Norfolk Southern's Atlanta headquarters 'supports thousands of high-quality jobs,' and operational degradation would 'ripple through our state's economy.' His relief request is conditional: if approved, the merger must 'clearly enhance competition, protect service quality, and support a robust and reliable freight rail system that serves all Americans.' Rep. Williamson positions his opposition as consistent with 'private-sector' and 'free enterprise' principles, suggesting the merger itself violates competitive markets rather than representing necessary consolidation. No settlement signals or detailed negotiable conditions provided.
key_arguments: Combined UP-NS system would control nearly 45 percent of U.S. rail tonnage and dominant market share in six key industries (chemicals, metals, lumber, motor vehicles, crushed stone, food products), eliminating transportation choice for shippers.
Merger would create 'captive customers' in smaller communities facing 'higher costs, service disruptions, and diminished access to markets' due to elimination of competing rail alternatives.

Norfolk Southern's Atlanta headquarters and operations are critical to Georgia's economy and thousands of high-quality jobs; adverse effects on NS would have ripple consequences for state economic development.

Consolidation contradicts principles of 'fair competition' and 'free enterprise' that drive 'efficiency, lowers costs, and sustains American economic growth'; merger approval would undermine these market dynamics.

Approval should be conditioned on demonstrable enhancements to competition (not mere preservation), service quality protections, and robust freight rail system access for all customer classes and regions.
key_excerpts: If approved, the combined UP-NS system would control nearly 45 percent of U.S. rail tonnage and hold dominant market share across key industries—chemicals, metals, lumber, motor vehicles, crushed stone, and food products. Such concentration would reduce transportation choices for shippers, drive up costs for manufacturers and farmers, and ultimately raise prices for consumers.

I am deeply troubled that this merger could leave many American businesses—particularly those in smaller communities—without viable rail alternatives. The result would be a new generation of captive customers facing higher costs, service disruptions, and diminished access to markets.
Norfolk Southern's headquarters in Atlanta supports thousands of high-quality jobs, and any adverse effects on its operations could ripple through our state's economy.

I respectfully urge the Board to scrutinize this merger carefully and ensure that any approved transaction clearly enhances competition, protects service quality, and supports a robust and reliable freight rail system that serves all Americans—not just a few dominant carriers.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Rep. Williamson urges the STB to 'scrutinize this merger carefully and ensure that any approved transaction clearly enhances competition, protects service quality, and supports a robust and reliable freight rail system that serves all Americans.' If approved, conditions must include: (1) Enhanced competition protections, (2) Service quality guarantees, (3) Preservation of robust and reliable freight rail access.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Rep. Williamson's framing as pro-business legislator opposing merger on competition-based (not populist) grounds may strengthen STB's analytical burden on competitive effects analysis under 49 U.S.C. § 11324(c)(1). His quantified market concentration claim (45% of tonnage) provides benchmark for competitive harm assessment. His conditional relief language ('ensure any approved transaction clearly enhances competition') may influence scope of required remedies by suggesting approval only justified if merger generates affirmative competitive benefits, not mere preservation of existing competition. His invocation of Norfolk Southern's corporate presence and employment may create state-level regulatory/political dimension STB must address in findings.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment filing; no response deadline to Rep. Williamson, but filing is part of public record for STB decision-making.

docket_entries.title: Individual Resident Comment - Josh Mercer (Ponchatoula, LA) - Competition and Consumer Protection Concerns
docket_entries.entry_summary: Josh Mercer, a 20-year Ponchatoula, LA resident and construction worker, opposes the UP-NS merger absent protective conditions. He argues: 'Mergers result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and history shows these expenses don't stop at the rail yard.' He frames the transaction as a consolidation risk that threatens 'a competitive freight rail system' essential for workers and families, and supplies needed for construction and retail commerce. He does not demand outright denial but instead requests that 'the Surface Transportation Board takes a closer look and makes sure the tenets of the merger and conditions imposed on the transaction meet the standards for enhancing competition and safety to stimulate a healthy economy.' His opposition is conditional: approval acceptable only if accompanied by substantive competitive safeguards. The filing reflects consumer concern about pass-through pricing effects of rail consolidation.
key_arguments: Mergers in freight rail historically result in reduced competition that drives higher costs, with those cost increases passing through to consumers and industries reliant on rail shipping
Rail industry consolidation threatens 'a competitive freight rail system' that is 'critical for the workers and families who need it,' particularly in small Louisiana communities
Without 'appropriate protections for competition,' a UP-NS merger creates unacceptable risk of higher consumer prices and weaker service quality in freight rail
Construction supplies and retail goods pricing are directly affected by freight rail competition; consolidation threatens affordable access to goods in rural/small-town communities
key_excerpts: Often, mergers result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and history shows these expenses don't stop at the rail yard.
A competitive freight rail system is critical for the workers and families who need it.
If approved without appropriate protections for competition, such a merger would be risky.
docket_entries.relief_requested: If merger proceeds, impose 'appropriate protections for competition' and conditions that 'enhance competition and safety to stimulate a healthy economy.' Requests STB to 'take a closer look' at conditions 'imposed on the transaction' to meet legal standards.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing establishes a consumer protection and public interest record supporting Board consideration of competitive effects beyond shipper-specific harm. It frames the merger review as implicating broad consumer welfare and economically disadvantaged rural communities—arguments that support conditions-based approval rather than unconditional denial. The filing's emphasis on 'standards for enhancing competition and safety' references the Board's statutory merger review standards under 49 U.S.C. § 11324(b), suggesting the merits of conditioning approval on competitive safeguards.

docket_entries.title: Joseph Summers (Minerva Defense) - Small Business Opposition to UP-NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: Joseph Summers, CEO of Minerva Defense (a defense contractor in Huntsville, Alabama), opposes the UP-NS merger on general competitive grounds. He argues: 'large mergers like this can create real challenges for small and mid-sized businesses' through 'slower service, increased delays, and higher shipping costs' that ultimately harm consumers. His core concern is that 'consolidation into the hands of just a few major rail companies' will reduce competition and raise prices for smaller shippers who lack the negotiating leverage of large corporations. He frames the issue as a choice between 'a rail system that's competitive, reliable, and fair — one that supports businesses of all sizes' versus one dominated by 'the biggest players.' However, he provides no quantified impacts on Minerva Defense operations, no specific service problems from past mergers, and no conditions that would satisfy him—making this fundamentally an ideological opposition to further consolidation rather than conditional opposition based on remedial feasibility.
key_arguments: Large rail mergers lead to slower service, increased delays, and higher shipping costs for small and mid-sized businesses that depend on rail
Merger will consolidate control into 'just a few major rail companies,' reducing competition and negotiating leverage for smaller shippers
Reduced competition 'almost always means higher prices and fewer options,' ultimately harming consumers through cost pass-through
Small businesses depend on competitive, reliable rail service; consolidation disadvantages them relative to large corporations with negotiating power
key_excerpts: When rail service slows or becomes unreliable, it directly affects our operations — and our bottom line.

If this merger goes forward, it will consolidate even more control into the hands of just a few major rail companies. Less competition almost always means higher prices and fewer options, especially for smaller businesses that don't have the leverage of large corporations.
We need a rail system that's competitive, reliable, and fair — one that supports businesses of all sizes, not just the biggest players.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the proposed merger. No specific conditions or fallback relief requested.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low. This is generic small-business opposition based on broad consolidation concerns rather than specific competitive analysis or market-based arguments relevant to the STB's statutory merger test under 49 U.S.C. § 11324. It does not identify markets, competitive impacts, or remedial measures, and thus will likely receive minimal weight in STB decision-making. It may be cited for the general proposition that small shippers perceive consolidation risk, but it provides no evidentiary or legal foundation that would shift the burden or scope of analysis.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Filed as a comment; no response deadline for the filer

docket_entries.title: Vinny Oliver (Texas Pecan Farmer) - Opposition to UP-NS Merger on Competition Grounds
docket_entries.entry_summary: Vinny Oliver, a multi-generational Texas pecan farmer, opposes the proposed UP-NS merger on competition grounds. He argues that approval would create 'a near duopoly' in freight rail, 'further reducing competition and leaving farmers with fewer options and higher costs at a time when margins are already razor thin.' Oliver frames rail service reliability and competitive pricing as existential to agricultural viability: 'When rail service falters — whether through higher rates, reduced options, or poorly executed mergers — it creates ripple effects across the entire supply chain. These changes can be the difference between a profitable season or closing the doors on a farm that has sustained the community for generations.' He requests the STB 'keep farmers and ranchers in mind' during formal review. This is an outright opposition with no conditions; Oliver does not propose remedies but rather advocates for merger denial to preserve competitive rail access.
key_arguments: Merger creates 'a near duopoly' that will further reduce competition in an already-concentrated freight rail industry
Farmer customers will face 'fewer options and higher costs' post-merger, particularly damaging when agricultural margins are 'already razor thin'
Rail service disruptions create cascading supply chain impacts that threaten farm viability and generational operations
Agriculture specifically requires competitive rail system to 'survive'; merger weakens that system
key_excerpts: If this merger is approved, the two companies would create a near duopoly, further reducing competition and leaving farmers with fewer options and higher costs at a time when margins are already razor thin.

When rail service falters — whether through higher rates, reduced options, or poorly executed mergers — it creates ripple effects across the entire supply chain. These changes can be the difference between a profitable season or closing the doors on a farm that has sustained the community for generations.
Agriculture needs a competitive rail system to survive, and we cannot afford changes that would weaken that system further.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Merger should not be approved. Applicant requests STB 'keep farmers and ranchers in mind when these companies formally file' and maintain competitive rail system.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low formal significance at this pre-filing stage. However, represents the class of agricultural shippers (high-volume bulk commodity users) whose competitive concerns are material to STB competitive analysis under 49 U.S.C. § 11324(c). Does not raise novel legal issues but documents agricultural sector opposition for the administrative record. May support intervenor standing for formal agricultural organizations (e.g., National Grain and Feed Association, American Farm Bureau) if they rely on this letter.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Pre-filing public comment; no formal deadline triggered

docket_entries.title: Miles Rihn - Small oilfield service contractor opposes merger on competition and cost grounds
docket_entries.entry_summary: Miles Rihn, a small oilfield service contractor, opposes the UP-NS merger on ideological grounds centered on competition and small business impact. He argues: 'If the merger is approved, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would form a near duopoly. This would be detrimental to competition.' He asserts that poorly executed rail mergers cause service disruptions and supply chain delays that disproportionately harm small businesses like his own. Rihn contends that 'less competition in rail service leads to higher costs across the board' and warns that when businesses cannot absorb these costs, 'they eventually get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for essential goods.' His opposition is fundamentally ideological—rooted in general principles about consolidation harm—rather than requesting specific operational remedies. He provides no conditions under which he would accept merger approval, instead calling for outright denial. The filing includes no quantified impacts, economic analysis, or service-specific evidence. Rihn's argument reflects broader small business constituency concerns but contributes limited substantive record material.
key_arguments: Merger would create a near duopoly: 'If the merger is approved, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would form a near duopoly. This would be detrimental to competition.'

Poorly executed rail mergers disrupt service and supply chains, harming small businesses: 'Poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers – and it's the mom-and-pop stores who are impacted the most.'

Loss of competition drives price increases that cascade to consumers: 'Less competition in rail service leads to higher costs across the board... when businesses can't absorb these costs, they eventually get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for essential goods.'
Competition is necessary for long-term viability and cost control: 'Competition drives long-term viability and lower costs.'
key_excerpts: 'If the merger is approved, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would form a near duopoly. This would be detrimental to competition.'
'Poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers – and it's the mom-and-pop stores who are impacted the most.'

'Less competition in rail service leads to higher costs across the board... when businesses can't absorb these costs, they eventually get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for the essential goods and products they need.'
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the merger. Rihn urges the STB to 'ensure the tenets of the merger meet the standards for enhancing competition and safety' but provides no alternative conditions that would satisfy approval.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing contributes to the record of small business opposition but carries limited legal weight. It raises no novel statutory issues, cites no specific regulatory standards, and provides no quantified analysis of competitive effects. Its significance is primarily atmospheric—documenting retail customer concern about consolidation—rather than substantive. The filing does not advance specific arguments about the merger's competitive effects under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 or establish measurable service/cost impacts that would inform STB analysis.
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is a comment filing; no response deadline applies to Rihn or the applicants.

docket_entries.title: Miles Rihn (Oilfield Service Contractor) - Opposition Based on Competition and Supply Chain Disruption Concerns
docket_entries.entry_summary: Miles Rihn, a small Texas-based oilfield service contractor, opposes the UP-NS merger on ideological grounds centered on competition and small business vulnerability. He argues: 'Poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers – and it's the mom-and-pop stores who are impacted the most.' His core concern is that a merged UP-NS entity would create 'a near duopoly' that 'would be detrimental to competition,' leading to higher rail costs that small businesses cannot absorb and must pass to consumers: 'when businesses can't absorb these costs, they eventually get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for the essential goods and products they need.' He frames competition as essential to 'the success of businesses, employees and customers across Texas' and calls on the STB to ensure any approved merger 'meet[s] the standards for enhancing competition and safety.' However, he does not propose specific remedial conditions or identify particular rail corridors, service levels, or rate impacts. His opposition is grounded in general consolidation concerns rather than transaction-specific harm analysis. No settlement signals are present.
key_arguments: UP-NS merger would create 'a near duopoly' detrimental to competition in rail services
Rail mergers historically cause service slowdowns and supply chain congestion that disproportionately harm small businesses
Reduced rail competition drives higher shipping costs that small businesses cannot absorb and must pass to end consumers
Small businesses and consumers across Texas depend on competitive rail service for viable operations
key_excerpts: 'If the merger is approved, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would form a near duopoly. This would be detrimental to competition.'
'Poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers – and it's the mom-and-pop stores who are impacted the most.'

'I've consistently seen how less competition in rail service leads to higher costs across the board. Unfortunately, when businesses can't absorb these costs, they eventually get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for the essential goods and products they need.'

docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing does not raise novel legal or regulatory issues but does contribute to the evidentiary record on small business impacts and market competition concerns. Under 49 U.S.C. § 11324(c), the STB must consider 'the effect of the proposed transaction on the adequacy of transportation to the public' and competitive effects. While Rihn's filing establishes that small business stakeholders perceive competition concerns and supply chain vulnerability, it lacks the specificity (geographic corridors, rate data, service metrics) needed to support detailed remedy design or factual findings. It may support general procedural arguments about notice to affected communities but will not independently drive legal standards or burden allocation.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No specific response deadline; this is a general comment filing in the pre-filing phase

docket_entries.title: Small Business Owner Opposition to UP-NS Merger – Competition and Service Reliability Concerns
docket_entries.entry_summary: Sunny Black, a small business owner in Madison, Alabama, opposes the UP-NS merger based on competition and service reliability concerns. She argues that merger-induced consolidation to a 'near duopoly' will 'inevitably' reduce competition, increase shipping costs, and diminish service reliability. She emphasizes that small businesses 'lack alternative shipping options' and cannot absorb cost increases, so they pass them to consumers: 'When businesses cannot absorb these rising costs, they are passed down to consumers, driving up prices for essential goods and materials.' She draws on experience with 'large consolidations' observing that 'service slows, congestion increases, and small businesses like mine bear the brunt of the disruption.' She frames the issue as preservation of 'a fair, competitive, and efficient rail system' and urges the STB to demand that approval demonstrate 'measurable benefits to competition, safety, and service performance – not just to shareholders.' Her opposition is principled (outright denial preferable) but includes a fallback condition for approval: measurable competitive and service benefits must be demonstrated.
key_arguments: Approval would create a 'near duopoly' that reduces competition across the rail network, inevitably leading to higher shipping costs and diminished service reliability
Small businesses 'lack alternative shipping options' and cannot absorb cost increases, forcing them to pass costs to consumers and driving up prices for essential goods
Prior rail consolidations have caused service slowdowns and congestion that 'small businesses like mine bear the brunt of' and ripple through local economies
Merger approval should be contingent on demonstrating 'measurable benefits to competition, safety, and service performance – not just to shareholders'
Competition is vital to 'ensuring affordability, reliability, and long-term economic growth'
key_excerpts: If this merger is approved, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would form a near duopoly, greatly reducing competition across the rail network. A reduction in competition inevitably leads to higher shipping costs and diminished service reliability.
When businesses cannot absorb these rising costs, they are passed down to consumers, driving up prices for essential goods and materials.
When major rail mergers are poorly executed, service slows, congestion increases, and small businesses like mine bear the brunt of the disruption.
Any merger approval should clearly demonstrate measurable benefits to competition, safety, and service performance – not just to shareholders.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the merger or, if approval is considered, require that 'any merger approval should clearly demonstrate measurable benefits to competition, safety, and service performance – not just to shareholders.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low direct legal significance but substantively important as evidence of consumer/small business impact. Does not change scope of review but provides factual testimony that merger harms (service disruption, cost increases, reduced competition) cascade through supply chain to end consumers. Supports arguments by major shipper intervenors that small businesses and consumers are the ultimate bearers of consolidation costs. May influence STB's public interest analysis and framing of competitive harms under 49 U.S.C. § 11324(c).
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing; no response deadline for this particular comment
