docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low. This is unrepresented individual comment expressing general policy objection to consolidation. Does not raise novel legal issues or create burdens for applicants. Demonstrates public concern about competitive impact but provides no specific factual record for STB analysis. May be cited as evidence of general business community concern, but lacks the specificity and institutional credibility to shift evidentiary burden.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment filed; no response deadline applicable

docket_entries.title: Summer Smith - Retail Customer Comment on UP-NS Merger (Pre-Filing Opposition)
docket_entries.entry_summary: Summer Smith, a 30-year Denham Springs, Louisiana resident, opposes the UP-NS merger absent conditions protecting competition and consumer welfare. She argues that 'Mergers are known to result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and these expenses don't stop at the rail yard. They trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.' She frames freight rail's role in her community as essential to affordability and local economic vitality, requesting that the STB impose conditions 'meet[ing] the standards for enhancing competition in the market' before approving the transaction. She does not specify what conditions would be acceptable, but her framing suggests conditional opposition: approval is acceptable IF adequate competitive protections are imposed. No settlement signals present.
key_arguments: Rail consolidation reduces competition, which directly increases freight costs that are passed through to consumers in the form of higher grocery and everyday goods prices
Freight rail is essential to local economy and job creation in southern Louisiana economic hubs like Denham Springs
Merger creates unacceptable risk of higher costs and weaker service to consumers unless STB imposes competitive protection conditions
Consumer welfare and protection from rail industry consolidation effects are appropriate STB merger review standards
key_excerpts: Mergers are known to result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and these expenses don't stop at the rail yard. They trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.

We need to protect consumers and prevent rail industry consolidation from leading to higher costs and weaker service. When Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern officially file, I hope that the Surface Transportation Board certifies that the tenets of the merger and conditions imposed on the transaction meet the standards for enhancing competition in the market which is essential to a capitalist society.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Surface Transportation Board must impose conditions on the merger to 'enhance competition in the market' before approval. Merger should be rejected if conditions adequate to preserve competition cannot be imposed. Specifically requests that STB 'certifies that the tenets of the merger and conditions imposed on the transaction meet the standards for enhancing competition in the market.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing does not establish new legal or evidentiary burdens but signals that consumer welfare arguments framed around price impacts may gain traction in public comment phase. The filer's invocation of competitive market standards as a basis for merger evaluation could support arguments by other intervenors that the STB should apply stricter competitive scrutiny under 49 U.S.C. § 11324.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Pre-filing comment; no response deadline applicable

docket_entries.title: Daniel Oneil (New Orleans resident) - Comment opposing UP-NS merger on consumer impact grounds
docket_entries.entry_summary: Daniel Oneil, a 20-year New Orleans resident, opposes the UP-NS merger without appropriate competitive protections. He argues that rail consolidation will reduce competition and drive higher freight costs, which 'trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.' Oneil identifies New Orleans as a critical port-to-rail distribution hub where freight 'plays a significant role...by importing nationwide goods, creating jobs, and helping families get what they need at a decent price.' He does not seek outright denial but rather conditions: he requests STB 'certif[y] that the tenets of the merger and conditions imposed on the transaction meet the standards for enhancing competition in the market which is essential to a capitalist society.' This is conditional opposition—he supports approval IF conditions adequately protect competition and consumer prices.
key_arguments: Rail consolidation reduces competition, which is 'known to result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs'
Higher rail costs directly harm consumer prices: 'These expenses don't stop at the rail yard. They trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods'
New Orleans specifically depends on freight rail for port-to-nationwide distribution: 'thousands of freight is brought in internationally by boat and then loaded on trains to distribute nationwide'
Competition in rail markets is essential: 'We need to protect consumers and prevent rail industry consolidation from leading to higher costs and weaker service'
key_excerpts: Mergers are known to result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and these expenses don't stop at the rail yard. They trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.

I hope that the Surface Transportation Board certifies that the tenets of the merger and conditions imposed on the transaction meet the standards for enhancing competition in the market which is essential to a capitalist society.
docket_entries.relief_requested: STB should 'certif[y] that the tenets of the merger and conditions imposed on the transaction meet the standards for enhancing competition in the market.' Merger approval only if conditions protect competition and prevent cost increases passed to consumers.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low legal significance as a standalone filing but contextually relevant: (1) Represents public interest concerns that STB must weigh under 49 U.S.C. § 11324(b) (public interest standard for rail mergers); (2) Demonstrates consumer awareness and potential political constituency for merger scrutiny; (3) Frames consumer welfare as condition-negotiable, not deal-breaking—consistent with STB's precedent allowing conditional approvals when public interest satisfied by remedies.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing (no response deadline applicable)

docket_entries.title: Jonathan Davis (Gator Roofing and Restoration) - Opposition to UP-NS Merger on Competition and Small Business Grounds
docket_entries.entry_summary: Jonathan Davis, owner of a small roofing business in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, opposes the UP-NS merger based on general competition and small business impact concerns. Davis argues that 'If the merger is approved, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would form a near duopoly. This would be detrimental to competition' and that 'Competition is the backbone of our economic system in America.' He asserts that 'less competition in rail service leads to higher costs across the board' and that small businesses like his 'cannot absorb these costs' and will pass them to consumers. Davis frames the merger opposition as protecting 'everyday Americans' and emphasizes his 8-year experience seeing 'the effect large consolidations can have on small business operations,' noting that 'poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain.' He does not propose specific conditions or remedies—his position is outright opposition based on competition principles and economic impact on small businesses generally.
key_arguments: The merger would create a 'near duopoly' that is 'detrimental to competition,' which Davis identifies as 'the backbone of our economic system in America.'

Less competition in rail service leads to higher costs that small businesses cannot absorb, forcing pass-through to consumers: 'when businesses can't absorb these costs—and most small businesses cannot, they eventually get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for the essential goods and products they need.'

Poorly executed rail mergers cause operational disruptions that disproportionately harm small businesses and emerging enterprises: 'Poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers—and it's the industrial industries and new businesses trying to get on their feet like mine, who feel it the most.'

A competitive rail system is essential to broader economic health: 'Competition drives long-term viability and lower costs. The success of businesses, employees and customers across Louisiana depend on a strong rail system.'
key_excerpts: If the merger is approved, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would form a near duopoly. This would be detrimental to competition. And competition is the backbone of our economic system in America.

I've consistently seen how less competition in rail service leads to higher costs across the board. Unfortunately, when businesses can't absorb these costs—and most small businesses cannot, they eventually get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for the essential goods and products they need.

Poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers—and it's the industrial industries and new businesses trying to get on their feet like mine, who feel it the most.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the merger. Davis requests that the STB 'consider the impact on local businesses and ensure[s] the tenets of the merger meet the standards for enhancing competition and safety' and that 'the railroad industry stays competitive and healthy in order to protect everyday Americans.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: While this filing does not create new legal issues, it serves as evidence of potential public interest concerns under 49 U.S.C. § 11324(c), which requires the STB to consider 'the effect of the proposed transaction on the adequacy of transportation to the public.' Individual small business customer comments can be cited by intervenors or the Board to support findings about competitive harm or rate impacts. However, the filing lacks the quantitative data or specific factual allegations that would carry significant evidentiary weight in a formal hearing.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing; no response deadline triggered

docket_entries.title: Sierra Schmidt (Walker, LA Resident) - Opposition to UP-NS Merger on Consumer Price Grounds
docket_entries.entry_summary: Sierra Schmidt, a 20-year Walker, Louisiana resident, opposes the UP-NS merger absent adequate consumer protections. She argues: 'Often, mergers result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and history shows these expenses don't stop at the rail yard. Instead, they trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.' Schmidt emphasizes freight rail's role in her community's economy—stocking store shelves, importing goods, creating jobs—and requests that the STB impose conditions ensuring the merger 'enhance[s] competition and safety' while preventing 'weaker service.' Her position is conditional: she would support approval IF appropriate competitive safeguards are implemented, but opposes approval without such protections.
key_arguments: Railroad consolidation reduces competition in freight rail, driving higher input costs that are passed through to consumers in the form of higher grocery and everyday goods prices
Freight rail is critical infrastructure for community economies—it stocks store shelves, enables nationwide goods distribution, creates jobs, and helps families afford necessities
Merger approval without 'appropriate protections for competition' poses unacceptable risk to consumer welfare and community economic stability
key_excerpts: Often, mergers result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and history shows these expenses don't stop at the rail yard. Instead, they trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.
A competitive freight rail system is critical not just for businesses, but for the families and communities that depend on it.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Approval should be conditioned on: (1) protections for competition; (2) conditions that 'enhance competition and safety'; (3) safeguards to prevent higher consumer prices and weaker service.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low procedural significance. Filing does not raise novel legal issues or challenge the regulatory framework. However, it may modestly strengthen the Board's record on consumer welfare considerations under the public interest standard (49 U.S.C. § 11324(d)). The filing demonstrates that residential constituents perceive merger risk to consumer prices, which could support a condition-based approval finding if the Board determines conditions are necessary to protect the public interest.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment filing; no response deadline applicable

docket_entries.title: Individual consumer comment expressing concerns about merger impact on grocery prices and family affordability
docket_entries.entry_summary: Shannon Burfield, a 40-year New Orleans resident and mother, opposes the merger without specific conditions, but frames her opposition as conditional on STB imposing adequate competitive and safety protections. She argues: 'Freight rail plays a significant role in Louisiana's economy - keeping store shelves stocked, creating jobs and helping families get what they need at a fair price.' Her core concern is the price pass-through mechanism: 'Often, mergers result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and history shows these expenses don't stop at the rail yard. Instead, they trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.' She does not request outright denial but rather asks that the STB 'ensure the tenets of the merger and conditions imposed on the transaction meet the standards for enhancing competition and safety' and 'keep the interests of everyday Louisiana residents in mind.' This is quintessential conditional opposition from a retail customer: she would not oppose if competitive safeguards are imposed. Settlement probability is high if applicants can articulate competitive protection measures.
key_arguments: Rail merger-driven cost increases in freight are passed through supply chains to consumer retail prices: 'Often, mergers result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and history shows these expenses don't stop at the rail yard. Instead, they trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.'

Reduced rail competition threatens affordable access to basic goods for families: 'Feeding my family high quality, healthy foods is one of my biggest concerns as a mother and the rail industry allows for these foods to get to me and at an affordable price.'

A competitive freight rail system is essential infrastructure for consumer welfare and community economics: 'A competitive freight rail system is critical not just for businesses, but for the families and communities that depend on it.'
key_excerpts: Often, mergers result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and history shows these expenses don't stop at the rail yard. Instead, they trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.
A competitive freight rail system is critical not just for businesses, but for the families and communities that depend on it.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Approval should be conditioned on 'ensuring the tenets of the merger and conditions imposed on the transaction meet the standards for enhancing competition and safety' and protecting consumer interests from higher costs and weaker service.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low. This comment does not raise novel legal issues or evidentiary challenges. It restates the consumer harm theory implicit in STB merger review (competition → service/price impacts → consumer welfare) without providing factual support. It will contribute to the administrative record demonstrating public concern about consumer impacts but does not affect scope of review, burden allocation, or substantive legal standards. It may be grouped with similar consumer comments in STB analysis.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing; no response deadline for STB

docket_entries.title: Trey Santos - Individual Rancher Opposition to UP-NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: Trey Santos, a Texas-Louisiana rancher whose family business depends on freight rail to move livestock and beef to market, opposes the UP-NS merger on grounds that it would create a 'near duopoly' in already consolidated rail industry, reducing options and raising costs for farmers and ranchers. He argues: 'Competition is the driver of our economic system' and 'Agriculture needs a competitive rail system to survive, and we cannot afford changes that would weaken that system further.' His opposition is ideologically framed around competitive principle and the existential threat consolidation poses to family farms operating on 'razor thin' margins. He provides no settlement conditions, instead asking the Board to 'keep farmers and ranchers in mind' and implicitly to deny approval. No specific service failures or rate impact data cited—the argument rests on general competitive harm theory.
key_arguments: The merger will create a 'near duopoly' in freight rail, further reducing competition in an already consolidated industry dominated by 'a small number of players'
Farmers and ranchers will face 'fewer options and higher costs' as a result of reduced competitive pressure, which is particularly damaging when 'margins are already razor thin'
Competition is foundational to economic system function: 'Competition is the driver of our economic system' and consolidation threatens agricultural sector's ability to compete globally

The merger threatens family farming operations: changes that 'weaken' competitive rail system 'can be the difference between a profitable season or closing the doors on a farm that has sustained the community for generations'
key_excerpts: If this merger is approved, the two companies would create a near duopoly, further reducing competition and leaving farmers with fewer options and higher costs at a time when margins are already razor thin and railroad companies are already hard to find.
Agriculture needs a competitive rail system to survive, and we cannot afford changes that would weaken that system further.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Request that the STB 'keep farmers and ranchers in mind' and reject the merger to preserve competitive rail system. No specific conditions offered; framed as outright opposition to consolidation that would harm agricultural competition.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Minimal direct regulatory significance. Does not introduce new substantive issues or evidentiary matters the STB has not already identified. Represents general customer/constituency concern that may factor into policy considerations but does not address specific merger effects analysis, competitive harm metrics, or remedy frameworks. Value is primarily political/constituency representation rather than technical legal or economic contribution.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment filing; no response deadline indicated

docket_entries.title: Brad Garafola (Walker, LA Resident) - Pre-Filing Comment on UP-NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: Brad Garafola, a 15-year Walker, Louisiana resident, opposes the proposed UP-NS merger without 'appropriate protections for competition.' He argues freight rail consolidation will harm consumers: 'Mergers are known to result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and these expenses don't stop at the rail yard. They trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.' Garafola frames the issue as fundamental to market capitalism: 'We need to protect consumers and prevent rail industry consolidation from leading to higher costs and weaker service.' He urges STB to condition any approval on meeting 'standards for enhancing competition in the market which is essential to a capitalist society.' The filing represents consumer-level concerns about downstream pricing effects rather than shipper-specific operational arguments, and signals openness to approval if competitive safeguards are imposed.
key_arguments: Freight rail consolidation from UP-NS merger will reduce competition, driving higher costs that pass through to consumer prices for groceries and everyday goods
Merger approval without 'appropriate protections for competition' poses unacceptable risk to community access to affordable goods
Rail industry consolidation weakens service quality while raising prices, harming working families in small Louisiana communities
Market competition is essential principle; merger conditions must affirmatively 'enhance competition' rather than merely mitigate harms
key_excerpts: 'Mergers are known to result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and these expenses don't stop at the rail yard. They trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.'

'We need to protect consumers and prevent rail industry consolidation from leading to higher costs and weaker service. When Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern officially file, I hope that the Surface Transportation Board certifies that the tenets of the merger and conditions imposed on the transaction meet the standards for enhancing competition in the market which is essential to a capitalist society.'
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny merger approval 'without appropriate protections for competition.' If approved, require conditions that 'enhance competition in the market' and prevent 'higher costs and weaker service.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Limited legal significance. Filing does not raise novel legal theories or regulatory issues. However, it creates record evidence of consumer/retail customer opposition to merger on grounds of competitive effects and downstream pricing. May be cited by STB or intervenors as representative of consumer interest in merger conditions focused on competitive preservation rather than rail-specific operational remedies.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Pre-filing comment; no response deadline. Filer is responding to merger announcement, not formal application. Likely to serve as basis for formal intervention if applicants file.

docket_entries.title: Bipartisan Senate Letter: Demand Rigorous Merger Review with Focus on Agricultural Impact and Long-Term Competition
docket_entries.entry_summary: A bipartisan coalition of 20 U.S. Senators filed a letter urging the STB to apply 'rigorous and comprehensive evaluation' to the UP/NS merger, with emphasis on long-term competitive effects and agricultural impact. The Senators argue: (1) The UP/NS merger represents the first major rail consolidation under the STB's heightened post-2001 standards designed to 'enhance, rather than merely preserve, competition,' setting critical precedent; (2) Further consolidation threatens agricultural producers who 'depend on reliable and competitive rail service' and 'already face limited competitive options for rail service'; (3) The current rail landscape is a 'fragile equilibrium' with only six Class I carriers, four controlling 90% of freight, and the proposed merger would disrupt this balance by reducing 'routing flexibility, constraining network fluidity, increasing market power, and limiting access'; (4) The 1996 UP-SP merger caused 'widespread service breakdowns,' nine worker fatalities, a Federal Railroad Administration finding of 'fundamental breakdown' in safety, and $4 billion in economic losses—risks amplified by the proposed merger's scale (40%+ of U.S. freight, 50,000 route miles across 43 states); (5) Agricultural producers face specific vulnerability: 'Time-sensitive shipments during harvest could be delayed or spoiled, export windows could be missed, and access to global markets could be sharply reduced.' The Senators condition their position on the STB establishing that the merger 'demonstrably strengthen[s] competition' and provides 'clear and tangible long-term improvements in competition' that are not merely short-term efficiencies.
key_arguments: The merger represents the first major Class I consolidation under the STB's post-2001 'Major Rail Consolidation Procedures,' which were 'adopted specifically to place heightened emphasis on whether Class I railroad mergers enhance, rather than merely preserve, competition.' The STB must 'establish a strong precedent and apply these heightened standards in the way they were intended.'

Current rail landscape is a 'fragile equilibrium' with six Class I carriers (four controlling 90% of freight). The proposed merger would 'alter this equilibrium' by reducing 'routing flexibility, constraining network fluidity, increasing market power, and limiting access for both producers and processors.'

Agricultural producers 'already face limited competitive options for rail service' and depend on reliable rail service to move products to domestic and international markets. Further consolidation would compound challenges by constraining 'network fluidity' and limiting 'access for both producers and processors.'

The 1996 UP-SP merger precedent shows the dangers: 'widespread service breakdowns and safety lapses,' 'nine worker fatalities,' a Federal Railroad Administration finding of a 'fundamental breakdown' in safety practices, and 'freight disruptions lasting more than a year and a half'—costing 'the broader economy an estimated $4 billion.'

The proposed UP/NS merger's scale creates unacceptable service disruption risk: 'a combined UP/NS would handle more than 40 percent of all U.S. freight rail traffic' across 'a transcontinental system spanning 50,000 route miles across 43 states.' Service interruptions could cause agricultural harm: 'Time-sensitive shipments during harvest could be delayed or spoiled, export windows could be missed, and access to global markets could be sharply reduced.'

Additional consolidation risks embedding 'higher costs, diminished service quality, and less innovation across the network' and may 'discourage future market entrants,' making these conditions 'difficult to reverse' once 'entrenched.'
key_excerpts: 'The STBs post-2001 "Major Rail Consolidation Procedures" were adopted specifically to place heightened emphasis on whether Class I railroad mergers enhance, rather than merely preserve, competition, and to ensure that any potential anticompetitive effects or other harms are outweighed by substantive and demonstrable gains to the public interest.'

'The current landscape of railroads as it exists today represents a fragile equilibrium with two in the west, two in the east, and two through the middle. As the STB reviews the proposed merger, it is important to consider how additional consolidation could alter this equilibrium.'

'Our producers already face limited competitive options for rail service. Further consolidation could compound these challenges by reducing routing flexibility, constraining network fluidity, increasing market power, and limiting access for both producers and processors.'

'The 1996 Union Pacific–Southern Pacific merger triggered widespread service breakdowns and safety lapses. Integration challenges led to nine worker fatalities, a Federal Railroad Administration finding of a "fundamental breakdown" in safety practices, and freight disruptions lasting more than a year and a half—delays that cost the broader economy an estimated $4 billion.'

'If approved, a combined UP/NS would handle more than 40 percent of all U.S. freight rail traffic... Service interruptions of this magnitude could have severe consequences, especially for agricultural producers. Time-sensitive shipments during harvest could be delayed or spoiled, export windows could be missed, and access to global markets could be sharply reduced.'
docket_entries.relief_requested: The Senators do not explicitly demand outright denial, but call for the STB to conduct a 'rigorous and comprehensive evaluation' under the heightened post-2001 merger standards. They implicitly condition approval on demonstrating 'clear and tangible long-term improvements in competition' and 'substantive and demonstrable gains to the public interest.' If the merger is approved, they demand the STB weigh specific harms: (1) impacts on agricultural supply chains including 'shipping costs and market access,' (2) preservation of competitive equilibrium across freight corridors, and (3) risks of service disruptions given the scale (40%+ of U.S. freight rail traffic, 50,000 route miles across 43 states).
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing invokes the STB's post-2001 Major Rail Consolidation Procedures as controlling legal standard, explicitly arguing that this merger is the first to test those heightened requirements and therefore sets precedent for how the Board will apply its statutory mandate to enhance (not merely preserve) competition. The Senators frame the merger as a test case for whether the STB will rigorously enforce its own rules. This changes the evidentiary burden: the applicants cannot merely show cost savings or operational efficiencies—they must affirmatively demonstrate 'clear and tangible long-term improvements in competition' and gains to the public interest that 'outweigh' anticompetitive effects. The letter also reintroduces the 1996 UP-SP merger as binding precedential warning, suggesting the STB failed in its duty to prevent similar catastrophes and must not repeat that error. This elevates both the scrutiny standard and the consequences of approval.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No formal response deadline specified, but filing date is October 30, 2025 (letter to Board); entered into record November 13, 2025. Applicants and interested parties will have opportunity to respond during comment period.

docket_entries.title: Joint East End Super Neighborhood Coalition - Request for Public Hearing, Impact Studies, and Community Mitigation Conditions
docket_entries.filer_name: Joint East End Super Neighborhood Coalition
docket_entries.entry_summary: The Joint East End Super Neighborhood Coalition represents three Houston neighborhoods (35,000+ residents) bisected by major rail corridors including Congress Yard, Englewood Yard, and Settegast Yard. The coalition does not oppose the merger outright but demands conditional approval with specific mitigation. They argue that Houston was inadequately served in the CP-KCS merger review (hearing held in Beaumont on weekday, limiting worker participation) and must be included this time. They assert that current STB analysis may underweight post-merger freight volume impacts and note that 'the densest lanes are projected to emerge post-merger' without localized forecasts for Houston. Critically, they argue the previous merger review's 'narrow scope failed to capture the real-world operational dynamics' because it ignored cascade effects: at-grade interchanges in Houston create secondary line bottlenecks where trains wait for priority routes to clear, causing blockages of 30+ minutes in East End neighborhoods. They request: (1) Houston public hearing with evening/weekend hours; (2) neighborhood-specific forecasts of freight volume increases, train frequency changes, crossing wait times, emergency response impacts, and school air quality; (3) comprehensive system study of secondary line interactions and cumulative Houston rail network effects; (4) robust comment period with meaningful weight to community input; and (5) extensive mitigation including air quality monitoring near schools, $5M for Preston Road underpass, 25% UP funding for ten grade separations, four Quiet Zones, operational rules preventing trains from blocking neighborhoods while awaiting yard space, dedicated local UP police liaison, park space creation on abandoned UP properties, and monthly right-of-way maintenance. The coalition frames this as a procedural justice issue: 'Our requests are not unreasonable. They represent the bare minimum of what our communities need to ensure that increased rail operations do not further degrade our quality of life.' This is a sophisticated conditional intervention combining procedural demands (Houston hearing, extended comment) with specific operational and environmental conditions.
key_arguments: Houston was inadequately served in CP-KCS merger review—hearing held in Beaumont on weekday prevented working residents from participating; East End residents deserve direct testimony opportunity in their own city about a merger that will significantly impact rail operations in their neighborhoods

STB may be underweighting post-merger freight volume impacts to expedite merger decision; industry projections indicate 'the densest lanes are projected to emerge post-merger' yet Houston has received no clear, localized predictions about impacts on East End communities

Previous merger review's narrow analytical scope failed to capture real-world operational dynamics; at-grade interchanges in Houston create cascade effects where trains on secondary lines must wait for priority routes to clear before proceeding, a primary cause of prolonged blockages lasting 30+ minutes in East End, Second Ward, and Fifth Ward neighborhoods

STB's system impact analysis must examine secondary line interactions and cumulative effects on entire Houston rail network, not only direct merger lines, to capture blockage patterns that directly harm community safety and access

Communities bearing direct operational burden deserve meaningful investment and protection if railroads benefit from merger; increased rail operations will further degrade quality of life, children's health, and neighborhood safety without specific mitigation measures
key_excerpts: Early analysis suggests that the STB may place less emphasis on post-merger freight volume impacts to expedite the merger decision process. Industry projections indicate that 'the densest lanes are projected to emerge post-merger,' yet Houston has not received clear, localized predictions about what this means for our communities.

In cities like Houston, where interchanges are at-grade, trains on secondary lines must wait for priority routes to clear before they can proceed. This cascade effect is one of the primary causes of prolonged blockages in neighborhoods like the East End, Second Ward, and Fifth Ward, where trains regularly block crossings for 30 minutes or more.
The previous merger review's narrow scope failed to capture the real-world operational dynamics that affect East End residents on a daily basis. This merger review must not repeat that mistake.
Our residents need transparent, data-driven projections—not generalized regional assessments that obscure local impacts.
If Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern stand to benefit from this merger, then the communities that make their operations possible deserve meaningful investment and protection in return.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Conditional approval contingent on: (1) public hearing in Houston during accessible hours; (2) detailed, neighborhood-specific freight volume, train frequency, crossing wait time, and air quality impact forecasts; (3) comprehensive system impact study examining secondary line interactions and cascade blockage effects; (4) robust public comment period with meaningful weight given to community input; (5) specific community mitigation measures including air quality monitoring, grade separations, Quiet Zones, operational constraints on train movements, local Union Pacific police representation, and park/community space development on specified railroad properties.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing raises several substantive issues within STB's merger review scope: (1) whether localized community impact studies are required or merely regional competitive analyses; (2) whether cascade effects from secondary line interactions (at-grade interchange bottlenecks) must be examined as part of system impact analysis; (3) whether post-merger operational intensity in major freight hubs like Houston warrants condition-setting beyond traditional competitive remedies; (4) scope of STB's authority to impose operational constraints (train movement rules, quiet zone implementation) and community benefit conditions (park development, police liaison) as merger approval conditions. The filing implicitly challenges whether the CP-KCS merger review precedent (focused on narrow merger lines, regional hearings) establishes adequate standards for reviewing a UP/NS merger affecting a major national freight hub. It also raises procedural questions about public comment period adequacy and hearing accessibility for affected communities. The specificity of requested operational conditions (preventing trains unable to fit in yards from moving through Houston Complex) suggests sophisticated analysis of local rail bottlenecks and potential basis for operational remedy conditions.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Public comment filing; no response deadline indicated

docket_entries.title: Canadian National Railway Comments on Proposed Procedural Schedule – Requests Extended Comment Period, Pre/Post-Hearing Briefs, and Ex Parte Window
docket_entries.entry_summary: Canadian National Railway opposes the Board's proposed procedural schedule as insufficiently protective of intervenor participation rights in this unprecedented major transaction. CN's core procedural complaint centers on Applicants' failure to provide an 'approximate filing date' as required by regulation—Applicants stated only 'on or before January 29, 2026' while publicly indicating potential filing as early as November 2025 or early December 2025. CN argues this creates information asymmetry: 'Applicants have retained at least three STB-facing law firms and five economic firms and, according to Applicants, have been hard at work evaluating the proposed transaction for well over two months. Other interested parties too must assemble teams, request and process extensive datasets and prepare analyses. Applicants' omission of an approximate filing date risks upending the critical pre-filing period.' CN further contends the 120-day comment period is unreasonably compressed given the transaction's unprecedented scope—combining two of the largest U.S. railroads into 'the largest Class I railroad by route miles, number of employees, states covered' with '$250 billion enterprise value, over $50 billion larger than the remaining three publicly traded Class I railroads combined.' CN also points to Applicants' inadequate discovery responses: despite CN serving pre-filing discovery requests in September 2025, 'as of the time of CN's filing, Applicants had failed to produce any of the discrete materials responsive to CN's first set of discovery requests, over a month after those requests were served,' including merger agreement disclosure schedules and documents regarding two-to-one customers. CN rejects Applicants' claim the transaction presents no complex competitive issues, noting: 'Applicants themselves have recognized, the proposed transaction involves overlapping markets and customers; therefore, it is inaccurate for Applicants to call it an "end-to-end" transaction.' CN proposes F+150 days (or May 29, 2026) for comments and responsive applications, limited pre-hearing briefs 20 days before hearing, and final briefs 20 days after hearing closes. On ex parte communications, CN argues the cutoff should extend to 20 days after rebuttals are filed, not Day 150, to enable 'public engagement' on 'issues likely to arise in rebuttal filings' involving 'technical data.'
key_arguments: Applicants violated regulatory requirements by failing to provide approximate filing date—stating only 'on or before January 29, 2026' despite public statements indicating potential November/December 2025 filing, creating unequal preparation time for competitors and other intervenors who lack access to Applicants' extensive legal/economic teams and merger information

The 120-day comment period is unreasonably compressed for unprecedented transaction combining two largest Class I railroads ($250B enterprise value, 50,000+ miles, 43 states) into entity larger than remaining three Class I railroads combined, requiring complex competitive analysis under new 'enhancement of competition' standard

Applicants' pre-filing discovery responses are obstructionist—over one month after CN's September 23, 2025 requests, Applicants have produced zero responsive documents despite requests for readily available merger agreement schedules and customer documents, demonstrating information asymmetry justifies longer comment period

Transaction is not truly end-to-end despite Applicants' characterization—Applicants themselves acknowledge 'overlapping markets and customers,' and even end-to-end mergers can pose competitive risks (citing Board's Canadian Pacific-Kansas City decision overturning prior end-to-end presumptions)
Pre-hearing and post-hearing briefs are standard in major federal court mergers and would benefit Board given complexity, new legal standard, and extensive factual record requiring developed analysis

Ex parte communications should extend to 20 days after rebuttals filed to permit stakeholder engagement on technical/competitive issues arising in rebuttal, consistent with AAR's reasoning that reply comments often present new issues requiring discussion
key_excerpts: Applicants' omission of an approximate filing date risks upending the critical pre-filing period, including both substantive and organizational efforts. Substantive work during the pre-filing notice period also includes important pre-filing discovery requests to allow interested parties to obtain the necessary data and documents to begin to understand the potential competitive impacts of the transaction.

If approved, the proposed transaction would bring together two of the largest railroad companies in the U.S., resulting in one spanning over 50,000 miles across 43 states. The combined railroad would become the largest Class I railroad by route miles, number of employees, states covered, and enterprise value with an anticipated enterprise value of $250 billion, over $50 billion larger than the remaining three publicly traded Class I railroads combined.

Although Applicants claim they have begun responding to discovery requests, as of the time of CN's filing, Applicants had failed to produce any of the discrete materials responsive to CN's first set of discovery requests, over a month after those requests were served.

Whether the proposed transaction raises complex competition or operating issues goes to the very heart of the Board's evaluation and should not be prejudged before the Board and interested parties have a meaningful opportunity to evaluate the proposed transaction.

Issues can and do arise in reply comments for which public engagement could be beneficial, especially in rulemakings in which technical data is sought or submitted. The current policy of prohibiting communications after the cutoff of 20 days before replies are due—even if such communications are publicly disclosed—inhibits discussions on all of the issues in the record.
Applicants themselves have recognized, the proposed transaction involves overlapping markets and customers; therefore, it is inaccurate for Applicants to call it an 'end-to-end' transaction.
docket_entries.relief_requested: CN requests three modifications to the Board's proposed procedural schedule: (1) Comments, requests for conditions, and responsive applications due by F+150 days or May 29, 2026 (whichever is earlier), not F+105/F+120; (2) Allow limited pre-hearing briefs 20 days prior to any public hearing and move final briefs to 20 days after the hearing (not 270 days before hearing); (3) Extend period for ex parte communications to 20 days after rebuttals in support of responsive applications are submitted (not Day 150).
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: CN's filing raises material questions about STB's regulatory framework for major transactions: (1) Whether lack of approximate filing date triggers exemption authority under 49 U.S.C. § 10502(a) to extend statutory 90-day deadlines for inconsistent/inclusion applications (CN suggests Board exempt proceeding from § 11325(b)(2) if necessary); (2) Whether information asymmetry and inadequate discovery warrant procedural accommodation to competitors; (3) Whether new 'enhancement of competition' standard under 2001 merger rules requires expanded briefing and ex parte procedures beyond historical merger precedent; (4) Whether Board's normal 270-day final brief deadline (before hearing) is suitable for major transactions, or whether pre/post-hearing brief format (standard in federal court mergers) better serves public interest. CN's conditional procedural framework could establish precedent for future major transactions if adopted.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Filing date—procedural request filed with Board for consideration in upcoming Decision on procedural schedule

docket_entries.title: Coy Fortenberry - Small Business Consultant Opposition to UP-NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: Coy Fortenberry, a small business consultant in Baton Rouge, opposes the UP-NS merger on grounds that it would create a 'near duopoly' harmful to competition and small businesses. He argues: 'Rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers - and it's the mom-and-pop stores and new business trying to get on their feet - who feel it the most.' He contends that reduced rail competition leads to higher shipping costs that small businesses cannot absorb and ultimately must pass to consumers. His opposition is framed in broad competitive policy terms rather than through specific market evidence or quantified impacts. He does not propose conditions that would remedy his concerns but instead urges the STB to ensure the merger meets standards for 'enhancing competition and safety' and to preserve a competitive railroad industry. No settlement signals or willingness to negotiate on specific remedies are evident.
key_arguments: A UP-NS merger would form a 'near duopoly' that is 'detrimental to competition,' which Fortenberry characterizes as 'the backbone of our economic system in America'
Rail mergers 'slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain' - harms that 'mom-and-pop stores and new business' feel most acutely
Reduced competition in rail service leads to 'higher costs across the board' that small businesses cannot absorb, forcing them to raise consumer prices
Competition is essential for 'long-term viability and lower costs' and for protecting 'businesses, employees and customers across Louisiana'
The railroad industry must remain 'competitive and healthy in order to protect everyday Americans'
key_excerpts: If the merger is approved, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would form a near duopoly. This would be detrimental to competition. And competition is the backbone of our economic system in America.

Poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers - and it's the mom-and-pop stores and new business trying to get on their feet - who feel it the most.

I've consistently seen how less competition in rail service leads to higher costs across the board. Unfortunately, when businesses can't absorb these costs - and most small businesses cannot, they eventually get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for the essential goods and products they need.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the merger. Fortenberry requests that 'the Surface Transportation Board considers the impact on local businesses and ensures the tenets of the merger meet the standards for enhancing competition and safety.' He emphasizes that 'it is essential that the railroad industry stays competitive and healthy in order to protect everyday Americans.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low. This filing presents general competitive concerns and public interest arguments but no legal analysis, evidentiary support, or specific regulatory claims that would alter the scope of STB review or create new legal issues. It does not challenge jurisdiction, raise procedural defects, or propose novel legal theories. The filing is consistent with standard public comment on merger applications expressing concern about consolidation effects.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing - no specific response deadline for applicants, though filing will be part of the administrative record

docket_entries.title: Edward Jelinek - Individual Comment Opposing UP-NS Merger Without Conditions
docket_entries.entry_summary: Edward Jelinek, an automotive industry veteran from Missouri, opposes the UP-NS merger on consumer protection grounds. He argues that rail consolidation will reduce competition, inevitably raising freight costs for manufacturers and retailers, which will "end up hitting consumers hardest, from higher prices at the grocery store to inflated costs for everyday essentials." He frames the merger as a threat to the "delicate balance of logistics that industries like auto manufacturing depend on" and to household budgets broadly. Jelinek urges the STB to "thoroughly examine the consequences" and ensure "any approval comes with enforceable safeguards that prioritize fair pricing, strong service, and open competition." However, his filing does not specify what those safeguards should be, does not provide quantified competitive analysis, and does not propose discrete remedies. The opposition is rooted in general principle (consolidation harms consumers and competition) rather than deal-specific harm modeling.
key_arguments: Rail consolidation reduces competing shipping options, which 'inevitably' increases freight costs that cascade to consumer prices: 'when shipping options shrink, costs inevitably rise—and those increases don't stop with manufacturers or retailers. They end up hitting consumers hardest, from higher prices at the grocery store to inflated costs for everyday essentials.'

The merger disrupts logistics equilibrium needed by capital-intensive industries like automotive: 'It can disrupt the delicate balance of logistics that industries like auto manufacturing depend on, while also putting added strain on household budgets.'
Rail consolidation has irreversible long-term consequences for competitive markets and consumer welfare: 'This kind of rail industry consolidation has long-term implications.'
key_excerpts: If approved without strong conditions, this consolidation could significantly reduce competition in the freight rail market. Based on my experience, when shipping options shrink, costs inevitably rise—and those increases don't stop with manufacturers or retailers.
This decision must reflect the interests of both the economy and the people who drive it.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the merger or, if approved, impose 'enforceable safeguards that prioritize fair pricing, strong service, and open competition.' No specific conditions articulated.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Minimal. This is a consumer-perspective comment that does not identify specific regulatory gaps, create new legal theories, or propose novel remedies. It is probative of public concern sentiment but does not materially advance the evidentiary record on competitive effects or remedial design. It may be cited by opposing parties to demonstrate broad consumer concern, but it carries limited weight in a merger analysis that requires quantified competitive harm and specific, enforceable conditions.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing; no response deadline

docket_entries.title: Parker Ward (Swamp Fire Seasoning) - Opposition to UP-NS Merger on Competition and Small Business Impact Grounds
docket_entries.entry_summary: Parker Ward, owner of Swamp Fire Seasoning in Shreveport, Louisiana, opposes the UP-NS merger on grounds that it would create a 'near duopoly' detrimental to competition. His argument centers on ideological commitment to competitive markets rather than specific, quantified harms to his business. Ward contends: 'Poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain' and 'less competition in rail service leads to higher costs across the board.' He characterizes small businesses like his own as most vulnerable to merger-induced service disruptions and cost increases, and warns that cost increases 'get passed down to consumers.' Ward frames the opposition around protecting 'everyday Americans' and maintaining a 'strong rail system' competitive and healthy. However, the filing contains no specific allegations of current service problems, pricing data, or evidence that the merger would harm his particular business operations. The opposition is framed as a matter of principle—'competition is the backbone of our economic system'—rather than concrete business impact. Ward does not propose conditions that would satisfy his concerns or indicate willingness to negotiate; his position is fundamentally that the merger threatens competition itself and should be denied.
key_arguments: The proposed merger would form a 'near duopoly' that is 'detrimental to competition,' which Ward characterizes as 'the backbone of our economic system in America.'

Rail consolidations cause service disruptions and supply chain delays, with small businesses bearing disproportionate impact: 'it's the mom-and-pop stores and new business trying to get on their feet like mine, who feel the most.'

Reduced competition in rail service leads to higher costs that small businesses cannot absorb, forcing them to pass costs to consumers: 'when businesses can't absorb these costs—and most small businesses cannot, they eventually get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more.'

A competitive rail system is essential to long-term business viability and consumer welfare: 'Competition drives long-term viability and lower costs. The success of businesses, employees and customers across Louisiana depend on a strong rail system.'
key_excerpts: If the merger is approved, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would form a near duopoly. This would be detrimental to competition. And competition is the backbone of our economic system in America.

Poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers—and it's the mom-and-pop stores and new business trying to get on their feet like mine, who feel the most.

I've consistently seen how less competition in rail service leads to higher costs across the board. Unfortunately, when businesses can't absorb these costs—and most small businesses cannot, they eventually get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for the essential goods and products they need.
It is essential that the railroad industry stays competitive and healthy in order to protect everyday Americans.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Implicit: Denial of the merger. Explicitly requests that 'the Surface Transportation Board considers the impact on local businesses and ensures the tenets of the merger meet the standards for enhancing competition and safety.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low. This is a general public interest comment articulating competitive policy concerns without specific evidentiary support or proposing remedial conditions. It does not raise novel legal arguments or challenge specific aspects of STB merger review standards under 49 U.S.C. § 11324. The filing does not require substantive response from applicants or raise factual disputes requiring hearing development. Its value is political/advocacy rather than legal; it illustrates public sentiment among small business operators but lacks the specificity needed to drive regulatory decision-making.

docket_entries.title: Eric Hare (Global K9 Protection Group) - Small Business Opposition to UP-NS Merger
docket_entries.filer_name: Eric Hare / Global K9 Protection Group
docket_entries.entry_summary: Eric Hare, CEO of Global K9 Protection Group (Opelika, Alabama), opposes the UP-NS merger on the grounds that it would create a 'near duopoly' reducing rail competition and driving cost increases that harm small businesses and ultimately consumers. He argues: 'When rail mergers are poorly executed, they slow service, cause congestion, and disrupt supply chains. It's often small and mid-sized businesses — the mom-and-pop operations — that end up paying the price.' key_arguments: UP-NS merger would create a 'near duopoly' and further reduce rail competition, which 'almost always leads to higher costs across the board'
Rail mergers that are 'poorly executed' cause service slowdowns, congestion, and supply chain disruption that disproportionately harm small and mid-sized businesses
Cost increases from reduced competition in rail service 'inevitably trickle down to consumers — the people who can least afford to pay more for essential goods'
Strong competition in the rail network is essential for 'efficiency, lower costs, and long-term success' of businesses and communities
key_excerpts: If this merger is approved, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would create what amounts to a near duopoly, further reducing competition. Less competition in rail service almost always leads to higher costs across the board.

When rail mergers are poorly executed, they slow service, cause congestion, and disrupt supply chains. It's often small and mid-sized businesses — the mom-and-pop operations — that end up paying the price.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the merger; ensure STB decision 'truly strengthens competition, reliability, and safety' and protects small business interests
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Minimal. This filing represents public comment from a small business customer but contains no novel legal arguments, no evidence of specific merger-related harm to this filer, and no actionable proposed conditions. It reflects a general policy concern about consolidation rather than analysis of merger-specific impacts under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 standards. The filing does not advance factual or legal theories that would alter the STB's analytical framework or evidentiary burdens.

docket_entries.title: Nancy Nabors - Small Business Owner Opposition to UP-NS Merger

It reflects public comment on the public interest standard (49 U.S.C. § 11324(c)), specifically the 'public interest' prong including effects on small businesses and consumers. While not legally novel, it establishes a record that small business customers voiced concerns about competitive effects and service reliability. Does not require specific STB response but documents stakeholder opposition.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Public comment period (date dependent on formal application filing)

docket_entries.title: City of Houston Comments: Conditional Support with Mandatory Procedural Safeguards and Community Mitigation Requirements
docket_entries.entry_summary: The City of Houston, representing the nation's fourth-largest city and a critical rail hub, supports the merger proceeding but conditions approval on extensive procedural safeguards and binding mitigation commitments. Houston's East End, Greater Fifth Ward, OST/South Union, and Northside neighborhoods—already among the most rail-impacted urban areas in the nation—experience hundreds of documented incidents annually where stopped trains delay emergency response vehicles, divide communities, and worsen air quality. The City notes that Union Pacific has identified Houston as a key node in its post-merger expansion strategy to capture Midwest freight bound for Gulf Coast ports, which will "intensify the operational pressures already affecting our city" without proper oversight. Houston explicitly rejects the procedural exclusion it experienced during the CP-KCS merger and demands: (1) at least one public hearing in Houston with evening/weekend access; sufficient time between filings and comment deadlines; a comprehensive regional impact study capturing cascading effects across multiple carriers; and community mitigation planning before final approval. On substantives, Houston requests binding commitments for grade separation funding at priority crossings, train length and idling restrictions in residential areas, formalized emergency coordination protocols with fire/EMS/police departments, incorporation of the City's Smart Railroad Crossing Monitor Pilot data into STB oversight, and ongoing community engagement. The City frames this as balancing "national freight efficiency with local public safety and environmental justice" and positions itself as ready to collaborate with the Board, applicants, and regional partners on an "equitable outcome."
key_arguments: Merger-driven traffic intensification will exacerbate existing emergency response crisis: Houston Fire Department documents 'hundreds of incidents each year' where stopped trains delay emergency vehicles or force reroutes, 'creating unacceptable risks to life and safety,' and Union Pacific has identified Houston as 'a key node in its expansion strategy, seeking to capture more Midwest freight bound for Gulf Coast ports'—this will 'intensify the operational pressures already affecting our city' absent proper oversight.

Houston neighborhoods experience documented environmental justice harm from rail operations: East End, Greater Fifth Ward, OST/South Union, and Northside are 'among the most rail-impacted urban areas in the nation' with 'frequent blocked crossings—sometimes lasting hours—causing delays for emergency responders, dividing communities, and contributing to air quality and noise issues that affect tens of thousands of residents.'

Previous regulatory exclusion of Houston during CP-KCS merger must not be repeated: 'During the previous CP–KCS merger, Houston was excluded from direct engagement despite being a major operational hub. That must not happen again,' requiring STB ensure meaningful community participation including at least one public hearing in Houston.

Comprehensive regional impact analysis is essential because Houston's rail congestion is interlinked across multiple carriers: 'Rail congestion in Houston is interlinked across multiple carriers and subdivisions; a narrow review will fail to capture cascading effects that cause prolonged blockages and emergency response delays.'
Procedural schedule must allocate time for community mitigation negotiation before final approval, not after, to give affected neighborhoods meaningful input on proposed measures.

Binding operational restrictions on train length and idling are necessary public health measures: 'Reasonable limits on train length and idling time within urban and residential areas to prevent gridlock and reduce diesel emissions' directly address documented air quality and congestion harms.
key_excerpts: As the nation's fourth-largest city and a critical hub for rail and port activity, Houston sits at the crossroads of the national freight network and is in the Gulf Coast Commodity Flow for both Union Pacific Railroad and Burlington Northern Santa Fe Railroad. Our rail system supports the movement of goods vital to the U.S. economy, but it also runs directly through densely populated residential neighborhoods, creating unique and ongoing challenges for public safety, emergency response, air quality, and community livability.
The Houston Fire Department documents hundreds of incidents each year where stopped trains delay emergency vehicles or force reroutes, creating unacceptable risks to life and safety.

The proposed $85 billion merger would create the first modern transcontinental railroad, and Union Pacific has identified Houston as a key node in its expansion strategy, seeking to capture more Midwest freight bound for Gulf Coast ports. Without proper oversight and mitigation, this will intensify the operational pressures already affecting our city.
During the previous CP–KCS merger, Houston was excluded from direct engagement despite being a major operational hub. That must not happen again.

Rail congestion in Houston is interlinked across multiple carriers and subdivisions; a narrow review will fail to capture cascading effects that cause prolonged blockages and emergency response delays.

Houston's economic vitality depends on efficient freight rail operations—but our residents and first responders cannot bear the escalating costs of congestion and inaction. This merger review presents an opportunity for the Surface Transportation Board to balance national freight efficiency with local public safety and environmental justice.
docket_entries.relief_requested: The City requests that any merger approval include: (1) Procedural safeguards ensuring meaningful Houston community participation including at least one public hearing in Houston at accessible times/locations; sufficient time between technical filings and comment deadlines; comprehensive system impact study examining primary and secondary lines throughout Houston region; community mitigation planning period before final approval. (2) Binding substantive commitments requiring: infrastructure investment for grade separation at priority crossings; operational restrictions on train length and idling in urban areas; community protections including quiet zones and rail safety measures; formalized emergency response coordination protocols with Houston Fire Department/EMS/Police; incorporation of Smart Railroad Crossing Monitor Pilot data into STB monitoring; ongoing community engagement for neighborhoods with highest blocked crossing frequency.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing raises procedural scope issues requiring STB response: (1) it demands local public hearings as part of merger review process, potentially expanding traditional STB hearing practice to include community-centered sessions; (2) it requires comprehensive regional impact analysis beyond typical merger environmental review, explicitly requesting examination of cascading effects across multiple carriers/subdivisions; (3) it seeks incorporation of local emergency response data (Houston Fire Department incident records) and pilot project data (Smart Railroad Crossing Monitor) into formal STB monitoring requirements, expanding the evidentiary record for operational oversight. The filing also creates a settlement negotiation baseline: the City is not opposing the merger per se but has identified specific, achievable, and quantifiable mitigation measures (grade separation funding, train length restrictions, emergency coordination protocols, data incorporation) that could satisfy its concerns. The reference to previous CP-KCS merger exclusion may trigger STB procedural fairness considerations and invite comparison to prior merger proceedings' community engagement practices.
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is a Comment filing submitted during the comment period; no specific response deadline is indicated. However, STB will need to address Houston's procedural requests (hearing location, scheduling) in procedural orders and address substantive conditions in any merger approval conditions or hearing procedures.

docket_entries.title: American Chemistry Council Files Notice of Intent to Participate
docket_entries.entry_summary: The American Chemistry Council filed a simple notice of intent to participate as a party of record in the UP-NS merger proceeding, dated October 21, 2025 (entered November 13, 2025). No substantive comments, conditions, or positions are stated in this filing. This is a procedural filing establishing the organization's standing to receive notice and participate in future phases of the docket. The filing signals that the chemical industry—a substantial user of rail transportation for bulk commodity shipment—intends to monitor and potentially engage in the proceeding. Given the chemical industry's reliance on railroad competition for rates and service, ACC's participation could indicate upcoming substantive filings on competitive impacts, rate implications, or service reliability issues specific to chemical shipments.
key_excerpts: The American Chemistry Council intends to participate in this proceeding as a party of record.
docket_entries.relief_requested: None stated. Filing establishes right to participate and receive notice in the proceeding.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing does not itself change the scope of review or burden of proof, but it establishes ACC as an official party with notice and participation rights. Under 49 CFR § 1104.2, this notice creates procedural entitlements to discovery, hearing participation, and filing opportunities. If ACC files substantive comments later in the Comment phase, those will be required responses for the applicants and carry evidentiary weight. The filing signals that the chemical shipping industry—a major customer class for UP and NS—is engaged and may present testimony on competitive effects specific to chemical commodity routes and rates.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.deadline_description: Procedural filing; no responsive deadline. ACC must participate within established STB comment/hearing deadlines for this docket.

docket_entries.title: Colorado Pacific Rio Grande Railroad LLC - Notice of Intent to Participate
docket_entries.entry_summary: Colorado Pacific Rio Grande Railroad LLC filed a notice of intent to participate in the UP-NS merger proceeding. The filing is purely procedural—the railroad seeks placement on the official service list and recognition as a party of record but does not express support, opposition, or any substantive position on the proposed transaction. No arguments, conditions, or analysis are provided. This is a standard notice establishing eligibility to receive service documents and participate in subsequent proceedings, likely filed to preserve the railroad's right to intervene or comment later if it chooses to do so.
key_excerpts: The Colorado Pacific Rio Grande Railroad LLC, hereby provides notice of its intent to participate in this proceeding as a Party of Record and requests that its undersigned counsel be placed on the official service list for this docket.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Placement on the official service list and recognition as a party of record to participate in the proceeding.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing establishes Colorado Pacific Rio Grande Railroad's formal status as a party of record in the docket, entitling it to receive all service documents and enabling future substantive participation (comments, testimony, discovery, cross-examination). It does not change the scope of review or evidentiary burdens but preserves the filer's procedural rights.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.deadline_description: No response required. This is a notice of participation, not a motion or petition requiring Board action.

docket_entries.title: Brittany Hollis - Small Business Retail Opposition to UP-NS Merger

She argues: 'As a small business person for several years, I've seen the effect large consolidations can have on small business operations. The merger creates a near-monopoly harmful to competition: 'If the merger is approved, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would form a near duopoly. This would be detrimental to competition.'

Reduced competition directly increases costs to small businesses and consumers: 'Less competition in rail service leads to higher costs across the board... eventually [costs] get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for the essential goods and products they need.'

key_excerpts: Poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers – and it's the mom-and-pop stores who are impacted the most.
If the merger is approved, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would form a near duopoly. This would be detrimental to competition.

Less competition in rail service leads to higher costs across the board. Unfortunately, when businesses can't absorb these costs, they eventually get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for the essential goods and products they need.

docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: None - filing provides general policy perspective without raising novel legal issues, evidentiary claims, or regulatory interpretation questions relevant to 49 U.S.C. § 11324 merger analysis. Does not engage with statutory merger standards (competition analysis, service impacts, labor impacts). Primarily a public comment supporting competitive markets.

docket_entries.title: Bill Coomer (Ohio Manufacturing/Textile/Storage Owner) - Opposition to UP-NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: Bill Coomer, owner of manufacturing, textile, and storage businesses in Ohio, opposes the proposed UP-NS merger based on competitive harm to small-to-mid-sized businesses. He argues that 'less competition leads to higher shipping costs' and that merger-driven service degradation 'cascades across every part of the supply chain,' disproportionately burdening small operators unable to absorb disruptions. Coomer explicitly frames the competitive risk as creating a 'near-duopoly in freight rail' and notes that cost increases will 'filter down to consumers, forcing families to pay more for everyday goods and services.' He does not demand outright denial but instead urges the Board to impose 'strict safeguards' to 'protect competition, safeguard service reliability, and prioritize the long-term stability of communities and businesses' if approval is granted. His framing emphasizes consumer and regional economic impact rather than technical competitive analysis, making this an accessible narrative for settlement—he identifies three specific categories of protective conditions (competition, service reliability, community stability) that could anchor negotiations with applicants.
key_arguments: Merger will create a 'near-duopoly in freight rail' that eliminates meaningful competitive choice for small-to-mid-sized shippers like his own businesses

Reduced rail competition historically leads to higher shipping costs, which small and mid-sized businesses 'are often the ones left to carry the burden' for, unlike large corporations that can absorb disruptions

Cost increases will not be contained to businesses but will 'filter down to consumers, forcing families to pay more for everyday goods and services,' making this a consumer welfare issue, not just a business-to-business problem

Service delays from reduced competition 'cascade across every part of the supply chain,' undermining the reliability that manufacturers, textile producers, and logistics operators depend on for operations across Ohio
key_excerpts: Service slows, costs rise, and delays cascade across every part of the supply chain. Large corporations may be able to absorb those disruptions, but small and mid-sized businesses like mine are often the ones left to carry the burden.

If this merger is approved without strict safeguards, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would effectively create a near-duopoly in freight rail. History has shown that less competition leads to higher shipping costs and those costs don't stop with business owners. They inevitably filter down to consumers, forcing families to pay more for everyday goods and services.

I urge the Board to carefully examine this proposal and ensure that any merger fully protects safeguards to competition, safeguards service reliability, and prioritizes the long-term stability of communities and businesses across Ohio.
