docket_entries.title: Sunflower State Industrial Railway Opposition to UP-NS Merger: Shortline Perspective on Merger Futility and Poor Class I Service
docket_entries.entry_summary: Sunflower State Industrial Railway files a passionate but largely rhetorical opposition to the UP-NS merger, arguing it represents yet another doomed consolidation that will not address rail's fundamental competitive problems. The filer contends: 'This merger is a joke' that offers 'NO improvements over the present lines.' Gorsline argues the real problem is not rail consolidation but Class I railroads' poor local service and their own strategic decision to abandon less-than-carload (LCL) traffic to trucking decades ago. He cites that trucks move 10.8 billion tons (72% of U.S. freight) versus rail's 27%, and that 82,859 trucking companies compete with Class I railroads—a competitive disadvantage no merger can fix. Most substantively, Gorsline attacks the applicants' core justification: NS CEO Mark George's claim that 'We can only go so far independently...We've been losing share to truck—and this is one way to reverse that trend.' Gorsline directly counters: 'This merger will do Nothing to change the onslaught of trucks!' He argues that by the time 'a railroad puts a MILE long train together on the east coast: a truck is halfway across the US!' Gorsline also criticizes the promised 24-48 hour service improvement as illusory because transcontinental shipments still require stops at Chicago and other gateways, negating efficiency gains. Most critically for STB review, Gorsline documents rail system contraction: U.S. rail mileage dropped from 200,000+ miles (1960) to under 100,000 miles (2020)—a 50% reduction despite decades of mergers. He argues this proves that 'Rail mergers and how many abandonments have changed the AMOUNT of track in the US? ZIP! NADA! Trackage continues to DROP—yet truck traffic GOES UP!' As a shortline operator, Gorsline provides personal testimony: 'As a shortline RR entity: I can TELL you how unhelpful UP is...I can't be the only shortline RR that's gone to the UP & sought their assistance—to get lip service.' He demands that instead of merger consolidation, Class I railroads should 'Start being BETTER partners 4 your Shortline & Regional RRs. THAT'S How ya get freight OFF trucks & BACK on railcars.' The filing also cites infrastructure destruction: UP's abandonment of the Missouri-Kansas-Texas (MKT) Railroad line (St. Louis-Kansas City, 240 miles) exemplifies how mergers lead to route abandonment, not expansion. Gorsline challenges the STB's historical approval of merger-driven abandonments, asking: 'When is the last time a merger Preserved trackage, saved jobs and didn't put Stockholders BEFORE the customers the RR claims it serves?' He concludes: 'The definition of crazy's allowing merger upon merger expecting the US rail system to Grow. It isn't & that should be something that worries STB.' While the filing lacks legal sophistication and makes broad market-level arguments about trucking competition that may be outside STB merger review scope, it provides authentic shortline operator perspective on class I service failures and raises specific infrastructure abandonment concerns that could inform regulatory findings on whether the merger enhances public interest.
key_arguments: The merger cannot reverse rail's market share losses to trucking because the Class I railroads caused those losses by abandoning LCL traffic to trucks themselves: 'the Class I RR's have NO ONE to Blame for truck traffic losses as it was the RRs WHO decided to let go of LCL & pass it on to the trucks & that truck traffic is NOT coming back to the Class I railroads!'
Trucks move 10.8 billion tons (72% of U.S. freight) versus rail's 27%, and 82,859 trucking companies compete for freight—a structural disadvantage no railroad merger can overcome.

The promised 24-48 hour transit time improvement is illusory because transcontinental shipments still require stops at intermediate hubs like Chicago: 'the railway would STILL need to STOP in Chicago. Ah so much for a New Transcontinental railway system!'

U.S. rail mileage has contracted from 200,000+ miles (1960) to under 100,000 miles (2020), proving that decades of mergers have not expanded rail infrastructure but destroyed it: 'Trackage continues to DROP—yet truck traffic GOES UP!'

Class I railroads provide poor local service to shortlines and regional operators, losing freight to trucks not because of network limitations but because of operational failures: 'Shippers divert rail shipments to trucks when a local regularly fails to show up, doesn't deliver the right empties, or can't pull loads on schedule.'

Union Pacific specifically has abandoned critical Midwest routes and provides inadequate service to shortline partners: 'UP's killed so Many MidWest lines it's Hard to say they Care about the Mid West!' and 'I can TELL you how unhelpful UP is.'

Prior rail mergers have consistently failed to deliver promised benefits while creating operational disruptions: 'When is the last time a merger Preserved trackage, saved jobs and didn't put Stockholders BEFORE the customers the RR claims it serves?'

The solution to rail's competitive problems is improved local service and better shortline partnerships, not consolidation: 'Skip the merger mania & Start being BETTER partners 4 your Shortline & Regional RRs. THAT'S How ya get freight OFF trucks & BACK on railcars.'
key_excerpts: 'This merger is a joke. By the time a railroad puts a MILE long train together on the east coast: a truck is halfway across the US!'
'This merger will do Nothing to change the onslaught of trucks! Trucks move 10.8 BILLION tons of freight or 720/o of all US freightll! Rail moves a puny 270/o of all US freight!'
'As a shortline RR entity: I can TELL you how unhelpful UP is. I can't be the only shortline RR that's gone to the UP & sought their assistance—to get lip service.'
'The definition of crazy's allowing merger upon merger expecting the US rail system to Grow. It isn't & that should be something that worries STB.'
'Rail mergers and how many abandonments have changed the AMOUNT of track in the US? ZIP! NADA! Trackage continues to DROP—yet truck traffic GOES UP!'
'the railway would STILL need to STOP in Chicago. Ah so much for a New Transcontinental railway system!'
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the proposed merger. Sunflower argues the merger should be rejected because: (1) it will not reverse rail's loss of market share to trucking; (2) it will not preserve or improve rail service in the Midwest; (3) prior mergers have consistently failed to deliver promised benefits while destroying regional rail infrastructure; and (4) Class I railroads should instead focus on improving local service and partnering with shortlines rather than pursuing consolidation.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing, while lacking legal formality, raises material factual arguments about whether the merger satisfies the STB's statutory obligation under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 to ensure the merger 'is consistent with the public interest' and enhances (not merely preserves) competition. Specifically: (1) Gorsline's documentation of 50% U.S. rail mileage contraction despite decades of mergers directly challenges the applicants' claim that consolidation serves the public interest; (2) his specific examples of route abandonments (MKT line) provide concrete evidence of prior merger-related infrastructure destruction; (3) his testimony about inadequate Class I local service to shortline partners raises questions about the merged entity's likely behavior toward competitors and regional operators; (4) his argument that trucks dominate freight because of Class I strategic decisions (not network limitations) undermines the merger's economic justification. However, Gorsline's broad claims about trucking competition, interstate commerce, and general railroad industry policy may exceed STB merger review scope, which focuses on competitive effects in specific freight markets and service corridors. The filing does not identify specific markets where the merger would reduce competition or cite the applicants' proposed service offerings that would allegedly be harmed.

key_arguments: Consolidating Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would create a duopoly in freight rail, eliminating competitive options for small business shippers
Weakened rail competition leads to service degradation, higher shipping costs, fewer transportation options, and increased delays
Supply chain cost increases from reduced competition ripple to consumers in the form of higher prices for groceries and household goods

docket_entries.entry_summary: The City of Greenville's Safety/Service Director opposes the merger absent specific safety conditions. He states: 'Our police, fire, and EMS teams depend on reliable coordination with rail operators to respond quickly and protect lives.' The filer does not seek outright denial but rather conditions approval on: (1) 'strong safety safeguards,' (2) 'clear emergency communication protocols,' and (3) 'sustained infrastructure investment.' This is framed as a public safety/quality-of-life issue rather than economic competition—the merger threatens emergency services coordination and crossing safety in Greenville specifically. The tone signals openness to approval if conditions are met, making this a conditional opposition.
key_arguments: Reduced competition from merger will lead to slower response times and longer blockages at railroad crossings, impairing emergency vehicle access and response
Consolidation reduces investment in maintenance and communication systems, undermining the infrastructure reliability that emergency responders depend on
First responders (police, fire, EMS) require reliable coordination with rail operators for emergency response; merger threatens this coordination
Public safety and community readiness must not be sacrificed for rail efficiency gains
Merger requires strong safety safeguards and emergency communication protocols to protect residents and motorists
key_excerpts: Reduced competition often leads to slower response times, longer blockages at crossings, and less investment in maintenance and communication systems. These challenges directly impact first responders and increase risks to residents and motorists.
Our police, fire, and EMS teams depend on reliable coordination with rail operators to respond quickly and protect lives.
Any merger of this scale must include strong safety safeguards, clear emergency communication protocols, and sustained infrastructure investment.
Rail efficiency cannot come at the expense of local safety and community readiness.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Approval conditioned on: (1) Strong safety safeguards; (2) Clear emergency communication protocols; (3) Sustained infrastructure investment in maintenance and communication systems
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing introduces a public safety dimension to the STB's merger analysis that may expand the evidentiary record beyond typical competitive/service/rate concerns. Under 49 U.S.C. § 11324, the STB must consider whether a merger is consistent with 'the public interest,' which includes safety and emergency response coordination. This filing signals that local government entities view the merger as implicating first-responder capabilities and crossing safety—factors the STB should address in its decision or conditional approval. If multiple municipalities file similar concerns, this could create pressure for systemwide safety conditions rather than ad-hoc negotiation.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment filing; no response deadline, but applicants may address in reply comments or hearing testimony

docket_entries.title: Amanda Suffecool (Portage County, OH business owner) opposes UP-NS merger as anti-competitive threat to small business shipping costs
docket_entries.entry_summary: Amanda Suffecool, a manufacturing business owner in northeastern Ohio, opposes the merger on ideological and competitive grounds. She argues that consolidating Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern—'two of the nation's largest railroads'—would 'create an even tighter grip on the market, pushing the freight rail industry closer to a duopoly.' She contends that weakened rail competition directly harms small businesses and consumers: 'When rail competition weakens, service suffers. Shipping costs rise, options shrink, and delays increase. Those burdens don't just hit businesses, they ripple through the supply chain until families feel them directly in the form of higher prices for groceries, household goods and other essentials.' She frames her opposition as capitalist principle: 'For business owners like me who rely on dependable, affordable shipping across sectors, that means fewer choices and greater risk.' No specific conditions or remedies are proposed; her position is that the merger should be denied to preserve competition. She urges the STB to consider impacts 'not only on large corporations but also on small businesses and the communities they anchor,' framing rail as 'the backbone of local economies.'
key_arguments: Consolidation of UP and NS would push the freight rail industry 'closer to a duopoly,' reducing competitive options for shippers
Weakened rail competition causes service deterioration, cost increases, and schedule delays that ripple through supply chains to consumers in higher prices for essential goods
Small businesses and local economies are particularly vulnerable to consolidation because they lack alternatives when rail competition weakens
The merger threatens safety alongside competition—'we cannot afford changes that weaken competition or compromise safety'
Rail consolidation creates 'an even tighter grip on the market' that disadvantages small shippers relative to large corporations
key_excerpts: 'Consolidating two companies of this size would create an even tighter grip on the market, pushing the freight rail industry closer to a duopoly. For business owners like me who rely on dependable, affordable shipping across sectors, that means fewer choices and greater risk.'

'When rail competition weakens, service suffers. Shipping costs rise, options shrink, and delays increase. Those burdens don't just hit businesses, they ripple through the supply chain until families feel them directly in the form of higher prices for groceries, household goods and other essentials.'
'Rail is more than a logistical system, it is the backbone of local economies, and we cannot afford changes that weaken competition or compromise safety.'
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the proposed merger between Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Minimal direct legal significance. This is a form comment expressing general merger opposition without specific allegations of competitive harm, service impacts, or market data. Does not introduce new legal theories or factual disputes requiring investigation. Represents constituency sentiment but lacks the specificity needed to support detailed conditions or to counter company arguments with concrete business impact data. Does not materially change evidentiary burden or scope of review.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing; no response deadline

docket_entries.title: Lance Urbach (Walker, LA resident) - Comments opposing UP-NS merger absent competitive protections
docket_entries.entry_summary: Lance Urbach, a 25-year Walker, Louisiana resident and steel/aluminum welder, opposes the UP-NS merger absent appropriate competitive protections. Urbach's business depends on rail transportation: 'the railroad is arguably our most important form of transportation' for shipping steel goods throughout the South. He argues that rail consolidation historically 'results in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and these expenses don't stop at the rail yard,' ultimately harming consumers and businesses in rural communities. Urbach does not demand outright denial but conditions approval on the STB certifying that merger conditions 'meet the standards for enhancing competition in the market which is essential to a capitalist society' and prevent cost increases and service deterioration. His opposition is conditional—he would support approval if meaningful competitive safeguards are imposed, though he does not specify what those safeguards should be beyond broad competition protection.
key_arguments: Rail industry consolidation historically drives higher freight costs that ultimately reach consumers and small businesses dependent on rail shipping
The merger threatens rural communities' access to affordable goods and services by removing competitive pressure on freight rates
Rail transportation is critical infrastructure for small regional manufacturers: 'the railroad is arguably our most important form of transportation' for steel/aluminum welding operations
Consumers and small businesses require STB-imposed conditions to protect competitive markets, which is 'essential to a capitalist society'
key_excerpts: The rail industry particularly is important to my business as a steel and aluminum welder. We build, assemble, and ship steel goods for the entire south and the railroad is arguably our most important form of transportation.
Mergers are known to result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and these expenses don't stop at the rail yard.
We need to protect consumers and prevent rail industry consolidation from leading to higher costs and weaker service.
docket_entries.relief_requested: STB should 'certify that the tenets of the merger and conditions imposed on the transaction meet the standards for enhancing competition in the market which is essential to a capitalist society.' Approval only if merger conditions protect competition and prevent higher costs and weaker service.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing establishes that small-business shippers and rural retail consumers are actively monitoring the merger and expect the STB to condition approval on demonstrable competitive protection. Urbach's invocation of competition standards as a capitalist principle may signal expectations among small-business constituencies that the STB will apply rigorous competitive analysis under 49 U.S.C. § 11324. The filing does not raise novel legal issues but reinforces that public comment period generated opposition from affected business communities beyond major shippers and competitors.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Public comment period filing; no response deadline triggered

docket_entries.title: Ray Griffin (Cochiara Marina) - Small Business Opposition to UP-NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: Ray Griffin, owner of Cochiara Marina in Lafitte, Louisiana, opposes the UP-NS merger on general competition and small-business impact grounds. He argues: (1) the merger creates a 'near duopoly' detrimental to competition; (2) rail consolidations historically cause service disruptions and supply chain delays that disproportionately harm small businesses; (3) reduced rail competition leads to higher shipping costs that small businesses cannot absorb and must pass to consumers; and (4) 'Competition is the backbone of our economic system in America' and essential to long-term business viability. He seeks Board consideration of the impact on local businesses but provides no specific operational data, service corridors, or measurable competitive harms. His opposition is framed in broad policy terms rather than the transactional mechanics or competitive effects the Board analyzes.
key_arguments: The merger would create a 'near duopoly' that is detrimental to competition
Poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting supply chains—harm felt most acutely by small businesses
Less competition in rail service leads to higher costs that small businesses cannot absorb and must pass to consumers
Competition drives long-term business viability and lower costs; without it, everyday Americans pay more for essential goods
key_excerpts: If the merger is approved, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would form a near duopoly. This would be detrimental to competition. And competition is the backbone of our economic system in America.

Poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers—and it's the mom-and-pop stores and new business trying to get on their feet like mine, who feel it the most.

I've consistently seen how less competition in rail service leads to higher costs across the board. Unfortunately, when businesses can't absorb these costs—and most small businesses cannot, they eventually get passed down to consumers who are forced to pay more for the essential goods and products they need.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the merger OR, if approved, ensure 'the tenets of the merger meet the standards for enhancing competition and safety' and that the railroad industry 'stays competitive and healthy in order to protect everyday Americans.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low. Filing does not raise issues that alter STB's analytical framework or evidentiary burden. It is representative comment from the shipper/business customer constituency but lacks the specificity (routing data, competitive alternatives, service metrics, market analysis) that would require substantive applicant response or Board engagement with competitive effects analysis. Does not challenge procedural framework or raise novel legal questions.

docket_entries.title: Senator Robert Clements (Nebraska) Supports UP-NS Merger for Economic Growth
docket_entries.entry_summary: Nebraska State Senator Robert Clements supports the UP-NS merger as beneficial to Nebraska's economy and national competitiveness. He argues the merger would 'improve reliability, reduce delays, open new market access, and support continued investment in infrastructure and safety,' thereby 'strengthen[ing] supply chains, enhance[ing] competitiveness, and provide[ing] lasting value for shippers, consumers, and communities alike.' He frames it as essential to 'maintaining America's leadership in freight rail' and requests STB approval. The filing contains no specific conditions, empirical analysis, or acknowledgment of potential competitive concerns—it is a straightforward political endorsement from a state legislator whose district depends on Union Pacific service.
key_arguments: Merger will improve reliability and reduce delays for shippers by creating 'a more seamless rail network'
Merger will 'open new market access' and support continued investment in infrastructure and safety
Merger is necessary to strengthen Nebraska's economy and maintain U.S. competitiveness in freight rail globally
key_excerpts: By creating a more seamless rail network, the merger would improve reliability, reduce delays, open new market access, and support continued investment in infrastructure and safety.
I respectfully urge the Surface Transportation Board to give full and favorable consideration to this proposal, recognizing the benefits it will bring to our state and to the national economy.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Urges STB to 'give full and favorable consideration to this proposal, recognizing the benefits it will bring to our state and to the national economy'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Minimal. This filing contributes to the public record as a statement of state political support for the merger, but does not raise novel legal issues, propose evidentiary burdens, or affect scope of STB review. It does not address competitive impacts under 49 U.S.C. § 11324(b) (which requires analysis of effects on competition, efficiency, or the public interest in rail services).
docket_entries.deadline_description: No deadline; statement of support submitted during comment period

docket_entries.title: City of Denison, Texas Support Letter for UP-NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: The City of Denison, Texas, represented by Mayor Robert Crawley and the City Council, files a letter of support for the proposed UP-NS merger, characterizing it as beneficial for the state's economy and transportation network. The City argues that the merger will deliver: (1) improved service reliability through more direct routes and greater operational flexibility to prevent service disruptions; (2) reduced transit times by eliminating certain interchanges, allowing local businesses to reach customers faster; (3) increased investment in modern infrastructure, advanced technology, and enhanced safety systems; and (4) expanded geographic reach to open new markets for Texas products and strengthen supply chain resilience. The filing emphasizes freight rail's role as 'a cornerstone of our state's economy' and 'one of the most sustainable modes of transportation available.' The City takes no conditional stance and does not request specific operational guarantees or service commitments. No settlement signals are present; this is a straightforward endorsement requesting STB approval.
key_arguments: The merger will improve service reliability through more direct routes and greater operational flexibility, preventing service disruptions and improving schedule dependability.
Eliminating certain interchanges will reduce transit times, allowing Denison-area businesses to reach customers faster and more competitively.
The combined entity will be better positioned to invest in modern infrastructure, advanced technology, and enhanced safety systems.
The expanded geographic footprint will open new markets for Texas products and strengthen supply chain resilience.
Freight rail is a critical sustainable transportation mode that reduces highway congestion and emissions while supporting economic growth.
key_excerpts: The proposed merger offers a unique opportunity to strengthen this network and deliver tangible benefits for shippers, consumers and communities
The merged transcontinental railroad will be better positioned to invest in modern infrastructure, advanced technology and enhanced safety systems.

This merger is about more than just railroads—it's about securing the future of our transportation network, supporting economic development and ensuring American freight rail remains globally competitive.
docket_entries.relief_requested: The Denison City Council respectfully urges the Surface Transportation Board to give full and favorable consideration to this proposal.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing has minimal legal significance. It is a non-substantive expression of community support that does not advance novel legal arguments, introduce empirical evidence, or propose specific remedial conditions that would affect STB's statutory analysis under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 (public interest standard). It may carry modest weight as evidence of local economic support but will not materially influence the competitive or service-quality analysis required in the proceeding.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No response required; comment filing

docket_entries.title: PA State Representative Shelby Labs: Support for Union Pacific/Norfolk Southern Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: Pennsylvania State Representative Shelby Labs (Bucks County, 143rd District) filed a letter of support for the UP/NS merger. Labs argues that 'freight rail is a cornerstone of our state's economy' and that 'a rail system that connects the entire country will only enhance the ability of our companies to deliver their goods across the nation.' He frames the merger as beneficial for environmental sustainability ('taking large trucks off the road is not only good for the environment'), economic development, and various constituencies: 'That is good for small businesses, farmers, consumers, and workers.' No specific conditions, concerns, or detailed analysis provided. The filing appears designed to demonstrate political support from Pennsylvania state-level government rather than to advance substantive arguments about merger effects.
key_arguments: Freight rail is essential to Pennsylvania's economy and the merger will strengthen that system
Consolidated rail network will enhance companies' ability to distribute goods nationally, benefiting small businesses and farmers
Rail consolidation produces environmental and congestion benefits by reducing truck traffic on roads
key_excerpts: Freight rail is a cornerstone of our state's economy. We depend on rail to safely move goods that support our industries and connect our communities.

A rail system that connects the entire country will only enhance the ability of our companies to deliver their goods across the nation. That is good for small businesses, farmers, consumers, and workers.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Give 'full and favorable consideration' to the merger proposal
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Minimal. This is a generic support letter that does not raise new legal issues, propose specific remedies, or provide evidence relevant to the STB's statutory review criteria under 49 U.S.C. § 11324. It demonstrates state-level political support but does not affect the scope, evidentiary burden, or substantive issues in the proceeding.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment filing - no response deadline

docket_entries.title: Bill Knapke - Individual Farmer Opposition to UP/NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: Bill Knapke, a multi-generational family farmer from Ohio, opposes the merger as harmful to agricultural competition. He argues that the freight rail industry is already concentrated among a limited number of carriers, and combining Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern—'two of the nation's largest railroads'—'would push the market closer to a duopoly.' Knapke contends that farmers 'would face fewer choices, higher costs, and even tighter margins at a time when agriculture is already under strain.' He frames rail service reliability and competitive pricing as existential to farm survival: 'For farms like ours, these changes can mean the difference between a successful harvest and the closure of operations that have supported our community for decades.' Knapke requests outright denial, stating the industry cannot 'afford changes that further erode' competitive rail access. No conditions are proposed; opposition is categorical based on consolidation concerns.
key_arguments: The freight rail industry is already controlled by a limited number of carriers; a UP/NS merger would push the market 'closer to a duopoly'
Farmers would face 'fewer choices, higher costs, and even tighter margins' as a result of reduced rail competition
Rail service consolidation poses an existential threat to multi-generational farming operations: merger effects 'can mean the difference between a successful harvest and the closure of operations'
Agriculture sector cannot sustain further erosion of competitive rail access: 'we cannot afford changes that further erode' the competitive rail system
key_excerpts: The freight rail industry is already controlled by a limited number of carriers, and combining these two giants would push the market closer to a duopoly. Farmers would face fewer choices, higher costs, and even tighter margins at a time when agriculture is already under strain.
Agriculture depends on a fair and competitive rail system, and we cannot afford changes that further erode it.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Denial of the proposed merger. Knapke urges the STB to 'keep farmers and ranchers front of mind when reviewing this merger' and states that 'Agriculture depends on a fair and competitive rail system, and we cannot afford changes that further erode it.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low. This is a retail customer comment without legal or regulatory precedent. However, it represents the category of individual shipper voices that STB considers under its public interest mandate (49 U.S.C. § 11324(b)). It establishes a factual record of farmer concerns about duopolistic consolidation, which may influence Board consideration of whether the merger is consistent with the public interest. No novel legal arguments or procedural issues are raised.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Filing is a comment; no response deadline applies to the commenter. Applicants may address in reply.

docket_entries.title: Matthew Aultman (Individual Farmer) - Opposition to UP-NS Merger on Competition and Agricultural Impact Grounds
docket_entries.entry_summary: Matthew Aultman, a multi-generational farmer in Greenville, Ohio, opposes the UP-NS merger on competition grounds. Aultman argues that the freight rail industry is already dominated by 'a small number of players' and that merger approval 'would create a near duopoly, further reducing competition and leaving farmers with fewer options and higher costs at a time when margins are already razor thin.' He emphasizes that rail service disruption—whether through rate increases, reduced routing options, or execution failures—cascades through agricultural supply chains: 'These changes can be the difference between a profitable season or closing the doors on a farm that has sustained the community for generations.' Aultman's core argument is that agriculture cannot survive with further consolidation: 'We already have reduced options and reducing them even further to allow one company to control the movements of goods will be detrimental to the future of feeding this country and the world.' He does not propose specific conditions or remedies, making this an ideological opposition rooted in competitive necessity for agricultural survival rather than conditional opposition. The filing provides consumer/shipper testimony on the competitive harm thesis but lacks operational details or economic data.
key_arguments: Merger would create a 'near duopoly' in freight rail, reducing farmer options and raising input/output transportation costs when agricultural margins are already thin

Freight rail consolidation cascades through agricultural supply chains: service disruptions, rate increases, and reduced routing options directly threaten farm viability and intergenerational sustainability
Agriculture fundamentally requires a competitive rail system; further consolidation is incompatible with maintaining competitive commodity markets and feeding domestic and global populations
key_excerpts: If this merger is approved, the two companies would create a near duopoly, further reducing competition and leaving farmers with fewer options and higher costs at a time when margins are already razor thin.

When rail service falters—whether through higher rates, reduced options, or poorly executed mergers—it creates ripple effects across the entire supply chain. These changes can be the difference between a profitable season or closing the doors on a farm that has sustained the community for generations.
Agriculture needs a competitive rail system to survive, and we cannot afford changes that would weaken that system further.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Implicit request to deny merger approval. Aultman requests that the Board 'keep farmers and ranchers in mind when these companies formally file' and warns that 'Agriculture needs a competitive rail system to survive, and we cannot afford changes that would weaken that system further.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: While not legally sophisticated, this filing establishes retail customer perspective in the administrative record on competitive necessity and anti-competitive harm. It may support broader shipper coalition arguments about competitive impact and provides testimony on real-world shipper dependency. Does not raise novel legal issues but reinforces the competitive harm narrative that will likely be central to the Board's analysis under 49 U.S.C. § 11324(b) (consideration of competitive effects).
docket_entries.deadline_description: Pre-filing comment; no formal response deadline

docket_entries.title: Rachel Neal - Retail Customer Opposition to UP/NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: Rachel Neal opposes the UP/NS merger as fundamentally anticompetitive and harmful to small businesses and working families. She argues the merger will create a rail industry 'dominated by a single player,' reduce competition, lead to higher shipping costs, and cause 'trickle down' economic damage to small businesses and railroad workers. She expresses concern that communities like hers will face reduced service options and additional economic hardship for 'working families.' The filing provides no specific conditions or remedies, opposing the merger outright on ideological grounds regarding market concentration and community impact.
key_arguments: The merger will create a rail industry dominated by a single dominant player, eliminating meaningful competition
Higher shipping costs will result from reduced competitive options, causing 'trickle down' effects to small businesses
Working families and rural communities will experience additional economic hardship from the transaction
The STB should reject mergers that concentrate market power without guardrails for competition and shipping cost protection
key_excerpts: Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern—two of the largest rail—do it without any guardrails this merger risks creating severe competition problems, and harm to small business and the additional burden on working families.
for communities like ours with small business and additional train on working families
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the merger. The filing opposes creation of a rail industry dominated by two mega-players without specific conditions or remedies.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low. This is a form letter / template-style opposition from a non-expert retail customer with no specific legal or evidentiary claims that would alter STB's statutory review framework under 49 U.S.C. § 11324. It does not identify specific markets, shipping lanes, service degradation, or measurable competitive harms requiring Board response.

docket_entries.title: Kent Davis - Individual Shipper Comment Opposing UP/NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: Kent Davis filed a comment opposing the UP/NS merger as an individual business operator with family-run operations that depend on rail service. The filing is severely corrupted with OCR errors and formatting failures that render most of the substantive content illegible. Discernible fragments suggest concerns about rail service reliability and competitive effects from consolidation, but specific arguments, quantified harms, and relief requested cannot be reliably extracted. The filing provides no usable information for merger arbitrage analysis.
key_arguments: Appears to argue that merger will harm rail service reliability and competitive options, but specific arguments cannot be extracted due to filing corruption
key_excerpts: Filing is substantially illegible; no reliable quotable excerpts can be extracted. The document contains pervasive OCR errors and formatting corruption that prevents confident citation of specific passages.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Filing is substantially illegible; relief cannot be determined with certainty
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: None discernible. The filing's corruption prevents assessment of whether it raises novel legal issues, evidentiary questions, or regulatory concerns.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No deadline applicable; individual comment during public comment period

docket_entries.title: Unreadable Filing - Document Quality Issue
docket_entries.entry_summary: This filing by Penny Treon (individual) was entered into the docket on November 13, 2025, but the document content consists entirely of corrupted text, random characters, and garbled formatting that prevents meaningful review. The filing header indicates it was received by the Office of Chief Counsel and made part of the public record, but the substantive comments/arguments are completely illegible. No position on the merger, specific arguments, or relief request can be discerned from the available text.
key_arguments: UNABLE TO EXTRACT - Document unreadable
key_excerpts: UNABLE TO EXTRACT - Document unreadable due to OCR/formatting failure
docket_entries.relief_requested: UNABLE TO DETERMINE - Filing content is illegible
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: If this represents an intended substantial intervention or comment, the illegibility creates a procedural issue regarding whether a valid filing was actually made. The STB record may need clarification on whether this constitutes an effective filing under the docket rules.
docket_entries.deadline_description: N/A - Filing content illegible

docket_entries.title: Individual St. Louis Resident Comment Opposing Merger Without Specific Conditions
docket_entries.entry_summary: Maryann Manion, a St. Louis resident, opposes the UP-NS merger based on general concerns that freight rail consolidation reduces competition and causes consumer price increases. She states: 'Often, mergers result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and history shows these expenses don't stop at the rail yard. Instead, they trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.' However, she does not specify quantifiable competitive harms, alternative scenarios, or detailed conditions that would satisfy her concerns. She requests only that the STB 'ensure the tenets of the merger and conditions imposed on the transaction meet the standards for enhancing competition and safety'—language that is general rather than actionable. Her opposition appears rooted in principle (consolidation is bad for consumers) rather than analysis specific to this transaction. She explicitly copied the Governor of Missouri and Members of Congress, indicating a broader advocacy strategy.
key_arguments: Freight rail consolidation reduces competition in rail markets, driving up input costs for retailers and shippers
Cost increases imposed by consolidated railroads are passed through to consumers in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods
A competitive freight rail system is essential to Missouri's economy, job creation, and consumer access to affordable goods
The merger poses risk to consumers without 'appropriate protections for competition'
key_excerpts: Often, mergers result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and history shows these expenses don't stop at the rail yard. Instead, they trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.
If approved without appropriate protections for competition, such a merger would be risky.
docket_entries.relief_requested: If the merger is approved, the Surface Transportation Board must ensure 'the tenets of the merger and conditions imposed on the transaction meet the standards for enhancing competition and safety.' Manion does not specify what those conditions should be.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low. This is a citizen comment expressing concern about consumer price impacts from consolidation. It does not raise novel legal theories, challenge STB jurisdiction, propose specific structural or behavioral remedies, or cite statutory provisions. It reflects the retail-customer perspective on consolidation (prices will rise) but provides no evidentiary foundation or specific conditions the Board could enforce. It illustrates the public concern base around this merger but does not advance the technical or legal analysis of competitive effects.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Pre-filing comment, no response deadline applicable

docket_entries.title: Josh Johnson (Missouri Farmer) - Opposition to UP-NS Merger on Grounds of Reduced Competition and Higher Freight Rates
docket_entries.entry_summary: Josh Johnson, a Missouri row crop farmer, opposes the UP-NS merger on the grounds that it will further reduce rail competition and lead to higher freight rates for agricultural producers. He argues that 'The rail industry has already seen major consolidation over the years, and if this deal goes forward, it would shrink competition even more-leaving Missouri farmers with limited options and likely higher freight rates.' Johnson contends that increased transportation costs directly harm independent farmers and rural economies: 'When transportation becomes more expensive or unreliable, the impact on agriculture is immediate and significant. These kinds of changes don't just affect big companies; they put pressure on independent farmers, strain rural economies, and can lead to long-term damage for communities that rely on farming.' He does not propose conditions that would make the merger acceptable, instead asking the STB to consider farmers' need for 'a strong, competitive rail network to stay viable' and warning that 'Fewer carriers mean fewer choices and higher costs.' This is a straightforward opposition grounded in general competitive concerns rather than deal-specific remedies.
key_arguments: The rail industry has already consolidated significantly; this merger will shrink competition further, leaving farmers with fewer options.
Higher transportation costs resulting from reduced competition directly harm independent farmers' viability and strain rural economies dependent on agriculture.
Farmers require access to a competitive rail network to remain viable; consolidation to fewer carriers increases costs that farmers 'cannot afford to carry.'
Rail consolidation has cascading effects on rural communities beyond individual farm operations, creating long-term economic damage.
key_excerpts: The rail industry has already seen major consolidation over the years, and if this deal goes forward, it would shrink competition even more-leaving Missouri farmers with limited options and likely higher freight rates.

When transportation becomes more expensive or unreliable, the impact on agriculture is immediate and significant. These kinds of changes don't just affect big companies; they put pressure on independent farmers, strain rural economies, and can lead to long-term damage for communities that rely on farming.
Farmers need access to a strong, competitive rail network to stay viable. Fewer carriers mean fewer choices and higher costs-and that's not a burden we can afford to carry.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Implicit denial request: 'I respectfully ask that you weigh the needs of farmers as you review this proposed merger.' No specific conditions offered that would make the merger acceptable.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low legal significance. This filing does not raise novel legal theories or evidentiary issues under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 standards. However, it provides evidentiary support for the general competitive harm argument—that end-users across multiple sectors (agricultural producers) will face higher costs due to reduced rail competition. It may be cited collectively with other shipper opposition to demonstrate consumer impact, but does not independently change the scope or burden of review.
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is a public comment filing; no formal response deadline applies to the filer, though parties may file responsive comments.

docket_entries.title: Donna Skipper - Individual Opposition on Historical and Competitive Grounds
docket_entries.entry_summary: Donna Skipper, a Republican Women activist and relative of a retired railroad conductor, opposes the UP-NS merger on fundamental grounds: that it represents a return to 'railroad baron' monopoly power that originally prompted America's antitrust laws. She argues the STB proceeding is predetermined theater: 'the STB will go through the motions of analyzing how the creation of the most powerful railroad monopoly in the country will increase competition and lower prices for shippers... [they will produce] a lengthy document that justifies what has already been decided.' She frames the merger as the creation of unchecked economic power over 'the nation's economic arteries' and uses the historical 1869 Golden Spike ceremony as a metaphor for celebratory acknowledgment of what will actually represent 'the losing of competition.' She concludes: 'Only at two would be celebration—it will be a warning that the balance of power has shifted decisively away from the many. And as it is done and all the dignitaries have left the stage, they will have to step up alone to try and secure the promise of better service and lower prices from a railroad with darker power unlike any other in the country.'
key_arguments: The merger recreates the 'railroad baron' monopoly power that originally prompted the creation of America's antitrust laws over a century ago: 'unchecked railroad power once spurred the very creation of America's antitrust laws. Those laws were intended to protect farmers, shippers, and consumers from the whims of railroad barons who dictated prices and routes.'

The STB proceeding is predetermined and lacks genuine independent analysis: 'for the next year and a half, the STB will go through the motions of analyzing how the creation of the most powerful railroad monopoly in the country will increase competition and lower prices for shippers. They will hold hundreds of hours of public hearings, review tens of thousands of pages of filings from affected parties, spend substantial sums on economic consultants, and produce a lengthy document that justifies what has already been decided.'

The merger represents an irreversible loss of competition: 'Unlike the 1869 Golden Spike ceremony and the telegraph message of 'Done,' this time the message our nation's system will hear loud and clear is 'You are Removed.' Only at two would be celebration—it will be a warning that the balance of power has shifted decisively away from the many.'

The merger will result in worse service and higher prices for shippers and consumers: 'they will have to step up alone to try and secure the promise of better service and lower prices from a railroad with darker power unlike any other in the country.'
key_excerpts: 'unchecked railroad power once spurred the very creation of America's antitrust laws. Those laws were intended to protect farmers, shippers, and consumers from the whims of railroad barons who dictated prices and routes.'

'the STB will go through the motions of analyzing how the creation of the most powerful railroad monopoly in the country will increase competition and lower prices for shippers... [they will produce] a lengthy document that justifies what has already been decided.'

'this time the message our nation's system will hear loud and clear is 'You are Removed.' Only at two would be celebration—it will be a warning that the balance of power has shifted decisively away from the many.'
docket_entries.relief_requested: Implicit denial of the merger; no conditional remedies or settlement path offered.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low direct legal significance. The filing does not present novel legal arguments or identify specific regulatory deficiencies in the STB's analysis framework. However, it may have political significance as evidence of organized grassroots opposition sentiment. The filer's affiliation with Republican Women of East Alabama suggests the opposition is not purely partisan and may reflect broader conservative/populist concern about monopoly power, potentially complicating any purely pro-business political narrative around the merger.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment filing; no response deadline for applicants

docket_entries.title: Mike and Rachel Fearon (Grave-Fearon Insurance, Courageous Creations) - Opposition to UP/NS Merger as Near-Duopoly Threat to Small Business
docket_entries.entry_summary: Mike and Rachel Fearon, owners of Grave-Fearon Insurance and Courageous Creations (retail/farm operations in Ohio), oppose the UP/NS merger as creating a 'near duopoly' that would eliminate competitive pressure. They argue: 'Competition drives long-term viability and lower costs. The success of businesses, employees and customers across Ohio depend on a strong rail system.' They contend that 'poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain' and that 'it's the mom-and-pop stores and farms who are impacted the most.' The Fearons seek outright denial, stating: 'When Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern officially file, I hope that the Surface Transportation Board considers the impact on local businesses and ensures the tenets of the merger meet the standards for enhancing competition and safety.' No conditions are proposed that would satisfy their concerns; this is principled opposition to consolidation itself on grounds that small businesses cannot survive in a two-player market.
key_arguments: The proposed merger would create a 'near duopoly' that is 'detrimental to competition' - reducing viable competitive options for small shippers.
Rail mergers historically 'slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain,' with disproportionate harm to small businesses ('mom-and-pop stores and farms').
Small businesses depend on 'reliable rail service to ship the supplies we need to operate' and 'consistent transport of our crops' - merger threatens supply chain viability.
Competition is necessary for 'long-term viability and lower costs' - consolidation removes this competitive pressure on pricing and service.
The merger does not meet statutory standards for 'enhancing competition and safety.'
key_excerpts: This proposed merger between Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would form a near duopoly and be detrimental to competition.

Poorly executed rail mergers slow service and cause congestion, disrupting the supply chain and our ability to get products to customers - and it's the mom-and-pop stores and farms who are impacted the most.
Competition drives long-term viability and lower costs. The success of businesses, employees and customers across Ohio depend on a strong rail system.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the merger. Applicants' merger proposal does not meet statutory standards for enhancing competition and safety.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing evidences small-shipper and agricultural customer opposition to the merger under the statutory 'public interest' standard (49 U.S.C. § 11324). While individual consumer/small business filings do not create independent legal burden, they contribute to the evidentiary record on competitive impact and may be cited by STB staff or intervenor groups (e.g., National Industrial Transportation League, agricultural associations) to support broader arguments about shipper harm. The filing also demonstrates that the merger creates concerns beyond the institutional shipper base, potentially supporting arguments that remedial conditions are inadequate to protect small-business users.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period submission; no response deadline for applicants, though filing will be part of public record for STB deliberation.

docket_entries.title: Kevin Selhorst (North Star Hardware & Implement) - Opposition to UP/NS Merger Based on Competition Concerns
docket_entries.entry_summary: Kevin Selhorst, owner of North Star Hardware & Implement in Northeastern Ohio, opposes the UP/NS merger on general competitive and economic grounds. He argues the merger would create a "duopoly" by consolidating two of the nation's largest railroads, weakening rail competition and ultimately harming small businesses and consumers. Selhorst frames his opposition in terms of market fragility: "When rail competition weakens, service suffers. Shipping costs rise, options shrink, and delays increase." He emphasizes downstream consumer impacts—"Those burdens don't just hit businesses-they ripple through the supply chain until families feel them directly in form of higher prices for groceries, household goods, and other essentials." However, the filing provides no specific quantification of harms to his business, no detailed analysis of competitive alternatives available to him, and no conditional remedies that would satisfy his concerns. The opposition is framed as ideological support for competition preservation rather than transaction-specific impact analysis.
key_arguments: Consolidating two of the nation's largest railroads into one entity would create a duopoly and push the freight rail industry closer to monopolistic control, reducing competitive options for shippers
When rail competition weakens, service deteriorates, shipping costs rise, options shrink, and delays increase—harms that ultimately flow through supply chains to consumers in higher prices
Small business owners depend on competitive, affordable rail shipping across multiple sectors; this merger eliminates options and increases risk to their operations and to local economies
key_excerpts: Consolidating two companies of this size would create an even tighter grip on the market, pushing the freight rail industry closer to a duopoly.

When rail competition weakens, service suffers. Shipping costs rise, options shrink, and delays increase. Those burdens don't just hit businesses-they ripple through the supply chain until families feel them directly in form of higher prices for groceries, household goods, and other essentials.
Rail is more than a logistical system—it is the backbone of local economies and we cannot afford changes that weaken competition or compromise safety.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the proposed merger between Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern; consider impact on small businesses and local economies, not just large corporations.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Limited significance. Filing articulates general policy objections to consolidation but does not raise novel legal issues, challenge evidentiary burdens, or identify procedural defects. Does not engage with 49 U.S.C. § 11324 merger standards or propose fact disputes requiring hearing. Reflects category of small shipper opposition but lacks the specificity and market data that would create significant discovery or hearing requirements.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing; no specific response deadline for applicants

docket_entries.title: Joyce Long - Individual Citizen Comment Opposing UP/NS Merger on Competition and Consumer Cost Grounds
docket_entries.entry_summary: Joyce Long, a retired manufacturing executive from Greenville, Ohio, opposes the UP/NS merger on grounds that it will reduce competition and harm consumers. She argues: 'Through the years, I saw what happens when competition in the rail industry is diminished. Reduced competition usually means slower service, higher shipping costs and fewer options for businesses. Those costs never stop at the factory gate-they trickle down, raising prices for everyday families in the form of more expensive groceries and essentials.' She contends the merger 'risks concentrating too much power in too few hands, leaving communities like Greenville with fewer choices, higher costs and unnecessary strain on working families and small businesses alike.' Her opposition is fundamentally ideological—based on general principles that excessive rail consolidation harms competition and consumer welfare—rather than conditional on specific remedial measures. She does not propose conditions that would satisfy her concerns, only urges the Board to 'protect competition and ensure safe, reliable rail service.'
key_arguments: Reduced competition in rail industry leads directly to slower service, higher shipping costs, and fewer options for businesses

Freight cost increases flow through to consumers: 'Those costs never stop at the factory gate-they trickle down, raising prices for everyday families in the form of more expensive groceries and essentials'
Merger of two largest railroads in the country concentrates excessive power, eliminating local economic resilience in rail-dependent communities like Greenville, Ohio
Without meaningful safeguards, merger will leave working families and small businesses with 'fewer choices, higher costs and unnecessary strain'
key_excerpts: Reduced competition usually means slower service, higher shipping costs and fewer options for businesses. Those costs never stop at the factory gate—they trickle down, raising prices for everyday families in the form of more expensive groceries and essentials.

Without meaningful safeguards, this merger risks concentrating too much power in too few hands, leaving communities like Greenville with fewer choices, higher costs and unnecessary strain on working families and small businesses alike.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Urges the Surface Transportation Board to 'take the long view' in protecting competition and ensuring safe, reliable rail service; implicit request to deny merger absent meaningful safeguards against competitive concentration.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low direct legal/regulatory significance. Filing does not engage with substantive merger analysis under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 or raise novel evidentiary issues. However, may be cited by opposing intervenors or the STB itself as evidence of consumer concern about competition and retail price pass-through—relevant to the Board's public interest analysis under the statute. Adds qualitative support to shipper and competitor arguments about competitive harm but provides no independent factual foundation.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing; no response deadline for individual citizen comments

docket_entries.title: Frank Granberry (Orange Farms) - Retail Customer Opposition to UP/NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: Frank Granberry, an Alabama farmer operating Orange Farms, opposes the UP/NS merger on grounds that agriculture operates on tight margins and cannot afford higher rail costs or reduced transportation options. He frames the merger as the latest in a series of industry consolidations that harm farmers: 'Higher rates, fewer options, or poorly planned mergers' all create supply-chain shockwaves that 'make the difference between a good year and shutting the gates on a farm.' He characterizes agriculture as 'already so concentrated' and argues the merger would 'leave even fewer options for shippers like us.' However, Granberry does not propose specific remedial conditions, does not quantify anticipated rate increases or service losses, and does not engage with the legal standard for merger review (competitive effects analysis). His opposition is framed as a plea to 'keep farmers and ranchers in mind' based on general principle that agriculture needs 'a fair competitive rail system,' not as a detailed competitive or economic argument.
key_arguments: The merger will further reduce transportation options for agricultural shippers in an already-concentrated industry, leaving farmers with fewer alternatives to Union Pacific's prices and service terms
Agricultural businesses operate on tight margins and cannot absorb higher rail costs or tolerate service degradation caused by merger-related disruptions

Consolidation of the two largest rail companies will create supply-chain shockwaves that cascade through farming operations, threatening the viability of long-established agricultural businesses and rural communities
key_excerpts: Agriculture already operates on tight margins - we simply can't afford higher costs or less competition in an industry that's already so concentrated.

For folks like us, up against all the challenges we face, whether it's higher rates, fewer options, or poorly-planned mergers - it's never just our problem. It sends shockwaves through the entire supply chain. For families like mine, it's the difference between a good year and shutting the gates on a farm that's been [operating] for decades.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Implicit denial of the merger to preserve competitive rail options for agricultural shippers
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low. This is a lay comment from a retail customer with no legal or economic analysis. It does not raise novel competitive issues, does not propose specific remedies, and does not engage with the statutory merger review framework under 49 U.S.C. § 11324. However, it may be cited by STB or by opposing parties as evidence of real-world competitive concerns among agricultural shippers and the human/community impact of rail consolidation. STB may acknowledge receipt in the public record but is unlikely to treat this as a material evidentiary submission requiring specific response.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period submission; no reciprocal deadline for applicants to respond to individual comments

docket_entries.title: Celeste Kososki - Individual Commercial Real Estate Professional Opposes Merger Without Conditions
docket_entries.entry_summary: Celeste Kososki, a commercial real estate professional with 35+ years of experience including 17 years managing industrial real estate for SUPERVALU, opposes the UP-NS merger without enforceable safeguards. She argues that 'Rail is not just a transportation option—it is a lifeline for the consumer products supply chain' and warns that consolidation historically 'reduces competition, increases costs, and degrades service.' Kososki emphasizes the downstream impact on retailers and consumers: 'When rail service falters or shipping costs climb due to reduced competition, the impact is swift and widespread. All retailers see their costs rise, and consumers—especially those in lower-income communities—bear the burden through higher prices at the checkout counter.' She frames the merger as a threat to local economies, job creation, and consumer access to affordable goods. However, she does not categorically demand denial—rather, she conditions approval on 'enforceable conditions that prevent monopolistic practices, protect access for shippers, and maintain the safety and reliability of our rail infrastructure.' This signals conditional opposition: she recognizes potential efficiencies but requires specific safeguards.
key_arguments: Rail consolidation from 2 major competitors to 1 integrated entity will reduce competition, increase shipping costs, and ultimately raise consumer prices through the retail supply chain
Lower-income communities will suffer disproportionately from higher consumer prices resulting from increased rail shipping costs
Historical precedent shows railroad consolidation reduces competition and service quality without offsetting consumer benefits
Retail distribution centers and municipal economic development depend on reliable, affordable freight rail access—merger threatens supply chain efficiency
Merger threatens thousands of jobs and local business viability that depend on competitive rail service
key_excerpts: Rail is not just a transportation option—it is a lifeline for the consumer products supply chain. It ensures that products move efficiently from farms and manufacturers to distribution centers and ultimately to store shelves.

When rail service falters or shipping costs climb due to reduced competition, the impact is swift and widespread. All retailers see their costs rise, and consumers—especially those in lower-income communities—bear the burden through higher prices at the checkout counter.
While there may be efficiencies to gain from combining operations, history has shown that consolidation often reduces competition, increases costs, and degrades service.
Any approval must come with enforceable conditions that prevent monopolistic practices, protect access for shippers, and maintain the safety and reliability of our rail infrastructure.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Urges the Board to 'prioritize competition, service quality, and consumer protection. Any approval must come with enforceable conditions that prevent monopolistic practices, protect access for shippers, and maintain the safety and reliability of our rail infrastructure.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low direct legal significance as individual commenter rather than formally intervening party. However, filing expands the record on consumer protection impacts and downstream retail supply chain effects, creating narrative support for conditions protecting shipper access. Establishes lower-income consumer advocacy dimension in the public record.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing; no specific deadline for response

docket_entries.title: Gabe Freeman - Louisiana Resident Comment on UP-NS Merger Consumer Impact
docket_entries.entry_summary: Gabe Freeman, a 20-year Bossier, Louisiana resident, opposes the UP-NS merger without specific protections for competition and consumer welfare. He argues: 'freight rail plays a significant role in Louisiana's economy—keeping store shelves stocked, creating jobs and helping families get what they need at a fair price' and warns that 'mergers result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs' which 'trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.' He specifically highlights Louisiana's agricultural dependence: 'In Bossier, produce and beef are king and many of the farmers throughout the great state of Louisiana rely on the railroad for distribution.' He requests conditional approval: 'please keep the interests of everyday Louisiana residents in mind' and 'ensure the tenets of the merger and conditions imposed on the transaction meet the standards for enhancing competition and safety.' This is a consumer-focused intervention emphasizing retail price impacts and agricultural commodity distribution rather than rail-to-rail competition dynamics.
key_arguments: Rail industry consolidation historically reduces competition, which increases freight costs that are passed through to consumers as higher grocery and everyday goods prices
Louisiana's economy is particularly vulnerable due to reliance on rail for agricultural commodity distribution (produce and beef), making price increases directly impact family affordability
Merger creates risk of service degradation and higher costs to farmers and retailers unless specific competitive protections are imposed
Competitive freight rail system is critical not just for business efficiency but for ensuring families and communities have access to affordable food
key_excerpts: Often, mergers result in reduced competition in freight rail that drives higher costs, and history shows these expenses don't stop at the rail yard. Instead, they trickle down to hardworking families in the form of higher prices on groceries and everyday goods.
In Bossier, produce and beef are king and many of the farmers throughout the great state of Louisiana rely on the railroad for distribution.
A competitive freight rail system is critical not just for businesses, but for the families and communities that depend on it.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Approval only if 'the tenets of the merger and conditions imposed on the transaction meet the standards for enhancing competition and safety.' Specifically requests STB ensure: (1) competition protections prevent rail industry consolidation from raising consumer costs, (2) service quality maintained, (3) effects on Louisiana farmers and produce/beef distribution chains mitigated.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low legal significance. Does not raise novel statutory interpretation issues or change scope of STB review. However, represents public constituency input on consumer welfare effects—a factor STB must consider under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 (public interest standard). May be cited by STB or intervenors as evidence that consumer/retail constituencies have concerns about merger effects on input costs and pricing. Does not affect evidentiary burdens or discovery scope.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment filing - no response deadline

docket_entries.title: Ben Terrill Comment: Small Business Impact of UP-NS Merger - Opposition Based on Competition and Cost Concerns
docket_entries.entry_summary: Ben Terrill, identifying himself as an entrepreneur and small business advocate, opposes the UP-NS merger on the grounds that railroad consolidation threatens competition, increases shipping costs, and harms small business owners and families. He argues: 'When shipping costs go up, the price of raw materials, products, and everyday essentials go up with them. For entrepreneurs trying to get a business off the ground, or families stretching every dollar, these increases can mean the difference between moving forward or falling behind.' Terrill frames the issue not as a technical transportation matter but as a threat to 'the American Dream' and 'community resilience.' He urges the STB to 'stand with the small business owners, future entrepreneurs, and hardworking Americans who rely on a competitive and accessible freight rail system.' His opposition is ideological rather than conditional—he does not specify remedial conditions that would make the merger acceptable, but rather articulates a general principle that consolidation in transportation threatens economic opportunity.
key_arguments: Unchecked consolidation in freight rail results in reduced competition, higher costs, and degraded service that threaten small business viability and family economic security
Merger-driven increases in shipping costs cascade through supply chains, raising prices for raw materials, products, and everyday essentials sold by small business owners operating on thin margins
Consolidation undermines 'community resilience' and the ability of entrepreneurs and families to pursue economic opportunity
key_excerpts: While collaboration in business can lead to innovation, unchecked consolidation in any industry often results in reduced competition, higher costs, and degraded service. This doesn't just hurt big corporations; it threatens the livelihoods of small business owners and everyday families who already operate on thin margins.

When shipping costs go up, the price of raw materials, products, and everyday essentials go up with them. For entrepreneurs trying to get a business off the ground, or families stretching every dollar, these increases can mean the difference between moving forward or falling behind.
Please stand with the small business owners, future entrepreneurs, and hardworking Americans who rely on a competitive and accessible freight rail system. The American Dream depends on it.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Ensure the merger 'does not come at the expense of fair competition, economic opportunity, or community resilience'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: No legal or regulatory significance. The filing does not raise novel legal issues, cite case law, invoke statutory provisions, or propose specific remedies within the STB's authority. It is a values-based, ideological statement about consolidation. It does not require or invite a substantive response on competitive grounds because it does not make falsifiable factual claims about market impact.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing; no response deadline applies

docket_entries.title: Lisa Chambers - Missouri Business Community Opposition to UP-NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: Lisa Chambers, representing Missouri businesses in manufacturing and industrial sectors, opposes the merger based on competitive and service concerns. She argues: 'Businesses across Missouri depend on reliable, efficient, and competitively priced rail service' and warns that 'A consolidation of this scale could lead to service disruptions, increased congestion, diminished reliability, and higher costs for rail users.' She frames the issue as a regional economic development concern: 'The strength of Missouri's economy, and that of the broader region, is closely tied to a robust freight transportation network.' She urges the STB to 'thoroughly assess the implications on competition, service quality, and operational efficiency, especially in states with significant manufacturing and freight-dependent industries like Missouri.' The opposition implicitly suggests that if the merger proceeds, conditions maintaining competitive pricing, service standards, and operational efficiency would be necessary.
key_arguments: Consolidation of two largest US railroads will reduce competitive options for shippers, leading to reduced bargaining power and higher costs for Missouri manufacturers and industrial businesses
The merger poses direct risks of 'service disruptions, increased congestion, diminished reliability' that would harm supply chain reliability for manufacturing operations
Missouri's economy is dependent on robust freight transportation competition; merger threatens regional economic development in a major manufacturing state
Fair pricing and high service standards require maintaining competitive freight rail environment; merger threatens these conditions
key_excerpts: Businesses across Missouri, particularly in the manufacturing and industrial sectors, depend on reliable, efficient, and competitively priced rail service to sustain operations and meet growing supply chain demands.

A consolidation of this scale could lead to service disruptions, increased congestion, diminished reliability, and higher costs for rail users. These effects would ripple throughout the business community and the local economies these businesses support.
Maintaining a competitive freight rail environment is essential to ensuring fair pricing, high service standards, and continued economic development.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the merger OR, if approved, maintain competitive freight rail environment with fair pricing, high service standards, and continued economic development safeguards
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing represents direct business community opposition on competitive and service grounds, relevant to the STB's analysis under 49 U.S.C. § 11324(c) regarding effects on competition and service. While not a formal party filing, it demonstrates organized shipper/business opposition in a strategically important manufacturing region. The geographic specificity (Missouri, broader region) and sector specificity (manufacturing, industrial) may be material to demonstrating regional competitive harm if corroborated by more detailed submissions or testimony. The filing's reference to ripple effects through local economies invokes broader regional economic impact arguments that may be relevant to the public interest analysis.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing; no specific response deadline for applicants, but may generate follow-up filings from other Missouri stakeholders

docket_entries.title: Rob Salvino (Commercial Packaging Executive) - Opposition to UP-NS Merger Based on Competition and Service Reliability Concerns
docket_entries.entry_summary: Rob Salvino, a 25-year veteran of commercial packaging and freight distribution, opposes the merger on grounds that consolidation reduces shipper choices and competitive discipline. He argues: 'Fewer rail operators often means fewer choices for shippers, which leads to increased transportation costs. And when those costs rise, the burden falls not just on businesses, but on consumers. The prices of everyday items usually spike.'
