docket_entries.title: STB Response to Nebraska Congressional Delegation Letter on UP/NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: The STB Board chairs (Chairman Patrick J. Fuchs, Vice Chairman Michelle A. Schultz, Member Karen J. Hedlund) responded to a December 2025 letter from Nebraska's congressional delegation (Senators Fischer and Ricketts and Representatives Smith, Bacon, and Flood) regarding the UP/NS merger. The delegation had expressed the view that the merger 'would promote competition and benefit the public.' The STB acknowledged their input but stated: 'The Board will conduct a rigorous and comprehensive review of the transaction as required by law.' The Board confirmed it will evaluate the transaction against statutory criteria including 'effective competition, carrier safety and efficiency, adequate service for shippers, environmental safeguards, and fair working conditions for employees,' and will 'ensure that any approved transaction would promote a competitive, efficient, and reliable national rail system' per 49 C.F.R. § 1180.1(b). The Board noted that on December 19, 2025, UP and NS filed their application, and the Board would determine completeness within 30 days. Public comments on completeness were due December 29, 2025, with applicant replies due January 2, 2026 at noon EST. The Board stated: 'Because this is a pending matter, we cannot comment further; however, please be assured that, should an application be filed, the Board will conduct a thorough and fair review of the evidence and argument and consider whether the transaction serves the public interest.'
key_arguments: The Board will apply a comprehensive statutory framework evaluating effective competition, carrier safety and efficiency, adequate service for shippers, environmental safeguards, and fair working conditions for employees
The Board must ensure any approved transaction promotes a competitive, efficient, and reliable national rail system
The Board will conduct a thorough and fair review and consider whether the transaction serves the public interest consistent with applicable law
key_excerpts: The Board will conduct a rigorous and comprehensive review of the transaction as required by law.
The Board must ensure that any approved transaction would promote a competitive, efficient, and reliable national rail system.
The Board will conduct a thorough and fair review of the evidence and argument and consider whether the transaction serves the public interest, consistent with applicable law.
docket_entries.relief_requested: No relief requested. Board states it will conduct required statutory review.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing confirms the STB's statutory review framework under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 and 49 C.F.R. part 1180. It establishes the procedural timeline: completeness determination within 30 days of December 19, 2025 application; completeness comments due December 29, 2025; applicant reply due January 2, 2026. The letter signals that the Board will not prejudge the transaction and will apply the full statutory criteria. It has minimal evidentiary significance but confirms the Board's multi-factor review standard that intervenors and applicants should address.
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is an outbound communication from the Board; no response required from merger parties or intervenors.

docket_entries.title: Senator Blumenthal Letter Opposing UP/NS Merger on Consumer Prices, Jobs, and Safety Grounds
docket_entries.entry_summary: Senator Blumenthal opposes the UP/NS merger on four grounds: (1) Consumer Price Impacts: 'When competition in rail transportation is reduced, higher shipping costs are often passed directly on to consumers in the form of higher prices at the checkout counter.' He argues that 'a merged UP/NS would control a transcontinental rail line, which they could then use to preferentially price their services to direct shippers,' jeopardizing intermodal partnerships and driving up costs for everyday goods including food, fuel, and household products; (2) Employment Consequences: Despite company promises, 'precedent shows us such promises are little more than hollow words,' citing the 1996 UP/Southern Pacific merger where 'thousands of employees were laid off or relocated despite assurances to protect workers'; (3) Shipper Competition: 'Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern largely serve different markets, and as a result, shippers are able to negotiate with each of them and their competitors for better prices.' A merger would eliminate this negotiating leverage; (4) Safety and Community Harms: The letter specifically references East Palestine derailment impacts, blocked highway-rail grade crossings causing emergency vehicle delays, and children forced to crawl under trains to reach school, arguing that 'cost-cutting efforts implemented by railroads only exacerbate these issues.' The filing frames opposition as protecting American families 'already struggling with the rising cost of groceries, household goods, and other essentials' from further inflation.
key_arguments: Merger will eliminate competitive options for shippers currently able to negotiate with both UP and NS separately on different market segments: 'Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern largely serve different markets, and as a result, shippers are able to negotiate with each of them and their competitors for better prices for various portions of their trip. Under the proposed merger, however, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would control a transcontinental rail line, which they could then use to preferentially price their services to direct shippers.'

Higher shipping costs will be passed directly to consumers in the form of higher prices: 'When competition in rail transportation is reduced, higher shipping costs are often passed directly on to consumers in the form of higher prices at the checkout counter.'

Company promises to protect union jobs are unreliable, citing historical precedent: 'While the companies have said they will protect all union jobs during a merger, precedent shows us such promises are little more than hollow words. For example, after Union Pacific and Southern Pacific merged in 1996, thousands of employees were laid off or relocated despite assurances to protect workers before the merger went through.'

Merger will jeopardize intermodal partnerships currently benefiting shippers and underserved areas: 'Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern currently have various intermodal partnerships with each other and their competitors to improve access to shipping containers and underserved areas around the country. The proposed merger between Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would jeopardize these partnerships.'

Merger will exacerbate safety and community harms including blocked highway-rail grade crossings, emergency service delays, and hazardous materials risks: 'In recent years, ambulances and emergency service vehicles have been delayed for extended periods of time as long trains roll through highway-rail grade crossings in towns. Similarly, to get to and from school, kids have been forced to climb under trains stopped at such crossings.'
key_excerpts: A merger between Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern – two of the four largest railroads in the United States – would further consolidate the nation's rail network, resulting in potential job insecurity for workers, higher costs and less competition for shippers, and safety and community harms.
When competition in rail transportation is reduced, higher shipping costs are often passed directly on to consumers in the form of higher prices at the checkout counter.

While the companies have said they will protect all union jobs during a merger, precedent shows us such promises are little more than hollow words. For example, after Union Pacific and Southern Pacific merged in 1996, thousands of employees were laid off or relocated despite assurances to protect workers before the merger went through.
Under the proposed merger, however, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern would control a transcontinental rail line, which they could then use to preferentially price their services to direct shippers.

In recent years, ambulances and emergency service vehicles have been delayed for extended periods of time as long trains roll through highway-rail grade crossings in towns. Similarly, to get to and from school, kids have been forced to climb under trains stopped at such crossings.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Oppose the proposed merger between Union Pacific Railroad and Norfolk Southern Railway
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing from a sitting U.S. Senator creates significant political pressure on the STB merger approval process. By directly addressing both the STB and DOJ Antitrust Division, Blumenthal is framing the merger as implicating consumer protection (FTC/DOJ domain) and safety/public interest (STB domain). The letter invokes the 1996 UP/SP merger as precedent for unreliability of employment protections, which may require the applicants to respond with more detailed labor commitments or independent monitoring provisions. The safety arguments (East Palestine references, blocked crossings) may expand the scope of the required Safety Integration Plan and force detailed examination of cost-cutting impacts on safety protocols post-merger. This is not a conditional opposition—no path to approval is offered—making it a high-priority response document for merger applicants.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Letter filed December 23, 2025; no specific STB deadline noted but as a Comment phase filing, subject to applicable comment period rules

docket_entries.title: American Rail Center Notice of Intent to Participate – Conditional Opposition Based on Gateway Foreclosure and Terminal Displacement Risk
docket_entries.entry_summary: American Rail Center (ARC) files a Notice of Intent to Participate opposing the UP–NS merger as a threat to independent terminal service providers and competitive routing. ARC argues the transaction creates 'systemic origin monopolies and routing control' by consolidating UP's dominant access to Western commodity origins (soda ash, plastics) with NS's control of Eastern destinations, enabling vertical foreclosure that would displace CSX-routed and independent facilities. ARC provides empirical foundation through its own post-Conrail experience: when Conrail was split between CSX and NS in 1999, ARC's volume collapsed from 'more than 10,000 carloads per year to fewer than 1,000' due to fragmentation of its service geography and loss of linehaul access, despite physical rail service remaining available. ARC characterizes this as foreclosure 'not due to inefficiency, but by regulatory redesign.' ARC explicitly states it does not oppose the deal outright but will support approval only if UP–NS accepts five specific conditions: (1) open gateway provisions maintaining all current UP–CSX and NS–CSX interchange points; (2) dual-service options at major markets for bulk commodities; (3) enforcement against diversion to proprietary terminals when neutral alternatives exist; (4) rate and service transparency monitoring; and (5) 7-year Board oversight period. ARC requests full party status and intends to submit operational data, verified statements, and testimony based on its historical merger experience.
key_arguments: The merged UP–NS entity would achieve vertical foreclosure by consolidating origin market dominance (UP controls 90%+ of soda ash production in Wyoming; serves Texas Gulf Coast plastic resin sources) with downstream destination control (NS serves Eastern markets), enabling single-line routing that bypasses CSX entirely and disqualifies independent transload terminals like ARC despite their operational viability

ARC's post-Conrail experience demonstrates that structural displacement occurs independent of terminal efficiency: when Conrail split between CSX and NS in 1999, 'ARC was effectively stranded: its service geography fragmented, its customer relationships disrupted, and its commercial role diminished not due to inefficiency, but by regulatory redesign,' with volumes collapsing 90% from 10,000+ to <1,000 carloads annually

The UP–NS merger poses 'network-level consolidation of routing power' across multiple commodity classes (fertilizers, aggregates, chemicals, food products, metals, paper) where UP controls origin access and NS controls destination access, creating systematic risk of loss of interchange competition and neutral service provider access

ARC's CSX-served facilities would face foreclosure not due to performance deficiency but due to 'lack of carrier neutrality,' as merged UP–NS gains ability to absorb soda ash and plastic traffic into single-line UP–NS routes and reroute commodity traffic 'to NS-served or proprietary terminals and bypass ARC's infrastructure'

The merger replicates and extends the Conrail consolidation pattern: carriers 'expanded their in-house proprietary terminals, eroding shipper discretion, and narrowing the role of neutral providers,' with 'formerly less-competitive terminals, now dual-served or linehaul-favored to rapidly gain market share, displacing ARC's historical volumes'
key_excerpts: As a neutral service provider, ARC's competitiveness is defined by the availability of interchange options, not proprietary access or captive routing. Any restructuring that consolidates end-to-end control by a single merged carrier places ARC's customers and operations at direct risk.

This is a textbook case of vertical foreclosure: a carrier with origin market dominance extends control to downstream destinations through elimination of competitive routing. ARC's terminals, though physically rail-served, would be excluded due to lack of carrier neutrality—not lack of demand or performance.

More than 90% of U.S. soda ash production originates in southwestern Wyoming, a region served exclusively by UP. ARC currently handles soda ash via UP–CSX interchanges into CSX-served Eastern markets. If UP gains control over NS, soda ash traffic could be absorbed into a single-line UP–NS route—bypassing CSX entirely and disqualifying ARC from participation.

ARC was effectively stranded: its service geography fragmented, its customer relationships disrupted, and its commercial role diminished not due to inefficiency, but by regulatory redesign. The merged carriers compounded these effects by expanding their in-house proprietary terminals, eroding shipper discretion, and narrowing the role of neutral providers. ARC's volume collapsed by over 90%, falling from more than 10,000 carloads per year to fewer than 1,000.

ARC supports the transaction only under the following conditions: Open Gateway Provisions, Dual-Served Market Protections, Neutral Access Enforcement, Rate and Service Transparency, and Oversight Period [of 7 years].
docket_entries.relief_requested: ARC urges the Board to 'avoid repeating the conditions that produced this displacement and to instead prioritize access continuity, interchange parity, and structural safeguards in its merger review.' ARC does not oppose the transaction but supports it only under the following mandatory conditions: (1) Open Gateway Provisions ensuring all current UP–CSX and NS–CSX interchange points remain open and commercially viable; (2) Dual-Served Market Protections requiring dual-service options at major origin and destination markets, particularly for bulk commodities; (3) Neutral Access Enforcement preventing post-merger diversion of traffic to proprietary terminals when neutral CSX-served terminals are operationally viable; (4) Rate and Service Transparency implementing post-merger monitoring and reporting for interline routing lanes; (5) Oversight Period retaining active Board jurisdiction over access conditions for no less than 7 years post-transaction.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: ARC's filing introduces a specific foreclosure theory grounded in 49 U.S.C. §§ 10101(b) (minimum rail service standards) and 11324 (merger review criteria requiring Board to consider public interest and competitive effects). ARC invokes the Board's prior Conrail divestiture orders as evidentiary foundation for structural foreclosure risk, arguing the Board's failure to impose effective access conditions in 1999 resulted in documented permanent displacement. ARC's detailed conditions framework—particularly the 'Neutral Access Enforcement' requirement and 7-year oversight period—establishes a specific remedy model for Board evaluation of whether approval conditions can adequately protect shipper choice and independent service providers. The filing expands the merger's competitive scope beyond shipper rates to include terminal access and routing discretion for downstream service providers, creating potential for broader remedy scope. ARC's quantified harm metrics (90% volume loss post-Conrail) provide evidentiary basis for speculative harm claims.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.deadline_description: Notice of Intent to Participate has been filed. ARC is now entitled to submit comments during the comment period and to participate in discovery and hearing phases. No specific response deadline applies to this notice itself, but ARC's participation creates ongoing discovery and hearing participation obligations.

Amtrak's Mardi Gras service has served over 59,000 passengers on Norfolk Southern track, demonstrating established public interest in maintaining passenger rail operations on merged carrier infrastructure

docket_entries.title: NGFA Comments on Application Completeness - Deficient Competition Enhancement and Service Assurance Plans
docket_entries.entry_summary: NGFA challenges the Application as incomplete on two critical 2001 Rules compliance fronts. On competition enhancement, NGFA argues the Application is 'deficient under both the letter and spirit of the 2001 Rules.' Applicants propose only three measures (2-to-1 facility protection, gateway preservation, Committed Gateway Pricing), but 'NGFA's review of the Application to date has not revealed any mention of any other proposed means to enhance competition' despite the Board's explicit citation of trackage rights, reciprocal switching, paper/steel barrier elimination, transload facilities, and shared access areas. NGFA contends 'the presentation of such a spare discussion in the Application of the potential competitive harms caused by the merger, combined with Applicants' silence on all the measures recommended by the Board to enhance competition, are deficient.' On Service Assurance, NGFA argues the proposed arbitration clause violates 2001 Rules by imposing a burden requiring customers prove 'substantial deterioration in service' caused 'direct damages'—undermining the Board's intent that compensation be 'readily handled.' The plan also allows Applicants to eliminate compensation by resuming service within 30 days of arbitration notice. On cooperation with other carriers, NGFA finds the Application's discussion 'devoid of specifics'—offering only 'generic statements' of willingness to work with competitors when 'the 2001 Rules require' detailed explanation of 'precise steps' to utilize other railroads during disruptions, tailored by geographic location and available carrier options. NGFA signals these deficiencies are fundamental regulatory violations requiring supplementation before the Board can accept the Application as complete.
key_arguments: The 2001 Rules explicitly require merger applications to include 'robust and detailed plan for how they expect to enhance competition to address every competitive harm that could result from the merger, not just the loss of rail-to-rail competition.' NGFA found no discussion of Board-recommended measures: trackage rights, reciprocal switching, paper/steel barrier elimination, shared/joint access areas, or transload facilities.

Applicants' argument that 'the merger in and of itself will enhance competition' cannot satisfy the regulatory requirement for a concrete 'plan' to enhance competition—these are representations about merger benefits, not compliance mechanisms.

The Service Assurance Plan's arbitration clause violates the 2001 Rules requirement for 'objective, easily administered dispute resolution process' by imposing burden on shipper to prove 'substantial deterioration in service' and 'direct damages,' when the Board anticipated pre-established service level benchmarks enabling payment to be 'readily handled' by arbitrator.

The 30-day cure provision eliminating compensation if service resumes within 30 days of arbitration notice 'further violates the 2001 Rules by eliminat[ing] any compensation for service failures,' contrary to the Board's intent to ensure 'applicants have no incentive to exaggerate' benefits.

The Application devotes 'only two paragraphs' to how Applicants would cooperate with other carriers during service disruptions, providing only 'generic statements' when 'the 2001 Rules require' Applicants explain 'precise steps' that will 'vary according to where such disruptions occur on the combined system and what railroads are available to provide alternative service.'
key_excerpts: The regulations require the Application to include a robust discussion of the broad potential competitive harms the merger may cause, and a plan to not only preserve existing competition but to enhance it moving forward should the merger be approved. The discussion should include an explanation of what measures to enhance competition were considered and why they were rejected, in particular the many potential measures specifically cited by the Board.

The present ation of such a spare discussion in the Application of the potential competitive harm s caused by the merger, combined with Applicants' silence on all the measures recommended by the Board to enhance competition, are deficient under both the letter and spirit of the 2001 Rules.

While the Application contains a proposal for submitting service claims to arbitration, the proposal falls short of a system that enables shippers to be compensated for the Applicants' failure to meet pre-established and agreed-upon service levels. On the contrary, the Application proposes a vague and onerous 'standard for relief.'

The 2001 Rules contain numerous provisions addressing the Board's desire that the applicant's Service Assurance Plan must 'identify[] the precise steps they would take to ensure adequate service and to provide for improved service' including 'how they would cooperate with other carriers in overcoming serious service disruptions on their lines during the transitional period and afterwards.' However, the Application devotes only two paragraphs to this critical issue that together set forth only generic statements.

To ensure that applicants have no incentive to exaggerate [the] projected benefits to the public, the Board expects applicants to propose additional measures that the Board might take if the anticipated public benefits fail to materialize in a time ly manner. [Applicants] must submit a precise, detailed Service Assurance Plan.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Require Applicants to supplement the Application with additional information before acceptance as complete. Specifically: (1) robust discussion of competitive harms and plan to enhance (not just preserve) competition addressing all Board-recommended measures (trackage rights, reciprocal switching, paper/steel barrier elimination, transload facilities, shared/joint access areas); (2) explanation of what enhancement measures were considered and why rejected; (3) redraft Service Assurance Plan with objective, pre-established service level standards enabling automatic compensation; (4) arbitration provision with defined failure metrics, not vague 'substantial deterioration' standard; (5) detailed explanation of 'precise steps' for cooperation with other railroads during service disruptions by specific geographic corridor and carrier availability.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing invokes 49 C.F.R. Part 1180 (Major Rail Consolidation Procedures, 2001 Rules from Ex Parte No. 582 Sub-No. 1) as the binding regulatory framework for application completeness. NGFA's procedural challenge could block STB acceptance of the Application as complete unless Applicants supplement the record. The filing establishes that the 2001 Rules require not merely preservation of competition but affirmative enhancement through specific mechanisms (trackage rights, reciprocal switching, etc.) and pre-established service level compensation formulas—not burden-shifting to shippers. This shifts the evidentiary burden: rather than shippers proving harm in hearing, the regulations require Applicants propose remedies upfront. If STB agrees with NGFA's completeness arguments, the Application cannot be deemed complete, delaying the proceeding and requiring substantial supplementation. The filing also suggests the Service Assurance arbitration clause language may violate the 2001 Rules by imposing vague standards contrary to the Board's explicit policy intent, creating a potential vulnerability in any approval conditions.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comments on Application completeness due by December 29, 2025. This is a procedural deadline for parties to identify deficiencies before STB determines whether to accept Application as complete.

docket_entries.title: CPKC Comments on Completeness of UP/NS Merger Application
docket_entries.entry_summary: CPKC files comments arguing the UP/NS merger application is incomplete and should be rejected. CPKC alleges applicants failed to provide critical underlying data for truck diversion analysis, withheld key merger agreement schedules, failed to analyze downstream merger effects, and provided insufficient horizontal competition analysis in violation of STB's 2001 Major Merger Rules.
key_arguments: Applicants failed to provide Transearch county-to-county truck flow data and DAT Freight & Analytics truck rate data required for evaluating truck-to-rail diversion claims underlying entire application

Applicants withheld Schedule 5.8 of Merger Agreement defining 'Non-Required Restriction' and 'Materially Burdensome Regulatory Condition' which reflects applicants' own assessment of merger's anticompetitive harms
Applicants provided only three-paragraph discussion of downstream effects instead of required rigorous analysis of whether two-railroad duopoly is in public interest

Dr. Elizabeth Bailey's horizontal competition analysis is incomplete and non-compliant with 2001 Rules; corridor analysis ignores effects where UP and NS serve different legs; 50/10 geographic competition screening merely identifies concerns without analyzing them
UP's own 2000 comments established that evaluating whether North American railroad duopoly is in public interest is the 'overriding public policy question' before the Board
Applicants' privilege claims for withheld merger agreement schedules are frivolous; contractual promises are not attorney-client privileged and were shared with investment bankers
key_excerpts: Applicants have not supplied the Board or interested parties with the data that allegedly support the core set of claims upon which the entire Application is predicated: that the merger 'will convert more than 2 million truckloads of traffic from long-haul trucking to rail.'

The withheld Schedule defines the nature of the conditions that NS can sue to require UP to accept and also those that would allow UP to walk away from the merger, and thus likely reflects the best glimpse that the Board and interested parties will get of Applicants' own assessment of the scope of the anticompetitive harms their proposed merger would cause

The important public policy questions in the next major Class I merger proceeding will focus on whether a North American railroad duopoly is in the public interest... This is an important choice that can be made only once, because mergers are likely to be permanent.
It strains credulity to even suggest UP and NS have not both considered this issue in depth when evaluating their future business prospects as a merged enterprise
Applicants' gambit fails to comply with the new rigor of the Board's 2001 rules. The Board should reject the Application as incomplete.

docket_entries.title: BNSF Railway Company Comments on UP/NS Merger Application - Procedural Deficiencies and Merits Opposition
docket_entries.entry_summary: BNSF Railway opposes the UP/NS merger application, arguing it cannot be approved on the merits and identifying significant procedural deficiencies. BNSF contends the application fails to adequately address competitive harms, product/geographic market impacts, downstream effects, projected market shares, controlled entities disclosure, and has not provided necessary discovery data. BNSF requests a longer procedural schedule and full compliance with discovery obligations before proceeding.
key_arguments: Applicants have not met their burden of proving substantial and demonstrable public benefits and lack of competitive harm
Application dismisses competitive harms and fails to recognize risks of consolidating nearly half of U.S. rail traffic under UP's sole control
Failure to conduct rigorous analysis of product and geographic market impacts as required by 49 C.F.R. § 1180.7(b)
Application lacks traffic flow analysis and does not model shifts in freight patterns or geographic competition effects
Inadequate discussion of downstream effects and 'end-game' of rail consolidation as required by 2001 rules
Missing projected market shares incorporating the over 2 million new units UP/NS claim they will attract
Failure to clearly identify controlled subsidiary carriers and applicant carriers, particularly regarding 50% ownership interests
Proposed Committed Gateway Pricing (CGP) is inadequate remedy that would apply to only small subset of affected routes and contains significant limitations
Applicants have failed to provide source data for modal share analysis, truck diversion analysis, and market share calculations
Discovery deficiencies: no emails produced, custodians not identified, incomplete merger agreement, no board materials or investment banker assessments provided
key_excerpts: A combined UP and NS would control nearly half of U.S. rail freight. The Application's discussion of harm to shippers is inadequate and does not offer the Board a clear picture of post-merger competitive dynamics.

UP and NS were obligated to submit a complete and well-supported record that demonstrates the merger is in the public interest. UP and NS made strategic choices regarding the scope, detail, and evidentiary support of their Application.

The Board should not be forced into a process to try to make it work. Nor should the Board allow the limited, proposed conditions to function as an anchoring mechanism for what UP and NS may view as a floor for subsequent negotiation with shippers and competitors.
Because there are so few remaining Class I carriers, and because of the interconnected nature of the rail industry, the Board cannot evaluate the merits of a major transaction in isolation.
UP and NS have not provided the source data that underlies their modal share and truck diversion analysis—the core of their purported benefits analysis.

docket_entries.title: Super Neighborhood 64 & 88 Opposition to UP-NS Merger with Extensive Mitigation Requirements
docket_entries.entry_summary: Community organization representing 23,000 residents in Houston's East End directly impacted by rail infrastructure opposes the UP-NS merger, citing decades of rail congestion, documented life-threatening blockages, and procedural improprieties in merger solicitation. If approved, requests binding mitigation including grade separations, blocked crossing time limits, quiet zones, emergency protocols, and community decision-making authority.
key_arguments: Procedural irregularities: Union Pacific solicited support letters through Griffin Communications before filing application and during period when STB requested only procedural comments, generating approximately 2,000 form letters with identical language

Houston experiences most freight rail congestion in United States with Union Pacific controlling 95% of trackage rights; eight of ten most-blocked rail crossings in entire U.S. located in affected communities
Merger will increase daily train traffic on Lafayette Subdivision by 36% within 5 years; projected 8-10 additional trains daily on lines directly impacting communities

Life-threatening impacts documented: emergency response times in East End average 11-12 minutes versus 5-6 minutes citywide; documented deaths in 2023-2024 attributed to blocked crossings preventing emergency access
Contradictory merger claims: applicants promise reduced truck traffic but disclose 209.8% increase in daily truck traffic at Settegast Yard (246 to 762 trucks daily)
Applicants withdrew previously announced $750 million in concessions and removed 'For Our Communities' section from promotional website
Existing infrastructure inadequate: no new significant railroad line built in Houston in nearly a century despite rail cargo tripling; 26% of trains on Galveston Subdivision stop (1 in 3 trains)
Chicago precedent: Union Pacific plans to double train traffic on two-mile stretch of Chicago's West Side with similar vague assurances about offset benefits
key_excerpts: Our community is directly traversed by the railroads involved in this merger and will bear disproportionate impacts from the proposed transaction.
In 2023, the Federal Railroad Administration confirmed that Houston experiences the most freight rail congestion in the United States.
26% of trains on the Galveston Subdivision through our neighborhood stop—essentially 1 in 3 trains.
Eight of the ten most blocked rail crossings in the entire United States are located in our communities.
In the East End, it takes 11-12 minutes because first responders must navigate around trains, which is more than double the citywide average.
The applicants' own STB filings reveal the merger will increase daily train traffic on the Lafayette Subdivision...by 36 percent within 5 years.
Houston's Settegast Yard would experience a 209.8 percent increase in daily truck traffic by year five—from 246 trucks daily to 762 trucks daily
The combined intermodal business will grow by more than 1.4 million annual loads.

docket_entries.title: CSX Transportation Comments on Completeness of UP/NS Merger Application
docket_entries.entry_summary: CSX Transportation submits comments opposing the Union Pacific/Norfolk Southern merger application, arguing it is incomplete and fails to meet statutory and regulatory requirements. CSX identifies multiple deficiencies including failure to seek proper control of NPBL, misclassification of TRRA transaction as minor, incomplete merger documentation, and failure to address downstream effects and net public benefits under the Board's New Rules.
key_arguments: Application improperly fails to seek separate control approval for Norfolk and Portsmouth Belt Line Railroad (NPBL), which NS owns 57.14% of without Board authorization

Terminal Railroad Association of St. Louis (TRRA) control should be classified as significant transaction, not minor, given UP's existing control of direct competitor Alton & Southern and complete gateway control implications
Application withholds material disclosure schedules including Section 5.8 defining 'Materially Burdensome Regulatory Conditions,' violating transparency requirements
Application fails to provide required evidence on downstream effects of proposed merger and potential cascade mergers (e.g., BNSF-CSX combination)
No identification of which claimed benefits could be achieved short of merger, contrary to New Rules requirement
Application provides no evidence that Committed Gateway Pricing mechanism would enhance rail-to-rail competition; conflates efficiency improvements with competitive enhancement
Application contains no suggested additional measures if claimed benefits fail to materialize, mandatory under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.6(b)(11)
Proposed procedural schedule combined with application deficiencies leaves non-applicants unable to respond adequately to applicants' prima facie case
key_excerpts: Each of these deficiencies renders the Application incomplete as originally filed. 49 U.S.C. § 11325(a)...These deficiencies render the Application incomplete and, as required by 49 U.S.C. § 11325(a), 'the Board shall reject it.'
To the extent UP seeks control over NPBL, the Application is fundamentally incomplete because it fails to include a separate control application for NPBL. 49 U.S.C. § 11323(a).
Common control of these two direct competitors alone precludes this being a 'clearly' harmless transaction.

Despite this clear mandate, the Application omits material aspects of Applicants' agreement 'pertaining to the proposed transaction.' Specifically, while Applicants have filed a copy of the 'Agreement and Plan of Merger,' they have not included the 'Company Disclosure Schedules'
The Board expects applicants to explain how additional Class I mergers would affect the eventual structure of the industry and the public interest.
Enhanced efficiency and enhanced competition, however, are not synonyms

docket_entries.title: Grand Trunk Corporation's Comments on Completeness of Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern's Application
docket_entries.filer_name: Grand Trunk Corporation (on behalf of itself and U.S. rail operating subsidiaries)
docket_entries.entry_summary: CN challenges the completeness of UP/NS merger application under 49 C.F.R. Part 1180, citing deficiencies in market analyses, failure to identify all 2-to-1 and 3-to-2 points, incomplete network maps showing overlapping lines, withholding of merger agreement schedules, and failure to propose competition-enhancing conditions. CN requests the Board reject the application and require resubmission with corrected deficiencies.
key_arguments: Applicants fail to disclose methodology for identifying 2-to-1 shippers and omit multiple 2-to-1 and 3-to-2 points from their analysis
Application contains conflicting conclusions about 2-to-1 points between different verified statements (Novak vs. Bailey)
Applicants omit projected market shares by traffic and revenue as required by regulation
Impact analysis relies on incomplete Class I traffic tape data despite CSX and CPKC data being available
Network map omits critical overlapping lines and trackage/haulage rights, including between Springfield, IL and Kansas City, MO
Merger Agreement incomplete - critical schedules and appendices withheld with improper privilege claims
Schedule 5.8 of Merger Agreement unlawfully withheld and not protected by attorney-client privilege, work product doctrine, or settlement privilege
Applicants fail to propose meaningful competition-enhancing conditions despite regulatory requirement
Transaction is not truly 'end-to-end' as Applicants claim - substantial overlap exists in watershed states
Committed Gateway Pricing proposal is temporary and extremely limited in scope
key_excerpts: Applicants fail to provide the complete market analyses required by section 1180.7. Despite submitting seven verified statements purportedly describing the alleged impacts of the proposed transaction as their 'market analyses' required by section 1180.7, Applicants fail to comply with the specific requirements of that section and exclude key information necessary for the Board's evaluation of the proposed transaction.

Applicants claim that there are only three 2-to-1 shippers, but they fail to disclose any of the information required by section 1180.7(a) regarding the methodology or data used to identify those three shippers.

The Board's new regulations 'significantly increase the burden on applicants to demonstrate that a proposed transaction would be in the public interest.' Consistent with this enhanced standard, any applicants seeking approval for a major transaction are expected to propose conditions that not only preserve, but enhance competition.
A quick glance at a rail map confirms that the eastern and western railroads do not simply meet end-to-end...there is a fair degree of overlap.

Schedule 5.8 merely reflects business terms negotiated between Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern. Moreover, the work product doctrine only covers materials created in anticipation of and for use in litigation.

docket_entries.title: Foresight Energy LLC Notice of Intent to Participate
docket_entries.entry_summary: Foresight Energy LLC filed a notice of intent to participate in the UP/NS merger proceeding, requesting placement on the service list for document service. The filing is purely procedural and contains no substantive position on the merger, no arguments regarding competitive effects, service impacts, or pricing concerns, and no conditions requested. Foresight's interests in the merger remain unstated at this stage. The filing indicates only that Foresight believes it has interests affected by the transaction and intends to monitor the proceeding. Further filings will be necessary to determine whether Foresight will oppose, support, or seek specific remedies.
key_excerpts: Foresight Energy LLC ('Foresight') hereby provides notice of its intent to participate in this proceeding as its interests may appear, and Foresight requests that the Board place it on the service list for this proceeding.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Request for placement on service list and email service of all documents in proceeding
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: No legal or regulatory significance at this stage. This is a procedural filing that formally establishes Foresight as an intervenor and ensures it receives all STB filings and orders. Under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 and STB Rules of Practice, intervenors must formally notify the Board of their intent to participate. This filing satisfies that requirement but does not advance any substantive issue in the merger review.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)

docket_entries.title: Maryland Department of Transportation Notice of Intent to Participate
docket_entries.entry_summary: Maryland Department of Transportation filed a notice of intent to participate in the UP-NS merger proceeding without stating a substantive position on the transaction. The filing is purely procedural: MDOT requests intervention status and placement on the service list to receive all documents and participate in any sub-proceedings 'as its interests may appear.' No opposition, support, or specific conditions are articulated. No facts are provided regarding Maryland's stake in the merger or what rail service issues Maryland DOT intends to address.
key_excerpts: The Maryland Department of Transportation (MDOT) respectfully submits its Notice of Intent to Participate in this proceeding and any related sub-proceedings before the Surface Transportation Board, as its interests may appear.
MDOT consents to email service of all documents, and requests that the undersigned be placed on the service list as representative for MDOT.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Intervention in the proceeding and placement on the service list for all documents and sub-proceedings
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: No legal or regulatory significance at this stage. This is a standard intervention notice establishing procedural participation. Maryland DOT has not yet disclosed the nature or scope of its interests, so the substantive implications remain unknown pending future filings.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.deadline_description: Intervention notice; no response deadline

docket_entries.title: STB Orders Applicants to File Workpaper Reconciliation Table and Complete ZIP Archive by January 5, 2026
docket_entries.entry_summary: The STB issued a procedural order responding to a pattern of undisclosed workpaper revisions. Between December 19-29, 2025, Applicants uploaded replacement files for Bailey, Hunt-Schabas, and Operating Plan workpaper collections without explaining what changed. The Board stated: 'To ensure transparency and clarity, Applicants will be directed to file in the docket a table providing, for each "replacement" file, (1) the name of the replacement file; (2) the name and file path of the file it replaces; (3) a brief description of the differences, if any, between the original file and the replacement file; and (4) for any such differences, an explanation of the reasons therefor.' Applicants must file this reconciliation table and upload a complete ZIP archive of all workpapers (original plus replacements/new files) by January 5, 2026. The order also establishes a prospective requirement that Applicants pre-notify the Board of any future workpaper changes and follow the same detailed disclosure process. Applicants must maintain original December 19 files on the SFTP site and provide file hashes with all transmissions.
key_arguments: Applicants' failure to disclose what changed in replacement workpaper files undermines transparency essential to the merger review process: 'Applicants' emails, however, did not indicate whether—and if so, how—the content of the replacement workpaper files differs from those originally uploaded on December 19 when the application was filed.'
Complete documentation of all workpaper revisions is necessary to preserve record integrity and enable proper intervenor review and Board evaluation of application materials.
key_excerpts: To ensure transparency and clarity, Applicants will be directed to file in the docket a table providing, for each 'replacement' file, (1) the name of the replacement file; (2) the name and file path of the file it replaces; (3) a brief description of the differences, if any, between the original file and the replacement file; and (4) for any such differences, an explanation of the reasons therefor.

Applicants' emails, however, did not indicate whether—and if so, how—the content of the replacement workpaper files differs from those originally uploaded on December 19 when the application was filed.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Applicants directed to file a detailed reconciliation table identifying all replacement and newly-added workpaper files, describing substantive differences from original submissions, and providing explanations for changes. Complete ZIP file of all workpapers (original plus replacements/additions) must be uploaded to SFTP site by January 5, 2026. All future workpaper changes must be pre-notified and follow same reconciliation process.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This order addresses a fundamental procedural gap in application completeness and record integrity. The Board has explicitly required ex post disclosure of undisclosed ex ante revisions to critical evidentiary materials (workpapers supporting competitive analysis, financial projections, operating plans). The order creates a precedent for documentary accountability in future large mergers and establishes that pre-notification and detailed reconciliation of document revisions is mandatory going forward. The January 5 deadline is immediately enforceable and noncompliance could affect application status. The order also signals Board concern about potential 'hidden' changes to substantive analysis materials, which may become relevant if intervenors challenge application completeness or if evidentiary disputes arise over which version of workpapers reflects the applicants' actual analysis.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Applicants must file reconciliation table in docket AND upload complete ZIP file of all workpapers (original plus replacements/additions) to SFTP site by January 5, 2026.

docket_entries.title: Norfolk Southern Reply Comments: UP/NS Application is Complete; Separate NPBL Control Filing Not Required
docket_entries.entry_summary: Norfolk Southern argues the UP/NS control application is complete and UP is not required to file a separate application to acquire control of NPBL. NS contends: (1) UP's application lawfully seeks 'whatever interests NS is legally authorized to hold at the time the Board may approve its application'; (2) the pending NS/NPBL control proceeding (FD 36836) will be decided by April 2026, before the Board rules on UP/NS, ensuring 'the Board's decision in the NPBL proceeding will determine whether NS's controlling shares of NPBL are among the assets UP would acquire'; (3) a separate UP/NPBL application is 'inconsistent with 49 C.F.R. § 1180.4(b) (applications must reflect actual operating plans), the Board's policy against contingent filings, and basic administrative law principles prohibiting agencies from requiring filings based on conjecture and speculation'; (4) the UP/NS application already incorporates NPBL's competitive, operational, and financial impacts because NS has 'de facto controlled NPBL since 1982' and 'NS's operating plan already anticipates NPBL routings...NS traffic data already includes NPBL movements...NS's consolidated reporting already includes amounts normally received from NPBL'; (5) requiring a separate UP/NPBL application would be 'duplicative' and 'would serve no regulatory purpose and contradict the Board's preference for efficient, non‑redundant filings'; and (6) CSX 'has engaged in a futile attempt to seek government intervention to provide it with a competitive advantage for intermodal traffic' and is using the NPBL issue as a 'back-up in the event it fails in its attacks' in other proceedings. NS argues the proper sequence is: NS's NPBL control decision in April 2026 → determines NPBL scope → then UP/NS decision incorporates that outcome. NS offers conditional supplementation: 'If the Board approves NS's NPBL control application with conditions that materially affect traffic flows or competitive dynamics separate from those already included in the UP/NS application, UP can supplement its application at that time.'
key_arguments: UP's application lawfully seeks to acquire 'whatever interests NS is legally authorized to hold at the time the Board may approve its application,' and a separate NPBL application is not required because the NS/NPBL control decision will be issued by April 2026, before the Board rules on UP/NS, ensuring proper sequencing.

Requiring a separate UP/NPBL control application would violate 49 C.F.R. § 1180.4(b) (requiring applications to reflect actual operating plans) and the Board's policy against contingent filings—it would force UP to submit 'a filing grounded in speculation rather than fact' based on 'assumptions the Board has not yet decided, conditions the Board may never impose, and ownership interests NS may never hold.'

The UP/NS application is complete because NS has de facto controlled NPBL for 42 years (since 1982), and thus 'NS's operating plan already anticipates NPBL routings based upon NPBL's current operations...NS traffic data already includes NPBL movements...NS's consolidated reporting already includes amounts normally received from NPBL,' meaning all competitive, operational, and financial impacts are already reflected.

A separate UP/NPBL application would be purely duplicative—'the information contained in such a separate application with respect to the competitive, operational, and financial impacts of NPBL would be exactly the same as what the current UP/NS application reflects and exactly the same as reflected in the NS/NPBL control application'—and would 'serve no regulatory purpose and contradict the Board's preference for efficient, non‑redundant filings.'

CSX is improperly attempting to use the NPBL issue as a 'back-up' strategy: 'CSX has engaged in a futile attempt to seek government intervention to provide it with a competitive advantage for intermodal traffic to/from the East Coast Ports' and is 'presumably' using NPBL as leverage 'in the event it fails in its attacks and requests for conditions' in related proceedings.

There is no statutory or regulatory precedent supporting CSX's position: 'CSX can cite to no precedent requiring such a speculative and hypothetical application,' and 'Nothing in 49 U.S.C. § 11323(a), et. seq., the Board's regulations, or its precedent requires an applicant to file a control application based on hypothetical future circumstances.'
key_excerpts: UP's application is forward‑looking and seeks authority to acquire whatever interests NS is legally authorized to hold at the time the Board may approve its application. By April 2026, long before the Board rules on the UP/NS application, the Board will have decided in the separate NS/NPBL control proceeding. That decision will determine whether NPBL is among the assets UP would acquire.

The entire point of this major application is that UP seeks STB approval to control NS and all subsidiary entities it controls. And the forthcoming STB decision in FD 36836...will determine whether NPBL is within, or outside, the scope of UP's application to acquire control of NS.

Although NS does not have 'authorized' control of NPBL, NS has de facto controlled NPBL since 1982. NS's operating plan already anticipates NPBL routings based upon NPBL's current operations. NS traffic data already includes NPBL movements in line with NPBL's current operations.

Requiring UP to file a separate application to acquire NPBL at this time based upon assumptions that may or may not occur is inconsistent with 49 C.F.R. § 1180.4(b) (applications must reflect actual operating plans), the Board's policy against contingent filings, and basic administrative law principles prohibiting agencies from requiring filings based on conjecture and speculation.

A separate NPBL control application would add nothing—no new data, no new analysis, and no new insight. It would simply duplicate what is already before the Board, contrary to the Board's preference for efficient, non‑redundant filings.

CSX asks the Board to require UP to file an application based on assumptions the Board has not yet decided, conditions the Board may never impose, and ownership interests NS may never hold. That is not what the statute requires, not what the regulations contemplate, and not what the Board has ever demanded.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Reject CSX's claim that UP's application is incomplete; proceed with review of the UP/NS application as filed; do not require UP to file a separate control application for NPBL
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing addresses a critical procedural and substantive issue: whether CSX can force a separate control application filing through a completeness challenge, effectively creating a second merger review track for NPBL. NS's arguments invoke administrative law principles (no speculative filings), regulatory framework (49 U.S.C. § 11323, 49 C.F.R. § 1180.4), and Board precedent on supplementation and efficiency. The filing establishes that the Board's procedural rules do not contemplate separate applications for subsidiaries already controlled by an acquiree, and that sequencing (NS/NPBL decided in April, then UP/NS incorporates that result) is legally sound. If successful, this prevents CSX from opening a second regulatory front on NPBL; if unsuccessful, it exposes the merger to extended NPBL-specific competitive review and potentially separate competitive impact analysis.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Reply comments; no specific response deadline stated, but CSX may file further response or the Board may issue a completeness ruling

docket_entries.title: Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern Reply to Comments on Application Completeness
docket_entries.entry_summary: Applicants filed a comprehensive reply defending the completeness of their 6,700-page merger application against challenges from competitors (CN, BNSF, CSX, CPKC) and the National Grain and Feed Association. Applicants argue they have fully complied with Surface Transportation Board merger rules by providing required system impact analyses, competitive impact studies, operating plans, and supporting data, and that remaining objections address merits rather than completeness.
key_arguments: Application contains all information required by 49 C.F.R. part 1180 and presents prima facie case for public interest consistency
Full system impact analyses provided using Bureau of Economic Analysis geographic definitions as permitted by rules
2-to-1 and 3-to-2 point analyses completed with identified 2-to-1 shipper protections; only one 3-to-2 point identified with competitive harm analysis
Market share analyses properly conducted using standard antitrust methodology comparing pre- and post-transaction shares
Vertical competitive effects thoroughly addressed by Dr. Mark Israel with no realistic prospect of material harm
Downstream effects adequately addressed through discussion of likely future mergers and required conditions
Public benefits enumerated and quantified in Summary of Benefits Exhibit with documented development process
Committed Gateway Pricing program proposed as competition-enhancing condition addressing Board concerns
Data underlying evidence provided in workpapers including Transearch truck flow data, DAT pricing data, and computer programs for replication
Merger agreement body provided as Exhibit 2; privilege assertions over disclosure schedules defensible
Competitor objections largely address merits rather than application completeness
Minor map omissions do not affect application substance or analytical integrity
key_excerpts: The Application contains all the information required by the Board's merger rules, 49 C.F.R. part 1180, and presents a prima facie case that the proposed transaction is consistent with the public interest.

The Board should reject the efforts of a few parties—primarily competitors of Applicants who will experience increased competition as a result of the merger—to delay and prolong this proceeding by claiming the Application is incomplete.
NGFA's concerns relate to the merits of the Application, not the completeness of the Application.

Applicants fully complied with § 1180.7(b)(2) by providing 3-to-2 and 2-to-1 information for 'each major point on the combined system.' The Board's rules do not require Applicants to conduct a station-level or facility-level analysis.
Dr. Bailey's approach is not only consistent with standard antitrust analysis, it is also consistent with the Board's requirement that Applicants identify a particular year for their impact analysis.

Applicants provided a Summary of Benefits Exhibit as Exhibit B to Volume 1 of the Application, and the Verified Statement of Grant Janke describes and thoroughly documents the development of the Summary of Benefits Exhibit.
Applicants' workpapers include all the truck movements identified for diversion at a county-to-county level of detail.

The schedule at issue is shielded from discovery by recognized privileges. Commenting parties may disagree with Applicants' privilege assertions, but such issues can and should be adjudicated through the discovery process.

docket_entries.title: Applicants' Supplemental Filing of Replacement and Additional Workpapers with Technical Accommodation Request
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern are submitting replacement and additional workpapers made available to the Board and parties on December 23, 24, and 29, 2025, in response to STB Decision No. 8's requirement for supplemental filings. The submission addresses three categories of materials: (1) intermediate datasets supporting Dr. Elizabeth M. Bailey's Verified Statement, re-produced after a party reported corruption issues (though Applicants determined the corruption arose post-upload); (2) files related to the Joint Verified Statement of David Hunt and Matthew Schabas, including re-productions due to apparent corruption in the production process, four previously unproduced files due to technical upload errors, one inadvertently omitted file, and twelve intermediate datasets provided as accommodation; and (3) three Operating Plan files (from the Joint Verified Statement of Eric Gehringer and John F. Orr), two originally produced with encryption keys preventing download access and one re-produced as part of folder consolidation. Applicants argue that combining the large number of files and massive data volumes into a single zipped file—as mandated by Decision No. 8—likely caused the file-corruption problems and would repeat those problems if attempted again. They further assert that the time required to complete such consolidation within Decision No. 8's timeframe was infeasible. As an alternative, Applicants are uploading three separate zipped files organized by witness/subject (Bailey workpapers, Hunt/Schabas workpapers, and Operating Plan workpapers) to the Kiteworks SFTP site in folder 'Updated Workpaper Files (1.5.2025),' and propose scheduling a technical conference with Board staff to discuss either a mechanism for single-file consolidation or development of another acceptable alternative.
key_arguments: The process of combining and processing a large number of files and massive amount of data into a single zip file contributed to file-corruption problems, and similar problems would likely recur if that process were repeated
The time required to combine all files into a single zipped file made it infeasible for Applicants to ensure completion within the Decision No. 8 timeframe

Three separate zipped files organized by witness statement/subject matter (Bailey, Hunt/Schabas, Operating Plan) provide all replacement and additional materials while avoiding the technical consolidation problems that caused corruption
key_excerpts: Applicants believe that the process of combining and processing the large number of files and massive amount of data contained in those files into a single zip file contributed to the file-corruption problems, and that similar problems would likely arise if they were to repeat that process.

In addition, because of the amount of time required to combine all the files into a single zipped file, Applicants could not ensure they could complete the process in the timeframe established by Decision No. 8.

Applicants propose that the Board schedule a technical conference between Applicants and Board staff to discuss a mechanism that would allow Applicants to reproduce all the workpapers in a single zipped file or to develop another acceptable alternative.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Schedule a technical conference between Applicants and Board staff to discuss a mechanism allowing reproduction of all workpapers in a single zipped file or develop an alternative acceptable to the Board
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing directly addresses compliance with a mandatory Board discovery order (Decision No. 8) and seeks a procedural accommodation/deviation from that order's consolidation requirement. The technical problems raise questions about the integrity and verifiability of the underlying economic analyses (particularly Dr. Bailey's analyses and the Operating Plan) that form the evidentiary foundation for the merger application. Intervenors may challenge the adequacy of file consolidation or data integrity, potentially impacting their ability to conduct effective discovery and prepare rebuttal evidence. The Board must decide whether the proposed three-file alternative satisfies the discovery mandate or whether stricter file consolidation is necessary. This precedent-setting technical accommodation could influence future discovery disputes in this and other complex proceedings.
docket_entries.document_type: Modify/Supplement Prior Filing Or The Record
docket_entries.deadline_description: No explicit deadline stated; Applicants are requesting Board action to schedule technical conference and approve proposed filing methodology. Board may issue directive via supplemental Decision order.

docket_entries.title: Union Pacific / Norfolk Southern - Joint Modification/Supplement to Prior Filing
docket_entries.entry_summary: UNABLE TO PROVIDE SUBSTANTIVE SUMMARY - Document metadata indicates this is a modification or supplement to a prior filing, but the actual content, arguments, and specific changes are not provided in the entry. To assess the materiality and substance of this modification (e.g., whether it includes new commitments, revised service guarantees, settlement-related conditions, or responses to intervenor objections), the full text of the filing is required. Merger arbitrage professionals need to know: (1) What was modified from the original application? (2) Are new conditions or commitments proposed? (3) Does this represent a concession to intervenor demands or discovery findings? (4) Does it signal potential settlement with major opponents?
docket_entries.relief_requested: Approval of the proposed merger, as modified/supplemented by this filing
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Modifications to merger applications can alter the evidentiary record, introduce new commitments enforceable by the STB, or indicate responsiveness to discovery challenges. If this supplement includes service guarantees, operating restrictions, or divestiture commitments, those would materially affect conditions analysis and intervenor settlement likelihood. Without the full filing content, the legal significance cannot be assessed.

docket_entries.title: STB Response to Representative Garcia Letter on UP/NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: The STB responds to Representative Sylvia Garcia's letter expressing concerns about the UP/NS merger's impacts on Harris County economy, shippers, passengers, and competition. The Board reiterates its statutory obligation to conduct 'rigorous and comprehensive review' considering 'effective competition, carrier safety and efficiency, adequate service for shippers, environmental safeguards, and fair working conditions for employees.' The Board confirms that applicants must submit: (1) an operating plan demonstrating effects on regional/national rail operations; (2) a Safety Integration Plan developed with the Federal Railroad Administration; (3) information on blocked crossing mitigation; and (4) a Service Assurance Plan describing how efficiencies translate to benefits for shippers and passenger rail operators. The Board notes it is currently reviewing the December 19, 2025 application for completeness under 49 C.F.R. Part 1180 (30-day review window) and will seek public comments on the merits at a later stage. The Board declines to comment further pending the review, but assures 'thorough and fair review' consistent with law.
key_arguments: Board's statutory review must address six specific public interest goals: effective competition, carrier safety and efficiency, adequate service for shippers, environmental safeguards, fair working conditions, and a competitive/efficient/reliable national rail system
Applicants must demonstrate operating plan impacts on 'regional and national rail operations'—establishing that scope extends beyond parties' own operations
Service Assurance Plan must demonstrate how operational efficiencies translate into 'present and future benefits for the shipping public,' not just applicants
Blocked crossings analysis is mandatory, requiring applicants to affirmatively address merger-caused traffic increases and crossing impacts
Passenger rail coordination is mandatory—applicants must show 'effective communications' with passenger operators to 'minimize potential transaction-related negative impacts'
key_excerpts: The Board must ensure that any approved transaction would promote a competitive, efficient, and reliable national rail system.

Applicants must also submit a Service Assurance Plan, which describes how operating plan efficiencies would translate into present and future benefits for the shipping public, and includes, among other things, a description of how the Applicants would ensure effective communications with passenger rail operators to minimize any potential transaction-related negative impacts.
docket_entries.relief_requested: No relief requested. Board confirms it will conduct rigorous review per statutory requirements.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This response establishes the formal evidentiary burden and scope of review for the merger. The Board's enumeration of mandatory submission categories (Operating Plan, Safety Integration Plan, blocked crossing analysis, Service Assurance Plan) and the public interest factors (49 C.F.R. § 1180.1(b)) defines what applicants must prove. The 30-day completeness review window (ending ~January 19, 2026) is the first critical juncture—failure to file complete applications could result in rejection without merits review. The requirement for Service Assurance Plans demonstrating shipper benefits (not just efficiency claims) and passenger rail coordination language suggests the Board will scrutinize service quality and network reliability arguments. The emphasis on 'regional and national rail operations' (not just merged entity operations) signals the Board will examine broader competitive impacts.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Completeness review deadline approximately January 19, 2026 (30 days from December 19, 2025 application filing)

docket_entries.title: Corrected Exhibit 1 Map - Trackage Rights Supplement
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern jointly filed a corrected Exhibit 1 map to replace the original version submitted with their application. The original map omitted three sets of operating rights: (1) Union Pacific's trackage rights over Norfolk Southern between Kansas City, Missouri and Springfield, Illinois; (2) Norfolk Southern's rights over Union Pacific between Salem, Illinois and Sidney, Illinois, consisting of haulage rights (Salem to Villa Grove) and trackage rights (Villa Grove to Sidney); and (3) Norfolk Southern's restricted haulage rights over Union Pacific between St. Louis and Iron Mountain, Missouri, specifically for ballast train operations supporting track maintenance. Applicants provided both PDF and JPG digital versions plus 25 printed copies. This filing suggests the applicants discovered the mapping errors while responding to completeness challenges and are correcting the record prospectively. The significance lies in what these omitted rights reveal: the carriers already have some reciprocal operating arrangements on key corridors, which may affect competitive analysis and remedy discussions.
key_arguments: The original Exhibit 1 map failed to depict existing trackage and haulage rights between UP and NS on three strategically important corridors: Kansas City-Springfield (UP over NS), Salem-Sidney (NS over UP with split haulage/trackage arrangement), and St. Louis-Iron Mountain (NS ballast haulage rights over UP).

Applicants characterize the omitted rights as requiring explicit correction and supplementation via formal filing, suggesting these were oversight-level errors in the initial application completeness that need Board acknowledgment.

The corrected map shows reciprocal rights arrangements already in place, indicating pre-existing operational interdependence between the carriers on multiple routes that a fully merged entity would internalize.
key_excerpts: With this letter, Applicants are submitting PDF and JPG files containing a corrected version of the map included as Exhibit 1 at Volume 1, page 71, of their Application. The corrected map shows three sets of rights not shown in the original: (i) Union Pacific's trackage rights over Norfolk Southern between Kansas City, Missouri, and Springfield, Illinois; (ii) Norfolk Southern's rights over Union Pacific between Salem, Illinois, and Sidney, Illinois, which consist of haulage rights between Salem and Villa Grove, Illinois, and trackage rights between Villa Grove and Sidney; and (iii) Norfolk Southern's haulage rights over Union Pacific between St. Louis, Missouri, and Iron Mountain, Missouri, which are restricted to haulage of ballast trains that allow Norfolk Southern to obtain ballast for maintenance of its railroad.
In Applicants' Reply to Comments on Completeness of Application (UP-17/NS-15), Applicants stated that they would file a corrected Exhibit 1 to their Application.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Submission and acceptance of corrected Exhibit 1 map to the Application replacing the original version filed at Volume 1, page 71.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing reveals potential completeness and accuracy issues with the original application. Under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 and STB procedure, applications must contain accurate and complete information about the applicants' networks and operating arrangements. The omission of existing trackage/haulage rights from the network map could be characterized by opposing parties as: (1) evidence of incomplete diligence by applicants; (2) material misrepresentation of competitive overlap (if the rights reduce apparent head-to-head competition); or (3) an attempt to downplay existing operational coordination. Conversely, applicants may argue the omissions were clerical mapping errors immaterial to substantive competitive analysis. The correction demonstrates applicants are policing their own record but also signals that intervenors should scrutinize whether other operating arrangements (joint ventures, informal coordination agreements, shared facilities) remain undisclosed. This may prompt discovery requests targeting existing service arrangements not yet in the application.
