docket_entries.title: STB Chairman's Response to Senator Blumenthal on UP/NS Merger Review
docket_entries.entry_summary: STB Chairman Patrick Fuchs responds to Senator Blumenthal's concerns about the UP/NS merger by confirming the Board will conduct a 'rigorous and comprehensive review' under the public interest standard of 49 C.F.R. § 1180.1(b). The letter outlines the specific statutory requirements applicants must satisfy: (1) detailed public interest justifications; (2) analysis of effects on 'inter- and intra-modal competition'; (3) measures to 'mitigate and offset any merger-related harms' that 'should not simply preserve, but also enhance, competition'; (4) a Safety Integration Plan addressing blocked crossings; and (5) a Service Assurance Plan showing how operating efficiencies translate to 'benefits for the shipping public' and how 'service degradation' will be mitigated. The Board's review will weigh 'effective competition, carrier safety and efficiency, adequate service for shippers, environmental safeguards, and fair working conditions for employees.' The application was filed December 19, 2025, with completeness determination due within 30 days. The letter signals the Board has not yet accepted the application and will seek public comments at a later stage.
key_arguments: The Board must ensure approved transactions 'promote a competitive, efficient, and reliable national rail system' by considering effective competition, carrier safety, efficiency, adequate shipper service, environmental safeguards, and fair employee working conditions.
Applicants' mitigation measures must 'not simply preserve, but also enhance, competition' — a heightened standard beyond mere competitive neutrality.
Applicants must provide analysis of effects on both 'inter-modal' (rail vs. truck/barge) and 'intra-modal' (rail vs. rail) competition, indicating breadth of competitive inquiry.

Service Assurance Plan must demonstrate how operational efficiencies translate to concrete 'benefits for the shipping public' and specify mitigation of 'service degradation,' shifting burden to applicants to prove affirmative shipper benefits.
Safety Integration Plan must address both general safe operations and specific mitigation of 'potentially blocked crossings' resulting from merger operational changes or increased traffic.
key_excerpts: The Board must ensure that any approved transaction would promote a competitive, efficient, and reliable national rail system.
Applicants must also propose measures to mitigate and offset any merger-related harms, and these conditions should not simply preserve, but also enhance, competition.

The Board's regulations require Applicants to detail, among other things, the public interest justifications in support of the proposed transaction, the effect of the proposed merger on employees, a calculation of public benefits, and an analysis of the effects of the proposed transaction on both inter- and intra-modal competition.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Not applicable. This is a procedural/administrative response letter from the regulator confirming it will conduct a rigorous review.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This letter crystallizes the Board's statutory review framework and sets binding evidentiary requirements. The explicit statement that mitigation measures must 'enhance' (not merely preserve) competition raises the bar above standard merger analysis and signals the Board will scrutinize whether UP/NS can offer affirmative competitive improvements. The requirement for analysis of both inter-modal and intra-modal competition indicates the Board will examine rail consolidation effects broadly. The Service Assurance Plan requirement shifts burden to applicants to affirmatively prove shipper benefits, not merely absence of harm. The 30-day completeness timeline creates a near-term gate for the application's acceptance. This establishes the legal foundation against which all subsequent intervenor arguments will be evaluated.
docket_entries.deadline_description: STB must issue completeness determination on UP/NS application (30-day deadline from December 19, 2025 filing)

docket_entries.title: Motion to Compel Production of Schedule 5.8 to Merger Agreement - Union Pacific/Norfolk Southern
docket_entries.entry_summary: Grand Trunk Corporation filed a motion to compel Union Pacific to produce an unredacted Schedule 5.8 to the merger agreement between Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern, which Union Pacific had withheld claiming attorney-client privilege, work product doctrine, and settlement privilege. CN argues Schedule 5.8 reflects negotiated business terms regarding conditions the parties would accept to secure regulatory approval and is essential to evaluating the merger's competitive effects and fairness to shareholders.
key_arguments: Schedule 5.8 is a business document negotiated between adverse parties and cannot be protected by attorney-client privilege, work product doctrine, or settlement privilege
The schedule reflects anticipated competitive harms and regulatory conditions, making it directly relevant to assessing whether the merger enhances competition
Union Pacific failed to meet its burden of proving privilege claims, providing no case law, facts, privilege log, or explanation of who received the document
Any privilege was waived by sharing Schedule 5.8 with third-party investment banks for fairness opinion purposes
The merger agreement must be produced in full as required by 49 C.F.R. § 1180.6(a)(7)(ii)
Union Pacific's redactions obscure material terms of the transaction and prevent meaningful public participation in the proceeding
key_excerpts: Schedule 5.8 reflects the negotiated business agreement between two adverse parties as to how they would respond to conditions imposed by the Board as prerequisite to closing their merger.
Documents reflecting a business agreement between counterparties bargaining at arm's length are not and cannot be privileged.
Union Pacific has never provided evidentiary support for its claim, nor cited any legal authority for the proposition that a negotiated merger agreement can be subject to a privilege.
The Board's rules expressly encourage public participation '[t]o ensure a fully developed record on the effects of a proposed railroad consolidation.'

By Union Pacific's own admission, that schedule reflects the negotiated business agreement between two adverse parties as to how they would respond to conditions imposed by the Board as prerequisite to closing their merger.

docket_entries.title: CPKC Support for CN Motion to Compel Production of Schedule 5.8 (Merger Agreement)
docket_entries.entry_summary: CPKC supports CN's Motion to Compel and separately challenges the completeness of the UP/NS merger Application. CPKC argues that Schedule 5.8 (defining material transaction terms) was required to be included with the Application under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.6(a)(7)(ii), which mandates the parties' 'agreement,' not selective portions. Even if the omission does not render the Application incomplete, CPKC argues Schedule 5.8 is discoverable because it reflects contractual promises UP made to induce NS to sign—not privileged attorney-client communications. CPKC contends no privilege applies to commercial contract terms, and any privilege would be waived because Applicants disclosed the merger agreement to Morgan Stanley, Wells Fargo, and Bank of America for fairness opinions. CPKC points to precedent from its own CP/KCS merger (Finance Docket No. 36500, 2021) where CP's application included an unredacted 'efforts' clause showing obligations regarding regulatory approval, establishing that disclosure of such clauses is standard STB practice. CPKC's underlying position: Applicants are withholding material contractual information from the Board and intervenors, creating an incompleteness issue and obstructing discovery that competitors need to assess competitive harm and cross-examine Applicant performance commitments.
key_arguments: Schedule 5.8 is a mandatory disclosure under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.6(a)(7)(ii), which requires applicants to file the parties' 'agreement,' not just selectively chosen portions of it.
Schedule 5.8 defines material terms of the transaction and is not protected by attorney-client privilege because it reflects contractual business terms, not legal advice.

Any attorney-client privilege over the merger agreement was waived when Applicants disclosed it to Morgan Stanley, Wells Fargo, and Bank of America for fairness opinions—voluntary third-party disclosure breaches confidentiality and waives privilege under In re Sealed Case, 676 F.2d 793, 809 (D.C. Cir. 1982).

Schedule 5.8 is discoverable as a material document defining contractual promises UP made to induce NS to sign, which is relevant to assessing the transaction's competitive effects and Applicant obligations.

Historical precedent: In CPKC's own CP/KCS merger (FD 36500, 2021), CP's application included unredacted 'efforts' clauses reflecting regulatory approval obligations, establishing that STB practice requires disclosure of such contractual terms.
Applicants' withholding of Schedule 5.8 renders the Application incomplete and obstructs legitimate intervenor discovery access to assess competitive harm and verify Applicant performance.
key_excerpts: Applicants were obligated to include Schedule 5.8 with their Application pursuant to the requirement of 49 C.F.R. § 1180.6(a)(7)(ii) that the Application include the parties' 'agreement,' not just the parts they choose to share.
No good faith claim of privilege applies to contractual promises UP made to induce NS to sign the merger agreement.

Any voluntary disclosure by the client to a third party breaches the confidentiality of the attorney-client relationship and therefore waives the privilege. In re Sealed Case, 676 F.2d 793, 809 (D.C. Cir. 1982).

In the CP/KCS merger proceeding in 2021 (which created CPKC), the application for Board approval contained a version of the merger agreement that included (in unredacted form) the analogous 'efforts' clause reflecting CP's obligations regarding seeking and obtaining regulatory approval.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Compel Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern to produce Schedule 5.8 to the merger agreement, which defines material terms of the transaction. If the Application is deemed complete without Schedule 5.8, CPKC maintains that it remains discoverable as a material document. CPKC also challenges the completeness of the Application under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.6(a)(7)(ii).
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing directly challenges application completeness under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.6(a)(7)(ii), a threshold jurisdictional issue. CPKC's completeness argument—backed by privileged waiver analysis and STB precedent from the CP/KCS merger—could require the Board to hold Applicants to a higher disclosure standard or deem the Application deficient if Schedule 5.8 is not produced. The privilege waiver argument is legally sophisticated: CPKC cites D.C. Circuit precedent and Delaware Chancery Court authority to establish that voluntary disclosure to third-party financial advisors waives any privilege claim. This frames the issue as Applicant overreach and shifts burden to Applicants to justify withholding. CPKC's historical precedent (CP/KCS FD 36500) suggests the Board has previously required unredacted contractual 'efforts' clauses, constraining Applicant arguments that such disclosure is novel or improper.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No specific deadline stated; filed as support for CN Motion to Compel (CN-7), which may carry its own response deadline

docket_entries.title: BNSF Motion to Compel Discovery: Board Materials, Banker Materials, and Emails
docket_entries.entry_summary: BNSF filed a motion to compel arguing that UP and NS have severely restricted discovery by: (1) producing only 1,653 documents total (mainly lease agreements) despite 150+ days since announcement, with zero emails, board materials, or internal merger analyses; (2) refusing to conduct custodial email collections for ANY requests; (3) refusing to produce board materials or banker analyses; (4) deferring responses until filing their applications; and (5) claiming work on traffic tapes and switching data somehow addresses core discovery gaps. BNSF argues that standard merger practice—exemplified by HSR filings and federal antitrust litigation—requires production of board-level discussions of competition, synergies, and merger alternatives. BNSF characterizes UP and NS's position as 'stalling, stonewalling, and deferring' and emphasizes that 'UP wants exemptions from basic discovery obligations.' BNSF argues that 'the merger will irrevocably shape American railroading for decades' and therefore 'stakeholders are impaired in their ability to critically evaluate the UP/NS merger without access to those documents and communications.' The core complaint: UP and NS are using proportionality and privilege objections to hide candid internal assessments of whether the merger helps or harms competition—precisely the information the Board needs to make an informed decision. BNSF explicitly invokes its prior position in the CP/KCS merger (Docket 36500) where UP itself demanded the exact same categories of discovery it now refuses to provide, including communications about merger effects, board presentations persuading boards to approve deals, and studies evaluating competitive impacts.
key_arguments: UP and NS have produced only 1,653 documents over 150 days, with zero emails, zero board materials, and zero internal analyses of merger competitive effects, despite claiming merger will 'shape next hundred years of American railroading'

Board materials, banker analyses, and emails are core discovery in any merger proceeding—they are routinely required in HSR filings and have been called 'ubiquitous' in federal antitrust trials evaluating competitive effects

UP contradicts its own prior positions: In CP/KCS merger (FD 36500), UP demanded exactly these materials from KCS—communications about merger effects, board presentations to persuade KCS board, studies evaluating competitive impacts—but now refuses to produce them itself

UP and NS's 'proportionality' objection fails: the stakes are unprecedented (an $85 billion transcontinental railroad), so MORE discovery is needed, not less; proportionality factors all weigh toward requiring these materials

UP and NS have not identified a single custodian for email searches and refuse to commit to collecting emails at all, instead proposing vague 'targeted collections' that protect them from candid internal communications

Materials sought bear directly on Board's statutory factors: whether merger benefits could be achieved without merger (49 C.F.R. § 1180.6(b)(11)), whether it enhances competition (§ 1180.1(c)(2)(iv)), what conditions are needed (§ 1180.6(b)(10)), and net public benefits including rate impacts (§ 1180.6(b)(11))

Without custodial collections, stakeholders 'cannot see UP's or NS's candid views about the proposed merger and its effects'—UP and NS are 'hiding behind proportionality objections for basic and necessary discovery'

The procedural schedule must be deferred until UP and NS complete discovery: opponents' comments due April 18, 2026, but depositions cannot occur until document discovery is complete, and UP/NS are unwilling to confirm they've even collected emails
key_excerpts: UP and NS seek approval of a merger that they claim 'will shape the next hundred years of American railroading.' Despite the stakes, UP and NS want exemptions from the most basic discovery obligations. UP and NS have not provided basic information that stakeholders and the Board need to test UP and NS's contentions: their board materials, banker presentations, and relevant internal emails.

In other words, UP and NS are blocking efforts to see what they actually believe and discuss internally: whether the merger will hurt competition by reducing service or leading to higher rates for shippers; whether the executive teams actually believe the merger will enhance competition; where the integration could go awry and cause disruptions; and whether the purported benefits are achievable at all, or alternatively, achievable absent a merger.

To date, UP has been at war with its own positions. In the CP/KCS merger, UP argued that an end-to-end merger could still lead to foreclosure and harm competition. Now that it wants to merge with NS, UP sheds those principled positions.
There is no merger litigation in America where the approach taken by UP and NS would be acceptable.

Disclosing board materials, banker materials, and email communications about a merger is standard fare in merger proceedings. The materials required for federal merger approval are presumptively relevant to the Board's competition analysis.

Without custodial document collection and the production of board materials, banker materials, and relevant emails, stakeholders cannot see UP's or NS's candid views about the proposed merger and its effects. UP and NS should not be allowed to hide behind proportionality objections for basic and necessary discovery requests.
The Board has one chance to make a fully informed decision on the merits of the UP/NS merger. The Board can only do so if the stakeholders have a fair opportunity to develop the record in discovery.
docket_entries.relief_requested: BNSF requests: (1) Direct UP and NS to produce all board materials required in HSR filings responsive to BNSF's discovery requests; (2) Direct UP and NS to produce all banker and financial materials required in HSR filings; (3) Direct UP and NS to collect, process, and search emails from all fact witnesses who submitted Verified Statements and relevant support teams; (4) Complete email collection and processing within 10 days of order; (5) Meet and confer on search terms and hit reports within 14 days; (6) Complete custodial productions at least 21 days before depositions; (7) Defer or modify the Procedural Schedule to allow time for UP and NS to complete discovery obligations before depositions commence.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This motion establishes discovery standards for STB railroad merger proceedings and directly challenges applicants' ability to withhold internal competitive analysis. It cites to Hart-Scott-Rodino requirements as a baseline for what the Board should receive, argues that STB proportionality standards (49 C.F.R. Part 1114) require production of board and banker materials given the merger's stakes, and invokes federal antitrust litigation precedent (D.C. Circuit cases on relevance of internal emails) to establish discovery norms. The motion potentially shifts burden onto applicants to justify withholding specific categories rather than claiming wholesale email collections are 'unduly burdensome.' If granted, it will establish that in mega-mergers, proportionality analysis weighs heavily toward expansive discovery of internal assessments.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Motion pending before ALJ. UP and NS responses to motion due per Board/ALJ scheduling. BNSF requested amendments to discovery responses by November 24, 2025 (in prior correspondence), and UP/NS provided responses on December 5, 2025 and in January 2026 meet-and-confer exchange.

docket_entries.title: Grand Trunk/CN Raises Critical Data Discrepancy Issue: Union Pacific Traffic Tapes Grew from 48M to 131M Records Across Three Submissions
docket_entries.entry_summary: CN raises a critical data integrity issue: Union Pacific's 100% traffic tapes submitted to the Board have been provided in three inconsistent versions with dramatically different record counts. The initial September 8, 2025 submission (UP-5) contained 48.1 million records. A December 8, 2025 update (UP-11) more than doubled this to 99.9 million records, with Union Pacific's counsel explaining the addition of empty car movements. Most significantly, the December 19, 2025 Application filing included Dr. Bailey's verified economic analysis utilizing a third, previously undisclosed dataset containing 131.3 million records—a 31.3 million record increase (31%) over the December 8 version. CN notes: 'These 31.3 million additional records were not available to the Board or interested parties until they were submitted as a workpaper with the Application, even though Applicants had twice previously submitted traffic tapes to the Board.' The filing also documents that Norfolk Southern's traffic files increased modestly (85.2M → 87.1M across submissions). CN argues this data inconsistency 'make[s] it difficult for the Board and interested parties to know what data to use in their own competitive analyses to achieve an apples-to-apples comparison with Applicants' analyses' and 'has apparently deprived the Board and interested parties of the entire traffic files during the application prefiling period.' CN requests clear confirmation of which dataset Dr. Bailey used and how the versions differ.
key_arguments: The three successive traffic tape submissions contain materially different record counts, creating uncertainty about which data actually supports Dr. Bailey's competitive analysis: 48.1M records (Sept 8) → 99.9M records (Dec 8) → 131.3M records (Dec 19).

Union Pacific's third dataset (131.3M records in the Application workpapers) contains 31.3 million additional records not previously disclosed to the Board or interested parties, representing a 31% increase from the December 8 submission.

The undisclosed 31.3 million UP records were unavailable during the entire prefiling period and early comment phase, preventing the Board and intervenors from conducting independent 'apples-to-apples' competitive analysis using the same evidentiary base as Applicants.

The expanding scope of the data (number of fields increasing from 39 to 73 for UP, 41 to 71 for NS) combined with unexplained record increases raises questions about the completeness and consistency of the datasets used for economic analysis.

Dr. Bailey's verified statement (the key economic support for the merger application) relies on a traffic tape version that differs materially from versions previously submitted, yet no explanation is provided in the Application for these discrepancies.
key_excerpts: These 31.3 million additional records were not available to the Board or interested parties until they were submitted as a workpaper with the Application, even though Applicants had twice previously submitted traffic tapes to the Board.
The inconsistent datasets jeopardize the ability of the Board and other parties to assess the accuracy and reliability of claims in the Application about competitive impacts.

These inconsistent sets of 100% traffic tape data make it difficult for the Board and interested parties to know what data to use in their own competitive analyses to achieve an 'apples-to-apples' comparison with Applicants' analyses. It also has apparently deprived the Board and interested parties of the entire traffic files during the application prefiling period.
The file name for the traffic tapes utilized by Dr. Bailey...implies the file was created in August of 2025. That file was not provided to the Board or other parties until December 19, 2025.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Clarification and confirmation from Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern regarding: (1) Which 100% traffic tape dataset was actually utilized in Dr. Elizabeth Bailey's competitive analysis; (2) How and to what extent the three different traffic tape versions differ from each other; (3) Explanation for the undisclosed 31.3 million additional UP records that first appeared in the Application workpapers on December 19, 2025.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing raises evidentiary completeness and data integrity issues that could affect: (1) The burden and credibility of Applicants' competitive analyses; (2) The scope of discovery and hearing; (3) The Board's ability to verify claims about competitive effects, service impacts, and shipper/consumer harms; (4) The admissibility or weight given to Dr. Bailey's economic testimony if the underlying data cannot be reconciled or independently verified; (5) Whether Applicants complied with STB Discovery decision requiring submission of 100% traffic tapes. The undisclosed third dataset—appearing only in workpapers—may trigger questions about whether applicants' pre-filing obligations were satisfied and whether interested parties had adequate notice to prepare responsive economic analyses during the comment period.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No explicit deadline stated, but this is addressed to Applicants' counsel as a request for clarification, likely requiring response during the comment/discovery phase before substantive hearing. The filing was served on ALJ Soulikias and the STB Office of Chief Counsel, creating a formal record.

docket_entries.title: CSX Reply Supporting BNSF Motion to Compel Discovery of UP/NS Board Materials, Banker Materials, and Internal Communications
docket_entries.entry_summary: CSX Transportation, a major Class I railroad competitor, filed a reply supporting BNSF Railway's motion to compel discovery of Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern's board materials, banker materials, and internal email communications. CSX argues that these materials are "highly relevant in evaluating the potential competitive effects of the proposed merger; potential conditions that would mitigate merger-related harms; alternatives to the proposed merger; and a variety of other issues central to this matter." CSX emphasizes that internal documents of this type are "ubiquitous" in merger litigation, citing FTC v. Whole Foods (548 F.3d 1028) and United States v. Aetna (240 F. Supp. 3d 1), and notes that courts have found withholding of relevant emails "indefensible." CSX further contends that discovery proportionality is satisfied given "the magnitude and importance of the merger to American railroading." CSX explicitly requests that the STB "defer the Procedural Schedule until the Applicants satisfy their discovery obligations." This filing reveals active competitor skepticism about applicant transparency and signals that CSX views the withheld materials as potentially damaging to the merger case, likely containing competitive analysis or strategy that would support denial or strict conditions.
key_arguments: Internal board materials, banker materials, and email communications are essential evidence 'highly relevant in evaluating the potential competitive effects of the proposed merger; potential conditions that would mitigate merger-related harms; alternatives to the proposed merger; and a variety of other issues central to this matter'
These categories of materials are 'ubiquitous' in merger litigation and routinely relied upon by courts (citing FTC v. Whole Foods and United States v. Aetna)
Withholding of relevant internal communications has been characterized by courts as 'indefensible' (citing Parsi v. Daioleslam)

Discovery proportionality is satisfied because the Applicants themselves have emphasized 'the magnitude and importance of the merger to American railroading,' making production of central materials proportional to the scope of the combination
The procedural schedule should be deferred until Applicants fully comply with discovery obligations
key_excerpts: the Applicants' board materials, banker materials, and email communications are highly relevant in evaluating the potential competitive effects of the proposed merger; potential conditions that would mitigate merger-related harms; alternatives to the proposed merger; and a variety of other issues central to this matter
these materials are routinely and regularly relied upon in merger litigations and have been referred to as 'ubiquitous' by courts evaluating mergers
requiring Applicants to turn over materials that are central to the issues is proportional to the magnitude of the proposed combination

CSXT agrees with the Motion's request that should the Board accept the Application for further proceedings, the Board should defer the Procedural Schedule until the Applicants satisfy their discovery obligations
docket_entries.relief_requested: CSX joins BNSF's motion to compel discovery of: (1) Applicants' board materials; (2) banker materials; and (3) email communications. CSX further requests that the STB defer the procedural schedule until the Applicants satisfy their discovery obligations.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This discovery motion and CSX's support for it directly impacts the evidentiary foundation for the merger review. If granted, compelled production of board materials, banker communications, and internal emails could substantially expand the factual record regarding applicants' internal competitive analysis, merger rationale, and consideration of alternatives. This could establish evidence of competitive intent or harm that would strengthen intervenor arguments for denial or conditions. The request to defer the procedural schedule also creates scheduling leverage: delay of the timeline pending discovery compliance could extend the proceeding, increase uncertainty, and create cost/business planning pressure on applicants. The reference to merger litigation standards (FTC and antitrust case law) signals that CSX is framing this discovery dispute in merger antitrust terms, not merely railroad regulatory language.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No explicit deadline stated, but reply to BNSF's January 9 motion—applicants will likely file response brief within STB procedural schedule

docket_entries.title: CSX Reply Supporting CN Motion to Compel Disclosure of Merger Agreement Schedule 5.8
docket_entries.entry_summary: CSX Transportation, a major Class I railroad competitor, filed a reply supporting Canadian National's (Grand Trunk Corporation's) Motion to Compel the disclosure of Schedule 5.8 and other schedules to the UP/NS merger agreement. CSX argues that: (1) Schedule 5.8 and all merger agreement schedules are 'plainly relevant' to the proceeding and are at the 'heart of this matter'; (2) no legal privilege protects these documents because they reflect 'contractual terms negotiated between two adverse entities' and are therefore not confidential; (3) work product privilege does not apply because the schedules were 'exchanged between adverse parties' and 'were not created in anticipation of or for use during litigation'; (4) common interest privilege fails because 'the common interest between the parties was a business interest rather than a legal interest'; (5) any privilege was waived when the schedules 'were shared with the Applicants' banks who provided fairness opinions.' Most significantly, CSX 'respectfully submits this Reply without waiving its argument that Applicants' omission of Schedule 5.8 or any other schedule, exhibit, or attachment to the merger agreement renders the Application incomplete as a matter of law.' This procedural challenge, if successful, could require the applicants to amend their application or face challenges to its legal sufficiency. CSX's framing ties the motion to the fundamental adequacy of the Application itself, not merely discovery convenience.
key_arguments: Schedule 5.8 and merger agreement schedules are 'at the heart of this matter' and 'plainly relevant' to the STB proceeding, making their disclosure essential to the record.
No attorney-client privilege applies because schedules reflect 'contractual terms negotiated between two adverse entities' that are not confidential.
Work product privilege is waived because schedules were 'exchanged between adverse parties' and were not 'created in anticipation of or for use during litigation.'
Common interest privilege fails because 'the common interest between the parties was a business interest rather than a legal interest,' not a legal interest qualifying for privilege.
Any residual privilege was waived when schedules were 'shared with the Applicants' banks who provided fairness opinions,' triggering waiver rules for voluntary disclosure to third parties.

Applicants' omission of Schedule 5.8 and merger agreement schedules from the application 'renders the Application incomplete as a matter of law,' creating a threshold defect in the application itself independent of discovery merits.
key_excerpts: the merger agreement, which is at the heart of this matter, is plainly relevant, as are any schedules, attachments, and exhibits to that merger agreement.
Schedule 5.8 and all other schedules, exhibits, and attachments to the merger agreement reflect contractual terms negotiated between two adverse entities and are therefore not privileged.
Applicants' omission of Schedule 5.8 or any other schedule, exhibit, or attachment to the merger agreement renders the Application incomplete as a matter of law.
docket_entries.relief_requested: CSX joins and supports Grand Trunk Corporation's Motion to Compel disclosure of Schedule 5.8 and all other schedules, attachments, and exhibits to the merger agreement. CSX also argues that the Applicants' omission of Schedule 5.8 from the application renders the Application incomplete as a matter of law.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing introduces a completeness challenge to the merger application itself—CSX is arguing that omission of merger agreement schedules is not merely a discovery dispute but a threshold defect rendering the application legally insufficient. If the ALJ or STB agrees, the applicants could be forced to amend the application or the ALJ could determine the record is incomplete as a matter of law. This is distinct from a simple discovery dispute; it challenges the adequacy of the filings that triggered STB jurisdiction. CSX's invocation of privilege waiver doctrine (particularly the fairness opinion disclosure) and its citation to commercial contract law precedents (In re Grand Jury Subpoena, In re Sealed Case) attempts to reframe what applicants likely claim are confidential transaction documents as business records entitled to no protection. The 'incomplete application' argument could provide a procedural basis to disrupt the hearing schedule or impose sanctions on applicants for filing defectively.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No explicit response deadline stated in the reply itself; applicants would typically have 10-14 days to respond to a compel motion unless the ALJ sets a different schedule. The Motion to Compel (CN-7) filed January 8 would govern deadlines.

docket_entries.title: Atlantic Systems Inc. challenges application completeness; demands IMC capital plans, environmental impact analysis, and verified testimony on 2-million-truck diversion feasibility
docket_entries.entry_summary: Atlantic Systems challenges whether Union Pacific's December 19, 2025 application is complete and factually supported. They argue the applicants have dramatically underestimated capital requirements and failed to provide essential evidence that Intermodal Marketing Companies (IMCs) can or will execute the merger's central promise: diverting 2 million trucks to rail annually. Specifically: (1) UPNS modified the Uniform Railroad Costing System (URCS) in ways that 'could materially misstate net revenues for diverted traffic'; (2) A single IMC handling all diverted traffic would require $2.69 billion in capital investment ($1.14B for containers, $550M for chassis, $900M for tractors, $100M for terminals/IT), yet applicants provided 'no such plan...for their prospective IMC partners'; (3) The Environmental Impact Statement ignores localized 'hot spots' of congestion and air pollution at urban terminals where millions of truck drayages will concentrate—'excluded from the Application's Environmental Impact Statement because technically caused by IMC partners not UPNS'; (4) STG Logistics, the fourth-largest IMC, declared bankruptcy on January 12, 2026, with UP holding $13.4M in unpaid claims, yet applicants have no verified testimony from solvent IMCs committing to the expansion. Robertson states: 'While laudable, it is an enormous undertaking that requires the total commitment of the IMC community. The application as it stands does not indicate whether the IMCs as a group have the capital, operational capability, or the willingness to expand.' The filing is NOT challenging the 2-million-truck diversion methodology itself, but demanding the STB not rely on it without proof of execution. They explicitly request the Application be deemed incomplete unless these four elements are provided.
key_arguments: URCS modification underestimates intermodal equipment costs, creating material misstatement of net revenues for traffic diversions claimed in the application

Applicants project 2 million annual truck diversions but provide zero capital plan, operating plan, or business case for IMC partners required to execute this—IMC expansion would require ~$2.69 billion in new assets (containers, chassis, tractors, terminals) not addressed in merger filing

A purpose-built or expanded IMC would be 'roughly the size of J.B. Hunt's entire current intermodal business' yet applicants have not demonstrated where IMCs would source 2 million units or whether they would cannibalize their own higher-margin operations

Environmental Impact Statement is incomplete because it excludes localized pollution and congestion 'hot spots' at urban intermodal terminals where millions of truck drayages would concentrate—impacts technically attributable to IMC operations rather than railroad, but inseparable from merger benefits

No verified sworn testimony from IMC partners confirming financial capability, operational readiness, or commitment to invest billions; STG Logistics (4th-largest IMC) filed bankruptcy January 12, 2026, with UP holding $13.4M in unpaid claims, raising questions about IMC financial viability

Application lacks answers to fundamental logistics questions: Would IMCs divert from their own over-the-road operations (cannibalizing higher-margin business)? Would they poach units from competing IMCs? The filing contains no credible sourcing strategy
key_excerpts: While the applicants made representations concerning the capital expenditures required for rail line and terminal upgrades, their modification of URCS (Uniform Railroad Costing System) costing appears to understate intermodal equipment costs. This could have the effect of materially misstating net revenues for the diverted traffic.

While UPNS offered plans for the operations on their combined railroad, no such plan was offered for their prospective IMC (Intermodal Marketing Company) partners. At present, railroads serve as wholesalers providing linehaul services to IMCs such as Hub Group, STG Logistics and J.B. Hunt.

If a purpose-built IMC were started to handle all new intermodal traffic, our estimate for the capital requirements is: 53' Containers 120,000 @ $9,500 = $1.14B; Chassis 100,000 @ $5,500 = $550M; Tractors 5,000 @ $180,000 = $900M; Terminals/IT = $100M; Total CAPEX = $2.69 Billion.

While this is a 'green' alternative on a macro scale, it creates severe localized environmental impacts. Consolidating millions of truck movements into a handful of urban intermodal terminals will create localized congestion and air quality 'hot spots.' Because these negative consequences are technically caused by the IMC partners not UPNS, they have been excluded from the Application's Environmental Impact Statement.
The fourth largest IMC, STG Logistics, declared bankruptcy on January 12, 2026. Importantly, STG's largest creditor is the Union Pacific, which is owed more than $13.4 million.

The UPNS central argument is that the merger will allow 2 million trucks to be taken off the highway. To be clear, currently we are not questioning UP's traffic diversion study methodology nor the net result of 2 million truck diversions. We are saying that such an enormous change to the country's logistics system will have require massive investments by UP and the IMC community that are not in the December 19th Application.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deem the Application INCOMPLETE and DEFICIENT until four specific items are provided: (1) Full equipment investment detail and accounting treatment for traffic conversions; (2) Comprehensive IMC business plan from either a purpose-built IMC or verified expansion programs by existing IMCs; (3) Amended Environmental Impact Statement covering congestion and pollution impacts at urban terminals; (4) Verified testimony from partner IMCs validating commitment and capability for the 2-million-unit growth model. 'In the absence of this information, it will be impossible to make a complete analysis of the market impact of the proposed UPNS Merger. Otherwise, the Application is deficient and should be deemed incomplete.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing creates a 'completeness' challenge under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 and STB merger review standards. If accepted, it shifts burden to applicants to prove not just that diversion is possible, but that execution partners (IMCs) have committed capital and operational capacity. The filing also creates an Environmental Impact Analysis adequacy issue—if IMC terminal impacts must be included in the merger's environmental review (because causally connected to merger benefits), applicants must amend their EIS. The identification of STG Logistics bankruptcy and UP's $13.4M claim introduces credit/counterparty risk that was not disclosed in the application. This is procedurally significant because STB may order supplemental filings before the comment period closes, potentially extending the timeline and imposing additional burden on applicants to prove execution feasibility.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (With Comment)
docket_entries.deadline_description: No explicit deadline stated; Atlantic Systems requests application be deemed incomplete until conditions met. STB will determine whether to require supplemental filings or allow applicants to respond during comment period.

docket_entries.title: Notice of Appearance of Additional Counsel - Anacostia Rail Holdings Short Lines
docket_entries.filer_name: Anacostia Rail Holdings (CSS, LIRA, NY&A, PHL)
docket_entries.entry_summary: Four short-line railroads under common ownership by Anacostia Rail Holdings Company filed a notice of appearance for additional counsel in the UP-NS merger proceeding. The filing adds Mark H. Sidman, General Counsel & Corporate Secretary of Anacostia Rail Holdings, as counsel of record and requests he be added to the service list for all future documents. This is purely procedural—no substantive position on the merger is stated, and no comments, conditions, or relief requests beyond the appearance itself are included. The engagement of experienced transportation counsel (Slover & Loftus LLP) suggests these short lines intend to actively monitor the proceeding and are preparing to submit substantive filings, but their specific concerns or positions remain unstated at this stage.
key_excerpts: Parties-of-Record Chicago South Shore & South Bend Railroad (CSS), Louisville & Indiana Railroad Company (LIRA), New York & Atlantic Railway Company (NY&A), and Pacific Harbor Line, Inc. (PHL), which are all part of Anacostia Rail Holdings Company, hereby file this notice of appearance of additional counsel representing the four railroads in this proceeding.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Addition of Mark H. Sidman (General Counsel & Corporate Secretary of Anacostia Rail Holdings) to the Board's service list as counsel of record for the four Anacostia-affiliated railroads.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing does not change the scope of review or evidentiary burden, but it formally establishes that a group of competitor short-line railroads—which may have competitive interests in markets overlapping with UP and NS operations—are now represented by counsel in the proceeding. The engagement of Slover & Loftus, a top-tier STB practice firm, indicates these carriers are preparing for substantive participation. This signals potential for future conditional opposition or settlement negotiations if Anacostia carriers identify specific harms (e.g., loss of interline service, rate discrimination, terminal access restrictions).
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.deadline_description: Procedural filing; no response required from other parties.

docket_entries.title: Notice of Appearance of Additional Counsel - Anacostia Rail Holdings short-line portfolio
docket_entries.entry_summary: Anacostia Rail Holdings Company, which owns four regional and short-line railroads (Chicago South Shore & South Bend Railroad, Louisville & Indiana Railroad Company, New York & Atlantic Railway Company, and Pacific Harbor Line, Inc.), filed notice that Aimee Nolan, its Chief Legal Officer, has appeared as additional counsel representing these four railroads in the UP/NS merger proceeding. The filing provides Nolan's contact information and confirms her consent to email service. This is a routine procedural filing establishing counsel of record and does not indicate the position these carriers will take on the merger's substance.
key_excerpts: Chicago South Shore & South Bend Railroad (CSS), Louisville & Indiana Railroad Company (LIRA), New York & Atlantic Railway Company (NY&A), and Pacific Habor Line, Inc. (PHL), which are all part of Anacostia Rail Holdings Company, hereby file this notice of appearance of additional counsel representing the four railroads in this proceeding.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Addition of Aimee Nolan, Chief Legal Officer of Anacostia Rail Holdings Company, as counsel of record for the four Anacostia-owned railroads in this proceeding.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This establishes formal counsel representation for Anacostia's four railroads as parties of record. These carriers are now positioned to receive all service copies, participate in discovery, and potentially file substantive comments or testimony. The involvement of in-house general counsel (rather than outside counsel only) suggests these carriers view the merger as material to their competitive position and plan active engagement. This is a low-significance procedural milestone but confirms that a significant regional competitor portfolio is actively monitoring the proceeding.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.deadline_description: Procedural notice only; no response deadline

docket_entries.title: Joint Shipper Associations' Support for BNSF Motion to Compel Discovery
docket_entries.filer_name: Joint Shipper Associations (ACC, ACD, AFPM, TFI)
docket_entries.entry_summary: Five major shipper associations (American Chemistry Council, Alliance for Chemical Distribution, American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers, National Industrial Transportation League, The Fertilizer Institute) filed a joint statement supporting BNSF's Motion to Compel discovery, arguing that UP and NS's failure to produce basic discovery materials prevents meaningful evaluation of 'the largest rail merger in U.S. history, the first major transaction the Board will decide under its 2001 merger rules, and a merger likely to trigger a complete restructuring of the North American rail industry.' The Associations reject the Applicants' implicit argument that only competitor railroads oppose the deal, emphasizing that shippers are among the Applicants' largest customers and have significant independent interests. They argue: 'Discovery is critical to clarifying the merger's effects. When UP and NS refuse to meet fundamental discovery obligations, they harm all interested parties by withholding information needed to develop informed comments.' The Associations note that UP and NS's contradictory positions 'undermine their claims that the merger will create tremendous public benefits with virtually no competitive consequences.' They emphasize that shipper access to discovery is essential because 'shippers cannot effectively assess and comment on the merger within the proposed procedural schedule' without it. Regarding confidentiality objections, the Associations argue that the Board's protective order—which permits designation of materials as 'Highly Confidential' with access limited to outside counsel and consultants—provides 'robust safeguards' that do not justify withholding core information. The filing signals that shippers will not be passive stakeholders but active participants demanding transparency and adequate time to evaluate competitive impacts.
key_arguments: UP and NS's discovery deficiency harms shippers' ability to participate in this proceeding: 'When UP and NS refuse to meet fundamental discovery obligations, they harm all interested parties by withholding information needed to develop informed comments.' The Associations specifically state shippers 'cannot effectively assess and comment on the merger within the proposed procedural schedule' without access to discovery.

Shipper opposition is independent of competitor interests: 'Applicants have implied that other Class I railroads oppose the UP/NS merger because they are UP and NS's primary competitors. But this ignores shippers' significant interest in this proceeding.' Shippers are among the Applicants' largest customers and have distinct concerns about pricing and service.

The Applicants' inconsistent positions undermine claimed pro-competitive benefits: 'To date, UP has been at war with its own positions' and '[t]his merger raises enormous concerns for our member companies' while 'Applicants' contradictions undermine their claims that the merger will create tremendous public benefits with virtually no competitive consequences.'

Confidentiality protections are sufficient to require full discovery: The Board's protective order permitting 'Highly Confidential' designation with access limited to outside counsel 'provides robust safeguards' that do not justify refusing to produce 'core information.'
key_excerpts: This merger will irreversibly shape American railroading for decades... To date, UP has been at war with its own positions. [This failure to provide discovery] is untenable in a transaction of this magnitude—the largest rail merger in U.S. history, the first major transaction the Board will decide under its 2001 merger rules, and a merger likely to trigger a complete restructuring of the North American rail industry.

When UP and NS refuse to meet fundamental discovery obligations, they harm all interested parties by withholding information needed to develop informed comments... shippers cannot effectively assess and comment on the merger within the proposed procedural schedule.

Applicants have implied that other Class I railroads oppose the UP/NS merger because they are UP and NS's primary competitors. But this ignores shippers' significant interest in this proceeding. This merger raises enormous concerns for our member companies, who are among the Applicants' largest customers by traffic volume.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Grant BNSF's Motion to Compel requiring UP and NS to produce discovery responses; ensure shippers have access to discovery materials needed to evaluate merger impacts within the procedural schedule
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing establishes that discovery disputes directly implicate the substantive evaluation rights of non-competing intervenors. It frames discovery adequacy as a procedural due process issue affecting shipper participation, not merely a competitive gamesmanship concern between railroads. This may strengthen arguments for compelling discovery by showing that withholding information harms the Board's information base for evaluating public interest impacts beyond competition. The filing also establishes a factual record that shippers were unable to develop informed positions within the procedural schedule due to discovery deficiency, which could support later arguments that procedural shortcuts disadvantaged substantive evaluation by affected customers.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Support filing for Motion to Compel; no response deadline created by this filing itself

docket_entries.title: Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern Joint Submission of 16 Additional Stakeholder Support Letters
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern jointly submitted 16 additional letters of support for the merger, including 13 from customers (representing coal, agricultural products, lumber, energy, and intermodal sectors), one from Mayor Wanda Williams of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania (highlighting NS's role as a major regional hub with 637,000 containers/trailers annually through Harrisburg and Rutherford Yards), one from Indiana House Representative Earl Harris (citing benefits for state economy and freight reliability), and one from the International Brotherhood of Boilermakers union (noting a prior historic labor agreement with Union Pacific protecting member jobs). The letters present a consistent set of claimed benefits: improved service reliability through more direct routes, reduced transit times by eliminating interchanges (claimed to remove 'several days' from shipping), increased investment in infrastructure and equipment, and expanded geographic reach. America's Power argues that the merger will benefit coal-fired electricity generation by ensuring timely coal deliveries and reducing congestion. Mayor Williams emphasizes reduced highway truck traffic and safer roads. The Boilermakers union specifically references an agreement already in place protecting member jobs 'for the length of their careers following the merger transaction.' The filing is a coordinated pro-merger campaign designed to demonstrate broad stakeholder support rather than new legal or economic analysis.
key_arguments: The merged railroad will offer more direct routes and greater flexibility, minimizing service disruption risks to coal power plants, agricultural producers, manufacturers, and energy companies that depend on rail
Transit time reduction by eliminating interchanges will remove several days from shipping times, allowing customers to deliver goods faster to more markets and reach new customers
The transcontinental railroad will be better positioned to invest in infrastructure, technology, and equipment, improving service quality, capacity, and safety across all industries served

America's Power argues railroads transport roughly 70 percent of coal used by U.S. power plants, and many plants depend solely on rail service; a merged network will improve reliability critical to maintaining coal stockpiles and matching electricity supply to demand
Mayor Williams argues the merger will reduce long-haul truck traffic on highways and bridges, alleviating congestion, improving safety, and saving taxpayers time and money

The International Brotherhood of Boilermakers has already negotiated an historic agreement with Union Pacific protecting member jobs for the length of their careers following the merger, laying groundwork for a stronger future

Indiana House Representative Harris emphasizes the merger strengthens the national transportation network, supports economic development, and ensures American freight rail remains globally competitive
key_excerpts: Railroads transport roughly 70 percent of the coal used by U.S. power plants, and many plants depend solely on rail service for coal deliveries. This dependence on rail transportation underscores the importance of ensuring that the Board's review of the proposed merger takes into account the role of coal-based electricity and the supply chain that supports it. Timely and consistent coal deliveries allow coal power plants to maintain stockpiles of fuel that enable plant operators to match electricity supply and demand at all times.
By eliminating interchanges where rail cars are handed off, the combination will remove several days from transit times, enabling us to deliver more goods to more customers, faster.

By establishing the nation's first seamless coast-to-coast rail network, this merger will enhance the efficiency and affordability of freight rail, encouraging more businesses to choose this safer and more sustainable mode of transportation. The resulting increase in freight traffic through our intermodal facilities will stimulate job growth in the rail sector and strengthen Harrisburg's position as a prime location for manufacturers seeking reliable, accessible transportation infrastructure.

Increased rail efficiency will reduce the number of long-haul trucks on our highways and bridges—vehicles that place significant strain on shared infrastructure and pose safety risks to our communities. Alleviating highway congestion will save taxpayers time and money while making our roads safer for everyone.

Recently, the Boilermakers union and Union Pacific entered into an historic agreement that protects our members' jobs for the length of their careers following the merger transaction. We believe the commitments already in place—and the shared understanding reflected in our agreement—lay the groundwork for a stronger, more resilient and more opportunity-rich future for every union Boilermaker serving the railroad industry.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Approval of the proposed merger between Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing demonstrates organized stakeholder mobilization on behalf of the applicants during the comment phase. While not legal arguments, the filing shows the applicants have secured commitments from major customer sectors (coal, agriculture, lumber, energy, intermodal), municipal government support (Harrisburg), state legislative support (Indiana), and labor union support (Boilermakers with an existing labor agreement already in place). The labor union letter is particularly significant as it references an already-negotiated historic agreement protecting jobs, suggesting the applicants may have resolved labor concerns that could have been raised as barriers to approval. The Mayor's letter detailing specific container/trailer volumes (637,000 annually) and the geographic/economic significance of NS facilities provides concrete evidence of local economic dependence on the merger proceeding. This coordinated filing may influence the Board's perception of deal support among directly affected stakeholders and could affect how contested intervenors (competitors, shippers with NS access concerns) frame their opposition.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Support submission; no response deadline

docket_entries.title: Union Pacific Response to Grand Trunk Data Production Inquiry – Clarification of Traffic Data Discrepancies
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific responds to Grand Trunk Corporation's inquiry about discrepancies in traffic data productions by explaining that different datasets were produced in response to different requests at different times. UP clarifies that the proper datasets for competitive analysis are 'the data in the workpapers submitted with the Application.' Regarding the '31.3 million additional records' in Dr. Bailey's dataset, UP explains that all but 1,227 records either fell outside the 2019-2024 period requested by the Board or involved non-waybilled movements, and that Dr. Bailey excluded even the 1,227 records because they involved locomotives or end-of-train devices excluded from her analyses. For Norfolk Southern, UP states that data produced to the Board reflects 'the Board's specific instructions' while application workpapers 'reflect certain adjustments to ensure accurate treatment of intermodal traffic, the removal of voided waybills, and the addition of shoulder months.' UP offers to help clarify such issues informally in the future, signaling openness to resolving data confusion without requiring formal motion practice.
key_arguments: The proper baseline for intervenor analysis is 'the data in the workpapers submitted with the Application,' not separately produced Board data, because workpapers reflect data adjusted for accurate intermodal treatment and removal of voided waybills.

The apparent 31.3 million 'additional' records in Dr. Bailey's dataset is substantially explained by inclusion of records outside the Board's requested 2019-2024 period and non-waybilled movements; only 1,227 records fell outside these categories, and those were properly excluded from analysis as locomotive/end-of-train movements.

Different data productions reflect Board-mandated production requirements (fields kept in ordinary course of business) versus Application workpaper adjustments for analytical purposes; this distinction explains apparent discrepancies rather than indicating data inconsistency.
UP characterizes the issue as resolvable confusion rather than evidentiary deficiency, offering informal resolution to avoid formal discovery disputes.
key_excerpts: Applicants' analyses used the data in the workpapers submitted with the Application.

Of the 31.3 million 'additional' records in Dr. Bailey's workpapers, all except 1,227 records—i.e., 0.000012 of the records that Union Pacific provided the Board—either had waybill dates outside of the 2019 to 2024 period requested by the Board or involved movements that were not waybilled traffic and thus had no waybill number or waybill date.

The data produced to the Board reflects the Board's specific instructions and its instruction to produce data as kept in the ordinary course of business. The data files in the Application workpapers that were used for the analyses in the Application reflect certain adjustments to ensure accurate treatment of intermodal traffic, the removal of voided waybills, and the addition of 'shoulder months.'
docket_entries.relief_requested: Implicit: to clarify that traffic data submitted with the Application represents the proper dataset for competitive analysis, addressing intervenor concerns about data consistency and comparability.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing addresses an evidentiary completeness and reliability issue that could affect the Administrative Law Judge's (ALJ's) assessment of Union Pacific's competitive impact analysis. If intervenors successfully argue that UP's datasets were manipulated or selected to support merger justification, it could undermine the foundational economic evidence in the Application. Conversely, UP's detailed explanation of data production rationale and Dr. Bailey's exclusion methodology may preempt challenges to the workpapers' reliability. The filing also signals UP's willingness to resolve data disputes informally rather than through motion practice, which may reduce friction in discovery and limit opportunities for procedural delay. The specific quantification (0.000012 of records; 1,227 properly excluded records) is designed to rebut insinuations of large-scale data manipulation.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Response to prior inquiry; no deadline imposed on other parties

docket_entries.title: Smart Sand, Inc. Notice of Intent to Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.entry_summary: Smart Sand, Inc. filed a notice of intent to participate in the UP/NS merger proceeding without submitting any substantive comments, positions, or conditions. The company designated Thompson Hine LLP (Sandra L. Brown and David E. Benz) as counsel and requested direct service of all filings. This is purely procedural—Smart Sand has secured party status in the docket but has not disclosed whether it opposes, supports, or is neutral on the merger, nor has it indicated what issues concern it (e.g., rate increases, service reliability, competitive access to transportation, or divestitures). As a sand/proppant shipper dependent on rail transport, the company likely has interests in maintaining competitive railroad options and stable freight rates, but those interests remain unstated.
key_excerpts: Smart Sand, Inc. hereby gives notice of its intent to participate in the above-captioned proceeding.
docket_entries.relief_requested: None specified. Filing is procedural notice only.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: None. This is a procedural filing establishing standing/intervention status only. It creates no new issues, discovery obligations, or substantive claims requiring STB response. However, the filing indicates that a significant sand/proppant supplier is monitoring the merger, suggesting the shipper community includes parties with material interests—though Smart Sand has not yet articulated what those interests are or whether they align with the applicants or opposing coalitions.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)

docket_entries.title: STB Waybill Access Approval for CPKC Outside Counsel (Sullivan & Cromwell Attorney)
docket_entries.entry_summary: The STB's Office of Economics approved CPKC's request to add C. Andrew Gerlach of Sullivan & Cromwell LLP to its existing waybill access authorization (WB25-53) in the UP/NS merger docket. CPKC sought this access 'for outside counsel and consultants working on behalf of CPKC' with the purpose remaining consistent with prior authorization granted in David Meyer's August 26, 2025 letter. The approval is conditioned on standard confidentiality agreement language requiring compliance with CCWS data release conditions, certification of data destruction/return within 30 days of expiration, and prior payment of the $72 per-person fee. This filing demonstrates CPKC's active preparation of a competitive impact analysis using confidential waybill data, likely to support opposition arguments regarding rail service diversion, competitive constraint loss, or rate impacts in the merger.
key_excerpts: CPKC wishes to provide access to an additional attorney at Sullivan and Cromwell LLP. The purpose of access by outside counsel remains the same as that set forth in David Meyer's August 26, 2025 letter.

I agree to comply fully with these conditions and the provisions of this confidentiality agreement. No later than thirty days before the agreement expires, I will request an extension of this agreement, if necessary. If no extension is requested, I will return or destroy all CCWS data and certify that I have done so.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Approval to grant waybill data access to C. Andrew Gerlach of Sullivan & Cromwell LLP for CPKC's use in Finance Docket No. 36873, subject to standard CCWS confidentiality agreement.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing does not alter the scope or burden of review, but documents CPKC's engagement of specialized transportation/railroad M&A counsel (Sullivan & Cromwell is a major M&A firm). The approval grants access to confidential waybill operational data under 49 C.F.R. § 1244.9(b)(4), indicating CPKC intends to support its opposition position (if taken) with empirical competitive impact analysis rather than relying solely on generic antitrust arguments. The fact that additional counsel is being added post-initial waybill authorization suggests CPKC is deepening its analysis or preparing for hearing phase testimony.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Administrative approval granted; no further action required from applicants or other intervenors.

docket_entries.title: Union Pacific Submission of Additional Workpapers and Supporting Materials
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific filed additional workpapers and supporting materials pursuant to STB Decision No. 8. The submission consists of four separate zip files containing intermediate datasets and materials supporting verified statements by Dr. Elizabeth M. Bailey, Hunt/Schabas, Gehringer/Orr, and Rocker/Elkins—all components of Applicants' December 19, 2025 Application. Applicants note that most files are 'provided as a courtesy to the requesting parties,' but some were 'inadvertently omitted from Applicants' original workpaper upload.' Materials were uploaded to the Kiteworks SFTP site in folder 'Updated Workpaper Files (1.15.2026).' Applicants express willingness to confer with the Board on alternative mechanisms for future workpaper submissions. This follows a prior January 5, 2026 supplemental workpaper submission (UP-18/NS-17) using the same upload methodology.
key_arguments: Applicants are providing intermediate datasets and related materials to support expert testimony on economics, financial projections, and operational analysis
Some files were inadvertently omitted from the original December 19, 2025 Application workpaper upload and are now being supplied
Applicants remain willing to work with the Board on alternative mechanisms for managing voluminous workpaper submissions
key_excerpts: Applicants are making available to the Board and parties in this proceeding...materials supporting four parts of the Application filed December 19, 2025

Most of the files are intermediate datasets or similar files that Applicants are providing as a courtesy to the requesting parties, but some are files that were inadvertently omitted from Applicants' original workpaper upload
docket_entries.relief_requested: Not explicitly stated; implicit: approval of merger application. This filing provides supporting workpapers and materials in compliance with STB Decision No. 8.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Procedural filing demonstrating compliance with STB discovery obligations under Decision No. 8. Completeness of workpaper submissions can affect: (1) evidentiary sufficiency of expert testimony at hearing, (2) ability of intervenors to conduct adequate discovery and rebuttal analysis, and (3) hearing schedule. Omission of materials from original Application could trigger follow-up discovery requests or hearing challenges to testimony foundation. Court-appointed special masters or ALJs commonly scrutinize whether workpaper records are sufficiently complete and accessible.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No specific deadline imposed by this filing; submission is responsive to prior Board order

docket_entries.title: Union Pacific - Filing/Workpapers (2026-01-15)
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific filed workpapers on January 15, 2026, in support of its acquisition of Norfolk Southern. As a Party filing during the Discovery phase, this submission likely contains detailed technical, financial, operational, and competitive analysis supporting the transaction. The specific contents of these workpapers are not detailed in the entry metadata, but such filings typically include: financial projections, operational integration plans, competitive analysis demonstrating procompetitive effects, service quality commitments, and responses to regulatory concerns. The filing establishes Union Pacific's affirmative case for approval and provides the evidentiary foundation against which intervenor oppositions and STB analysis will be measured.
key_arguments: Unable to determine specific arguments from metadata - requires access to full filing content
key_excerpts: Unable to provide verbatim excerpts from metadata - requires access to full filing content
docket_entries.relief_requested: Approval of Union Pacific's acquisition of control of Norfolk Southern Corporation and Norfolk Southern Railway Company
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Party filings establish the evidentiary record in merger proceedings. Union Pacific's workpapers will define the scope of competitive analysis, operational feasibility claims, and service/financial benefits arguments. The adequacy and completeness of these workpapers will determine whether STB staff has sufficient information to evaluate the transaction and will likely be subject to discovery requests and cross-examination from intervenors. Any deficiencies in supporting documentation could undermine UP's burden of proof.
