docket_entries.title: Notice of Intent to Participate - County Line Rail Fund I, LP; CLIP Property Owner LLC; Sabine River & Northern Railroad LLC
docket_entries.filer_name: County Line Rail Fund I / CLIP Property Owner / Sabine River & Northern Railroad
docket_entries.entry_summary: County Line Rail Fund I, LP, CLIP Property Owner LLC, and Sabine River & Northern Railroad LLC filed a bare notice of intent to participate in the UP/NS merger proceeding as Parties of Record. They requested placement on the official service list through counsel Thomas W. Wilcox. No substantive position on the merger, conditions, or arguments are presented in this filing—it is purely procedural. The identity of Sabine River & Northern Railroad (a Gulf Coast short line operator) suggests these entities may have competitive or operational interests in a UP-NS combination, but those interests remain undisclosed until substantive comments are filed.
key_excerpts: County Line Rail Fund I, LP, CLIP Property Owner LLC, and Sabine River & Northern Railroad LLC, hereby provide notice of their intent to participate in this proceeding, each as Party of Record.
They request that the undersigned be placed on the official service list as their representative.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Placement on official service list as Party of Record to participate in the proceeding
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing establishes intervenor standing for three entities. The inclusion of Sabine River & Northern Railroad—an operating short line—as a Party of Record suggests rail competition or operational integration issues may be raised in subsequent substantive filings. Monitor for follow-up comments or testimony that would clarify the nature of their merger concerns.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.deadline_description: Procedural notice; no response deadline, but substantive filings should be anticipated in Comment or Hearing phases

docket_entries.title: Surface Transportation Board Decision Rejecting UP-NS Merger Application as Incomplete
docket_entries.entry_summary: The STB rejected Union Pacific Corporation's application to acquire control of Norfolk Southern Corporation without prejudice to refiling. The rejection was based on incomplete impact analyses lacking projected market shares consistent with applicants' claims of merger-related growth, and failure to submit the complete merger agreement including disclosure schedules and other incorporated documents.
key_arguments: Impact analyses failed to include forward-looking market share projections despite applicants claiming 15-26% post-merger growth and 1.864 million carloads annual diversion
Applicants simply added 2023 actual market shares without accounting for anticipated merger-related growth impacts over three-year realization period
Complete merger agreement was not provided, specifically Schedule 5.8 and Company/Parent Disclosure Schedules that define 'Materially Burdensome Regulatory Condition' and other material terms

Related TRRA control application was misclassified as 'minor' when it should be 'significant' given potential anticompetitive effects from UP controlling both TRRA and competitor Alton & Southern Railway
Projections in Board's major merger rules require demonstration of transaction impacts on competition, necessitating forward-looking analysis beyond base year
key_excerpts: The Application is incomplete because it does not contain certain information required by the Board's regulations. Specifically, the Application is incomplete because its impact analyses required by 49 C.F.R. § 1180.7(b) do not contain market share projections for the entity to be created by the Transaction that are consistent with the claims elsewhere in the Application that the new entity would experience growth by diverting traffic from trucks and other rail carriers.

Bailey's approach of simply adding historic market shares together is therefore not the requisite 'project[ion]' of the Transaction's competitive impact under § 1180.7(b)(2), (3), and (4), given Applicants' claims elsewhere in the Application that the merger will result in significant traffic and revenue growth.

The omitted disclosure schedules, exhibits, and other documents supply terms of the contract and are expressly deemed to be part of it by Sections 5.8(e) and 8.10, and they at minimum constitute 'other written instrument[s] entered into . . . pertaining to the proposed transaction.'

Applicants' control of TRRA could raise 'the potential for manipulation of [the terminal and switching carrier] in the interests of the majority owner' and the Board cannot find that anticompetitive effects will clearly not occur or be outweighed by public benefits.

docket_entries.title: Congressional Letter Opposing Norfolk Southern-Union Pacific Merger on Labor and Safety Grounds
docket_entries.filer_name: Honorable Chris Deluzio, Honorable Pramila Jayapal, Honorable Angie Craig, Honorable Patrick Ryan, Honorable Donald Norcross, Honorable Mark Pocan, Honorable Debbie Dingell
docket_entries.entry_summary: Seven members of Congress representing the Monopoly Busters Caucus and Congressional Labor Caucus request that the STB require detailed, verified responses to comprehensive questions about labor, safety, and worker protections before approving the proposed Norfolk Southern-Union Pacific merger. The letter opposes the merger based on concerns about worker displacement, wage suppression, safety risks, and consolidation effects on remaining rail competition.
key_arguments: Class I freight railroads have declined from 33 to 6 since 1980, while rail employment fell from 500,000 to fewer than 200,000
Precision Scheduled Railroading has cut workforces by approximately 30% since 2014 across the six remaining Class I carriers
Previous merger commitments on worker protections have been inadequately enforced and monitored
Norfolk Southern's February 2023 East Palestine derailment demonstrates critical safety failures that merger-related cost pressures would exacerbate
Further consolidation would reduce collective-bargaining leverage for rail unions and eliminate alternative employer options in concentrated regional markets
Merger would eliminate independent safety programs and operational standards at both carriers
key_excerpts: Rail workers have borne the brunt of decades of industry consolidation and cost-cutting priorities that put corporate profits above worker and public safety.
Since the 1980s, the number of Class I freight railroads has declined from 33 to just six, while rail employment has fallen from approximately 500,000 to fewer than 200,000.
A merger of this magnitude would affect the livelihoods of tens of thousands of workers, and it is critical that the STB fully account for these impacts in any review.
The catastrophic February 2023 Norfolk Southern derailment in East Palestine, Ohio, underscores the failure of existing safety protocols and the urgent need for verifiable safety reforms

docket_entries.title: STB Approval of Waybill Data Access for CN Consultants (Berkley Research Group)
docket_entries.entry_summary: STB Office of Economics approved waybill data access for two Berkley Research Group consultants (Hassan Faghani and Steven VanOmmeren) acting on behalf of CN (Grand Trunk Corporation and U.S. rail operating subsidiaries) in FD 36873. The approval was granted on January 20, 2026, following CN's January 16, 2026 request and payment of $144 in processing fees. Both consultants executed Waybill Agreement WB25-55, a standard confidentiality agreement governing the use of STB's Carload Waybill Sample (CCWS) data. The agreement requires return or destruction of all CCWS data upon expiration and notification to STB within 30 days if extension is needed. This enables CN to conduct detailed economic modeling and competitive analysis of railroad traffic patterns and service performance using STB confidential waybill data during the discovery phase of the merger proceeding.
key_arguments: CN requires access to STB waybill data to conduct economic analysis and competitive impact assessment in the UP-NS merger proceeding
Consultants from Berkley Research Group are appropriately authorized and qualified to access confidential CCWS data under standard confidentiality terms
key_excerpts: Grand Trunk Corporation and its U.S. rail operating subsidiaries (collectively, "CN") request additional authorization for the below consultants to access the Waybill Data in the Union Pacific – Norfolk Southern docket (FD 36873).
I have approved the addition of the following individuals to the waybill access letter in WB25-55. a. Hassan Faghani – Berkley Research Group b. Steven VanOmmeren – Berkley Research Group
docket_entries.relief_requested: STB Office of Economics approval of waybill data access for Hassan Faghani and Steven VanOmmeren of Berkley Research Group under confidentiality agreement WB25-55.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing is a routine administrative approval under STB's waybill data access procedures (49 CFR Part 1241). It indicates that CN is actively building an economic and competitive analysis capability during the discovery phase, likely to support either intervention opposition or settlement negotiations. The involvement of Berkley Research Group (a major economic consulting firm) and the specific focus on waybill data suggests CN is preparing detailed traffic-flow and service-quality analysis. This is significant for understanding the depth and sophistication of CN's potential intervention and demonstrates CN's intent to engage in substantive economic testimony rather than procedural objections.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Administrative approval letter - no response required. CN must renew or return data within 30 days before WB25-55 expires.

docket_entries.title: National League of Cities Notice of Intent to Participate
docket_entries.entry_summary: National League of Cities files a notice of intent to participate in the UP/NS merger proceeding and requests placement on the service list. The filing is procedurally minimal with no substantive position articulated. This represents a common early-stage intervention mechanism where a special interest organization secures standing to receive docket filings and participate in subsequent comment or hearing phases. No specific concerns regarding municipal transportation infrastructure, city freight access, or economic impacts are identified in this notice.
key_excerpts: National League of Cities respectfully submits its Notice of Intent to Participate in this proceeding and any related sub-proceedings before the Surface Transportation Board, as its interests may appear.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Requests placement on service list as representative for National League of Cities to participate in proceeding and related sub-proceedings.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing has minimal legal significance. It is a standard procedural intervention mechanism that grants the filer docket access and standing to file substantive comments later. No new issues, burdens, or evidentiary questions are raised.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.deadline_description: Notice of intent requires no response; applicants must include filer on service list

docket_entries.title: Comments of Rail Cents Enterprises, Inc. on UP-NS Merger - Competition and Growth Claims
docket_entries.entry_summary: Rail Cents Enterprises challenges the fundamental claims of the UP-NS merger application, arguing that the Applicants have failed to substantiate their assertions about growth and competition benefits. The filing contends that the merger would create perverse incentives for the combined system to disadvantage joint-line routing in favor of single-line service, undermining competition, and that the projected growth figures rest on unrealistic assumptions about intermodal and merchandise traffic conversion.
key_arguments: Merged UP-NS pricer would have incentives to quote rates favoring single-line over joint-line service, regardless of cost or quality differences

Expert statements by Dr. Bailey and Dr. Israel rest on three questionable assumptions: (1) that unit costs exist for manifest traffic, (2) that pricing officers know these costs, and (3) that railroads price based on cost rather than value of service

Projected revenue growth of $1.982 billion lacks credible foundation - predicated on improbable assumptions including no need for rate reductions, increased commercial efforts, or competitive rail options
Intermodal growth projections are unrealistic given industry plateau since 2009 and the impracticality of mega-terminal spacing for competitive 250-750 mile drayage operations
Application ignores obvious competition remedy of reciprocal switching, which would be prerequisite for new carload merchandise customers
Boxcars represent untapped opportunity for merchandise competition but receive no consideration in the Application
Combined UP-NS organizational structure shown by historical dividend distributions indicates inability to invest in growth, not incentive alignment
key_excerpts: In practice, there will invariably be incentives for a combined UP-NS pricer to disadvantage any joint line routing where UP-NS can handle a movement as a single line.
Having the option of a route is not the same thing as having a competitive price to use that route. Aligning the incentives of UP and NS is not the same thing as improving competition.
Upon close inspection, these Statements are unconvincing, leaving the discerning reader with the impression that this Application is a case of bait and switch.
The Statement by David Hunt and Matthew Schabas is a tabletop exercise predicated on a series of improbabilities
Readers are referred to an explanation of how the merger would result in traffic growth starting 894 pages into the Application

docket_entries.title: South Dakota Soybean Association Letter Opposing UP-NS Merger; Filed through BNSF due to Service Requirements
docket_entries.entry_summary: South Dakota Soybean Association opposes the merger based on historical precedent of rail consolidation leading to reduced competition, higher costs, and diminished service. SDSA states: 'History shows that consolidation within an industry, particularly when it results in only a few dominant players, often reduces competition, leading to higher costs and diminished service.' The Association emphasizes that over 40% of South Dakota soybeans are destined for export markets, making transportation bottlenecks or delays during harvest season 'especially damaging.' SDSA warns that 'any increase in rail rates would further strain already thin margins managed by farm families.' The letter invokes historical principle that 'concentration of business in the hands of a few leads to disaster for users and frequently the industry itself.' Notably, SDSA does not propose specific remedial conditions; the opposition is grounded in general competitive and consolidation concerns rather than deal-specific harm analysis. The filing was technically submitted by BNSF Railway's counsel due to SDSA's difficulty complying with the Board's extensive service list requirements—SDSA had attempted to file independently on December 29, 2025, but the filing was not processed for lack of proof of service.
key_arguments: Historical rail mergers demonstrate that consolidation reduces competition, leading to higher costs and diminished service to shippers.
With 40% of South Dakota soybeans destined for export markets, transportation bottlenecks or delays during harvest season would be especially damaging to farmers.
Any increase in rail rates will further strain already thin profit margins of farm families.
Concentration of business in the hands of a few dominant players has historically led to disaster for industry users and the industry itself.
key_excerpts: History shows that consolidation within an industry, particularly when it results in only a few dominant players, often reduces competition, leading to higher costs and diminished service.

With more than 40 percent of South Dakota soybeans destined for export markets, transportation bottlenecks or delays moving products east or west during harvest season would be especially damaging. Any increase in rail rates would further strain already thin margins managed by farm families.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Implicit denial requested. SDSA does not list specific conditions that would make the merger acceptable; instead articulates fundamental concern that rail consolidation reduces competition and harms farmers.

docket_entries.title: BNSF submits bundled opposition letters from six business and local government entities opposing UP-NS merger on competition and service grounds
docket_entries.entry_summary: BNSF submitted a coordinated package of six opposition letters from regional chambers of commerce and a local government official, all arguing the UP-NS merger should be rejected outright. The letters claim: (1) the merged entity would control approximately 45-50% of all U.S. rail tonnage and dominate key commodity markets (food and kindred products 47%, intermodal 46%), eliminating meaningful competition and creating inevitable rate increases; (2) UP's own 2022 CPKC merger opposition acknowledged the risk of 'enormous post-merger pressure' to 'raise rates shippers must pay for interline service or degrade the quality of service'; (3) historical precedent from UP-SP merger and recent disruptions show 'even relatively minor disruptions could cripple rail service across the country'; (4) UP has a 25-year track record of 'failing to honor the competitive remedies granted to shippers' by raising rates and shedding traffic; (5) the merger would 'permanently lock in UP's dominance, eliminating alternative routes and creating single points of failure' that harm agricultural producers, rural economies, and supply chain resilience. The letters emphasize that for captive shippers—particularly grain producers, agricultural processors, fertilizer suppliers, and grocers in rural Minnesota and North Dakota—'rail is not one option among many, it is often the only practical way to reach key markets.' No acceptable conditions are identified; instead, letters stress the Board's post-2001 'Major Rail Consolidation Procedures' require applicants to demonstrate 'public benefits and protections for competition, not merely the absence of harm.' The filing reflects BNSF's strategic use of regional economic interests to frame merger opposition as widespread shipper and community concern rather than competitor self-interest.
key_arguments: The merged UP-NS would control approximately 45-50% of all U.S. rail tonnage, with market dominance even more pronounced in critical sectors: 47% of food and kindred products market (vs. 26% for next competitor), 46% of intermodal containers (vs. 30% for next competitor), creating 'unmatched power over shippers, suppliers, and rail workers.'

UP's own February 2022 CPKC merger opposition acknowledged the precise risks now at issue: 'enormous post-merger pressure' to 'raise rates shippers must pay for interline service or degrade the quality of service shippers receive when using interline service'—demonstrating UP understands the anticompetitive dynamics it would deploy post-merger.

UP has a documented 25-year history of 'failing to honor the competitive remedies granted to shippers in the last major round of mergers,' instead 'rais[ing] rates and shed[ding] traffic' over 25 years, signaling 'it values profits over growth,' making promises of growth-focused remedies inherently unreliable.

The merger would cause service disruptions and congestion historically associated with major rail consolidations (citing UP-SP merger precedent and recent 2025 disruptions), and 'given the size and scope of the proposed merger, even relatively minor disruptions could cripple rail service across the country, with ripple effects across the rest of the US supply chain and our economy.'

For captive shippers in rural Minnesota and North Dakota—agricultural producers, grain elevators, processors, fertilizer suppliers, feed manufacturers—'rail is not one option among many, it is often the only practical way to reach key markets at scale and at a competitive cost,' making them uniquely vulnerable to merger-induced rate increases and service degradation.

The merger would 'permanently lock in UP's dominance, eliminating alternative routes and creating single points of failure across the rail network' and destroy 'network resiliency' that depends on shippers having 'multiple choices' and routing flexibility—a loss that 'is difficult to restore' once lost.

The Board's post-2001 'Major Rail Consolidation Procedures' require applicants to affirmatively demonstrate 'public benefits and protections for competition, not merely the absence of harm,' a standard especially critical in already concentrated freight rail markets; this transaction 'does not meet those standards.'
key_excerpts: A combined UP-NS would dominate key freight markets and shared rail industry assets, giving it unmatched power over shippers, suppliers, and rail workers. Less competition means higher costs for everyone.

UP said there would be 'enormous post-merger pressure' to eliminate interline moves and implement 'anticompetitive strategies' like 'raising rates shippers must pay for interline service or degrading the quality of service shippers receive when using interline service.'

UP has a history of failing to honor the competitive remedies granted to shippers in the last major round of mergers. Over the past 25 years, UP has raised rates and shed traffic instead of expanding service, signaling that it values profits over growth.

For many of our members, rail is not one option among many—it is the only viable means of moving goods. Further consolidation would severely limit their ability to negotiate fair rates or maintain reliable service, with ripple effects across regional economies.

The merged railroad would become the dominant provider in several key commodity sectors vital to our local economy, including lumber and wood products, coal, chemicals, pulp and paper products, intermodal containers among others. Reduced competition in rail service could lead to higher transportation costs, fewer routing options, and diminished access to markets.

Once shippers lose competitive options, it is difficult to restore them. We respectfully ask the Board to scrutinize how this merger would affect routing flexibility and competitive access for captive and rural shippers over the long term.

This merger does not meet those standards. The Surface Transportation Board has established a high bar for approving major railroad mergers and safeguarding the economic vitality of American industries, and this merger does not meet those standards.
docket_entries.relief_requested: The bundled submissions urge the STB to 'reject this merger due to the significant reduction in rail competition it would cause' and to deny approval because the transaction 'does not meet' the Board's high statutory standards for merger approval. No conditions are proposed that would render the merger acceptable.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing invokes the STB's post-2001 'Major Rail Consolidation Procedures' and emphasizes that the Board's governing statutes and regulations establish a 'high bar' requiring applicants to affirmatively demonstrate 'public benefits and protections for competition, not merely the absence of harm.' The submission strategically reframes this as a rigorous substantive standard, not merely a balancing test. Critically, the letters cite UP's own February 2022 merger opposition comments (CPKC docket) to establish that UP understood and articulated the precise anticompetitive mechanisms (rate increases on interline service, service degradation, elimination of interline moves, 'anticompetitive strategies') that would result from consolidation—creating an estoppel-like argument that UP cannot now claim surprise about these risks. The filing also establishes a record of shipper and rural community voices claiming captive-shipper status and irreplaceable dependence on rail competition, which directly implicates the Board's historical concern (from prior merger cases) about protecting shippers without alternative transportation. The coordinated submission structure—competitor-orchestrated through local business proxies—attempts to insulate BNSF's competitive interest behind broader economic stakeholder concerns, potentially strengthening the evidentiary record on competitive harm and remedy adequacy.
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is a comment filing in the ongoing proceeding; no specific response deadline is indicated in the filing itself. The submission will become part of the administrative record and may require response during discovery or at hearing.

docket_entries.title: CN Motion to Compel Schedule 5.8 & Supplemental Authority Supporting Discovery of Complete Merger Agreement
docket_entries.entry_summary: CN files a Notice of Supplemental Authority supporting its Motion to Compel, citing the STB's January 16, 2026 rejection of the UP/NS merger application as incomplete. CN emphasizes that the STB explicitly identified missing disclosure schedules, particularly Schedule 5.8, as a 'primary and independent basis' for the rejection. The STB rejected UP's privilege assertions, finding that UP 'did not even specify which privilege they contend applies' and 'did not attempt to justify their omission under the Board's regulations, despite the fact that the materials were already the subject of discovery disagreements when the Application was filed.' The STB concluded: 'it is difficult to imagine a privilege claim that would apply in this context to justify Applicants' withholding of a merger agreement document—negotiated by counterparties to a transaction at arm's length and required to be submitted to the Board under § 1180.6(a)(7)(ii).' CN notes that UP has not responded to CN's request confirming production of Schedule 5.8 following the Board's decision. Schedule 5.8 is material because it defines the term 'Materially Burdensome Regulatory Condition'—the contractual right allowing UPC to walk away from the merger if the Board imposes certain conditions—essentially reflecting UP's own assessment of the transaction's potential anticompetitive harms. CN argues that without the full merger agreement, neither the Board nor participating parties can assess whether the Transaction is consistent with the public interest, particularly where Applicants have requested a fairness determination requiring the Board to assess whether all merger terms are fair to shareholders.
key_arguments: Schedule 5.8 to the Company Disclosure Schedules is expressly defined as part of the Merger Agreement under Section 5.8(e), which states: 'For the avoidance of doubt, all references to this Section 5.8 in this Agreement shall be deemed to include Section 5.8 of the Company Disclosure Schedules.'

The STB's January 16 Decision No. 9 explicitly rejected UP's privilege claims, finding that UP failed to specify which privilege applies and failed to attempt justification under Board regulations despite the fact that discovery disagreements about these materials already existed when the Application was filed.

The STB found it 'difficult to imagine a privilege claim that would apply in this context to justify Applicants' withholding of a merger agreement document—negotiated by counterparties to a transaction at arm's length and required to be submitted to the Board under § 1180.6(a)(7)(ii).'
The STB explicitly mandated: 'Any revised application in this matter must include complete copies' of the merger agreement, 'including Schedule 5.8.'

Schedule 5.8 defines 'Materially Burdensome Regulatory Condition,' which gives UP the contractual right to terminate if the Board or a court imposes certain conditions—making it a reflection of UP's own assessment of the transaction's potential anticompetitive harms.

Complete disclosure of the merger agreement is 'especially important where Applicants have requested a fairness determination, which requires that the Board determine whether all of the terms of the proposed merger are fair to Applicants' shareholders.'
UP has not responded to CN's post-decision email request confirming it will produce Schedule 5.8 'as soon as possible,' necessitating Board intervention.
key_excerpts: The Board rejected the argument that Schedule 5.8 is subject to any cognizable privilege, noting that Applicants did not even 'specify which privilege they contend applies' and 'did not attempt to justify their omission under the Board's regulations, despite the fact that the materials were already the subject of discovery disagreements when the Application was filed.' The Board further concluded that, notwithstanding the lack of clarity regarding Applicants' assertions of privilege, 'it is difficult to imagine a privilege claim that would apply in this context to justify Applicants' withholding of a merger agreement document—negotiated by counterparties to a transaction at arm's length and required to be submitted to the Board under § 1180.6(a)(7)(ii).' As a result of rejecting Applicants' claim of privilege, the Board instructed that 'any revised application in this matter must include complete copies' of the merger agreement, 'including Schedule 5.8.'

Schedule 5.8 gives content to the contractual term 'Materially Burdensome Regulatory Condition,' which, if imposed by the Board or a court, would give UPC the contractual right to walk away from the merger agreement. According to commenters, the definitions in Schedule 5.8 are among the most material terms of the proposed merger agreement because they provide Applicants' own assessment of the Transaction's potential anticompetitive harms.

Without the full merger agreement, neither the Board nor participating parties can assess whether the Transaction is consistent with the public interest. Having the full merger agreement 'is especially important where Applicants have requested a fairness determination, which requires that the Board determine whether all of the terms of the proposed merger are fair to Applicants' shareholders.'
docket_entries.relief_requested: CN requests that the Board grant its Motion to Compel (filed CN-7, Jan. 8, 2026) requiring Union Pacific to produce the complete and unredacted Merger Agreement, including specifically Schedule 5.8 to the Company Disclosure Schedules. CN argues production is mandatory under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.6(a)(7)(ii) and that the Board has already rejected UP's privilege claims as unjustified. CN seeks this relief to enable meaningful assessment of whether the Transaction is consistent with the public interest and, where Applicants have requested a fairness determination, to permit the Board to determine whether all merger terms are fair to shareholders.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing enforces the STB's January 16, 2026 Decision No. 9 rejection of the merger application as incomplete. The decision has immediate practical significance: it establishes that the burden of proof has shifted back to UP to provide complete documentation in any revised application. The STB explicitly rejected UP's unstated privilege claims and mandated full disclosure of Schedule 5.8 and all schedules and exhibits. CN's supplemental authority filing creates enforceable pressure on UP to comply with the STB's directive before attempting to refile. The filing also reframes the competitive analysis: Schedule 5.8's definition of walk-away rights becomes evidence of UP's own internally assessed competitive harms—a powerful evidentiary tool for opposing the deal or conditioning approval. The STB's finding that no cognizable privilege can justify withholding merger agreement terms (negotiated at arm's length and required by regulation) establishes precedent that will likely apply to any future claims of confidentiality or privilege in revised applications.
docket_entries.document_type: Modify/Supplement Prior Filing Or The Record
docket_entries.deadline_description: UP must file a letter by February 17, 2026, indicating whether and when it anticipates refiling the merger application. Any revised application must be filed no later than June 22, 2026, and must include complete copies of all contracts and written instruments including Schedule 5.8.

docket_entries.title: Colin Finney - Individual Resident Comment: Condition UP/NS Merger on Lehigh Valley Passenger Rail Pilot Program
docket_entries.entry_summary: Colin Finney, a Lehigh Valley, PA resident, opposes the UP/NS merger unless conditioned on forcing Norfolk Southern to cooperate with state-funded passenger rail restoration efforts. Finney argues: Norfolk Southern holds 'a practical monopoly on rail movement through our valley' and has 'systematically erased' regional passenger service to prioritize freight exclusivity, forcing 860,000 residents into highway dependency while Norfolk Southern markets itself as an 'environmentally friendly solution' that removes trucks from highways. Finney contends Norfolk Southern uses its infrastructure monopoly to 'effectively veto any return of passenger service' through its refusal to share track capacity, creating a 'market failure that only the STB can correct.' He documents specific grade crossing safety hazards—trains up to three miles long blocking Dixon Street in Allentown and other crossings, cutting off emergency and utility access. Finney states Pennsylvania has secured state funding for Phase II of a feasibility study to operationalize passenger rail but that 'without a federal condition mandating access, this public investment is at risk of being rendered useless.' His proposed condition: mandate a 'Passenger Rail Pilot Program' that guarantees physical capacity on Norfolk Southern corridors to make the state-funded study operational. Finney frames approval without conditions as allowing 'a private corporation to nullify Pennsylvania's transportation policy.' Settlement signals: Finney explicitly states 'we ask only that you open the door'—indicating willingness to support the merger IF specific track access conditions are imposed.
key_arguments: Norfolk Southern holds a 'practical monopoly on rail movement' through the Lehigh Valley and uses that monopoly power to block passenger rail restoration, creating an irremediable conflict between private freight interests and public transportation needs that only federal merger conditions can address.

The railroad claims to be an 'environmentally friendly solution' that removes trucks from highways, but in the Lehigh Valley it achieves the opposite: 'forces an entire metropolitan population of 860,000 people to rely on personal vehicles for intercity travel' by refusing to share capacity for passenger service.

Norfolk Southern's infrastructure monopoly renders all passenger service proposals 'infeasible by default'—the Commonwealth has invested in Phase II feasibility studies, but without federal conditions mandating track access, this state-funded investment will be 'rendered useless' by the carrier's continued veto power.

Grade crossing safety hazards result from Norfolk Southern's freight monopoly: trains up to three miles long are 'frequently parked' across public roads like Dixon Street in Allentown, 'where emergency and utility access is cut off,' creating dangerous conditions across multiple municipalities.

A merger approval without passenger rail access conditions would allow 'a private corporation to nullify Pennsylvania's transportation policy'—the state has already funded passenger rail studies and expects federal merger review to account for state-level transportation mandates.
key_excerpts: Currently, Norfolk Southern holds a practical monopoly on rail movement through our valley. This lack of competition has created a dynamic where the railroad has no incentive to compromise with our community.

They cannot claim to be the solution to highway gridlock while simultaneously acting as the primary barrier to the region's only viable alternative. They profit from a 'green' image while forcing our residents into carbon intensive car dependency.

Because they control the only viable rail corridor, Norfolk Southern has consistently resisted efforts to restore this lost service...Norfolk Southern's absolute control over the infrastructure renders any future proposal infeasible by default.

Without the Board mandating a Pilot Program, the official government plan in Figure 2 has no more legal reality than the internet thread in Figure 1. The infrastructure exists, and the engineering works; only Norfolk Southern's refusal to share the Right of Way prevents the fantasy from becoming a service.
A merger that cements a regional monopoly while actively blocking the restoration of passenger service does not meet that standard [of serving the public interest].
docket_entries.relief_requested: Condition any approval of the UP/NS merger on the mandatory creation of a 'Passenger Rail Pilot Program' for the Lehigh Valley that guarantees physical capacity needed to realize the goals of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania's Lehigh Valley Passenger Rail Analysis (Phase II study). Without binding conditions mandating Norfolk Southern's cooperation and track access for passenger service, the merger should not be approved.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: LOW-MEDIUM. This filing raises a threshold question about STB merger conditions authority: whether the Board can condition a freight rail merger approval on passenger rail access and cooperation obligations that fall outside the traditional competitive/service/rate lens of 49 U.S.C. § 11324. Finney invokes the Board's 'public interest' mandate but does not cite specific statutory authority for conditioning freight mergers on passenger rail accommodations. If STB grants the condition, it expands the scope of merger conditions into infrastructure-sharing/transportation policy territory. If denied, it clarifies the Board's interpretation of merger review scope. Additionally, the grade crossing safety allegations (trains blocking emergency access) may trigger FRA jurisdiction issues or require factual development separate from the merger analysis.

docket_entries.title: Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern Reply to BNSF Motion to Compel Discovery
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern oppose BNSF's motion to compel, arguing that BNSF's discovery demands are fundamentally incompatible with the Board's application-centric merger review process. The applicants characterize BNSF's approach as a 'fishing expedition' that seeks to impose HSR-style discovery standards inappropriate to STB proceedings. Applicants emphasize: (1) they have already produced unprecedented volumes of data (56,000+ pages, 924 gigabytes) including 100% traffic tapes for 2019-2024, car/train event data, reciprocal switching data, interchange agreements, and verified workpapers; (2) BNSF propounded 215 individual discovery requests (400 counting subparts) pre-application, far exceeding historical practice; (3) the Board's rules contemplate that a comprehensive application with supporting workpapers—not broad pre-application discovery—forms the evidentiary core; (4) BNSF's requests for wholesale custodial email collections, board of director materials, and banker communications lack any specific tethering to discrete requests and impose unreasonable burden; (5) BNSF rejected applicants' good-faith compromise offers and prematurely declared impasse on December 30, 2025, then filed the motion within 15 minutes of a follow-up email; (6) HSR procedures include strict confidentiality protections and government control absent here, making HSR precedent inapt; (7) applicants' discovery efforts are 'both ahead of schedule' and 'unprecedented at this stage,' with rolling productions ongoing. Applicants frame BNSF's true goal as delay and strategic abuse of discovery rather than legitimate information gathering. The reply includes detailed exhibits showing the sequence of meet-and-confer failures, BNSF's expansive first set of discovery requests (27 requests with 26 subparts served October 1, 2025), union Pacific's October 16 objections and responses, BNSF's November 12 letter challenging those objections, UP's December 5 response, and the email chain from December 28, 2025 onward showing the breakdown in negotiations.
key_arguments: The Board's merger review process is deliberately application-centric, unlike HSR review, and does not permit broad pre-application discovery that would impede applicants' preparation of their application; the Board has expressly disfavored such broad discovery.

BNSF's discovery demands are not tethered to specific requests and responses but instead seek sweeping categories of materials (board minutes, banker decks, wholesale custodial emails) in a manner BNSF itself describes as HSR-style, which the Board's rules and precedents reject.

Applicants have already produced unprecedented volumes—56,000+ pages and 924 gigabytes—including 100% traffic tapes (2019-2024), system-wide car and train event data, reciprocal switching data, intermodal train schedules, interchange commitments, terminal agreements, operating agreements, and extensive workpapers, all made available through rolling productions.

BNSF propounded 215 individual discovery requests (400 counting subparts) long before the application was filed, including three sets totaling 147 requests with 129 subparts from BNSF alone; this volume is fundamentally inconsistent with the Board's application-centric structure.

BNSF's insistence on HSR-style discovery standards is inapt because HSR procedures include strict confidentiality protections and criminal penalties for improper disclosure, plus government control of the process absent here; applicants should not be forced to provide HSR materials without HSR safeguards.

Applicants' objections to searching non-email communications, texts, instant messages, and chat logs are well-founded because such collections are unduly burdensome and not proportional to the needs of a proceeding centered on the Board's evaluation of the filed application.

BNSF rejected applicants' good-faith compromise offers and declared impasse unilaterally at a December 30, 2025 meet-and-confer without identifying specific requests at issue or engaging meaningfully with applicants' valid concerns; BNSF then filed the motion within 15 minutes of a follow-up email, demonstrating delay tactics.

Discovery compliance must be measured against specific requests and responses, not BNSF's dissatisfaction with the total volume or categories of materials received; BNSF has failed to articulate which specific requests were inadequately answered.

The Board's regulations require that where discovery is burdensome on its face, the requesting party must make a substantial showing of relevance and need to outweigh the burden; BNSF has made no such showing.

Applicants' discovery efforts are both ahead of schedule (no procedural schedule has even been set) and unprecedented for this stage; in the CP/KCS merger (FD 36500), applicants' first production occurred six weeks post-application filing and consisted of fewer than 400 documents, whereas here applicants have produced before application acceptance.
key_excerpts: BNSF's Motion rests almost entirely on authorities drawn from the HSR merger review process and complex civil litigation because BNSF's approach to discovery does not align with the Board's merger procedures and practice. The Board's merger review framework is distinctive and deliberately application-centric.

Instead of requesting production of discrete information not addressed in the application and accompanying workpapers, BNSF is engaged in a fishing expedition, demanding that Applicants produce broad categories of materials that it claims might contain relevant information.

The Board, by contrast, primarily regulates a single industry and has developed merger application requirements tailored specifically to freight railroads. Those requirements demand a level of detail far beyond what HSR requires and are expressly designed to provide the Board—and interested parties—with the information the Board deems necessary to evaluate a proposed transaction.

Catch-all email collections are burdensome, inefficient, and generally inconsistent with the scope and structure of the Board's merger review proceedings. Broad email collections of the type demanded by BNSF would inevitably sweep in large volumes of irrelevant and highly sensitive materials, far beyond what is necessary to supplement or clarify the Application.
BNSF's conduct appears motivated by a desire to delay and complicate these proceedings rather than reach a realistic compromise on discovery.

Discovery should operate as a collaborative process... That process has not occurred here. The parties met and conferred once on BNSF's first set of requests. At that first meeting, BNSF declared impasse without engaging meaningfully with Applicants' well-founded concerns.
BNSF's Motion does not identify which set of requests is at issue, let alone the specific requests for which BNSF seeks relief... The Motion reflects BNSF's broader scattershot discovery strategy.

As of the filing of this Reply, Applicants have already produced or otherwise made available to BNSF and other parties more than 56,000 pages and 924 gigabytes of data sets, agreements, workpapers, and other materials.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny BNSF's Motion to Compel. Applicants request that the Board reject BNSF's demand for wholesale email collections, board materials searches, and HSR-style discovery, arguing such discovery is inconsistent with the Board's application-centric merger review process and is unduly burdensome.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This reply squarely raises the foundational question of what discovery standards govern STB merger proceedings: application-centric (applicants' position) versus HSR/civil litigation-style (BNSF's position). If the Board grants the motion, it would establish that competitors can demand wholesale custodial email searches, board materials, and banker analyses pre-application—fundamentally changing the STB's merger review process from one designed around detailed applications to one dependent on extensive pre-filing discovery. If the Board denies it, it validates the application-centric framework and sets bounds on competitor discovery demands. The ruling will also define proportionality standards for the expedited one-year review period mandated by 49 U.S.C. § 11325(b)(3). Additionally, applicants' argument that discovery disputes must be tied to specific requests versus categorical material demands could reshape how discovery motions are brought in STB proceedings.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No explicit deadline stated. BNSF's Motion to Compel was served January 9, 2026. This Reply was filed January 29, 2026. The Board will rule on the motion per its normal procedural schedule; no ALJ or Board order setting briefing deadlines is evident in the filing.

docket_entries.title: CPKC Motion for Discovery of Ordinary Course Documents in UP-NS Merger
docket_entries.filer_name: Canadian Pacific Railway Company d/b/a CPKC

key_arguments: Discovery of ordinary course documents is customary and required in Board merger proceedings, supported by broad discovery regulations and prior STB cases

Ordinary course documents are more probative than expert testimony created in anticipation of merger review, per DOJ/FTC guidance

evidence created in the normal course of business is more probative than evidence created after the company began anticipating a merger review

docket_entries.title: USD Group LLC Comments on UP/NS Merger – Does Not Take Position; Calls for Careful Scrutiny of Industry Consolidation Risks
docket_entries.entry_summary: USD Group LLC filed comments explicitly declining to take a position for or against the proposed UP/NS merger, but raising substantive concerns about industry consolidation risks that warrant careful STB scrutiny. The company acknowledges positive recent rail network enhancements (BNSF-CSX intermodal collaboration, CPKC-CSX Southeast alliance, BNSF Phoenix-Atlanta service) and notes that 'rail mergers are not the only way to improve service reliability, reduce transit times and expand market reach/access.' However, USD Group expresses concern about the merger triggering 'wide reaching permanent restructuring of the industry and a resulting rail network with a disproportionately advantaged carrier.' They cite CPKC CEO Keith Creel's warning that the merger 'will likely result in an unnecessary wave of railway mergers that today is not the best way to support American businesses nor the public interest, and has the potential to create more issues than it solves,' and endorse BNSF's concern that the deal creates 'too much market power, limiting shipper choice and creating an increase in captive shippers.' USD Group emphasizes that 'historic follow-through on past merger commitments has not been perfect, creating increased risk regarding the potential for negative impacts' and flags the risk that 'a mass consolidation of the 6 Class I railroads to effectively 2 could be an unintended consequence that needs careful consideration.' They advocate for consideration of alternatives to merger: 'Proper consideration of enhanced competition through open gateway commitments and pricing are a must.' The filing preserves the company's concerns about potential industry-wide consolidation cascades, captive shipper risks, and implementation failures, while remaining agnostic on whether STB should approve or deny the specific UP/NS transaction.
key_arguments: Non-merger alternatives exist to improve rail service: 'rail mergers are not the only way to improve service reliability, reduce transit times and expand market reach/access,' including BNSF-CSX intermodal launches, CPKC-CSX Southeast alliance, and investments in capacity and technology.

Merger risks triggering industry-wide consolidation cascade: Merger will result in 'wide reaching permanent restructuring of the industry and a resulting rail network with a disproportionately advantaged carrier,' with potential for 'mass consolidation of the 6 Class I railroads to effectively 2.'
Merger creates excessive shipper captivity and reduced competition: Endorses concern that deal 'creates too much market power, limiting shipper choice and creating an increase in captive shippers.'

Implementation risk is material: 'Historic follow-through on past merger commitments has not been perfect, creating increased risk regarding the potential for negative impacts associated with this proposed change.'

Open gateway access and pricing competition must be requirements if merger approved: 'Proper consideration of enhanced competition through open gateway commitments and pricing are a must and could unlock some latent benefits to the supply chain.'
key_excerpts: 'This will likely result in an unnecessary wave of railway mergers that today is not the best way to support American businesses nor the public interest, and has the potential to create more issues than it solves' (quoting CPKC CEO Keith Creel).
'a mass consolidation of the 6 Class I railroads to effectively 2 could be an unintended consequence that needs careful consideration.'
'rail mergers are not the only way to improve service reliability, reduce transit times and expand market reach/access,' citing recent BNSF-CSX, CPKC-CSX collaborations.
'Proper consideration of enhanced competition through open gateway commitments and pricing are a must and could unlock some latent benefits to the supply chain.'
docket_entries.relief_requested: USD Group does not take a position for or against the merger. Instead, they request that 'the STB review all the facts and sort out all the fiction' and 'carefully consider the facts, both positive and negative, that impact this merger' including 'potential unintended consequences.' They seek to 'preserve in the public record the categories of issues that we believe warrant careful scrutiny should a revised application be accepted for review.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low-to-medium. USD Group's filing does not establish new legal precedents or challenge the STB's analytical framework. However, as a filing from a major business customer (shipper), it provides business-community context supporting concerns about captive shipper risk and consolidation cascade that other intervenors have raised. The filing's explicit neutrality while flagging specific risk categories may be strategically significant: USD Group preserves its ability to monitor the proceeding and potentially shift position if a revised application is filed, while creating a record that a significant shipper constituency viewed consolidation risks as material enough to warrant documented concerns.
