docket_entries.title: DOJ Antitrust Division Motion for Supplemental Protective Order to Permit Law Enforcement Access to Confidential Transaction Data
docket_entries.entry_summary: The DOJ Antitrust Division filed a motion seeking modification of the Board's existing Protective Order to accommodate federal law and DOJ's law enforcement function. The Division does not challenge the underlying protective order's confidentiality protections but argues that three specific provisions conflict with DOJ's statutory obligations. First, paragraph 12 requires destruction of Designated Material upon case completion, which DOJ contends 'may run afoul of the Department's obligations to retain materials that are subject to the Federal Records Act. See 44 U.S.C. § 3101 et. seq.' Second, paragraph 11's blanket prohibition on use of Designated Material for purposes outside the Board proceeding 'would unnecessarily hamper the Department's ability to carry out its law enforcement function,' as DOJ must retain ability to use information obtained in any proceeding 'for any law enforcement purpose.' Third, paragraphs 7-8 requiring all DOJ employee signatories to execute specific undertakings are 'unnecessary given the Department's confidentiality policies,' which are codified in Justice Manual 1-7.100 and impose strict internal protocols on disclosure of non-public sensitive information. DOJ's proposed Supplemental Protective Order would: (1) permit retention of Designated Material when required by law or for law enforcement purposes; (2) allow use of Designated Material for law enforcement outside this proceeding; and (3) require only a signature by an authorized DOJ official rather than individual employee undertakings. DOJ acknowledges that unrestricted disclosure 'could cause competitive injury to the parties' and states the proposed order 'protects against such disclosure while accommodating the Department's legal obligations and law enforcement function.' This motion reflects DOJ's intent to conduct substantive antitrust investigation into the transaction's competitive effects and positions DOJ as an active, scrutinizing intervenor.
key_arguments: DOJ's obligation to retain materials under the Federal Records Act (44 U.S.C. § 3101 et seq.) creates conflict with the Protective Order's mandatory destruction requirement; blanket destruction 'may run afoul' of federal records retention law

DOJ's law enforcement function requires retention of ability to use information obtained in any proceeding 'for any law enforcement purpose'; a blanket prohibition on law enforcement use would 'unnecessarily hamper the Department's ability to carry out its law enforcement function'

DOJ's internal confidentiality policies (Justice Manual 1-7.100) impose strict protocols equivalent to or exceeding the Protective Order's undertaking requirements; individual employee signatures are therefore 'unnecessary'

The proposed Supplemental Protective Order adequately protects against competitive injury while accommodating DOJ's legal obligations without undermining the original Protective Order's confidentiality protections
key_excerpts: Destruction of Designated Material as required by the Protective Order may run afoul of the Department's obligations to retain materials that are subject to the Federal Records Act. See 44 U.S.C. § 3101 et. seq.

Given the Department's law enforcement function, the Department routinely retains the ability to use information it obtains in any proceedings or investigation for any law enforcement purpose and a blanket requirement for the Department to destroy all Designated Material would unnecessarily hamper the Department's ability to carry out its law enforcement function.
Such a requirement is unnecessary given the Department's confidentiality policies. See Justice Manual 1-7.100.

The Department recognizes that unrestricted disclosure of confidential, proprietary, or commercially sensitive information and data could cause competitive injury to the parties. Issuance of the proposed Supplemental Protective Order protects against such disclosure while accommodating the Department's legal obligations and law enforcement function.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Enter a Supplemental Protective Order modifying the Board's August 5, 2025 Protective Order (Decision No. 1) to permit DOJ: (1) to retain Designated Material when required by the Federal Records Act; (2) to use Designated Material for law enforcement purposes outside this proceeding; and (3) to avoid individual employee undertaking signatures, relying instead on DOJ's internal confidentiality policies (Justice Manual 1-7.100)
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This motion raises the legal hierarchy issue between STB protective order requirements and federal law obligations (Federal Records Act). It establishes a precedent for how DOJ's statutory intervention right under 49 U.S.C. § 11325(b)(1) interacts with procedural confidentiality rules. The motion also implicitly signals DOJ's intention to conduct substantive antitrust investigation (not passive monitoring) and suggests DOJ may be preserving the possibility of parallel antitrust enforcement proceedings outside the STB context. Approval would expand DOJ's investigative access and flexibility; denial could constrain DOJ's review capacity or force DOJ to limit its intervention scope. The motion does not prejudge the merger's legality but does confirm DOJ views the transaction as warranting active scrutiny.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Motion; Board response date not specified in filing

docket_entries.title: Petition for Mandatory Passenger Coexistence Condition on Lehigh Valley Corridor — Atlantic City Model Proposed
docket_entries.entry_summary: Colin Finney, a Drexel environmental engineering student with documented personal need for regional rail connectivity, petitions the STB to condition UP/NS merger approval on a mandatory passenger coexistence model for the Lehigh Valley corridor. Finney argues the merger cannot meet the 'substantial demonstrable public benefit' standard required for significant transactions unless the applicants adopt a public-private infrastructure model similar to Norfolk Southern's successful Atlantic City Line operations. Under this model, a public entity (LVPC) would assume maintenance of way and capital responsibility for infrastructure upgrades (leveraging Pennsylvania Governor Shapiro's proposed $300M annual transit fund), while Norfolk Southern retains 100% freight operational exclusivity and revenue. Finney frames this not as anti-merger but as pro-efficiency: the railroad offloads depreciating real estate liabilities, achieves tax shielding, and preserves capital for rolling stock while gaining a 'strategic shield' against rival carriers seeking entry. The petition cites documented infrastructure saturation: FRA data on blocked at-grade crossings (12th and Vultee Streets, Allentown), Allentown Terminal overflow creating mainline parking lots for 3-mile consists, and systemic saturation identified in 2024 Lehigh Valley passenger rail analysis. Finney argues this condition aligns with the Board's environmental mandate (addressing US-22/I-78 gridlock affecting 860,000 residents) and fulfills 'substantial public benefit' by integrating Phase II Passenger Rail Analysis into approval conditions, preventing merger approval from nullifying $400K in state transportation investments. The filing strategically positions the condition as revenue-neutral or beneficial to the applicants while serving regional public interest and stabilizing NS's market dominance.
key_arguments: The Board's January 2026 rejection of the initial merger application on grounds of incompletion and reclassification as 'significant transaction' mandates that applicants prove the merger provides 'substantial and demonstrable public benefits' rather than merely lacking anticompetitive effects — current operational assumptions are insufficient to meet 2001 major rail consolidation standards.

Norfolk Southern successfully operates the Atlantic City Line model where public entity (NJ Transit) maintains ownership and maintenance of way while NS retains exclusive freight rights; this precedent demonstrates viability for Lehigh Valley, allowing railroad to shed infrastructure liabilities while preserving operational exclusivity required for successful merger.

Lehigh Valley corridor operates at documented physical saturation point: FRA data shows disproportionate blocked crossing delays (3-mile trains at 12th and Vultee Streets, Allentown), Allentown Terminal overflow creates mainline parking lots forcing idling on mainlines, and 2024 analysis identifies lack of adequate terminal infrastructure as critical choke point.

Exclusive freight monopoly contradicts merger applicants' stated environmental/sustainability goals: by precluding passenger service, applicants force 860,000-person metropolitan population to rely on personal vehicles for intercity travel, creating net-negative environmental outcome that offsets supposed freight-shift-to-rail benefits.

Public-private model provides railroad competitive advantage by allowing NS to argue physical corridor is fully utilized in public interest, which prevents entry of rival freight operators (BNSF, CPKC) and preserves NS's regional exclusivity while satisfying public demand for sustainable infrastructure.

Mandatory coexistence model creates engineering buffer of certainty forcing optimization of yard entries/exits, ensuring Lehigh Valley is no longer treated as temporary storage for transcontinental freight and solving documented Dixon Street bottleneck.

Public assumption of maintenance/capital responsibility leverages Pennsylvania Governor Shapiro's February 2026 budget proposal ($300M annual transit fund) and $400K in Lehigh County/Senator Nick Miller transportation investments, preventing merger approval from nullifying state-level infrastructure commitments.
key_excerpts: Approval of this merger should be strictly conditioned on the establishment of a passenger coexistence model for the Lehigh Valley corridor. This transition of the Lehigh and Reading Lines toward a public private stewardship framework aligns the Applicants' operational efficiency with the public's right to essential transportation services.

The Board's January 2026 rejection of the initial merger application on the grounds of incompletion confirms that the Applicants' current operational assumptions are insufficient to meet the 2001 major rail consolidation standards. More importantly, the Board has reclassified this transaction as a significant transaction, which mandates that the Applicants prove the merger provides substantial and demonstrable public benefits rather than merely lacking anticompetitive effects.

By maintaining an exclusive freight monopoly that precludes passenger service, the Applicants are forcing a metropolitan population of 860,000 people to rely on personal vehicles for intercity travel. This creates a net-negative environmental outcome that offsets the supposed benefits of the merger, as residents are left with no viable alternative to the heavily gridlocked highway system.

Maintenance of Way (MOW) Offload: Public entities assume responsibility for maintaining tracks to high speed passenger safety standards, providing the railroad with premium infrastructure at a fraction of the private capital cost... Tax Shielding: Transferring rights of way to a public authority removes significant property tax liabilities from the railroad's balance sheet. This model effectively transforms a depreciating real estate liability into a pure operational asset, allowing for higher profit margins on every carload moved through the Lehigh Valley.

A mandated passenger coexistence model is the only engineering solution that creates a buffer of certainty. It forces the optimization of yard entries and exits, which ensures the Lehigh Valley is no longer treated as a temporary storage area for transcontinental freight.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Approval of merger STRICTLY CONDITIONED on establishment of a passenger coexistence model for the Lehigh Valley corridor. Transition of Lehigh and Reading Lines toward public-private stewardship framework where public entity assumes maintenance of way and capital responsibility while railroad retains exclusive freight rights (Atlantic City Line model).
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing invokes two critical regulatory developments: (1) the Board's January 2026 rejection of the initial merger application and reclassification as 'significant transaction,' which shifts the evidentiary burden from 'no anticompetitive effects' to 'substantial demonstrable public benefits' under 49 U.S.C. § 11324; (2) the application of this heightened public benefit standard to condition approval. The petition creates a framework for conditioning major consolidations on infrastructure stewardship models aligned with regional planning, potentially establishing precedent for regional authority assumption of maintenance and capital responsibility in exchange for freight exclusivity. This directly addresses the Board's January rejection by proposing specific structural remedy (public-private model) that converts alleged deficiencies into public benefits. The filing also establishes nexus between merger conditions and state-level transportation planning (Pennsylvania budget initiatives, Lehigh Valley Planning Commission Phase II), potentially requiring Board analysis of whether merger conditions must integrate with state infrastructure investments to satisfy 'substantial public benefit' test.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Petition filed; no deadline indicated. Responses from applicants/other parties possible but not mandated by filing itself.

docket_entries.title: Congressional Letter from 47 Republican Members Urging Rigorous STB Review of UP-NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: Forty-seven congressional members, predominantly Republican, oppose the proposed UP-NS merger absent clear demonstration of public benefits. They argue the transaction would further concentrate an already-consolidated industry (30 Class I railroads reduced to six since 1980), creating a 55,000-mile carrier controlling almost half U.S. rail freight. The members place the burden squarely on applicants: 'the responsibility to demonstrate clear, measurable, and substantial benefits...rests squarely with the applicant railroads. Absent such a showing, the Board should not permit this transaction to proceed.' They invoke the STB's 2001 merger rules requiring that future consolidations enhance (rather than merely preserve) competition, citing USDA's prior position that 'effective competition must include effective inter-railroad competition—the kind that minimizes the number of captive shippers.' The delegation warns of risks to constituent sectors: domestic manufacturers, agricultural producers, and energy companies remain burdened by pricing and service problems from prior consolidations in the 1990s-2000s. Members express concern that applicants have submitted inadequate competitive safeguards: 'the UP-NS application...lacks serious and meaningful commitments to enhance competition and protect against service meltdowns.' They frame the merger review through a Trump Administration pro-growth lens, cautioning that approval could 'result in the costs of goods and services going up for American businesses and consumers.' This establishes a foundational argument that if approved, the deal must affirmatively enhance competition, reduce captive shippers, and prevent service degradation.
key_arguments: Further consolidation from 6 Class I railroads creates a 55,000-mile carrier handling almost half U.S. rail freight, reducing already-limited shipping options and repeating past consolidation harms: 'A number of those shippers are still complaining about railroad pricing and service issues since the last major round of industry consolidation in the mid to late 1990s and early 2000s.'

Applicants bear the burden to demonstrate clear, measurable, substantial benefits; absent such proof, 'the Board should not permit this transaction to proceed.' This reverses any presumption of approval.

STB's 2001 merger rules require competition enhancement, not preservation. Applicants must affirmatively prove the merger 'enhance[s] competition for rail shippers, ensure[s] reliable rail service, and [is] in the interest of the public.'

The transaction threatens constituent economic sectors dependent on rail competition: domestic manufacturers, agricultural producers, energy companies. Congressional members 'remain keenly focused on ensuring government decision-making does not result in the costs of goods and services going up for American businesses and consumers.'

Past mergers created service disruptions and excessive market power generating 'tremendous backlash from rail customers, employees, passenger rail operators and riders along with communities cut in half by congested rail lines.' This merger risks repeating those harms.
Effective competition requires reducing 'captive shippers'—those dependent on a single carrier. Merger would expand captive shipper problem by reducing competitive alternatives.
key_excerpts: The responsibility to demonstrate clear, measurable, and substantial benefits for domestic manufacturers, agricultural producers, the energy sector, and the American consumer—all of whom rely on an efficient, competitive, and cost-effective freight rail system—rests squarely with the applicant railroads. Absent such a showing, the Board should not permit this transaction to proceed.
A 55,000-mile railroad handling almost half the nation's rail freight...could decrease already limited options for shippers around the country.

Rather than just preserving competition, the Board should use enhancement of competition as a deciding factor [when reviewing mergers]. To USDA, effective competition 'to meet the needs of the public' must include effective inter-railroad competition – the kind that minimizes the number of captive shippers and the need for regulatory control over rates and services.
Some of us are already hearing initial concerns about the UP-NS application and its lack of serious and meaningful commitments to enhance competition and protect against service meltdowns.

complaints about increased market power and major service disruptions resulting from those past mergers generated tremendous backlash from rail customers, employees, passenger rail operators and riders along with communities cut in half by congested rail lines.
docket_entries.relief_requested: STB must 'conduct a rigorous and comprehensive review' and 'should not permit this transaction to proceed' absent clear demonstration that applicants meet burden to show 'clear, measurable, and substantial benefits for domestic manufacturers, agricultural producers, the energy sector, and the American consumer.' If approved, merger must 'enhance competition for rail shippers, ensure reliable rail service, and be in the interest of the public.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing directly invokes the STB's 2001 merger rules and establishes congressional authority framing that would require UP and NS to meet an explicit burden: affirmatively demonstrating competition enhancement (not preservation) under 49 U.S.C. § 11324. The filing cites USDA's prior position during 2001 rule revision, suggesting STB must apply that precedent. It establishes on-the-record claim that applicants lack adequate competitive safeguards, shifting evidentiary burden and potentially requiring UP/NS to submit additional evidence during discovery. Congressional pressure may influence STB composition, decision timeline, and breadth of conditions imposed. The filing frames the public interest test around constituent harm (manufacturers, farmers, energy companies), potentially expanding the scope of beneficiaries the Board must consider when evaluating whether merger serves the public interest.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Congressional letter—no formal response deadline; however, may trigger STB clarification of merger review standards or procedural schedule.

docket_entries.title: STB Chair Fuchs Response to Congressional Letter on UP/NS Merger Labor and Safety Concerns
docket_entries.entry_summary: STB Chair Fuchs responds to congressional concerns about labor impacts, worker safety, and competition by confirming that the Board rejected the December 19, 2025 UP/NS merger application as incomplete on January 16, 2026. The application failed to include "projected market shares" required under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.7(b) and did not contain the complete merger agreement and all pertinent contracts as required under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.6(a)(7). The Board directed applicants to file a letter by February 17, 2026 indicating when they will file a revised application. Fuchs emphasizes that any revised application must address employee impacts with detailed geographic specificity and three-year forecasts, must include labor implementing agreements and Service Assurance Plans (SAP), must submit a Safety Integration Plan prepared with the Federal Railroad Administration, and must demonstrate how operating efficiencies will translate into service benefits. The Board will conduct "rigorous and comprehensive review" considering "effective competition, carrier safety and efficiency, adequate service for shippers, environmental safeguards, and fair working conditions for employees." The letter establishes that if approved, the Board will maintain formal oversight for at least five years, requiring annual evidence that conditions are working as intended and benefits are being realized, with retained jurisdiction to impose additional conditions. The proceeding remains open with opportunities for public participation from rail labor, shippers, carriers, and other interested parties.
key_arguments: The initial application was statutorily deficient and properly rejected without prejudice, permitting resubmission of a revised application that must satisfy all regulatory completeness requirements including projected market shares and complete merger agreements.

Applicants must provide detailed employee impact analyses specifying geographic points, time frames of at least three years post-consolidation, and any negotiated employee protection agreements, with Service Assurance Plans addressing labor implementing agreements and comprehensive employee training.

A Safety Integration Plan prepared in consultation with FRA must be submitted addressing deferred maintenance, capital improvements, system rehabilitation, and how these activities will yield promised service improvements and operating economies.

The Board's public interest standard requires demonstration that the merger will promote effective competition, carrier safety and efficiency, adequate shipper service, environmental safeguards, and fair working conditions for employees.

If approved, the Board will maintain five-year formal oversight requiring annual evidence that conditions are working, applicants are adhering to merger representations, no unforeseen harms have emerged, and promised benefits are being realized, with Board authority to impose additional conditions as needed.
key_excerpts: On January 16, 2026, the Board issued a unanimous decision finding that the application was incomplete because it did not contain certain information required by the Board's regulations at 49 C.F.R. part 1180. Specifically, the Board found that the December 19 application was incomplete because, in its impact analyses necessary to demonstrate the impacts of the transaction on competition and the provision of essential services, it did not include 'projected market shares' as required under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.7(b).

The Board's decision rejecting the December 19 application does not result in the dismissal of the merger proceeding, and Applicants are permitted to file a revised application in the docket, which would commence a new review by the Board for completeness. The Board directed Applicants to file a letter in the docket by February 17, 2026, indicating if and when they anticipate filing a revised application.

With regard to employee impacts, in a major merger application, Applicants must detail the effects of the proposed transaction on their employees, the geographic points where the impacts will occur, the time frame of the impacts (for at least 3 years after consolidation), and whether any employee protection agreements have been reached.

Applicants are required to submit a Service Assurance Plan (SAP), which must include, among other things, a plan for reaching necessary labor implementing agreements and include a plan for providing necessary training to employees involved in fields including operations, safety, hazardous materials compliance, and other functions affected by the acquisition.

In deciding whether a major merger transaction is in the public interest, the Board considers goals including effective competition, carrier safety and efficiency, adequate service for shippers, environmental safeguards, and fair working conditions for employees. The Board must ensure that any approved transaction would promote a competitive, efficient, and reliable national rail system.

In the event a proposed transaction is approved, the Board establishes a formal oversight process for at least five years following approval of a transaction... the Board retains jurisdiction to impose additional conditions it determines are necessary.
docket_entries.relief_requested: No direct relief requested. Filing is a procedural notice to Congress regarding the Board's January 16, 2026 rejection of the merger application for incompleteness and the applicants' obligation to file a revised application by February 17, 2026.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing establishes several critical procedural and substantive benchmarks: (1) the initial application failed statutory completeness review under 49 U.S.C. § 11325(a), specifically regarding projected market shares and complete merger documentation; (2) any revised application triggers a new completeness review with new statutory time periods computed from the revised filing date; (3) the Board's regulatory framework mandates detailed competitive analysis (49 C.F.R. § 1180.7(b)), employee impact documentation (49 C.F.R. § 1180.6(a)(2)(v), (b)(9)), Service Assurance Plans (49 C.F.R. § 1180.10), Safety Integration Plans (49 C.F.R. § 1180.8(a)(1)), and 'full system' analyses including Canadian and Mexican operations (49 C.F.R. § 1180.1(k)); (4) labor protections are mandatory at the level required by 49 U.S.C. § 11325(a) with possible enhancement for unusual circumstances (49 C.F.R. § 1180.1(e)); (5) post-approval oversight for minimum five years with retained Board jurisdiction to impose additional conditions creates ongoing regulatory exposure; and (6) the Board must affirmatively find the merger serves the public interest on multiple dimensions including competition, safety, service, environment, and labor conditions before approval is possible. The rejection without prejudice resets the procedural clock and requires applicants to address the specific deficiencies identified.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Applicants (Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern) must file a letter by February 17, 2026, indicating if and when they anticipate filing a revised merger application that remedies the completeness deficiencies identified in the January 16, 2026 Board decision.

docket_entries.title: BNSF Motion for Hearing on Motion to Compel Discovery from Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern
docket_entries.entry_summary: BNSF, competing directly with Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern, seeks an immediate hearing on its Motion to Compel discovery. BNSF emphasizes that over six months have passed since the merger announcement and it has been serving discovery requests for four months, yet UP and NS continue to withhold "ordinary course documents" and "internal, candid assessments and conversations." BNSF characterizes the applicants' discovery posture as "sweeping, 'trust us' approach" and "months of stonewalling," arguing that continued withholding "would deprive the Board a full record on which to consider the to-be re-filed application." BNSF frames this as a procedural necessity to "put discovery on the right track" and avoid further delay. While this is technically a procedural motion (requesting a hearing on a prior motion), it reflects BNSF's active opposition to the merger—BNSF needs these materials to substantiate competitive harm arguments. The motion signals BNSF's serious litigation posture and aggressive discovery strategy.
key_arguments: Applicants' withholding of board materials, banker materials, and email communications prevents BNSF from mounting a complete competitive harm case and deprives the Board of a full evidentiary record.
Four months of serving discovery requests have yielded no meaningful document production, demonstrating applicants' intent to stonewall unless compelled by court order.
The applicants' 'trust us' approach is unprecedented and inconsistent with the stakes of a transaction claimed to 'shape the next hundred years of American railroading.'
Without immediate judicial intervention, discovery delays will continue indefinitely—only a hearing and order to compel will move the proceeding forward.
key_excerpts: Months of stonewalling make clear that, until ordered to do so, UP and NS will not meaningfully advance discovery of ordinary course documents and email.

The sweeping, 'trust us' approach that UP and NS adopt in their reply (UP-24/NS23) is unprecedented. If permitted, it would deprive the Board a full record on which to consider the to-be re-filed application.
To avoid further delay—and to put discovery on the right track—BNSF respectfully requests a hearing on its Motion to Compel at Your Honor's earliest convenience.
docket_entries.relief_requested: BNSF requests a hearing on its Motion to Compel at Judge Soulikias's earliest convenience to compel Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern to produce case-relevant board materials, banker materials, and email communications.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing highlights a critical discovery dispute that affects the procedural integrity of the merger review. Under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 and STB discovery rules, applicants in merger proceedings must produce documents relevant to competitive impact, market concentration, and financial viability. BNSF's motion challenges applicants' assertion of privilege/confidentiality over board minutes, banker communications, and internal strategy emails. The ALJ's ruling will establish the boundaries of discoverable materials in this mega-merger case and determine whether BNSF and other intervenors can access the internal decision-making documents necessary to credibly challenge competitive effects. A ruling favoring BNSF would expand the evidentiary record significantly; a ruling favoring applicants would constrain intervenors' ability to cross-examine merger rationale. This motion is consequential for the overall fact-finding process.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No specific deadline stated; BNSF requests hearing 'at Your Honor's earliest convenience.' ALJ Soulikias will set hearing schedule in her discretion.

docket_entries.title: Supplemental Verified Comments on Union Pacific-Norfolk Southern Merger Control Application
docket_entries.filer_name: Andrew C. Robertson, President of Atlantic Systems Inc
docket_entries.entry_summary: Andrew Robertson challenges the incomplete UPNS merger application, arguing that the Applicants failed to provide proper market share calculations and lack clear definitions of relevant markets. Robertson contends that without proper equipment accounting and market segmentation by origin-destination-commodity flows, accurate competitive impact analysis is impossible. He requests the STB provide guidance on relevant market definitions and require new diversion studies with full IMC participation before approval.
key_arguments: UPNS failed to account for multibillion-dollar equipment and capital expenditures required by TTX, shippers, and IMCs
Market share calculations require clearly defined relevant markets segmented by origin-destination-commodity flows
UPNS's expansive 'Seamless Transcontinental Network' framing trivializes local and regional competitive impacts
The 237,000 carload diversion from other railroads involves shippers with existing sidings and limited truck competition alternatives, creating captive shipper concerns
Truck-to-intermodal diversions (1.23 million units) rest on unverified assumptions that UPNS-aligned IMCs lack capacity to execute
UPNS has not consulted with or secured commitments from Hub, Knight-Swift, and ONE regarding operational capacity for projected intermodal growth
Watershed and Committed Gateway Pricing benefits are speculative and not quantified in proper market context
UPNS-aligned IMCs will gain commanding market position in intermodal drayage, harming competing IMCs and motor carriers
key_excerpts: Without the equipment accounting identified in my previous filing, the market share calculations requested by the Board on January 18 remain a mathematical impossibility

Because market share calculations are only meaningful within properly defined markets, the STB cannot evaluate UPNS's competitive impact without segmenting the traffic flows into distinct, economically coherent markets
The principal beneficiaries of UPNS diversions are UPNS and its allied IMCs. By these calculations, these 'friendly' IMCs will take a commanding position in the intermodal drayage market
UPNS has planned for massive intermodal growth without securing the full participation of the IMCs who would be required to execute it
To evaluate whether the merger enhances or harms competition, the STB must determine whether UPNS's increased scale translates into dominance in specific O-D commodity markets
docket_entries.document_type: Modify/Supplement Prior Filing Or The Record

docket_entries.title: Union Pacific Reply: Motion to Strike CPKC's Improper Reply-to-Reply and Reinforce Discovery Scope Limitations
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific filed a motion to strike CPKC's February 2 letter as a prohibited reply-to-reply under STB rules strictly enforced in recent decisions. UP argues that CPKC improperly responded to UP's January 29 reply to BNSF's motion to compel. UP contends that tolerating such filings would create 'chaos' with 'multiple parallel threads of briefing' and undermine 'orderly and efficient administration' of the proceeding. Even if not struck, UP argues CPKC's letter actually reinforces UP's core position that discovery must proceed through 'specific requests' rather than 'sweeping demands for vague categories of documents.' UP criticizes CPKC and BNSF for demanding 'undefined categories of ordinary course documents' and broad email collections without justifying why 'appropriately targeted collections and productions are not sufficient and proportional to the needs of this proceeding.' UP commits to conferring on specific requests but refuses wholesale collections: 'Applicants have not issued a blanket refusal to produce ordinary course documents. Instead, Applicants have committed to conferring with parties regarding their specific discovery requests.' UP cites the CP/KCS merger (FD 36500) as precedent where CPKC itself negotiated narrow discovery scopes and produced 'a fraction of the material that Applicants have already produced in this proceeding, and at a far slower pace'—a pointed suggestion that UP is being more cooperative than competitors were in prior cases.
key_arguments: CPKC's letter violates STB Rule 49 C.F.R. § 1140.13(c) prohibiting replies-to-replies, a rule the Board recently committed to enforcing 'more strictly' for orderly case administration (Sunflower State Indus. Ry., FD 36714, March 2025; Norfolk S./Portsmouth Belt, FD 36836, March 2025)

Permitting routine replies-to-replies would create procedural chaos: 'With numerous parties of record, it is likely any motion would devolve into multiple parallel threads of briefing. The parties would have little incentive to reduce the burden on the Board, other parties, and the public by fully addressing issues in initial filings'

Discovery disputes must be resolved through conferral on specific requests with proportionality analysis, not abstract demands: 'The only practical way to resolve discovery disputes is to have the parties confer regarding individual requests, address objections and negotiate the scope of reasonable searches in light of the relevance of the materials sought and the burden of collection'

Sweeping categorical demands for 'ordinary course documents' and wholesale email collections lack legal basis: 'The Board's merger rules do not require Applicants to conduct wholesale collections and productions of emails and other internal materials without regard to the relevance of the materials sought or the burden of their collection'

UP has been more cooperative with discovery than CPKC was in the prior CP/KCS merger, producing 'a fraction of the material' faster than competitors in predecessor cases, suggesting good faith compliance

BNSF and CPKC have failed to explain proportionality: requesting parties 'failed to offer any explanation why appropriately targeted collections and productions are not sufficient and proportional to the needs of this proceeding'
key_excerpts: '[A] reply to a reply is not permitted.' Although the Board sometimes found good cause to accept such filings in the past, it has made clear in the last year that it will now 'more strictly' enforce this rule to ensure 'the orderly and efficient administration of cases.'

If the Board permits routine replies to replies in this proceeding, it will be impossible to ensure 'the orderly and efficient administration' of this proceeding. Nothing would stop the parties of record from attempting to get the last word on every dispute regardless of whether they are even a party to the dispute.

Discovery disputes must be evaluated within the context of specific discovery requests... demanding sweeping productions of materials without justifying those productions with specific relevant and reasonable discovery requests is not conducive to a reasonable and efficient discovery process.

Applicants have not issued a blanket refusal to produce 'ordinary course documents.' Instead, Applicants have committed to conferring with parties regarding their specific discovery requests in order to identify an appropriately narrow set of materials that can be reasonably searched consistent with the Board's merger review process.

The Board's merger rules do not require Applicants to conduct wholesale collections and productions of emails and other internal materials without regard to the relevance of the materials sought or the burden of their collection.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Strike CPKC's February 2, 2026 letter from the record as an improper reply-to-reply under 49 C.F.R. § 1140.13(c). In the alternative, use CPKC's filing to reinforce that discovery must proceed through specific requests, not sweeping categorical demands.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing attempts to establish a procedural precedent limiting discovery scope in the merger review. Union Pacific is relying on recent STB board orders (Sunflower State, Norfolk S./Portsmouth Belt, US Rail/Brookhaven, all 2025) to argue strict enforcement of the reply-to-reply ban. The substance is important because broad discovery demands by competitors (BNSF, CPKC) could materially extend the proceeding timeline and impose compliance burdens on UP/NS. UP is attempting to frame the discovery dispute as one about proportionality and specificity rather than withholding. This could influence how ALJ Soulikias (copied on filing) rules on pending and future discovery motions. The invocation of the CP/KCS precedent also suggests UP may be attempting to create a record that it is being more accommodating than its competitors were in prior cases.
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is a motion requesting Board action. No explicit deadline stated, but CPKC may seek leave to respond or defend its February 2 letter. The motion should be ruled on before substantive discovery disputes are resolved.

docket_entries.title: Susquehanna Union Railroad Company Notice of Intent to Participate

SURC has retained experienced STB counsel (KMA Zuckert), suggesting potential for substantive participation if terms threaten their operational model.

SURC relies on shared interchange locations with Norfolk Southern at multiple Central Pennsylvania locations
SURC operates on shared trackage with Norfolk Southern in multiple locations, creating vulnerability to post-merger service or access changes

No substantive legal issues are raised in this filing; significance lies in establishing that short-line dependent operations may later present evidence of merger-induced service degradation, rate increases, or access restrictions. The filing does not change the scope of review but confirms that interconnected third-party operational relationships will be part of the evidentiary record.

docket_entries.title: ALJ Denies BNSF Motion to Compel Discovery and Request for Hearing; Strikes CPKC Letter as Improper Reply to Reply
docket_entries.entry_summary: The ALJ denied BNSF's motion to compel discovery documents (board materials, banker analyses, internal emails) and BNSF's request for a hearing on the motion. The ALJ held that the Major Merger Rules, 5 S.T.B. 539 (2001), distinguish between pre-application and post-application discovery phases. In the pre-application phase, applicants are required to provide only what the Board has specifically ordered: (1) 100% traffic tapes for January 1, 2019 through December 31, 2024; (2) timetables, station lists, track charts; (3) geospatial information system maps; (4) joint facilities data; and (5) interchange commitments. The ALJ reasoned: "This is a question about timing, not scope of discovery. Here, the Board found the Application incomplete and gave Applicants leave to file a revised application. There is not an application pending for the Board to review. Applicants are preparing their revised application." The ALJ clarified that BNSF may be entitled to "basic discovery" (board materials, banker analyses, emails) after a revised application is accepted by the Board and the appropriate scope of discovery is reviewed. The ALJ also noted that pre-application discovery may be voluntarily conducted by the parties. Additionally, the ALJ granted UP's request to strike CPKC's February 2, 2026 letter as an improper reply to a reply, finding that although CPKC styled its letter as seeking affirmative relief rather than as a reply, CPKC's own characterization in its February 11 reply letter admitted the reply-to-reply purpose.
key_arguments: The Major Merger Rules establish a distinction between pre-application and post-application discovery: broad pre-application discovery is not proposed by the Board, and early access to traffic tapes should not impede applicants' preparation of their application.

During the pre-application phase, only discovery specifically ordered by the Board is required: traffic tapes, timetables, station lists, track charts, geospatial information system maps, joint facilities, and interchange commitments.

BNSF's request for 'basic discovery' (board materials, banker analyses, internal emails) falls outside the scope of pre-application discovery under the Major Merger Rules and cannot be compelled at this stage.
The current posture is pre-application: the Board found the initial application incomplete, applicants are preparing a revised application, and no application is currently pending for Board review.
BNSF may renew its motion to compel after a revised application is accepted by the Board, at which point the appropriate scope of discovery will be reviewed.
Pre-application discovery may be voluntarily conducted by the parties, but cannot be compelled at this stage.
CPKC's letter filed after UP's reply constitutes an improper reply to a reply, regardless of how CPKC styled the request for relief.
key_excerpts: This is a question about timing, not scope of discovery. Here, the Board found the Application incomplete and gave Applicants leave to file a revised application. There is not an application pending for the Board to review. Applicants are preparing their revised application.

BNSF may be entitled to these things after a revised application is accepted by the Board; however, the Major Merger Rules do not support compelling them now during the pre-application phase. See 5 S.T.B. at 591. Accordingly, BNSF's motion to compel is denied without prejudice and may be renewed, if appropriate, after Applicants' revised application is accepted.

Early access to this critical traffic data would aid interested parties in the preparation of their own submissions but (unlike broad pre-application discovery, which we are not proposing) would not impede the prospective applicants in the preparation of their application.
To be clear, pre-application discovery may be voluntarily conducted.
docket_entries.relief_requested: DENIED: BNSF's motion to compel Applicants to produce board materials, banker presentations, and internal emails; DENIED: BNSF's request for a hearing on the motion to compel; GRANTED: UP's request to strike CPKC's February 2, 2026 letter as an improper reply to a reply.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This ruling clarifies a critical distinction in the Major Merger Rules framework: pre-application discovery is limited in scope and timing, even for major rail consolidations. The ALJ's interpretation of 5 S.T.B. 539 (2001) establishes that broad discovery (board materials, internal communications, banker analyses) cannot be compelled until after a revised application is accepted by the Board. This significantly restricts competitors' ability to obtain discovery during the pre-application phase and creates a procedural hurdle for intervenors seeking to conduct expansive factual investigation before the formal hearing phase. The ruling also establishes that intervenors must distinguish between pre- and post-application discovery rights, effectively creating a two-stage discovery regime. This may affect the evidentiary burden and the pace of the proceeding, as competitors cannot compel internal documents until the application is formally accepted. The denial without prejudice preserves BNSF's and other competitors' rights to renew the motion post-acceptance.
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is a final procedural ruling; however, Applicants must file a letter by February 17, 2026, informing whether and when they anticipate filing a revised application, and may file a revised application no later than June 22, 2026. Upon acceptance of a revised application, BNSF may renew its motion to compel.

docket_entries.title: CPKC Response to UP/NS Motion to Strike: Opposes Discovery Limitations, Demands Ordinary Course Documents
docket_entries.entry_summary: CPKC filed in response to UP/NS motion to strike CPKC's prior discovery letter, seeking to preserve and expand its discovery rights. CPKC demands that UP and NS produce zero internal ordinary course documents to date despite nearly five months of discovery requests since September 2025. CPKC argues: 'Applicants have produced voluminous data and various agreements with other railroads, but they have still produced zero internal documents prepared by UP or NS personnel in the ordinary course of their business reflecting how those railroads think about, analyze, and communicate about the issues raised by the Application when they are doing so in more candid contexts outside of Board advocacy.' CPKC characterizes UP/NS production as fundamentally inadequate, contrasting it with CP and KCS in the CP/KCS merger, which produced extensive email, memos, spreadsheets, board materials, and strategic planning documents. CPKC argues discovery scope must expand relative to CP/KCS because: (1) UP-NS combination is 'orders of magnitude larger, blankets the entire country,' and applicants claim it will 'fundamentally transform U.S. railroading for centuries'; (2) this is the first application of the 2001 Major Merger Rules, which 'significantly increased Applicants' burden of demonstrating that their proposal serves the public interest and enhances competition'; (3) discovery requirements must be 'broader and more expansive, not less' given the transaction's scope and regulatory framework. CPKC explicitly requests hearing participation to present these arguments and remains actively engaged in opposing discovery limitations. This filing signals conditional opposition: CPKC will accept the merger IF adequate discovery is provided to test applicants' claims, but current discovery withholding is unacceptable.
key_arguments: UP and NS have produced zero internal ordinary course business documents (board materials, strategic plans, traffic forecasts, integration plans, email communications) nearly five months after initial discovery requests, despite producing voluminous agreements with other railroads—a production strategy fundamentally different from CP/KCS merger precedent

CP and KCS produced extensive ordinary course documents on pre-merger traffic forecasts, marketing strategies, board deliberations, service improvement efforts, and pricing analysis, whereas UP/NS have produced 'no board materials, no strategic plans, no growth forecasts, no business documents explaining their pre-existing standalone plans, none of their employees' communications about actual integration plans, and no email whatsoever (other than about 50 cover emails)'

Discovery scope must expand far beyond CP/KCS precedent because UP-NS combination is 'orders of magnitude larger, blankets the entire country' and applicants claim it will 'fundamentally transform U.S. railroading for centuries to come'

This proceeding is the first application of the 2001 Major Merger Rules, which 'expanded the scope of the Board's public interest inquiry and significantly increased Applicants' burden' of proving public interest and competitive enhancement—making discovery scope 'inevitably and commensurately broader and more expansive, not less'

UP/NS characterization that CP/KCS produced 'only a fraction of the material' that UP/NS have produced is 'nonsense on multiple levels' because it misrepresents both the nature of applicants' production and the relative complexity and scale differences between the transactions
key_excerpts: Applicants have produced voluminous data and various agreements with other railroads, but they have still—nearly five months after receiving the first discovery requests in this proceeding last September—produced zero internal documents prepared by UP or NS personnel in the ordinary course of their business reflecting how those railroads think about, analyze, and communicate about the issues raised by the Application when they are doing so in more candid contexts outside of Board advocacy.

CP and KCS produced [on such topics as] their pre-merger traffic forecasts, their marketing strategies, consideration of merger issues by their boards of directors, their efforts to improve service and grow traffic through interline collaborations, and their approach to and analysis of rail pricing, among many others. In contrast, Applicants have produced no such documents: no board materials, no strategic plans, no growth forecasts, no business documents explaining their pre-existing standalone plans, none of their employees' communications about actual integration plans, and no email whatsoever (other than about 50 cover emails to which agreements were attached).

This proceeding involves the first-ever application of the 2001 Major Merger Rules, which expanded the scope of the Board's public interest inquiry and significantly increased Applicants' burden of demonstrating that their proposal serves the public interest and enhances competition. Discovery in such a proceeding will inevitably and commensurately be broader and more expansive, not less.
docket_entries.relief_requested: CPKC seeks: (1) Denial of UP/NS motion to strike CPKC's February 2 letter; (2) Scheduling of discovery hearing at which CPKC counsel may participate; (3) Compulsory production of UP and NS ordinary course business documents (board materials, strategic plans, traffic forecasts, integration plans, employee communications, and email); (4) Rejection of Applicants' discovery limitations that CPKC characterizes as 'strident' and lacking merit.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing raises critical evidentiary burdens under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 and the 2001 Major Merger Rules (49 C.F.R. Part 1180, Subpart C). CPKC's argument that applicants must satisfy an enhanced 'public interest and competitive enhancement' burden is legally significant because it reframes the discovery scope question: production of internal planning documents becomes essential to testing whether applicants' public interest claims are supported by contemporaneous business analysis. The filing also establishes on the record that CPKC contests the sufficiency of applicants' document production compared to CP/KCS precedent, potentially supporting later challenges to ALJ evidentiary rulings. The reference to 2001 Major Merger Rules as applying 'for the first time' in this proceeding may affect burden allocation and expert testimony standards.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Implied deadline for ALJ response or hearing scheduling on discovery issues; no explicit deadline stated in letter but standard STB discovery response timeframe is 7 business days

docket_entries.title: SEDA-COG Joint Rail Authority Notice of Intent to Participate
docket_entries.entry_summary: SEDA-COG filed a notice of intent to participate without submitting substantive comments on the merger. The authority established standing based on: (1) its status as a Pennsylvania state rail authority operating a nine-county rail system, (2) physical interconnection between its rail lines and Norfolk Southern's network, and (3) existing contractual relationship with Norfolk Southern for trackage rights on the Selinsgrove Industrial Track. The filing requests only procedural relief—placement on the service list with three designated counsel representatives. SEDA-COG signals intent to monitor the proceeding but takes no position on approval/denial and presents no arguments regarding competitive harm, service quality, or merger conditions. This is a classic 'watching brief' by a stakeholder with direct operational exposure but insufficient immediate concern to lodge opposition.
key_excerpts: The JRA further respectfully requests that its representatives and undersigned solicitors be placed on the service list as the authorized representatives for the JRA in these proceedings

The SEDA-COG Joint Rail Authority (the 'JRA') hereby submits its Notice of Intent to Participate in this proceeding and any related proceedings before the Surface Transportation Board ('STB'), consistent with the JRA's role as a Pennsylvania nine (9)-county joint rail authority, and independent agency of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, whose lines interconnect with those of Norfolk Southern Rail Corporation's lines, and as a contracting partner with Norfolk Southern Corporation, relative to the Selinsgrove Industrial Track and certain other trackage rights.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Request to participate in the proceeding and placement of representatives on the service list
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low procedural significance. The filing establishes SEDA-COG's legal standing to participate based on state agency status and operational interconnection with Norfolk Southern. It does not advance novel theories of harm or propose remedies, but its contractual relationship with NS (trackage rights) could become relevant if applicants propose operational changes affecting the Selinsgrove Industrial Track post-merger. The filing suggests SEDA-COG may later submit comments raising service level or access concerns if merger conditions threaten existing arrangements.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.deadline_description: Procedural filing; no response deadline triggered

docket_entries.title: Steven Connolly - Request for STB Consideration of Grade Crossing Aggregation Impacts
docket_entries.entry_summary: Steven Connolly, a Jacksonville resident, submits public comments asking the STB to consider 'the impacts of aggregation' resulting from the proposed merger. He references local news coverage showing how long trains block grade crossings in Jacksonville, citing an example where a motorist was able to order food delivery while waiting for a train to clear. His core argument is that railroad mergers produce 'aggregation' - characterized by longer trains and single-line service - which 'will impact many communities across this proposed merger.' He frames this as a consequence of rail consolidation that the Board should weigh in its analysis. The filing contains no specific requests to deny, condition, or approve the merger, no quantified traffic impact analysis, and no proposed remedies. It is a general plea for procedural consideration of community-level grade crossing impacts.
key_arguments: Railroad mergers inevitably result in 'aggregation' that produces longer trains blocking grade crossings for extended periods, affecting community traffic flow and quality of life
Single-line railroad service (cited as justification for mergers) comes with a 'price' of operational consolidation that will negatively impact communities across the merger territory
Grade crossing delays demonstrated by Jacksonville news coverage illustrate a real, recurring problem that merger analysis should explicitly consider
key_excerpts: Single line railroad service is often stated as a reason to approve railroad mergers and single line railroad service also comes at a price: longer trains and a reality that will impact many communities across this proposed merger.
I'm asking your office to consider the impacts of aggregation as this complex finance docket is considered before the Surface Transportation Board.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Request that the STB 'consider the impacts of aggregation as this complex finance docket is considered before the Surface Transportation Board.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Minimal. Filing does not raise novel legal issues, cite regulatory standards, or propose enforceable remedies. It is a general public interest comment requesting consideration of community impacts. Does not create evidentiary burdens or change scope of review. Signals that local constituencies may be monitoring grade crossing impacts, but does not establish a factual record requiring response.

docket_entries.title: BNSF/Montana Grain Elevators Association Letter: UP-NS Merger Presents Unacceptable Competition and Supply Chain Risks
docket_entries.filer_name: Montana Grain Elevators Association (via BNSF Railway Company)
docket_entries.entry_summary: Montana Grain Elevators Association, filing through BNSF's counsel, opposes the UP-NS merger entirely and states that 'no form of the transaction (including any conditions intended to remedy competitive harms or enhance rail-to-rail competition) is capable of meeting the appropriately rigorous standards.' The Association argues the merger will: (1) eliminate competition on key freight markets, giving combined UP-NS 'unmatched power over shippers, suppliers, and rail workers' with inevitable rate increases; (2) cause service disruptions comparable to the UP-SP merger, potentially crippling national rail service and supply chains; (3) lock in UP's dominance by eliminating alternative routes and creating 'single points of failure'; and (4) be untrustworthy given UP's 25-year history of 'raising rates and shedding traffic instead of expanding service' despite remedies granted in prior mergers. The Association explicitly invokes UP's own 2022 opposition to the CPKC merger, where UP warned of 'enormous post-merger pressure to eliminate interline moves and implement anticompetitive strategies like raising rates shippers must pay for interline service or degrading the quality of service.' The filing signals that shippers view the merger as fundamentally restructuring competitive options with irreversible consequences, and that no behavioral conditions can restore lost competition.
key_arguments: A combined UP-NS would dominate key freight markets and shared rail industry assets, giving it unmatched power over shippers, suppliers, and rail workers, with less competition meaning higher costs for everyone.

The merger will cause service disruptions and supply chain vulnerabilities similar to the UP-SP merger; even minor disruptions in a combined network of this size could cripple rail service across the country with ripple effects across the entire U.S. economy.

UP has a documented 25-year track record of failing to honor competitive remedies from prior mergers—raising rates and shedding traffic instead of expanding service—which strongly suggests merger commitments cannot be trusted.

The merger would permanently eliminate alternative routes and create single points of failure across the rail network, destroying the resilience and shipper optionality necessary for a functioning competitive rail system.

UP's own 2022 arguments against the CPKC merger—that consolidation causes 'enormous post-merger pressure to eliminate interline moves and implement anticompetitive strategies like raising rates'—directly apply to and undermine UP's current merger arguments.
key_excerpts: Montana Grain Elevators Association believes that Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern's proposed merger presents significant risk for businesses like ours and the U.S. economy. We are concerned the merger will harm shippers and their customers by eliminating competition, disrupting service, weakening the U.S. supply chain, and increasing transportation rates.

we respectfully ask the Board to carefully consider the following concerns as it scrutinizes whether any form of the transaction (including any conditions intended to remedy competitive harms or enhance rail-to-rail competition) is capable of meeting the appropriately rigorous standards set forth in the Board's governing statutes and regulations
A combined UP-NS would dominate key freight markets and shared rail industry assets, giving it unmatched power over shippers, suppliers, and rail workers.

UP has a history of failing to honor the competitive remedies granted to shippers in the last major round of mergers. Over the past 25 years, UP has raised rates and shed traffic instead of expanding service, signaling that it values profits over growth.

The merger would permanently lock in UP's dominance, eliminating alternative routes and creating single points of failure across the rail network. Resilience depends on shippers having multiple choices and a rail network that can shift to changes in supply, demand, and shipping patterns.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the proposed transaction in any form, including any conditions intended to remedy competitive harms or enhance rail-to-rail competition. The Board should reject the merger as incapable of meeting the rigorous standards set forth in 49 U.S.C. § 11324.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing is significant because it represents organized shipper opposition and explicitly rejects conditional approval as a remedy—stating that no conditions can satisfy statutory standards. This narrows the settlement space considerably. The filing also weaponizes UP's own prior merger opposition arguments (CPKC, 2022), forcing applicants to distinguish their earlier competitive concerns or concede internal inconsistency. The invocation of UP-SP merger harms (a well-documented historical precedent involving service catastrophe) creates a high evidentiary burden on applicants to prove this merger differs. The shipper association's participation signals potential for coordinated discovery and hearing testimony on market-specific rate impacts and service degradation risks.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period deadline applies; this is a substantive filing within the record for Board consideration in merger review

docket_entries.title: STB Response to Congressional Letter on UP/NS Merger - Procedural Status and Review Standards
docket_entries.entry_summary: The STB responds to a Congressional letter from 47 House Republicans regarding the proposed UP/NS merger. The Board confirms that on December 19, 2025, UP and NS filed a major merger application, which the Board rejected as incomplete on January 16, 2026. The application lacked: (1) 'projected market shares' required under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.7(b) in impact analyses demonstrating effects on competition and essential services, and (2) the complete merger agreement and all contracts/written instruments required under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.6(a)(7). The Board reiterates its statutory review obligations: merger approval requires demonstrating that the transaction promotes 'a competitive, efficient, and reliable national rail system' and advances public interest goals including 'effective competition, carrier safety and efficiency, adequate service for shippers, environmental safeguards, and fair working conditions for employees.' The Board emphasizes that applicants must propose conditions to 'mitigate and offset merger-related harms' and that conditions 'should not only preserve, but also enhance, competition.' The Board also requires a Service Assurance Plan identifying steps to ensure projected service levels are attainable and describing how operating efficiencies translate to benefits for shippers. The Board directed applicants to file a letter by February 17, 2026 indicating whether and when they will refile, and confirmed it will 'conduct a thorough and fair review' if a revised application is submitted. The Board also noted that the review process includes opportunities for public participation.
key_arguments: The December 19, 2025 UP/NS merger application was incomplete under 49 U.S.C. § 11325(a) and 49 C.F.R. part 1180 because it did not include 'projected market shares' required by 49 C.F.R. § 1180.7(b) in impact analyses necessary to demonstrate transaction effects on competition and essential services

The application was also incomplete because it did not include the complete merger agreement and all contracts or written instruments pertaining to the transaction as required by 49 C.F.R. § 1180.6(a)(7)

Merger approval requires Board determination that the transaction would promote 'a competitive, efficient, and reliable national rail system' considering: effective competition, carrier safety and efficiency, adequate service for shippers, environmental safeguards, and fair working conditions for employees, per 49 C.F.R. § 1180.1(b)
Applicants must propose conditions that 'should not only preserve, but also enhance, competition' per 49 C.F.R. § 1180.6(b)(10)

Applicants must submit a Service Assurance Plan under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.10 identifying steps to ensure projected service levels are attainable and describing how operating plan efficiencies translate into benefits for the shipping public, including contingency plans for managing merger-related service disruptions

The application must include 'full system' competitive analyses and operating plans including operations in Canada and Mexico to allow Board determination of competitive, service, employee, safety, and environmental impacts within the United States, per 49 C.F.R. § 1180.1(k)
key_excerpts: The Board found that the December 19 application was incomplete because, in its impact analyses necessary to demonstrate the impacts of the transaction on competition and the provision of essential services, it did not include 'projected market shares' as required under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.7(b).
Applicants must propose conditions to mitigate and offset merger-related harms, and these conditions should not only preserve, but also enhance, competition.

In deciding whether a major merger transaction is in the public interest, the Board considers goals including effective competition, carrier safety and efficiency, adequate service for shippers, environmental safeguards, and fair working conditions for employees.

Should they file a revised application in the docket, the Board would commence a new review for completeness... the Board will conduct a thorough and fair review of the evidence and argument and consider whether the transaction serves the public interest, consistent with applicable law.
docket_entries.relief_requested: No relief requested. Board confirms it will conduct rigorous review and directs applicants to file letter by February 17, 2026 indicating timing of revised application submission.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing establishes the definitive regulatory framework and evidentiary burden for UP/NS merger review. The STB's January 16, 2026 incompleteness ruling (cited here) rejected the initial application on substantive grounds - lack of projected market share analysis directly addressing competitive effects. This creates a critical requirement that any revised application must include detailed quantitative competitive impact analysis. The Board's emphasis on conditions that 'enhance' competition (not merely preserve it) and the requirement for full-system analyses including Canadian/Mexican operations sets a high bar. The Service Assurance Plan requirement creates an obligation for applicants to affirmatively demonstrate that service improvements will offset any degradation. This is the foundational procedural order defining what the record must contain.
docket_entries.deadline_description: UP and NS directed to file letter indicating whether and when they will file revised application remedying the January 16, 2026 incompleteness findings

docket_entries.title: CN (Grand Trunk Corporation) Consents to DOJ Supplemental Protective Order for Access to CN's Confidential Information
docket_entries.entry_summary: CN (Grand Trunk Corporation) filed a one-page letter confirming it does not object to DOJ's Supplemental Protective Order filed February 4, 2026. CN states: 'CN does not object to DOJ's requested Supplemental Protective Order to facilitate their access to CN's information and thus their participation in these proceedings.' CN explicitly noted it has provided 'certain information designated Highly Confidential or Confidential under the existing Protective Order to the Applicants in these proceedings, including CN's 2019-2024 traffic tapes.' The filing frames DOJ's access as necessary for DOJ to 'access the information necessary to evaluate the proposed transaction and participate fully, consistent with its statutory right to intervene as a party under 49 U.S.C. § 11325(b)(1).' This is a technical procedural consent that permits government antitrust counsel to review CN's competitive data, suggesting CN is cooperating with DOJ scrutiny of the merger rather than opposing or supporting it outright.
key_arguments: CN's confidential operational data (2019-2024 traffic tapes and other highly confidential information) should be made available to DOJ under supplemental protective order to enable rigorous antitrust evaluation
DOJ's participation in these proceedings is statutorily contemplated and necessary for full evaluation of the transaction
key_excerpts: CN does not object to DOJ's requested Supplemental Protective Order to facilitate their access to CN's information and thus their participation in these proceedings.
CN has provided certain information designated Highly Confidential or Confidential under the existing Protective Order to the Applicants in these proceedings, including CN's 2019-2024 traffic tapes.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Confirmation of non-objection to DOJ's Supplemental Protective Order to facilitate DOJ access to CN's Highly Confidential and Confidential information (including CN's 2019-2024 traffic tapes) produced in these proceedings.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing confirms that a competing Class I railroad (CN) is voluntarily making detailed operational and competitive intelligence available to DOJ for antitrust analysis. This removes any potential objection from CN as an intervenor that would otherwise delay or impede DOJ's access to competitive data necessary for antitrust evaluation. The filing facilitates government scrutiny by ensuring DOJ has confidentiality protections to access sensitive competitive information. It suggests CN is neither opposing nor supporting the merger, but enabling robust government review—a neutral but cooperative posture.
docket_entries.document_type: Modify/Supplement Prior Filing Or The Record
docket_entries.deadline_description: No response required; this is a consent filing confirming CN's non-objection to existing procedural motion

docket_entries.title: Solutionary Rail Notice of Intent to Participate
docket_entries.entry_summary: Solutionary Rail filed a notice of intent to participate in the UP/NS merger proceeding. The filing contains no substantive arguments, conditions, or position on the merger's merits. It is solely a procedural notice establishing the filer's right to receive service of all documents and participate in the proceeding. Solutionary Rail provides contact information for Bill Moyer and consents to electronic service. No indication is given regarding whether the organization supports, opposes, or has neutral stance on the proposed transaction.
key_excerpts: Solutionary Rail hereby gives notice of its intent to participate in the above-captioned proceeding.
Copies of all pleadings and other documents filed or served in this proceeding, as well as all decisions and orders, should be served upon the representative below.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Notice of intent to participate in the proceeding; request for service of all pleadings, documents, decisions, and orders via email.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing establishes Solutionary Rail as an intervenor of record and triggers service obligations on all parties. However, the filing itself creates no legal burdens, changes to the scope of review, or substantive evidentiary issues. It is a straightforward participation notice.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)

docket_entries.title: Union Pacific Notice of Revised Application Filing (April 30, 2026)
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific filed notice that it and Norfolk Southern anticipate filing a revised application on April 30, 2026, pursuant to STB Decision No. 9. This is a procedural notice indicating the applicants will amend their merger application, but the filing does not specify what substantive changes or remedies will be included in the revised application. The notice was copied to all parties of record and ALJ Soulikias.
key_arguments: Applicants are signaling an amendment to their application consistent with Board requirements in Decision No. 9, suggesting they are responding to Board directives or factual development in discovery
key_excerpts: Union Pacific Corporation, Union Pacific Railroad Company, Norfolk Southern Corporation, and Norfolk Southern Railway Company are filing this letter to inform the Board that they anticipate filing a revised application in this docket on April 30, 2026.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Notice of intent to file revised application on April 30, 2026, pursuant to STB Decision No. 9.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This notice indicates the applicants have agreed to or been directed to revise their application. Without seeing Decision No. 9 or the eventual revised application, the legal significance is procedural rather than substantive, but the revision may signal material changes to the merger terms, remedies, or factual record. The April 30, 2026 deadline becomes a critical juncture for intervenor strategy and Board scheduling.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Anticipated filing date for revised application

docket_entries.title: Cherokee County Commission Support for UP/NS Merger - Georgia Local Government Endorsement
docket_entries.entry_summary: Cherokee County Commission (Georgia) expresses strong support for the UP/NS merger as beneficial to regional economic development and transportation infrastructure. The Commissioner argues the merger will 'reduce congestion on our roads, enhance public safety, and create efficiencies in shipping for businesses and consumers.' The County characterizes the merger as offering 'improved service reliability' through 'more direct routes and greater operational flexibility,' 'reduced transit times' by 'eliminating certain interchanges,' and 'expanded reach' with 'broader geographic footprint' opening new markets. The filing emphasizes Cherokee County's direct stake given its rapid growth, recent voter approval of a Transportation Special Purpose Local Option Sales Tax, and dependence on efficient freight rail for economic competitiveness. No conditions or qualifications on support are requested.
key_arguments: The merger will reduce congestion on county roads and enhance public safety by consolidating rail operations and reducing service disruptions
Direct routes and greater operational flexibility under merged entity will improve schedule dependability and prevent service disruptions
Eliminating interchanges will reduce transit times and allow local businesses to reach customers faster and more competitively
The broader geographic footprint of merged entity will open new markets for Georgia products and strengthen supply chain resilience
The merger directly benefits Cherokee County as one of Georgia's fastest-growing counties with significant transportation infrastructure needs
key_excerpts: Freight rail is a cornerstone of our state's economy, safely moving the goods that power our industries and connect our communities to markets nationwide.
this merger can reduce congestion on our roads, enhance public safety, and create efficiencies in shipping for businesses and consumers
More direct routes and greater operational flexibility will help prevent service disruptions and improve schedule dependability
Eliminating certain interchanges will speed the movement of goods, helping our businesses reach customers faster and more competitively
docket_entries.relief_requested: The filer 'respectfully urges the Surface Transportation Board to give full and favorable consideration to this proposal, recognizing the benefits it will bring to our state and the national economy.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Minimal legal significance. This is a supportive comment from local government expressing political backing for the merger. Does not introduce novel legal theories, substantive competitive arguments, or conditions that would alter the scope of STB review.
