Serves primarily as evidence of regional stakeholder support and political feasibility rather than as substantive technical or economic analysis.

docket_entries.title: Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern Response to DOJ Motion for Supplemental Protective Order – No Objection
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern jointly filed a response on February 18, 2026 to the DOJ's February 4, 2026 Motion for Supplemental Protective Order. The applicants confirm they do not object to the DOJ's request for access to information produced under the existing Protective Order's confidentiality provisions. This is a straightforward procedural accommodation that demonstrates the parties' cooperation with DOJ review during the discovery phase. The filing indicates no substantive disputes between applicants and DOJ regarding information access for the merger investigation.
key_arguments: Applicants have previously produced material designated as Confidential and Highly Confidential and anticipate producing additional Designated Material
The DOJ's requested Supplemental Protective Order is acceptable to the applicants as parties who have produced such materials
key_excerpts: As parties that have previously produced material designated as Confidential and Highly Confidential under the existing Protective Order and that anticipate producing additional Designated Material in the future, Applicants write to confirm that they do not object to the DOJ's requested Supplemental Protective Order.

Applicants in response to the Motion for Supplemental Protective Order filed by the United States Department of Justice ("DOJ") on February 4, 2026...confirm that they do not object to the DOJ's requested Supplemental Protective Order
docket_entries.relief_requested: Applicants confirm they do not object to the DOJ's requested Supplemental Protective Order to facilitate DOJ access to information produced pursuant to the existing Protective Order's confidentiality provisions.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing confirms procedural cooperation between applicants and DOJ during the competitive review discovery phase. The non-objection to supplemental protective order language signals applicants' proactive compliance posture and willingness to provide DOJ with full access to confidential competitive materials. This may indicate confidence in the applicants' competitive analysis or reflect standard practice; the lack of objection eliminates a potential procedural friction point that could have delayed discovery.
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is a response filing; no further action required from applicants.

docket_entries.title: TUCO Inc. (Submitted via BNSF) Opposition to UP-NS Merger: Competitive Harm, Service Disruption, and Track Record Concerns
docket_entries.entry_summary: TUCO Inc., a Texas-based shipper, opposes the UP-NS merger as fundamentally harmful to shippers, workers, and the U.S. economy. TUCO argues the combined entity would 'dominate key freight markets and shared rail industry assets, giving it unmatched power over shippers, suppliers, and rail workers,' inevitably leading to higher costs. TUCO specifically cites UP's own 2022 comments opposing the CPKC merger—in which UP warned of 'enormous post-merger pressure' to 'raise rates shippers must pay for interline service or degrade the quality of service'—as evidence that UP understands the anticompetitive dynamics of consolidation. TUCO further argues that service disruptions are predictable (citing UP-SP merger history and recent rail congestion), that UP has a 25-year track record of raising rates and shedding traffic rather than expanding service after prior mergers, and that the merger would 'permanently lock in UP's dominance, eliminating alternative routes and creating single points of failure.' Critically, TUCO does not propose specific conditions; instead, it challenges whether 'any conditions intended to remedy competitive harms or enhance rail-to-rail competition' can possibly satisfy statutory standards, signaling a conviction that the deal cannot be remedied through conditioned approval and implicitly requesting outright denial.
key_arguments: A combined UP-NS would 'dominate key freight markets and shared rail industry assets,' giving it 'unmatched power over shippers, suppliers, and rail workers,' with inevitable rate increases and reduced service quality—using UP's own 2022 language against it from its CPKC merger opposition.

Service disruptions are inevitable and historically severe: 'As seen with prior rail mergers, the proposed transaction would likely cause service disruptions and congestion,' with UP gaining control of 'key facilities and terminal railroads' and having 'incentives to favor its own trains while creating bottlenecks and service problems for others.'

UP has a 25-year track record of failing to honor competitive remedies: 'Over the past 25 years, UP has raised rates and shed traffic instead of expanding service, signaling that it values profits over growth,' demonstrating that 'a merger with NS will only shrink the rail network further.'

The merger would 'permanently lock in UP's dominance, eliminating alternative routes and creating single points of failure across the rail network,' destroying resilience and shipper optionality that depend on 'multiple choices and a rail network that can shift to changes in supply, demand, and shipping patterns.'

No form of remedial conditions can adequately address these harms: TUCO 'respectfully ask[s] the Board to carefully consider' whether 'any form of the transaction (including any conditions intended to remedy competitive harms or enhance rail-to-rail competition) is capable of meeting the appropriately rigorous standards' of governing statutes, implicitly rejecting the viability of conditioned approval.
key_excerpts: A combined UP-NS would dominate key freight markets and shared rail industry assets, giving it unmatched power over shippers, suppliers, and rail workers. Less competition means higher costs for everyone. UP recognized this dynamic itself when it opposed the much smaller CPKC merger just a few years ago. UP said there would be 'enormous post-merger pressure' to eliminate interline moves and implement 'anticompetitive strategies' like 'raising rates shippers must pay for interline service or degrading the quality of service shippers receive when using interline service.'

As seen with prior rail mergers, the proposed transaction would likely cause service disruptions and congestion... UP would also gain control of key facilities and terminal railroads, having incentives to favor its own trains while creating bottlenecks and service problems for others.

Over the past 25 years, UP has raised rates and shed traffic instead of expanding service, signaling that it values profits over growth. This history strongly suggests that a merger with NS will only shrink the rail network further.

The merger would permanently lock in UP's dominance, eliminating alternative routes and creating single points of failure across the rail network. Resilience depends on shippers having multiple choices and a rail network that can shift to changes in supply, demand, and shipping patterns.

We respectfully ask the Board to carefully consider the following concerns as it scrutinizes whether any form of the transaction (including any conditions intended to remedy competitive harms or enhance rail-to-rail competition) is capable of meeting the appropriately rigorous standards set forth in the Board's governing statutes and regulations.
docket_entries.relief_requested: TUCO requests the Board 'carefully consider' and scrutinize 'whether any form of the transaction (including any conditions intended to remedy competitive harms or enhance rail-to-rail competition) is capable of meeting the appropriately rigorous standards set forth in the Board's governing statutes and regulations.' The filing does not propose specific conditions; instead, it argues that no remedial structure can adequately address the merger's fundamental harms.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: TUCO's opposition is legally significant because it explicitly challenges the viability of remedial conditions as a path to approval. By stating it questions whether 'any form of the transaction (including any conditions)' can satisfy statutory standards, TUCO signals skepticism about the fundamental adequacy of the Board's traditional remedy framework (trackage rights, operational conditions, etc.) to address merger-specific competitive harm. This frames the merger as presenting structural/systemic harm that conditions cannot remedy—a position that shifts the burden toward the applicants to prove that conditions ARE sufficient. Additionally, TUCO's use of UP's own 2022 language against the CPKC merger creates a direct precedential challenge: if UP acknowledged in that proceeding that consolidated railroads have incentive to degrade interline service, how can UP-NS conditions prevent identical behavior? This cuts to the internal consistency of UP's positions across proceedings.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing; no specific response deadline for TUCO itself, though applicants will likely address in reply comments or hearing.

docket_entries.title: Metra Notice of Intent to Participate - No Position Stated
docket_entries.entry_summary: Metra filed a notice of intent to participate in the UP-NS merger proceeding without expressing any specific position on the transaction. The filing is procedural in nature—Metra seeks formal intervenor status and placement on the service list to monitor how the merger may affect its operations. The filing does not articulate concerns, request conditions, or state whether Metra supports or opposes the transaction. This is a placeholder intervention that preserves Metra's right to submit substantive comments or participate in hearing proceedings as the case develops.
key_excerpts: The Commuter Rail Division of the Regional Transportation Authority d/b/a Metra ('Metra') hereby provides notice of its intent to participate in this proceeding as its interests may appear, and requests to be placed on the service list for this proceeding.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Formal notice of intent to participate in the proceeding and placement on the service list. Requests email service of all filings and documents.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing establishes Metra as a recognized intervenor in the proceeding and ensures it receives all subsequent notices and filings. No substantive legal issues are raised. The filing's significance lies in formal participation rights rather than evidentiary or procedural burden.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.deadline_description: No response deadline; this is a notice of intent filing that does not require applicant or other party response

docket_entries.title: Arkansas State Representative James P. Eaton supports UP-NS merger for economic development
docket_entries.entry_summary: Arkansas State Representative James P. Eaton supports the merger as beneficial to Arkansas's economy. He argues that a 'stronger, more integrated rail system can reduce delays, improve supply-chain reliability, and continue to make Arkansas a more attractive place for investment and job creation.' Eaton emphasizes that rural and small-town Arkansas depend on 'access to markets' for economic success and that strengthening freight infrastructure is 'a practical step toward ensuring Arkansas continues to be a place where businesses invest and families can build lasting futures.' He frames the merger as essential infrastructure modernization, but provides no specific analysis of competitive effects, service impacts, or economic data. The filing is supportive advocacy without engagement with substantive merger conditions or safeguards.
key_arguments: A stronger, more integrated rail system resulting from the merger will reduce delays and improve supply-chain reliability for Arkansas industries (manufacturing, agriculture, energy, logistics)
The merger represents critical infrastructure modernization needed to maintain Arkansas's competitive position for business investment and job creation
In rural and small-town Arkansas, reliable freight transportation access to markets is directly tied to local economic success; this merger strengthens that infrastructure link
key_excerpts: A stronger, more integrated rail system can reduce delays, improve supply-chain reliability, and continue to make Arkansas a more attractive place for investment and job creation.
Strengthening our freight infrastructure is a practical step toward ensuring Arkansas continues to be a place where businesses invest and families can build lasting futures.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Approval of the proposed Union Pacific-Norfolk Southern merger
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Minimal. This is a supportive statement from a state legislator without legal or regulatory arguments. It does not raise new antitrust issues, propose conditions, or engage with substantive merger criteria under 49 U.S.C. § 11324. It may be cited by applicants as evidence of local political support but carries no evidentiary weight regarding competitive effects or public interest analysis.
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is a public comment; no response deadline applies

docket_entries.title: Arkansas State Representative McElroy Supports UP-NS Merger for Rural Agriculture Benefits
docket_entries.entry_summary: Arkansas State Representative Mark D. McElroy, representing six agricultural counties, supports the UP-NS merger based on anticipated benefits to rural agriculture and small-town economies. McElroy argues: 'A stronger, more connected rail network would help reduce shipping delays, improve reliability, and lower transportation costs for farmers and agribusinesses across the state.' He contends that improved transportation infrastructure attracts processing facilities and manufacturing plants to rural communities, helping retain population and investment. McElroy's support is conditional on 'appropriate oversight' and 'rightful leadership' with 'focus on service and safety,' though he provides no specific operational conditions or enforcement mechanisms. The letter represents political support from a state official with agricultural constituency interest, but offers no technical analysis or detailed conditions that would substantively constrain the merger if approved.
key_arguments: A merged UP-NS network would reduce shipping delays and improve reliability for agricultural freight movements, directly benefiting Arkansas farmers competing in national and global markets
Lower transportation costs resulting from merger will improve farm margins and rural livelihoods in agricultural communities

Improved rail reliability attracts downstream investment in processing facilities, storage operations, and manufacturing plants to rural Arkansas, providing stable employment and retaining young families in small towns
key_excerpts: A stronger, more connected rail network would help reduce shipping delays, improve reliability, and lower transportation costs for farmers and agribusinesses across the state.
When transportation works, rural communities are better positioned to attract processing facilities, storage operations, and manufacturing plants that provide stable jobs and keep small towns viable.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Approve the proposed Union Pacific-Norfolk Southern merger, conditioned on 'appropriate oversight' with 'rightful leadership' prioritizing 'focus on service and safety'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Minimal. This is a constituent/political support letter from a state legislator, not a regulatory filing presenting technical arguments or proposing enforceable conditions. While STB may note state political support, the filing contains no novel legal theories, competitive analysis, or specific operational remedies that would alter the evidentiary burden or scope of review. The vague conditions ('appropriate oversight,' 'service and safety focus') are too general to create enforceable obligations or trigger specific STB remedial authority.

docket_entries.title: Amtrak Notice of Appearance and Intent to Participate
docket_entries.entry_summary: Amtrak has filed a Notice of Appearance to participate in STB Docket FD-36873 concerning the proposed Union Pacific acquisition of Norfolk Southern. The filing is purely procedural—Amtrak designates counsel (Landman Corsi Ballaine & Ford P.C.) and requests placement on the service list, but states no position on the merger, requests no relief, and provides no substantive comments. This is a minimal intervention filing, indicating Amtrak intends to monitor the proceeding and reserves the right to file substantive comments later. The filing signals Amtrak's recognition that the merger could materially affect its access to and operations over both carriers' rail networks, but Amtrak has not yet disclosed its specific concerns or policy positions.
key_excerpts: Notice of Appearance only—no substantive excerpts available. Filing limited to service list notice and counsel designation.
docket_entries.relief_requested: None stated. Filing is limited to notice of appearance and service list entry.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Low for substantive analysis; procedurally significant only as it establishes Amtrak's formal intervention status. The filing preserves Amtrak's right to file substantive comments, motions, and potentially testimony later in the proceeding without losing intervenor standing. No new legal or regulatory issues are raised in this notice.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.deadline_description: No deadline applies to notices of appearance.

docket_entries.title: BNSF Railway Company Appeal of ALJ Order Denying Discovery Until Application is Accepted
docket_entries.entry_summary: BNSF appeals an ALJ order that denied its motion to compel discovery from UP and NS, ruling that party-led discovery is premature until a merger application is accepted. BNSF argues the ALJ's timing-based ruling contradicts Board precedent, blocks ordinary course document production until June 2026, and will compress the discovery schedule to less than three months before the F+120 deadline, preventing adequate development of the record on this major industry merger.
key_arguments: Board precedent permits party-led discovery before application acceptance, as demonstrated in Canadian Pacific, CSX, and Norfolk Southern cases
The proceeding is no longer in a pre-application phase; an application was filed December 19, 2025, and a revised application will be filed
The ALJ's decision will delay discovery until June 2026, compressing the discovery window to approximately 90 days before the F+120 deadline
BNSF's tailored discovery requests for board materials, banker analyses, and emails are within the broad scope of permissible discovery under 49 C.F.R. § 1114.21
UP and NS have systematically obstructed discovery and stalled production of ordinary course documents
The ALJ ruled on timing grounds not pressed by UP and NS in their brief
The ALJ was appointed in August 2025 with immediate effect to address discovery matters, undermining the premise that discovery should await application acceptance
key_excerpts: This appeal seeks review of an ALJ order that all but blocks discovery in Class I merger proceedings before an application is accepted. The ruling is contrary to Board rules, Board practice, and Board precedent.
Unless overturned, the ALJ's order will delay discovery. That delay and compression of the schedule will fundamentally undermine the process.

Board precedent does not categorically prohibit pre-application discovery... The Board has 'permitted discovery after the initiation of a proceeding under 49 U.S.C. § 11323 but before the filing of an application' in past cases.

Under the Decision, discovery of ordinary course documents and the like cannot be compelled until that date—saying nothing of the time needed to tee up a motion to compel. The compression in the schedule then compounds: under the Board's proposed schedule, the parties would then likely only have about 90 days to conduct both written discovery and depositions prior to filing their comments.

UP and NS have systematically stalled and obstructed discovery. They have produced little more than what is required by regulation; refused to collect emails; and have yet to produce the limited board and banker materials they recently committed to producing.

docket_entries.title: CPKC Support for BNSF Appeal of ALJ Discovery Order in UP-NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: CPKC supports BNSF's appeal of the ALJ's February 11, 2026 order prohibiting non-voluntary discovery prior to Board acceptance of the application. CPKC argues this discovery ban will prevent parties from building a full record on the UP-NS merger, citing Applicants' pattern of withholding ordinary-course documents and the impracticality of completing meaningful discovery within statutory timelines.
key_arguments: The ALJ Order's prohibition on non-voluntary pre-application discovery violates Board rules and will prevent informed Board review
Applicants have engaged in discovery stonewalling for seven months, refusing to produce internal documents on merger-related topics
The compressed procedural schedule (90 days post-acceptance) makes post-application discovery practically impossible
The heightened burden under 2001 Merger Rules requires more discovery, not less, to verify Applicants' public interest claims
Board precedent supports broad discovery in merger cases to test veracity of claims and analyze ordinary-course business documents
Expert opinions from Applicants' economists (Israel, Bailey) have been discredited in court when contradicted by ordinary-course documents
Unlike CP/KCS proceeding, Applicants have refused to produce traffic forecasts, board materials, strategic plans, and internal communications
Applicants' proposal for 45-day comment period is designed to 'run out the clock' and prevent meaningful discovery
key_excerpts: Applicants have repeatedly stonewalled attempts to obtain relevant documents, including those generated by Applicants in the ordinary course related to topics raised by their proposed merger.

Applicants have produced zero internal documents prepared by UP or NS personnel in the ordinary course of their business reflecting how those railroads think about, analyze, and communicate about the issues raised by the Application
This is the first-ever merger to be considered under the 2001 Merger Rules, which established 'a heavier burden to show that a major rail combination is consistent with the public interest.'
The Board's review of their merger should be based on advocacy documents and table-top exercises by paid experts shorn of any records reflecting how their railroads actually conduct business.
And hopefully, the STB looks at that and says, they don't need the 90 days for that and give them 45 days because they've already been looking at that application for a while.

docket_entries.title: CSX Transportation service list update - counsel notification
docket_entries.entry_summary: CSX Transportation filed a routine service list update adding Connor Ahearn from Crowell & Moring LLP and updating Shawn R. Johnson's attorney information. This is a procedural administrative filing that does not address the substantive merits of the proposed merger. The filing demonstrates CSX is actively monitoring the proceeding and has retained sophisticated antitrust counsel (Crowell & Moring is known for high-profile merger defense work), but provides no insight into CSX's position on the transaction or anticipated arguments.
key_excerpts: Please add the following attorneys to the service list in the above-referenced proceeding as counsel for CSX Transportation, Inc.: Connor Ahearn

Please modify the service list in the above-referenced proceeding to reflect the updated affiliation and email address of the following attorney as counsel for CSX Transportation, Inc.: Shawn R. Johnson
docket_entries.relief_requested: Add Connor Ahearn (Crowell & Moring LLP) to service list as counsel; update service list to reflect Shawn R. Johnson's new affiliation (Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson LLP) and email address
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: No substantive legal significance. This is a housekeeping filing to ensure proper service of documents. The retention of Crowell & Moring may signal CSX intends to file substantive opposition or conditional comments, but this filing itself is neutral on procedure and substance.

docket_entries.title: BNSF Support for DOJ Supplemental Protective Order Motion
docket_entries.entry_summary: BNSF filed a brief statement supporting the DOJ's February 4, 2026 motion for a Supplemental Protective Order to govern DOJ access to confidential information in the proceeding. BNSF states: 'The Supplemental Protective Order will allow the DOJ to meaningfully participate in these proceedings and assess the proposed merger, pursuant to its right to intervene under 49 U.S.C. § 11325(b)(1).' Critically, BNSF expressly waives confidentiality objections, stating: 'To the extent materials submitted in these proceedings contain BNSF's Confidential or Highly Confidential information, BNSF does not object to DOJ's request to access this information.' This filing suggests BNSF is not pursuing a confidentiality-based strategy to limit DOJ scrutiny and may indicate confidence in the merger's competitive effects or strategic neutrality on the transaction itself. The filing is purely procedural and does not address substantive merger support or opposition.
key_arguments: DOJ's statutory intervention right under 49 U.S.C. § 11325(b)(1) requires meaningful access to confidential materials in the proceeding
Original Protective Order (August 5, 2025) contains requirements that impede DOJ participation; Supplemental Order is necessary remedy
BNSF will not object to DOJ access to its own Confidential or Highly Confidential Information as barrier to government review
key_excerpts: The Supplemental Protective Order will allow the DOJ to meaningfully participate in these proceedings and assess the proposed merger, pursuant to its right to intervene under 49 U.S.C. § 11325(b)(1).
To the extent materials submitted in these proceedings contain BNSF's Confidential or Highly Confidential information, BNSF does not object to DOJ's request to access this information.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Support for DOJ Motion for Supplemental Protective Order to allow DOJ meaningful participation in proceedings and assessment of merger; consent to DOJ access to BNSF's Confidential and Highly Confidential Information
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing clarifies that at least one major competitor is not using confidentiality/protective order procedures as a litigation tactic to obstruct government antitrust review. By consenting to DOJ access to its confidential competitive information, BNSF may have waived any basis to later challenge DOJ's use of such information in settlement negotiations or eventual decision. The filing also confirms the STB is operating under a tiered confidentiality regime (original Protective Order plus Supplemental Order) designed to accommodate DOJ's heightened access needs under 49 U.S.C. § 11325(b)(1).
docket_entries.deadline_description: No responsive deadline; procedural support motion with no reply period indicated

docket_entries.title: CPKC Reply: No Objection to DOJ's Motion for Supplemental Protective Order
docket_entries.entry_summary: CPKC filed a one-paragraph response to DOJ's February 4, 2026 Motion for Supplemental Protective Order. CPKC has no objection to the relief sought and consents to DOJ access to any CPKC-produced material designated Confidential or Highly Confidential, provided such access is governed by the terms of the protective order if entered by the Board. The filing is purely procedural and reveals no CPKC position on merger approval, competitive concerns, or requested relief regarding the UP/NS transaction.
key_excerpts: CPKC has no objection to the relief sought by DOJ. To the extent CPKC produces material designated Confidential or Highly Confidential in this proceeding, CPKC does not object to DOJ having access to that material subject to the terms of the Supplemental Protective Order, if entered by the Board.
docket_entries.relief_requested: CPKC states it has no objection to DOJ's Motion for Supplemental Protective Order and consents to DOJ access to CPKC's Confidential or Highly Confidential material subject to the terms of any protective order entered by the Board.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: No legal or regulatory significance. This is a routine consent to a protective order modification—a standard discovery procedure. It does not advance substantive issues regarding merger control analysis, competitive effects, or merger conditions.

docket_entries.title: Texas State Senator Tan Parker Opposition to UP-NS Merger: Competition, Service Disruption, and Supply Chain Risks
docket_entries.entry_summary: Texas State Senator Tan Parker opposes the UP-NS merger entirely, framing it as presenting 'significant risk for the Texas and the U.S. economies.' Parker identifies four core harms: (1) Reduced competition and rate increases—'A combined UP-NS would dominate key freight markets and shared rail industry assets, giving it unmatched power over shippers, suppliers, and rail workers'; (2) Service degradations citing history of 1990s rail mergers that caused Texas businesses to lose '$100 million per month' during the UP-SP integration, arguing that 'even relatively minor disruptions could cripple rail service across the country'; (3) UP's failure to honor competitive remedies from prior mergers, noting 'UP has raised rates and shed traffic instead of expanding service, signaling that it values profits over growth'; (4) Loss of resilience and optionality through permanent elimination of alternative routes. Notably, Parker does not propose specific conditions that would make the merger acceptable—instead questioning whether 'any form of the transaction' can meet statutory standards, signaling ideological/fundamental opposition rather than conditional opposition amenable to remedy. The filing emphasizes Texas's particular vulnerability: '800 different shippers that are captive to Union Pacific' and 'almost 25% of UP's total revenue comes from freight moving to and from the Lone Star State.' Parker's language ('any form of the transaction') and refusal to propose remedial conditions distinguishes this from conditional opposition.
key_arguments: A combined UP-NS would dominate key freight markets and shared rail industry assets, creating unmatched power over shippers, suppliers, and rail workers; Texas alone has 800+ captive UP shippers representing approximately 25% of UP's total revenue, making Texas uniquely vulnerable to monopolistic pricing and service degradation.

Prior rail mergers, particularly the 1990s UP-SP merger, caused severe supply chain disruptions; Texas businesses lost $100 million per month during that integration, and 'even relatively minor disruptions could cripple rail service across the country' given the size and scope of the proposed UP-NS merger.

UP has systematically failed to honor competitive remedies from prior mergers—'over the past 25 years, UP has raised rates and shed traffic instead of expanding service, signaling that it values profits over growth'—making promises of integration success and competitive safeguards unreliable.

The merger would permanently eliminate alternative routes and create 'single points of failure across the rail network,' destroying resilience that depends on shippers having 'multiple choices and a rail network that can shift to changes in supply, demand, and shipping patterns.'
The merger is unnecessary; 'collaboration opportunities can already be pursued today,' questioning the justification for taking on supply chain risk.
key_excerpts: A combined UP-NS would dominate key freight markets and shared rail industry assets, giving it unmatched power over shippers, suppliers, and rail workers. Less competition means higher costs for everyone.

Texas leads the nation today with over 800 different shippers that are 'captive' to Union Pacific (UP), which may explain why almost 25% of UP's total revenue comes from freight moving to and from the Lone Star State.

The Houston Chronicle in 1998 reported that Texas businesses were losing $100 million per month as the UP–Southern Pacific merger crashed the supply chain. Despite improvements in technology, each railroad continues to operate its own unique and complex systems, which will need to be integrated seamlessly on day one across a new 55,000-mile railroad to avoid disruption.

UP has a history of failing to honor the competitive remedies granted to shippers in the last major round of mergers. Over the past 25 years, UP has raised rates and shed traffic instead of expanding service, signaling that it values profits over growth.

The merger would permanently lock in UP's dominance, eliminating alternative routes and creating single points of failure across the rail network. Resilience depends on shippers having multiple choices and a rail network that can shift to changes in supply, demand, and shipping patterns.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Respectfully asks the Board to 'carefully consider' whether 'any form of the transaction (including any conditions intended to remedy competitive harms or enhance rail-to-rail competition) can meet the appropriately rigorous standards set forth in the Board's governing statutes and regulations.' The framing suggests the filer believes the merger, in any form, cannot satisfy statutory standards.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing is significant not because it proposes novel legal theories but because it represents high-level state government opposition grounding merger harm in concrete economic data (25% of UP revenue from Texas, 800 captive shippers, $100M/month precedent losses) and challenges UP's credibility as a merger partner based on documented history of failing to honor competitive remedies from prior STB approvals. The 'any form of the transaction' language potentially signals to the Board that a major state with substantial shipper constituency cannot be satisfied by conditions alone, raising questions about whether conditional approval is politically/economically viable. This may influence STB calculus on whether even extensive conditions can satisfy the 'public interest' standard of 49 U.S.C. § 11324.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period filing; no deadline for response applies to intervenor comments

docket_entries.title: Pinsly Railroad Company Notice of Intent to Participate
docket_entries.entry_summary: Pinsly Railroad Company, a short-line holding company controlling nine regional carrier subsidiaries across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic, filed notice of intent to participate in the UP-NS merger proceeding. The filing is purely procedural: it does not state any position on the merger (support, opposition, or conditional support), make any substantive arguments, request any conditions, or allege any competitive harms. Pinsly merely requests addition of its General Counsel and external counsel to the service list and access to confidential materials. This is a typical placeholder intervention by a regional railroad with potential competitive interest but no disclosed strategy at this stage. The filing signals that Pinsly will monitor the proceeding and likely file substantive comments or testimony later if competitive concerns emerge.
key_excerpts: Pinsly Railroad Company, LLC ('Pinsly'), on behalf of itself and its rail carrier subsidiaries (Grenada Railroad, LLC, Florida, Gulf & Atlantic Railroad, LLC, Camp Chase Rail, LLC, Chesapeake & Indiana Railroad, LLC, Vermillion Valley Railroad Company, LLC, Pioneer Valley Railroad Company, LLC, Hondo Railway, LLC, North Florida Industrial Railroad, LLC, and Georgiana & Andalusia Railroad, LLC) hereby gives notice of its intent to participate in the above-captioned proceeding as a party of record.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Notice of intent to participate and request for service of all pleadings and discovery materials. Requests addition of Kristin Bevil (General Counsel) and Theodore L. Hunt (counsel at Dentons) to service list, including provision of highly-confidential materials.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Procedurally establishes Pinsly as a party of record entitled to service of all filings, discovery responses, and confidential materials. Creates obligation on other parties to include Pinsly in future service lists. No change to scope of review or evidentiary burden. Does not trigger any response obligation from applicants or other parties, though Pinsly's subsequent substantive filings would.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.deadline_description: No deadline for response. This is a notice of intent; substantive comments from Pinsly would follow applicable comment deadlines set by STB.

docket_entries.title: UP Motion to Strike CPKC's Letter Supporting BNSF Interlocutory Appeal as Untimely and Procedurally Defective
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific filed a motion to strike CPKC's February 23, 2026 letter that supported BNSF's interlocutory appeal of ALJ Decision No. 10. UP argues three grounds for striking: (1) BNSF's underlying appeal is untimely under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.9(b), as separately established in UP-29/NS-28; (2) even if timely, CPKC's letter fails to satisfy the substantive standards for interlocutory review under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.9(a) and § 1115.1(c), which require showing the ruling may be appealed, reflects clear error, and reversal is necessary to prevent manifest injustice; and (3) CPKC's primary purpose is impermissible—to resubmit claims that Judge Soulikias already struck in an earlier decision as an improper 'reply to a reply.' UP argues the letter is essentially an end-run around the ALJ's prior procedural ruling. This motion reflects the increasingly contentious interlocutory skirmishing between the merger applicant and competing railroad intervenors (BNSF and CPKC) over discovery timing and scope.
key_arguments: BNSF's interlocutory appeal is untimely under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.9(b), with the timeliness defect separately detailed in companion filing UP-29/NS-28

CPKC's letter fails to establish that ALJ Soulikias's ruling on discovery timing could result in 'substantial irreparable harm, substantial detriment to the public interest, or undue prejudice to a party' as required by 49 C.F.R. § 1115.9(a)
CPKC's letter does not demonstrate that the ruling reflects clear error or that reversal is necessary to prevent manifest injustice, as required by 49 C.F.R. § 1115.1(c)

CPKC's real motivation is to resubmit claims that Judge Soulikias previously struck as an impermissible 'reply to a reply' in Decision No. 10, making the letter an impermissible circumvention of the ALJ's prior ruling
key_excerpts: CPKC's letter fails to establish that Judge Soulikias's ruling may be appealed under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.9(a), much less that the ruling reflects a clear error or judgment or that reversal is necessary to prevent a manifest injustice, as required by 49 C.F.R. § 1115.1(c).

CPKC's main motivation for filing its letter appears to be to resubmit claims from a prior pleading that Judge Soulikias struck as an impermissible 'reply to a reply' in Decision No. 10. The Board should therefore strike CPKC's letter as an impermissible attempt to circumvent Judge Soulikias's prior decision.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Strike CPKC's February 23, 2026 letter supporting BNSF's interlocutory appeal of Judge Soulikias's Decision No. 10 as untimely under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.9(b) and as an impermissible attempt to circumvent the ALJ's prior ruling striking similar claims as a 'reply to a reply'.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This motion implicates procedural rules governing interlocutory appeals in STB proceedings (49 C.F.R. §§ 1115.1(c), 1115.9(a)-(b)) and the ALJ's authority to manage pleading sequences and prevent circumvention of prior rulings. A grant of UP's motion would eliminate a procedural vehicle by which competitors sought to delay or scope-limit discovery, potentially clearing the path for expedited hearing progression. Denial would signal the Board's openness to broad interlocutory review and competitor input on discovery disputes, affecting hearing timeline and competitive intervenor leverage.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No explicit deadline stated in the motion; response deadline would be determined by ALJ or Board procedural order.

docket_entries.title: Union Pacific/Norfolk Southern Reply to BNSF's Interlocutory Appeal of ALJ Discovery Ruling
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern oppose BNSF's interlocutory appeal of ALJ Decision No. 10, which denied BNSF's motion to compel broad pre-application discovery. The applicants argue the appeal fails on three independent grounds. First, BNSF's appeal is untimely: Decision No. 10 was issued February 11, 2026, triggering a 7-day deadline under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.9(b) that expired February 18, 2026, but BNSF filed February 23, 2026—five days late. The applicants cite Finch Paper LLC precedent (2017) that clarified the 7-day deadline applies to interlocutory appeals of ALJ discovery rulings, and argue BNSF, as a sophisticated party, should have known this rule. Second, BNSF's appeal fails to satisfy the threshold inquiry under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.9(a), which requires appeals to meet one of four enumerated circumstances (denial of participation, document inspection not ordinarily available, privilege override, or substantial irreparable harm). The applicants note BNSF did not even cite § 1115.9(a) and cannot establish any of these four bases. Third, on the merits under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.1(c), BNSF fails to establish clear error or manifest injustice. The applicants argue Judge Soulikias correctly interpreted the Major Rail Consolidation Procedures to limit pre-application discovery to Board-ordered materials (100% traffic tapes, timetables, station lists, track charts, geospatial maps, joint facilities, interchange commitments) and did not address scope but only timing. The applicants emphasize they have voluntarily produced over 56,000 pages and hundreds of gigabytes of data pre-application and will continue discovery post-application under a Board-established schedule. The applicants further argue BNSF's own 2000 comments on the Major Merger Rules stated that more detailed application requirements would enable merger review without third-party discovery, depositions, or evidentiary proceedings—a position the applicants cite back to BNSF. The applicants characterize BNSF's manifest injustice claim as 'overwrought' and note that post-application discovery with a Board-established schedule will be adequate.
key_arguments: BNSF's appeal is facially untimely under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.9(b): filed February 23, 2026, five days after the February 18, 2026 deadline (7 days from February 11 decision). Finch Paper (2017) clarified this rule nearly a decade ago; BNSF, as a sophisticated party familiar with Board rules, has no excuse.

BNSF's appeal fails the threshold inquiry under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.9(a) because BNSF did not cite the regulation and cannot establish any of the four enumerated circumstances: it does not deny participation, grant unusual document inspection, override privilege, or result in substantial irreparable harm, detriment to public interest, or undue prejudice.

ALJ Decision No. 10 addresses only timing of discovery, not scope. It does not preclude BNSF from conducting permissible discovery post-application under the Board's procedural schedule. No manifest injustice results from limiting general discovery to the post-application period.

Judge Soulikias reasonably interpreted Major Merger Rules and Board regulations to prohibit broad pre-application discovery, limiting pre-application discovery to Board-ordered materials. This interpretation is supported by Board precedent and the express statement in Major Merger Rules that the Board was not proposing broad pre-application discovery.
The applicants have voluntarily produced over 56,000 pages and hundreds of gigabytes of data pre-application and continue voluntary pre-application discovery with BNSF and other parties.

BNSF's own 2000 comments on the Major Merger Rules stated the Board should 'process most mergers without the need to supplement the initial filings of the parties with third-party discovery, depositions, or other evidentiary proceedings,' as FERC does—BNSF's current position is inconsistent with its own prior advocacy.
Requiring parties to follow clearly defined procedural deadlines is essential in this complex proceeding involving numerous parties, hundreds of filings, and significant Board resource demands.
key_excerpts: Decision No. 10 was issued on February 11, 2026, and thus the deadline for an appeal of that decision was February 18, 2026. Yet, BNSF did not file its appeal until February 23, 2026.
BNSF did not even bother to cite § 1115.9(a) in the Appeal, and it provides no basis to conclude that any of those circumstances apply.

Decision No. 10 addresses only the proper timing of discovery. Nothing in Decision No. 10 precludes BNSF from pursuing discovery to the extent permitted under Major Merger Rules and the Board's regulations.
The Board's more detailed application process under Major Merger Rules should require parties to engage in less discovery, not more.
Judge Soulikias's ruling is supported by Board precedent and procedure and was in no way a 'clear error of judgment.'
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny BNSF Railway Company's interlocutory appeal of ALJ Decision No. 10 on three independent grounds: (1) timeliness—BNSF filed five days after the seven-day deadline under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.9(b); (2) failure to satisfy threshold inquiry under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.9(a) requiring one of four enumerated circumstances; (3) failure to establish clear error of judgment or manifest injustice under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.1(c).
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing establishes the applicants' aggressive procedural defense to intervenor discovery challenges during the pre-application phase. It raises three separate legal barriers to BNSF's appeal: (1) strict timeliness under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.9(b) with a 7-day hard deadline; (2) a narrow threshold test under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.9(a) requiring one of four specific enumerated circumstances, which the applicants argue creates a high bar to interlocutory appeal of discovery rulings; (3) the 'clear error of judgment' or 'manifest injustice' standard under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.1(c), applied with a 'highly deferential' standard of review favoring the ALJ. The filing leverages Finch Paper precedent (2017) to establish that the 7-day deadline is a settled rule, not ambiguous. The applicants' interpretation of Major Merger Rules to limit pre-application discovery to Board-ordered materials (not broad discovery) has significant implications for the scope of information available to competitors and other intervenors during the critical pre-application period when they are forming positions on the merger. If upheld, this ruling constrains the factual record competitors can develop before the formal application is filed and accepted. The applicants' citation to BNSF's own 2000 comments supporting limited discovery in merger review may influence how the Board views BNSF's current position.
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is applicants' reply to BNSF's appeal filed February 23, 2026. The Board will determine whether to accept/grant/deny BNSF's appeal in a future order.

docket_entries.title: City of Decatur, Illinois Notice of Intent to Participate - Grade Crossing Blockage Concerns
docket_entries.entry_summary: The City of Decatur filed a Notice of Intent to Participate to preserve its right to submit comments and seek mitigation measures related to potential increases in blocked grade crossings resulting from the merger. The City emphasizes that it is "traversed by multiple rail corridors" with "numerous at-grade crossings that are integral to daily traffic circulation and public safety" and states that "Prolonged or recurrent blockage of rail crossings may affect emergency response times, traffic operations, and neighborhood access within the City." The City explicitly takes "no position at this time regarding the merits of the proposed transaction" but seeks to ensure the Board considers "potential for increased frequency and duration of blocked grade crossings, including effects associated with changes in train volumes, train length, scheduling, and yard or switching operations." The filing reserves Decatur's right to request "reasonable mitigation measures if warranted." This is a procedurally-protective filing that identifies a specific local impact category without yet opposing or supporting the merger.
key_arguments: The City of Decatur's rail corridors contain numerous at-grade crossings that intersect local arterial streets, emergency response routes, and school transportation routes, making any increase in blockage duration a public safety concern.
Merger-related changes in train volumes, train length, scheduling, and yard/switching operations could increase the frequency and duration of blocked grade crossings.
Prolonged or recurrent blockage of rail crossings directly affects emergency response times, traffic operations, and neighborhood access within the City.
The City requires location-specific consideration of crossing conditions and operational impacts in the Board's review.
key_excerpts: The City of Decatur is a municipal government located in Macon County, Illinois and is traversed by multiple rail corridors that intersect local arterial streets, emergency response routes, school transportation routes, and access to critical facilities.
Prolonged or recurrent blockage of rail crossings may affect emergency response times, traffic operations, and neighborhood access within the City.

The City seeks to ensure that the Surface Transportation Board's review considers the potential for increased frequency and duration of blocked grade crossings, including effects associated with changes in train volumes, train length, scheduling, and yard or switching operations.
docket_entries.relief_requested: The City reserves the right to provide location-specific information regarding crossings, emergency routes, and operational conditions, and to request reasonable mitigation measures if warranted by the Board's evaluation.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing establishes that local public safety and traffic circulation impacts from grade crossing blockages are a cognizable issue in the Board's public interest review under 49 U.S.C. § 11324. Decatur's intervention signals that the Board will likely receive detailed evidence on crossing blockage frequency, duration, and emergency response impacts during the Comment phase. This creates a potential condition category (grade crossing mitigation measures, operational protocols limiting blockage duration) that could be required as a remedy if the Board determines the merger would materially worsen crossing impacts. The filing also establishes that municipalities with significant rail exposure may seek operational commitments on train scheduling and yard operations.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (With Comment)
docket_entries.deadline_description: Notice of Intent to Participate; no response deadline, but City reserves right to file substantive comments later in the Comment phase.

docket_entries.title: DOJ Antitrust Division Urges Compulsion of Ordinary Course Business Documents in Discovery Disputes
docket_entries.entry_summary: The DOJ Antitrust Division intervenes in the pending discovery disputes between the Applicants and third parties (BNSF, CPKC) to argue that ordinary course business documents are essential to a well-informed decision. The Department states: 'evidence created in the normal course of business is more probative than evidence created after the company began anticipating a merger review.' The DOJ specifically cites BNSF's requests for 'executive-level and board documents evaluating the merger's effect on competition and proposed synergies or efficiencies' and 'documents and communications relating to potential joint ventures, marketing alliances, or other forms of cooperative agreements between UP and NS' as the types of materials it would request under HSR Act Second Request authority and finds 'highly relevant' to merger evaluation. The Department emphasizes that the Board's 'enhanced competition' standard under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.1 may create an 'even more imperative' need for ordinary course documents than exists under Clayton Act Section 7 analysis. The DOJ does not oppose or support the merger itself but urges the Board to 'compel the Applicants to produce relevant ordinary course documents at the appropriate time' to prevent the Applicants from limiting the record to 'hand-picked materials' supporting their position. The filing signals that the DOJ may seek its own discovery and will monitor Applicants' compliance with document production obligations.
key_arguments: Ordinary course business documents are more probative than advocacy, expert analysis, and self-serving statements: 'evidence created in the normal course of business is more probative than evidence created after the company began anticipating a merger review. Similarly, the Agencies give less weight to predictions by the parties or their employees...Where the testimony of outcome-interested merging party employees contradicts ordinary course business records, the Agencies typically give greater weight to the business records.'

BNSF's requested documents—executive board materials evaluating competitive effects and synergies—are the identical categories required under HSR Act initial screening and Second Request stages, establishing their relevance and appropriateness for discovery in STB proceedings.

The Board's 'enhanced competition' standard under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.1 creates an even more compelling case for ordinary course document discovery than exists under Clayton Act Section 7, which aims only to prevent substantial lessening of competition.

Applicants' refusal to produce ordinary course documents 'limits the ability of the Board and interested third parties to test the assertions, projections, and analyses set forth in the Application and related hand-picked materials,' creating an asymmetric evidentiary record.

The Department relies on ordinary course documents to assess merger effects in its own antitrust review, and the Board should similarly avail itself of such documents to have 'a robust record, not limited to materials supporting the Applicants' position.'
key_excerpts: evidence created in the normal course of business is more probative than evidence created after the company began anticipating a merger review. Similarly, the Agencies give less weight to predictions by the parties or their employees, whether in the ordinary course of business or in anticipation of litigation, offered to allay competition concerns. Where the testimony of outcome-interested merging party employees contradicts ordinary course business records, the Agencies typically give greater weight to the business records.

the Board and interested third parties should be able to obtain documents created in the Applicants' ordinary course of business because they are often 'more probative' than documents hand-picked after the Applicants 'began anticipating a merger review.'

Given the heightened 'enhanced competition' standard applicable to this matter, it may be even more imperative for the Board and interested third parties to obtain ordinary course documents than is the case under Section 7.

The Applicants' refusal to produce these types of documents, and their rejection of other requests for ordinary course documents, limits the ability of the Board and interested third parties to test the assertions, projections, and analyses set forth in the Application (now withdrawn but soon to be refiled) and related hand-picked materials.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Compel Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern to produce relevant ordinary course business documents at the appropriate time, subject to the Protective Order and related orders, to ensure the Board and interested third parties have access to well-informed advocacy and a robust record.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This DOJ filing establishes a federal evidentiary standard for discovery in STB railroad merger proceedings by importing principles from antitrust enforcement under the Clayton Act and Merger Guidelines. The DOJ argues that the STB's heightened 'enhanced competition' standard under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.1 (which requires affirmative evidence of enhanced competition benefits, not merely prevention of lessening competition) creates an even more stringent burden on applicants to support their position, thereby necessitating broader discovery of ordinary course documents. The filing directly impacts the ALJ's and Board's discretion to compel discovery by establishing that ordinary course documents are more probative than party advocacy—shifting the evidentiary burden and suggesting that document withholding by Applicants will result in an incomplete record. The DOJ's invocation of the heightened standard also subtly reframes the merger as requiring more substantial proofs of competitive benefit than standard antitrust merger review, potentially expanding the scope of permissible discovery.
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is a statement of position on pending discovery disputes with no deadline imposed, but it will influence ALJ Soulikias' rulings on BNSF's Motion to Compel and CPKC's related requests.

docket_entries.title: BNSF Request for Protective Waiver of Seven-Day Appeal Deadline in Pre-Application Discovery Dispute
docket_entries.entry_summary: BNSF filed a letter requesting a protective waiver of any seven-day deadline applicable to its appeal of ALJ Decision No. 10. The ALJ's decision interpreted the Major Merger Rules as a 'matter of first impression,' limiting discovery of ordinary-course documents in Class I merger proceedings before an application is accepted. BNSF argues it timely filed its appeal under 49 C.F.R. § 1115.1 and that a protective waiver is justified because: (1) the appeal addresses a first-time interpretation of pre-application discovery scope under the new rules; (2) a waiver would not prejudice UP/NS, who identified no prejudice and made no decisions in reliance on the seven-day deadline; and (3) a waiver would ensure Board review on the merits and clarify the process for all stakeholders. BNSF is not opposing the merger on substantive grounds in this filing—it is solely addressing the procedural issue of discovery access.
key_arguments: ALJ Decision No. 10 interpreted the Major Merger Rules in a manner that 'blocks discovery of ordinary-course documents in Class I merger proceedings before an application is accepted,' creating a novel limitation on pre-application discovery
BNSF timely filed its appeal pursuant to 49 C.F.R. § 1115.1 and the ten-day deadlines in 49 C.F.R. §§ 1115.1(c), 1011.6(b), and 1104.7(a)

A protective waiver of any seven-day deadline would not prejudice UP/NS because they 'did not identify any prejudice in their brief' and 'made no decision—discovery or otherwise—in reliance on a seven-day appeal deadline'

A waiver would ensure the Board decides 'the first interpretation of the scope of pre-application discovery in a major merger under the new rules' on the merits and clarifies the process for all stakeholders
key_excerpts: BNSF appealed an ALJ order that interpreted, as a matter of first impression, the Major Merger Rules in a manner that blocks discovery of ordinary-course documents in Class I merger proceedings before an application is accepted.
Rather than create any prejudice, a waiver would ensure a Board ruling on the merits of BNSF's appeal and allow the Board to clarify the process it wants stakeholders to follow in this proceeding.
docket_entries.relief_requested: BNSF requests a protective waiver of any seven-day deadline for its appeal of ALJ Decision No. 10, which interpreted the scope of pre-application discovery under the Major Merger Rules.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing raises a first-impression issue under the newly implemented Major Merger Rules regarding the scope of discovery available in pre-application proceedings. The ALJ's Decision No. 10 apparently established a restriction on ordinary-course document discovery before formal application acceptance. BNSF's appeal challenges this interpretation, and the outcome could materially affect how much competitive and operational information competitors can obtain to develop substantive merger objections. A Board waiver of procedural deadlines to allow full merits review could establish important precedent for the scope of competitor discovery rights in future Class I merger proceedings. The filing suggests potential ambiguity in how the new rules define pre-application discovery boundaries.
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is BNSF's response to a procedural question raised by UP/NS. The filing requests Board action (a waiver), but does not impose a responsive deadline on other parties.

docket_entries.title: Pattison Company LLC - Notice of Intent to Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.entry_summary: Pattison Company LLC, a sand and aggregate mining and logistics firm shipping over 20,000 railcar equivalents annually across Class I railroads, filed a notice of intent to participate in the UP-NS merger proceeding. Pattison explicitly states it is submitting a notice to participate 'Without Comment,' indicating the company is monitoring the proceeding but reserving judgment pending discovery or hearing phase developments. The filing establishes standing to intervene and request documents but signals no current opposition or support.
key_excerpts: Pattison Company LLC is a sand and aggregate mining, railroad services, and logistics company which currently ships 20,000 + railcar equivalents across Class I railroads annually.
Please accept this letter as Pattison Company's Notice of Intent to Participate (NOIP) in the UP -NS Merger Proceeding.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Intervention only; no specific relief or conditions requested

It grants the company rights to receive service of documents, participate in discovery, and potentially file comments or testimony in later phases. No substantive legal or regulatory issues are presented; however, Pattison's status as a major shipper (20,000+ railcar equivalents/year) across multiple Class I carriers means any future substantive comments would carry weight on competitive or service-level impacts.
