docket_entries.title: Fort Worth Mayor Letter Opposing UP-NS Merger: Competition, Service Reliability, and Community Safety Concerns
docket_entries.filer_name: City of Fort Worth / Mayor Mattie Parker
docket_entries.entry_summary: Mayor Mattie Parker, on behalf of Fort Worth, opposes the UP-NS merger based on competition reduction, service reliability concerns, and community safety impacts. Fort Worth describes itself as 'one of the most important freight rail cities in Texas and the nation' with economy dependent on competitive rail service. The Mayor argues: 'A merger of this scale could further reduce competition in an already highly concentrated freight rail industry. Many Fort Worth–area businesses depend on competitive rail service to control costs and remain viable. A loss of competition risks higher shipping costs that are ultimately passed along to consumers.' Beyond economics, Parker emphasizes operational impacts: 'Rail corridors in Fort Worth run directly through or alongside growing residential areas and major roadway networks. Increased congestion or service disruptions could lead to longer and more frequent blockages at grade crossings – particularly in areas near industrial corridors and intermodal activity – affecting local traffic flow, emergency response times, and daily commuting.' Parker frames the issue as requiring affirmative proof of public benefit: 'Any merger of this magnitude should clearly demonstrate that it will improve outcomes for consumers, businesses, and communities – not merely reallocate market power among carriers.' The conditions requested are substantive rather than technical, requiring applicants to affirmatively show competition strengthening, service reliability improvements, and avoidance of community congestion/safety harms. This reflects a conditional opposition posture—rejection unless applicants meet specific, articulated standards.
key_arguments: Merger will further reduce competition in an already highly concentrated freight rail industry, limiting Fort Worth-area businesses' ability to control shipping costs through competitive options
Loss of rail competition will result in higher shipping costs passed to consumers in increased prices for goods and services across the region

Merger will increase rail congestion and service disruptions leading to longer and more frequent blockages at grade crossings in residential and industrial areas, affecting traffic flow and emergency response times
Rail integration disruptions will add truck traffic to already strained roadways, undermining city infrastructure investments and increasing safety concerns for nearby communities
Merger applicants must affirmatively prove the transaction will improve outcomes for consumers, businesses, and communities rather than merely reallocate market power among carriers
Public interest standard requires demonstration of meaningful competition strengthening, enhanced service options and reliability, and avoidance of adverse community impacts before approval
key_excerpts: Fort Worth is one of the most important freight rail cities in Texas and the nation. Our economy depends on reliable and competitive rail service to support many industries including manufacturing, logistics and distribution, construction materials, energy, and agriculture.

A merger of this scale could further reduce competition in an already highly concentrated freight rail industry. Many Fort Worth–area businesses depend on competitive rail service to control costs and remain viable. A loss of competition risks higher shipping costs that are ultimately passed along to consumers in the form of increased prices for goods and services across our region.

Rail corridors in Fort Worth run directly through or alongside growing residential areas and major roadway networks. Increased congestion or service disruptions could lead to longer and more frequent blockages at grade crossings – particularly in areas near industrial corridors and intermodal activity – affecting local traffic flow, emergency response times, and daily commuting.
Any merger of this magnitude should clearly demonstrate that it will improve outcomes for consumers, businesses, and communities – not merely reallocate market power among carriers.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Reject the proposed merger UNLESS the applicants demonstrate that the merger will: (1) meaningfully strengthen competition in freight rail service; (2) provide greater service options and reliability for rail-dependent businesses; and (3) avoid adverse impacts to congestion, safety, and quality of life in communities the rail system serves. Mayor Parker states: 'Any merger of this magnitude should clearly demonstrate that it will improve outcomes for consumers, businesses, and communities – not merely reallocate market power among carriers.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing introduces a municipal/public interest dimension beyond traditional shipper competition arguments. Under 49 U.S.C. § 11324, STB must consider whether a merger is in the 'public interest,' which encompasses not only business competition but also community welfare, safety, and infrastructure impacts. The Fort Worth letter shifts burden to applicants to affirmatively prove public benefit—not merely absence of harm. The conditions framed (competition strengthening, service reliability, community impact mitigation) differ from typical carrier-focused remedies and may require applicants to address operational integration planning and grade crossing management protocols. This could expand discovery scope to include community impact assessments and operational integration plans.

docket_entries.title: Colin Finney Individual Intervention: Lehigh Valley Transit System Proposal Conditioned on UP/NS Merger Approval
docket_entries.entry_summary: Colin Finney proposes conditional approval of the UP/NS merger premised on establishment of a 'Public-Private Stewardship Framework' for the Lehigh Valley region. His core argument: 'Infrastructure Recycling' of underutilized freight assets into a high-capacity transit spine will serve the public interest by relieving congestion on I-78 and US-22 while providing Norfolk Southern with infrastructure upgrades (universal crossovers, modernized signaling) that generate 'net benefit to freight fluidity.' Finney's proposal centers on transferring Maintenance of Way and liability burdens to public entities (PennDOT, NJ Transit) under an 'Atlantic City Model' structure, while NS retains exclusive freight rights—framing the deal as advantageous to the carrier. He proposes a four-phase implementation: (1) heavy rail spine on existing NS corridors; (2) light rail extensions on abandoned rights-of-way and utility corridors; (3) BRT integration to serve logistics warehousing; (4) dual-mode bus-on-rails on historical industrial spurs. Finney argues this approach provides 'significantly higher return on investment than traditional highway expansion' (citing highway widenings exceeding '$100 million per mile') while 'diverting thousands of daily commuters' from congested road corridors. He emphasizes operational separation: 'passenger activity stays separated from active freight leads and switching zones, allowing Class I carriers to support maximum fluid throughput in high volume logistics districts without the safety or scheduling conflicts of localized transit stops.' The filing presents the LVT System as both a regional resilience strategy and a merger condition that enhances rather than constrains NS operations. Settlement signals are implicit: Finney's detailed engineering baselines, references to existing models (Atlantic City), and emphasis on NS operational benefit suggest openness to negotiation with applicants on implementation mechanics.
key_arguments: The merger should be approved CONDITIONED on implementation of the Lehigh Valley Transit System, which will provide Norfolk Southern with infrastructure upgrades (crossovers, signaling) that generate net freight benefits rather than liabilities: 'LVT investment would include capital improvements (e.g., universal crossovers and modernized signaling) that provide a net benefit to freight fluidity, turning passenger service into an infrastructure upgrade for NS rather than a liability.'

Public entities must assume Maintenance of Way and liability burdens through an 'Atlantic City Model' stewardship structure, eliminating private carrier infrastructure maintenance costs: 'By shifting these corridors from private freight liabilities to public transit assets, we establish a mechanism where infrastructure maintenance is decoupled from freight profitability.'

The LVT system will reduce highway congestion demand by 'diverting thousands of daily commuters' from I-78 and US-22, providing public interest relief at far lower cost than traditional highway expansion: 'Modern highway widenings, such as those projected for US-22 and I-78, often exceed $100 million per mile when accounting for land acquisition and interchange reconstruction.'

Regional transit can be implemented via infrastructure recycling of abandoned rail corridors and utility rights-of-way, minimizing environmental impact and avoiding complex legal hurdles of active freight mainlines: 'By using abandoned rail corridors and utility rights-of-way (such as high voltage electric transmission and pipeline paths), the system avoids the bottlenecking typical of shared-track environments.'

Operational separation between passenger and freight movements (through independent corridors, dedicated BRT buffers, and separation of passenger stops from freight switching zones) ensures merger approval enhances rather than constrains freight operations: 'By establishing dedicated BRT corridors that link rail stations directly to major warehouse clusters and industrial parks, the system effectively solves the last-mile challenge while providing a critical operational buffer for Norfolk Southern.'

Four-phased implementation strategy (heavy rail spine, light rail extensions, BRT integration, dual-mode bus-on-rails) allows for 'immediate regional impact with long-term best expansion capability' without burdening NS with passenger service management.
key_excerpts: By shifting these corridors from private freight liabilities to public transit assets, we establish a mechanism where infrastructure maintenance is decoupled from freight profitability.

LVT investment would include capital improvements (e.g., universal crossovers and modernized signaling) that provide a net benefit to freight fluidity, turning passenger service into an infrastructure upgrade for NS rather than a liability.
By using abandoned rail corridors and utility rights-of-way (such as high voltage electric transmission and pipeline paths), the system avoids the bottlenecking typical of shared-track environments.

By establishing dedicated BRT corridors that link rail stations directly to major warehouse clusters and industrial parks, the system effectively solves the last-mile challenge while providing a critical operational buffer for Norfolk Southern.
Modern highway widenings, such as those projected for US-22 and I-78, often exceed $100 million per mile when accounting for land acquisition and interchange reconstruction.
The LVT System is designed around a shared use philosophy that respects the operational integrity of Class I carrier Norfolk Southern (NS).
docket_entries.relief_requested: Approve the UP/NS merger CONDITIONED upon: (1) Implementation of a 'Public-Private Stewardship Framework' transferring Lehigh and Reading Line corridors from private freight to public transit assets under PennDOT/NJ Transit maintenance; (2) Norfolk Southern retains exclusive freight rights but is relieved of Maintenance of Way (MOW) and liability responsibilities for underlying right-of-way; (3) Mandatory implementation of 'universal crossover modernization and signaling upgrades' at Dixon Street bottleneck and Allentown Terminal; (4) Adoption of Finney's 'Atlantic City Model' where public entities assume infrastructure maintenance burdens; (5) Approval and facilitation of the phased Lehigh Valley Transit (LVT) System implementation (heavy rail spine, light rail extensions, BRT integration, dual-mode bus-on-rails development).
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Finney's filing introduces a novel merger condition argument: that approval should be conditioned on implementation of a third-party regional transit infrastructure project dependent on state/local government cooperation not within the applicants' direct control. This raises interpretive questions about the scope of conditions the STB may impose under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 (merger approval authority). His 'Public-Private Stewardship Framework' proposes de facto operational separation of passenger and freight functions on merged rail corridors, potentially implicating (1) operational integration requirements in merger approval, (2) liability allocation for rail infrastructure, and (3) the Board's authority to condition approval on state/local government action. His emphasis on the 'fair mandate' (congestion relief, public interest) may invoke the Board's general statutory obligation to consider public interest factors. The filing does not explicitly cite specific legal authority for the proposed conditions, but references the 'fair mandate' and invokes comparative public benefit analysis (rail vs. highway expansion efficiency).
docket_entries.deadline_description: Filing submitted as Executive Summary and Operational Narrative; no explicit deadline stated. Likely subject to Board procedural schedule for subsequent reply/hearing phases.

docket_entries.title: CN Motion to Compel Production of 2025 Traffic Tape, Reciprocal Switching, and Interchange Data
docket_entries.entry_summary: CN seeks a Board order compelling Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern to immediately produce their complete 2025 traffic tape data, reciprocal switching records, and interchange volume data, arguing that Applicants' refusal to produce this data unless they voluntarily include it in their revised application violates discovery rules and the Major Merger Rules. CN contends: (1) The Major Merger Rules explicitly require applicants to make traffic tapes available 'as soon as practicable' following notice of intent, and production must occur before the revised application is filed—Applicants cannot unilaterally condition disclosure on their own strategic decisions; (2) 2025 data is 'critical' and 'highly relevant' to evaluating the proposed transaction because it reflects 'the most recent and therefore, arguably the most accurate pre-merger status' of Applicants' traffic and networks, and is essential to assessing Applicants' claimed merger-related growth and efficiencies, post-merger projected market shares, and competitive implications; (3) The Board's regulations impose no limitation restricting interested parties' review to only materials Applicants elect to submit—the STB encourages 'a fully developed record' and recognizes that 'ordinary course' materials 'may be more probative than party advocacy, expert analysis, and self-serving statements'; (4) Applicants' own use of non-2023 data (experts Bailey and Israel used 2019-2024 data; density maps used 2024 data) demonstrates inconsistency in their argument that 2025 data is 'out of scope'; (5) Judge Soulikias's denial of BNSF's motion to compel does not preclude CN's request because CN seeks only traffic tapes and minimal related data—precisely the category the Major Merger Rules contemplate being produced pre-application, distinguishing it from the broader discovery BNSF sought. CN characterizes Applicants' position as an attempt to 'limit the Board's and interested parties' review of the proposed transaction to only those materials Applicants themselves elect to submit rather than the universe of available relevant information.' Settlement signal: Union Pacific's March 23, 2026 email indicates willingness to produce 2025 data 'to the extent it relies on 2025 data' in the revised application, but this conditional commitment does not satisfy CN's demand for unconditional pre-application production.
key_arguments: The Major Merger Rules mandate that applicants make 100% traffic tapes available 'as soon as practicable after the filing of the notice of intent,' before the application is filed, and the Board has emphasized such early access is 'critical' to interested parties' evaluation—Applicants cannot withhold data pending their discretionary decision to include it in the revised application

2025 traffic tape data is 'indisputably relevant' because it reflects the most current pre-merger operational status and is essential to evaluate Applicants' merger-related growth and efficiency claims and post-merger competitive effects, which CN cannot properly assess without 'the context of the most recent available data'

Applicants' position that 2025 data is 'out of scope' is contradicted by the Board's own prior request for 2024 data in Decision No. 2 (demonstrating years beyond the base year are contemplated), and by Applicants' own inconsistent use of non-2023 data throughout their initial application (experts relied on 2019-2024; density maps used 2024)

Applicants cannot unilaterally restrict the Board's and interested parties' review to 'only those materials Applicants themselves elect to submit'—the Board's regulations impose no such limitation and expressly encourage 'a fully developed record' and recognize that 'ordinary course' materials 'may be more probative than party advocacy, expert analysis, and self-serving statements'

CN's requests are targeted and minimally burdensome: Applicants produced 2019-2024 traffic tapes without issue, other Class I railroads have exchanged 2025 data, and CN stands ready for reciprocal exchange; data maintained in ordinary course of business is not unduly burdensome to produce

Judge Soulikias's Decision No. 10 denying BNSF's motion is distinguishable because BNSF sought broader pre-application discovery; here, CN seeks only traffic tapes and related data—the precise category the Major Merger Rules contemplate being produced pre-application
key_excerpts: Traffic tape data is critical to the competitive, operational, and environmental analyses the Board will undertake in reviewing the proposed transaction. Indeed, in recognition of the important role that traffic tapes play in evaluating proposed transactions such as this one, the Major Rail Consolidation Procedures ('Major Merger Rules') require applicants contemplating a major merger transaction to 'make their highly confidential 100% traffic tapes available to outside counsel or consultants for interested parties . . . as soon as practicable after the filing of the notice of intent.'

The 2025 data, which reflects the most recent year of Applicants' traffic data available prior to the filing of their revised application, is indisputably relevant. Traffic tape data is recognized by the Board to be so 'critical' that early production of prospective applicants' traffic tapes is required by the Major Merger Rules. As the Board has emphasized here, access to Applicants' traffic tapes is necessary for interested parties' and the Board's review of the proposed transaction. Applicants do not get to dictate what information is relevant to the proposed transaction or what information interested parties evaluate to analyze it.

Applicants' position is that CN's requests are either premature or seek information that is irrelevant — they are premature even if Applicants later choose to use 2025 data in their revised application, but they seek information that is irrelevant if Applicants choose to ignore 2025 data in their revised application. CN's request is neither premature nor irrelevant.

Applicants cannot be permitted to limit the Board's and interested parties' review of the proposed transaction to only those materials Applicants themselves elect to submit rather than the universe of available relevant information. The Board's regulations impose no such limitation, and such a restriction would be blatantly inconsistent with the broad discovery permitted in Board proceedings.

The 2025 data is thus 'critical' and highly relevant to interested parties' and the Board's evaluation of the proposed transaction and revised application, including in evaluating Applicants' merger-related growth and efficiencies claims. Applicants' position that interested parties' and the Board's review of the revised application should be limited exclusively to traffic data that is at least 16 months old is nonsensical.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Order requiring Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern to produce complete traffic tape data for 2025 (January 1 – December 31, 2025), reciprocal switching data for 2025, and interchange volume data for 2025, 'as soon as practicable' and expeditiously, prior to filing the revised application.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This motion directly implicates the scope of pre-application discovery obligations under the 2001 Major Rail Consolidation Procedures (49 C.F.R. § 1180.4(b)(4)(iii)) and challenges whether applicants can unilaterally condition production of statutorily required data on their voluntary inclusion in merger filings. The motion also raises questions about the interaction between pre-application discovery obligations and post-application discovery rights, and whether the Board's silence regarding 2025 data in Decision No. 2 (which requested only 2019-2024 data because 2025 was unavailable at that time) effectively removes 2025 from the scope of required disclosure. A ruling on this motion will establish whether applicants control the evidentiary scope of merger review or whether interested parties and the Board have independent discovery rights to obtain relevant operational data regardless of applicants' strategic decisions. This also implicates the completeness of the record for evaluating merger-specific claims (growth, efficiencies) against the most current pre-merger baseline.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Motion to Compel filed April 10, 2026; response deadline depends on Board or ALJ ruling; procedural schedule for responding would be set by Board order.

docket_entries.title: Shipper Associations' Motion to Redesignate Schedule 5.8 (Merger Agreement Regulatory Conditions) from Highly Confidential to Public
docket_entries.entry_summary: Shipper Associations jointly move to compel public disclosure of Schedule 5.8 of the Merger Agreement, which applicants designated as 'Highly Confidential.' Schedule 5.8 identifies regulatory conditions that would trigger Union Pacific's $2.5 billion termination right—essentially UP's list of conditions it refuses to accept. The shipper groups argue: (1) Schedule 5.8 contains no traffic data, shipper identities, rates, cost data, or trade secrets that would qualify it as confidential under the Protective Order—it is merely a contractual allocation of regulatory risk; (2) applicants have no legitimate competitive interest in protecting it, as it reveals no business strategies, customer relationships, or proprietary operations usable outside this proceeding; (3) the Highly Confidential designation prejudices interested parties by preventing them from seeing applicants' own candid assessment of the merger's potential harms and necessary remedies, which is essential to informed participation. The motion documents applicants' concealment tactics: redacting Schedule 5.8 from pre-filing discovery, omitting it from the December 2025 merger application despite regulatory requirements, claiming privilege (which the Board rejected), then designating it Highly Confidential without justification. Shipper Associations argue that 'rigorous and comprehensive review' of the merger requires transparency: shippers cannot assess whether to intervene, what experts to retain, or what conditions to propose without seeing applicants' own identification of significant potential harms. The motion emphasizes the strategic significance: conditions UP would pay $2.5 billion to escape are 'not hypothetical concerns—they are the conditions Applicants fear as likely outcomes of this proceeding,' providing a credible roadmap to the merger's greatest risks to public interest. The Shipper Associations present themselves as unable to make informed decisions about participation without access to this document, and note that even parties with outside counsel cannot discuss the contents with their own organization members and decision-makers.
key_arguments: Schedule 5.8 falls entirely outside the Protective Order's definition of 'Confidential Information' or 'Highly Confidential Information'—it contains no traffic data, shipper identities, waybill data, cost workpapers, confidential contract terms, or shipper-specific rate data. It is merely a contractual allocation of regulatory risk between the two applicants.

Applicants have no legitimate competitive interest in protecting Schedule 5.8 because it contains nothing—no trade secrets, business strategies, proprietary rate data, or customer contract terms—that competitors or customers could exploit outside this proceeding. A customer 'could not use it to bargain for better rates. A supplier would find nothing relevant. And a competitor could not learn anything about Applicants' business strategy or operations that the public merger application does not already reveal.'

Schedule 5.8's identification of conditions UP would pay $2.5 billion to avoid proves their significance and represents applicants' own candid assessment of the merger's greatest potential harms and necessary remedies—a 'credible roadmap to what Applicants have identified as the merger's greatest potential risks to the public interest.'

The Highly Confidential designation prevents meaningful participation by shippers, elected officials, and the public—only outside counsel and consultants may access it, barring parties from discussing it with their own organizations, making informed resource allocation and participation decisions, or assessing conditions against their own supply chains.

Applicants engaged in deliberate concealment: they redacted Schedule 5.8 from pre-filing discovery, omitted it from the merger application despite 49 C.F.R. § 1180.6(a)(7)(ii) requirements for 'any contract or other written instrument entered into, or proposed to be entered into, pertaining to the proposed transaction,' claimed unspecified privilege (rejected by Board as showing 'it is difficult to imagine a privilege claim that would apply'), and only then designated it Highly Confidential.

Rigorous and comprehensive Board review—as promised to lawmakers—'demands informed participation. Parties cannot participate meaningfully if they cannot see Applicants' own assessment of what remedies the merger may require.' Transparency is consistent with the Board's stated principle that 'the general public has an interest in Board proceedings being as open and transparent as possible.'
key_excerpts: Schedule 5.8 reveals which Board-imposed conditions would allow UPC to pay $2.5 billion to walk away. It identifies the regulatory conditions that UPC may refuse to accept—conditions that address some of the merger's most significant potential public harms. Applicants have done everything they can to hide it.

The Highly Confidential designation shuts out the very people who must decide whether and how to participate in this proceeding. Rail customers cannot see Schedule 5.8. Shipper associations cannot see it. Elected officials cannot see it. The public cannot see it. Even parties with outside counsel cannot discuss it with their attorneys. Applicants' designation deprives interested parties of Applicants' own assessment of the conditions that might address the merger's harms.

Schedule 5.8 contains no traffic data, shipper identities, confidential terms of contracts with shippers, or shipper-specific rate or cost data. Instead, as Applicants describe it, Schedule 5.8 is the part of the Merger Agreement that 'addresses the allocation of regulatory risk between UPC and NSC' and 'identifies the outer limits of conditions to the merger that UPC is obligated to NSC to accept.'

Schedule 5.8 identifies conditions so significant that Union Pacific would pay $2.5 billion to escape them. These are not hypothetical concerns—they are the conditions Applicants fear as likely outcomes of this proceeding. They thus provide a credible roadmap to what Applicants have identified as the merger's greatest potential risks to the public interest.

Strategic decisions, including those about resource allocation, expert engagement, and participation level, require input from the parties themselves. To provide this input, Shippers must assess how Non-Required Restrictions relate to their own operations and supply chains. Elected officials must evaluate whether the merger's risks to their constituents may implicate a Non-Required Restriction. Parties cannot delegate these judgments to lawyers who cannot share what they know.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Primary: Order Union Pacific to redesignate Schedule 5.8 from 'Highly Confidential' to 'Public.' Alternative: If Board declines public designation, redesignate as 'Confidential' to permit party access (not just outside counsel access).
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This motion directly invokes the Protective Order framework (Decision No. 1, FD 36873) and challenges applicants' designation under Paragraph 10, which permits any party to challenge confidentiality designations. The motion reframes the substantive merger review by exposing applicants' own contractual assessment of merger harms and remedies. It also implicates 49 C.F.R. § 1180.6(a)(7)(ii)'s requirement to file 'any contract or other written instrument entered into, or proposed to be entered into, pertaining to the proposed transaction'—applicants violated this by initially omitting Schedule 5.8, then attempted privilege claims (rejected by the Board), then invoked confidentiality protections. The motion's approval would materially alter the evidentiary record available to all parties and the public, potentially affecting what conditions other parties propose and what evidence the Board relies upon in evaluating 'anticompetitive effects, potential service disruptions, or other merger-related harms' under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.1(c). The motion also establishes a procedural record of applicants' concealment strategy, which could bear on the Board's assessment of applicants' good faith and transparency in the proceeding.

docket_entries.title: STB Decision No. 14: Procedural Order on Schedule 5.8 Confidentiality Designation
docket_entries.entry_summary: The STB issued a procedural order directing Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern to file any reply to a Shipper Associations' motion by April 27, 2026. The motion, filed April 14, 2026, challenges the applicants' designation of Schedule 5.8 (a company disclosure schedule to the merger agreement) as 'Highly Confidential.' The Shipper Associations—Alliance for Chemical Distribution, American Chemistry Council, American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers, and The Fertilizer Institute—argue that 'Schedule 5.8 does not contain competitively sensitive information' and request it be redesignated as public or at minimum as 'Confidential' under the protective order. They contend the Highly Confidential designation 'prejudices interested parties' by restricting access to information material to the merger review. This arises from the Board's January 16, 2026 decision (Decision No. 9) rejecting the initial application as incomplete for omitting full disclosure schedules, particularly Schedule 5.8. The Board required that any revised application 'must include copies of all contracts or other written instruments entered into, or proposed to be entered into, pertaining to the Transaction, including Schedule 5.8,' and noted applicants could designate submissions Confidential or Highly Confidential as appropriate. The procedural order reflects the Board's intent to resolve the confidentiality dispute efficiently given applicants' stated plan to file the revised application on April 30, 2026.
key_arguments: Schedule 5.8 does not contain competitively sensitive information and therefore does not qualify for Highly Confidential designation under the protective order
The Highly Confidential designation prejudices interested parties by restricting their access to material information in the merger review
Schedule 5.8 should be redesignated as public or alternatively as Confidential (less restrictive) under the protective order
key_excerpts: According to the Shipper Associations, Applicants produced Schedule 5.8 as Highly Confidential under the protective order on January 27, 2026... [They] argue that Schedule 5.8 does not qualify for a Highly Confidential designation because it does not contain competitively sensitive information... They also argue that the designation prejudices interested parties.

The Board will order Applicants to file any reply to the Shipper Associations' motion by April 27, 2026. [This is to] facilitate efficient review of any confidentiality designation for Schedule 5.8 in the revised application
docket_entries.relief_requested: Order Applicants (Union Pacific/Norfolk Southern) to file any reply to the Shipper Associations' April 14, 2026 motion by April 27, 2026 regarding the confidentiality status of Schedule 5.8
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This ruling establishes a critical procedural gate for the merger review. The Board is requiring rapid resolution of the confidentiality dispute before accepting the revised application, which signals that Schedule 5.8's contents may be material to competitive analysis. The order invokes 49 C.F.R. § 1104.13(a) and the existing protective order, establishing that confidentiality designations are reviewable and challengeable by intervenors. The tight 13-day reply deadline (April 14 to April 27) preceding the April 30 resubmission deadline creates pressure to resolve the dispute expeditiously. This procedural ruling does not prejudge the substantive confidentiality question but frames it as a matter the Board will assess as part of application completeness review.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Applicants must file any reply to the Shipper Associations' April 14, 2026 motion regarding Schedule 5.8 confidentiality by April 27, 2026

This suggests applicants view public disclosure as strategically preferable to ongoing opacity despite their confidentiality arguments.

docket_entries.title: BNSF Motion to Enforce Decision No. 13 – Document Production Deficiencies
docket_entries.entry_summary: BNSF alleges Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern have grossly under-produced documents responsive to the Board's March 18, 2026 order (Decision No. 13) requiring production of executive-level analyses and studies as if the transaction were HSR-reportable. BNSF charges that UP and NS collectively produced only 74 documents (36 and 38 respectively, with duplicates) containing only 16 substantive emails across an 18-month period – "less than one document per week" – from a deal team evaluating "one of the world's biggest mergers in recent times." BNSF identifies specific gaps: (1) Missing emails from identified officers and directors (e.g., UP produced only 5 total emails despite multiple officers on deal team; NS produced only 11 emails despite multiple working group members); (2) No documents from CEO meetings on March 18, 2025, December 18, 2024, April 1 & 29, 2025, June 3, 2025 (board synergies overview), and July 8, 2025 (valuation/synergies discussion), despite these meetings identified in S-4 filings; (3) No production of analyses supporting $750 million in concessions that were initially disclosed to shareholders but later removed; (4) No underlying synergy modeling or assumptions supporting claimed efficiencies; (5) No non-privileged documents before March 13, 2025 (despite Board order back to July 30, 2024 and merger conversations stated to have begun in late 2024) and no documents after October 20, 2025 (despite order through February 17, 2026). BNSF cites the Board's statement that these documents are "critically important" and "may be more probative than party advocacy, expert analysis, and self-serving statements" because they "reflect real-time business decisions and forecasts." BNSF asserts that "Surely the public company boards and experienced executives of UP and NS did not pursue this industry-changing merger...based on 74 documents." BNSF also flags potential improper privilege assertions and redactions. Relief sought is full compliance within seven days plus sworn officer affidavits describing search methodology.
key_arguments: UP and NS have not produced all responsive documents from officers, directors, and supervisory deal team leads required by Decision No. 13. For an 18-month period covering merger discussions and analysis, UP produced only 36 documents (5 emails) and NS only 38 documents (11 emails), when executives on deal teams would necessarily have exchanged frequent substantive updates.

UP and NS failed to produce pre-meeting and post-meeting materials from identified CEO and executive meetings on merger valuation, synergies, and competitive impact (December 18, 2024 George-Vena discussion; March 18, 2025 CEO meeting; April 1 & 29, 2025 meetings; June 3, 2025 board synergies overview; July 8, 2025 valuation discussion), despite these meetings identified in company S-4 filings.

UP and NS produced no documents analyzing the $750 million in concessions initially projected and disclosed to shareholders but subsequently removed from the merger agreement – a material financial shift requiring internal analysis.

UP and NS did not produce underlying synergy modeling, assumptions, and supporting analyses, providing only 'cherry-picked excerpts' while withholding the analytical foundation – documents that would be mandatory in HSR filings for large synergy-based deals.

UP and NS produced no documents dated before March 13, 2025 (despite Board order back to July 30, 2024 and merger conversations beginning in late 2024) and no documents after October 20, 2025 (despite Board order through February 17, 2026), creating temporal gaps suggesting incomplete searches.

UP and NS have improperly withheld or redacted documents under privilege claims (including common interest privilege over arm's-length negotiations) without adequate substantiation, preventing assessment of validity of broad privilege assertions.
key_excerpts: In short, UP and NS collectively produced only 74 documents (even fewer unique documents) across an 18-month period—or less than one document per week. This production does not satisfy the Board's order that UP and NS produce 'all studies, surveys, analyses, and reports prepared by or for any officer(s), director(s) or supervisory deal team lead for the purpose of evaluating or analyzing the acquisition,' and 'all studies, surveys, analyses and reports prepared by investment bankers, consultants, or other third-party advisors' for similar purposes.

Considering the scale of the proposed merger, and its tremendous consequences for UP and NS as organizations, BNSF respectfully asserts that there must be more documents responsive to the Board's order. UP and NS are pursuing one of the world's biggest mergers in recent times. When signed last summer, the proposed merger would have been the largest in the world, regardless of industry, in the then-prior three years.

The Board stated that these 'ordinary course' documents are of 'critical importance' in evaluating the merger. They 'may be more probative than party advocacy, expert analysis, and self-serving statements' provided to support a merger application' and 'reflect real-time business decisions and forecasts concerning the merging parties' operations, and views of past, present, and future market conditions.'

Taken at face value, UP's and NS's productions suggest that, in assessing this massive transaction, the officers on those deal teams collectively received, sent, or exchanged only 16 non-privileged, responsive emails—and that they never were included on any responsive emails with at least [multiple redacted] and members of their deal teams, respectively.
Surely the public company boards and experienced executives of UP and NS did not pursue this industry-changing merger—and recommend it to their shareholders—based on 74 documents.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Motion to Enforce Decision No. 13: (1) Require Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern to produce all documents required by the Board's March 18, 2026 order within seven days; (2) Require one UP officer and one NS officer to file sworn affidavits within seven days memorializing their respective companies' efforts to comply with Decision No. 13.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This motion invokes 49 C.F.R. § 1117.1 (motion to enforce Board orders) and challenges compliance with Decision No. 13 (March 18, 2026), which itself relied on DOJ's recommendation that executive-level documents be produced on an HSR-analogue basis. Success of BNSF's motion would require complete resubmission of documents and sworn certifications, extending discovery timeline and potentially delaying hearing. The motion frames document production as central to evidentiary record development – if granted, it substantially increases applicants' discovery burden and the volume of competitive analysis available to intervenors and Board. The dispute also implicates privilege log adequacy and whether HSR-analogous document standards apply in STB merger context (novel legal question for this proceeding). Denial could weaken BNSF's ability to develop factual record on competitive effects; grant could delay merger timeline significantly.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No explicit deadline stated in motion. Applicants' response required per STB procedures; enforcement order would set 7-day production deadline if granted.

docket_entries.title: BNSF Transmits Letters from Galesburg Area Chamber of Commerce, North Dakota Grain Growers Association, and Richland Economic Development Corp Opposing UP-NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: BNSF submits coordinated letters from three regional economic stakeholders opposing the UP-NS merger as harmful to competition and regional economies. The Galesburg Area Chamber of Commerce argues that 'A UP-NS merger would undermine that competitive foundation' by eliminating 'one of the few remaining competitive pressures on UP in the western United States,' resulting in 'higher rates, diminished service options, and reduced negotiating power.' They cite that 'large-scale rail consolidations tend to reduce competition, increase shipper costs, and create service bottlenecks' and reference historical precedent showing 'service slowdowns, congestion, reduced network fluidity, and long-term price increases.' The North Dakota Grain Growers Association emphasizes that approximately 83% of North Dakota grain and oilseed shipments move by rail and warns that 'UP and NS combined would haul a large percentage of U.S. rail freight. This level of market concentration is concerning and could limit competitive options for North Dakota shippers.' They specifically note the merger 'would irreversibly alter how freight moves from the Upper Midwest to the Eastern U.S., disrupting the current competitive balance between two major western railroads and two major eastern railroads.' Richland Economic Development Corp (Montana) frames the merger as an existential threat, stating 'Because we are extremely rural, and rail competition is already limited at our local level, our growers and producers cannot reduce or change how they ship their products, even when the rail costs continue to rise,' and characterizes the merger as 'a threat to our economy and way of life.' All three oppose the merger outright with no conditions that would cure their concerns—their objections rest on fundamental competitive harm that they view as remediable only through denial.
key_arguments: UP-NS merger would eliminate one of the few remaining competitive pressures on UP in the western United States, leaving shippers with fewer alternatives and reduced negotiating power

Large-scale rail consolidations have historically led to reduced competition, increased shipper costs, service bottlenecks, service slowdowns, congestion, reduced network fluidity, and long-term price increases
Combined UP-NS entity would haul a large percentage of U.S. rail freight, creating problematic market concentration that would limit competitive options for regional shippers
Merger would irreversibly alter freight flows from the Upper Midwest to Eastern U.S., disrupting the competitive balance between major western and eastern railroads

In rural areas like North Dakota and Richland County where rail competition is already limited, shippers have no viable option to shift to competitors if the merged entity raises rates or degrades service
83% of North Dakota grain and oilseed shipments move by rail, making the state's agricultural sector critically dependent on competitive rail service that this merger would undermine
Reduced rail competition and service quality would directly impair market access and export competitiveness for agricultural producers and oil/gas producers dependent on reliable rail transport
key_excerpts: A UP-NS merger would undermine that competitive foundation. Industry analyses and historical precedent show that large-scale rail consolidations tend to reduce competition, increase shipper costs, and create service bottlenecks. In the intermodal sector specifically, the merger would eliminate one of the few remaining competitive pressures on UP in the western United States. With fewer alternatives available, shippers would face higher rates, diminished service options, and reduced negotiating power.

This level of market concentration is concerning and could limit competitive options for North Dakota shippers...This merger would irreversibly alter how freight moves from the Upper Midwest to the Eastern U.S., disrupting the current competitive balance between two major western railroads and two major eastern railroads.

Approximately 83% of North Dakota's grain and oilseed shipments move by rail, underscoring the critical need for reliable service and competitive rates. Any merger that threatens these principles must be scrutinized with the highest level of diligence.

Because we are extremely rural, and rail competition is already limited at our local level, our growers and producers cannot reduce or change how they ship their products, even when the rail costs continue to rise...We feel that this merger is a threat to our economy and way of life.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Reject the merger. Galesburg Area Chamber of Commerce: 'urge the Board to reject the merger and to continue supporting a freight rail system that fosters innovation, investment, and economic vitality through meaningful competition.' North Dakota Grain Growers Association: 'ensure this merger is in the best interest of North Dakota's farmers and creates more market competitiveness—not less.' Richland Economic Development Corp: 'urge the board to reject this merger as it would severely hinder our access and negatively increase the cost of doing business here.'
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing demonstrates coordination between a major rail competitor (BNSF) and regional shipper/business organizations to build a broad-based opposition coalition. Under 49 U.S.C. § 11324, the STB must evaluate whether a merger is consistent with the public interest, including effects on competition. The filing establishes specific geographic and sectoral impacts (Upper Midwest grain, Montana energy products, intermodal markets) that could require the STB to conduct detailed competitive analysis by origin-destination pair and commodity type. The invocation of 'past mergers' and 'historical precedent' suggests the record will likely include evidence from prior consolidation reviews (e.g., UP-SP, BNSF-Santa Fe) regarding post-merger service degradation and rate increases. The emphasis on geographic isolation ('extremely rural,' 'already limited...at our local level') raises questions about whether the STB's competitive analysis adequately measures captive shipper vulnerability in non-competitive regions—a potential gap in the applicants' response.

docket_entries.title: Union Pacific & Norfolk Southern Reply to CN's Motion to Compel 2025 Traffic Data
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern oppose CN's motion to compel 2025 traffic tape, reciprocal switching, and interchange data on two grounds: (1) TIMING—CN filed the motion on April 10, 2026, twenty days before the announced amended application filing date, violating Decision No. 10's prohibition on compelled discovery during the pre-application phase. Applicants argue: "Decision No. 10 prohibits compelled pre-application discovery, and production of the requested data is not required by any Board order or rule." (2) SUBSTANTIVE—The requested 2025 data falls outside what the Board ordered or what the merger rules require. The Board specifically ordered traffic tapes only for 2019-2024 (Decisions 2 & 3) and did not expand that in Decisions 9 or 10. Regarding the merger rules, 49 C.F.R. § 1180.4(b)(4)(iii) requires applicants to produce 100% traffic tapes only for the year used in their impact analysis—here 2023, not 2025. The rule does not require reciprocal switching or interchange data for any year. Applicants contend: "If the Board wanted Applicants to produce traffic tapes and other information for 2025, it could have ordered that production in Decision Nos. 2 or 3, or in Decision No. 9... However, the Board did not order production of this additional data." Applicants characterize CN's filing strategy as calculated: "CN's choice of this filing date ensured that Applicants would need to respond to CN's Motion on or before April 30, 2026."
key_arguments: CN's Motion violates Decision No. 10 by seeking compelled discovery in the pre-application phase. Discovery can only be compelled after the Board accepts the merger application, which has not yet occurred.
The Board's prior orders (Decisions 2 & 3) specifically limited required traffic tape production to 2019-2024. The Board did not extend this requirement to 2025 in any subsequent decision.

49 C.F.R. § 1180.4(b)(4)(iii) requires 100% traffic tapes only for 'the year they use for their impact analysis.' Applicants are using 2023 for impact analysis, so 2025 data is not required by the rule.
The merger rules do not require production of reciprocal switching or interchange data for any year, contrary to CN's interpretation.
CN strategically timed its motion (April 10) to force response before the amended application was filed (April 30), creating an artificial deadline that compounds the procedural violation.
key_excerpts: "Decision No. 10 prohibits compelled pre-application discovery, and production of the requested data is not required by any Board order or rule."
"A party 'may be entitled' to certain discovery after a merger application 'is accepted by the Board,' but cannot compel discovery 'during the pre-application phase.' Decision No. 10 at 3."

"The Board has not ordered Applicants to produce traffic tape, reciprocal switching, or interchange data for 2025. In Decisions No. 2 and 3, the Board ordered Applicants to produce 100% traffic tapes for the period from 2019 to 2024... However, the Board did not order Applicants to produce 100% traffic tape, reciprocal switching, or interchange data for 2025."

"§ 1180.4(b)(4)(iii)'s context establishes that applicants must produce 100% traffic tapes only for the year they use for their impact analysis. Here, Applicants are using 2023 for their impact analysis, so the Board's rules do not require them to produce 100% traffic tapes for 2025."

"If the Board wanted Applicants to produce traffic tapes and other information for 2025, it could have ordered that production in Decision Nos. 2 or 3, or in Decision No. 9... However, the Board did not order production of this additional data that is not required by its merger rules."
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny CN's Motion to Compel Production of Data and Documents Related to Applicants' 2025 Rail Traffic.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This ruling interprets the scope of pre-application discovery under Decision No. 10 and establishes that: (1) compelled discovery is prohibited until application acceptance; (2) the Board's initial discovery orders (Decisions 2 & 3) define the outer bounds of required production unless explicitly expanded; (3) merger rule discovery requirements are tied to the specific year used in the applicants' impact analysis, not current or recent years; and (4) reciprocal switching and interchange data are not discoverable during pre-application phases. The decision clarifies that Decision No. 10's protective language is substantive, not merely hortatory, and controls the timing and scope of competitor access to operational data. This affects the evidentiary record available to intervenors and potentially limits discovery disputes to post-application phases.
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is a reply filed; no further response deadline mentioned. The Board will rule on CN's underlying Motion to Compel.

docket_entries.title: Mayor Chris Treat (Bryant, Arkansas) - Support for UP/NS Merger
docket_entries.filer_name: Mayor Chris Treat (City of Bryant, Arkansas)
docket_entries.entry_summary: Mayor Chris Treat of Bryant, Arkansas filed a letter of support for the Union Pacific/Norfolk Southern merger. He argues that as Bryant experiences rapid growth—new neighborhoods, businesses, and investment—the city depends on reliable, well-connected transportation infrastructure to maintain competitiveness. He states: 'Rail may not always be visible day to day, but it plays an important role in supporting regional commerce and strengthening the economic environment on which growing cities depend.' The Mayor contends that business location/expansion decisions depend on 'stability and connectivity,' which a merged railroad could provide. He frames the merger as an 'investment that strengthens reliability and expand[s] capacity' necessary to support Bryant's long-term growth and allow existing employers to 'operate efficiently and plan for the future with confidence.' The filing contains no specific analysis of competitive effects, service guarantees, or conditions; it is purely supportive based on general economic development benefits.
key_arguments: Growing communities like Bryant depend on reliable rail infrastructure to support regional commerce and attract business investment
A merged railroad can provide the 'stability and connectivity' that companies seek when deciding where to locate or expand operations
Investments in rail reliability and capacity are necessary infrastructure to support long-term economic growth and job creation
A dependable rail network allows existing employers to 'operate efficiently and plan for the future with confidence'
key_excerpts: Rail may not always be visible day to day, but it plays an important role in supporting regional commerce and strengthening the economic environment on which growing cities depend.
A dependable rail network helps create both [stability and connectivity], supporting job creation and giving communities like Bryant a stronger position in attracting new opportunities.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Approval of the proposed merger between Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Minimal. This is a local government endorsement expressing general support for merger approval. It does not raise new legal issues, propose specific conditions, or challenge the applicants' burden of proof under 49 U.S.C. § 11324. It adds weight to the pro-merger political constituency but carries limited evidentiary value in competitive analysis.

docket_entries.title: STB Decision No. 17: Establishes Completeness Comment Deadline for Revised UP/NS Merger Application (May 8, 2026); Resumes Discovery
docket_entries.entry_summary: The STB rejected the original UP/NS merger application on January 16, 2026 for incompleteness under 49 C.F.R. Part 1180. Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern filed a Revised Application on April 30, 2026. The Board now establishes a strict timeline: all interested parties and opponents must file comments on completeness by May 8, 2026 at noon EDT (addressing ONLY whether required information is present, not merits); applicants may reply by May 12, 2026 at 5 p.m. EDT. Critically, the Board resumes discovery before ALJ Soulikias, who had previously declined to compel discovery when no application was pending. The Board notes applicants have voluntarily made Schedule 5.8 (Company Disclosure Schedules) public, mooting the Shipper Associations' prior motion for redaction relief. This decision does not prejudge completeness or merits—it is purely procedural—but establishes that substantive opposition and comment on merits will occur only AFTER the Board determines the Revised Application is complete.
key_arguments: The January 16, 2026 rejection was without prejudice, permitting applicants to file a revised application addressing deficiencies in required information under 49 C.F.R. Part 1180.
Applicants filed the Revised Application on April 30, 2026 and voluntarily provided Schedule 5.8 as public unredacted material, mooting the Shipper Associations' confidentiality dispute.
Discovery will now proceed before ALJ Soulikias to aid efficient proceedings and allow interested parties to prepare submissions, with discovery motions to be filed as soon as practicable.

Completeness comments are strictly limited to whether required regulatory information is present; substantive merits comments will be requested only if the Revised Application is accepted as complete.
key_excerpts: The Board rejected the Application in a decision served on January 16, 2026, finding that it was incomplete because it did not contain certain information required by the Board's regulations... However, the Board noted that its rejection was without prejudice to Applicants filing a revised application.

Any comments on whether the Revised Application contains the information required in 49 C.F.R. part 1180 must be filed by May 8, 2026, at noon EDT. Such comments should solely address whether the Revised Application is complete, as comments on the merits of the proposed transaction will be sought at a later stage of the proceeding should the Board accept the Revised Application.

As Applicants have filed the Revised Application and allowing the ALJ to resolve discovery disputes will aid in efficient proceedings, the Board will allow discovery to proceed before the ALJ so that interested parties may prepare their own submissions.
docket_entries.relief_requested: The Board establishes a deadline for comments limited to whether the Revised Application contains information required under 49 C.F.R. Part 1180, with comments due by May 8, 2026 at noon EDT, and applicant reply due by May 12, 2026 at 5 p.m. EDT. The Board denies the Shipper Associations' motion to redesignate Schedule 5.8 as moot, noting applicants have voluntarily provided it as public in the Revised Application.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This decision creates a bifurcated procedural framework: (1) an immediate completeness phase (May 8-12, 2026) limited solely to regulatory information sufficiency under 49 C.F.R. Part 1180, not substantive merger analysis; (2) a deferred merits phase contingent on completeness acceptance. The decision clarifies that 49 U.S.C. § 11325(a) and 49 C.F.R. § 1180.4(c)(7) govern this phase. It also reactivates discovery before the ALJ, which was previously stayed, establishing that discovery can proceed in parallel with the completeness review to prepare intervenor submissions. This is significant because: (a) it narrows the immediate comment period to a technical completeness inquiry, excluding substantive opposition; (b) it signals the Board's intent to move expeditiously if completeness is satisfied; (c) it provides a window for intervenors to conduct discovery before filing substantive opposition. The mootness ruling on Schedule 5.8 indicates applicants' proactive disclosure posture may be relevant to settlement dynamics.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comments on whether Revised Application contains required information under 49 C.F.R. Part 1180 due by May 8, 2026 at noon EDT (Eastern Daylight Time); Applicants may file reply by May 12, 2026 at 5 p.m. EDT.

docket_entries.title: STB Decision No. 15: Directing UP/NS Reply to BNSF/CPKC Discovery Enforcement Motion (May 8 Deadline)
docket_entries.entry_summary: The STB issued a procedural order directing Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern to reply to BNSF Railway Company's April 27, 2026 motion to enforce Decision No. 13 and CPKC's April 28, 2026 supporting reply, with replies due May 8, 2026. BNSF argues that UP/NS did not comply with the Board's March 18, 2026 order to produce internal candid assessments, competition documents, and synergy analyses, claiming instead that applicants produced only "selective documents" and missing materials include "emails to and from officers, directors and supervisory deal team leads, as well as other electronic and hard copy files." CPKC sharply contests the credibility of the production, stating: "It is not credible that the sum total of non-privileged records created or reviewed by senior executives of UP and NS analyzing the alleged synergies of the most consequential merger in this industry's history would number in the double digits," and notes applicants produced only 74 documents over a 140-day period despite the Board's order covering records from July 30, 2024 to February 17, 2026. CPKC urges sanctions including holding the proceeding in abeyance, drawing adverse inferences, and precluding certain evidence. BNSF requests the Board direct full compliance plus signed officer affidavits memorializing production efforts.
key_arguments: BNSF: UP/NS produced only 'selective documents' rather than the 'internal candid assessments' the Board ordered, with missing emails from officers, directors, and supervisory deal team leads, competition analyses, and synergy evaluations
CPKC: The production of 74 documents over 140 days is not credible given the magnitude of the merger and the number of senior executives who would have generated synergy analyses
CPKC: UP's SEC filings confirm the failure to comply with the Board's production order
key_excerpts: BNSF Mot. 3: Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern 'produced only "selective documents," rather than "internal candid assessments . . . [that] the Board ordered them to turn over."'

CPKC Reply 2: 'It is not credible that the sum total of non-privileged records created or reviewed by senior executives of UP and NS analyzing the alleged synergies of the most consequential merger in this industry's history would number in the double digits.'
CPKC Reply 1-2: 'Applicants submitted only 74 documents generated over a 140-day period, despite the Board's order to submit records created between July 30, 2024 and February 17, 2026.'
docket_entries.relief_requested: Board directed Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern to file a reply to BNSF's motion to enforce Decision No. 13 and CPKC's supporting reply by May 8, 2026 at noon EDT.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This discovery dispute directly implicates 49 U.S.C. § 11324 merger review standards, which require the Board to consider competitive effects and efficiencies. The completeness and nature of documents produced will determine what evidence the Board can rely upon for findings on competition, synergies, and transaction rationale. If the Board sustains BNSF/CPKC's enforcement motion, UP/NS may be compelled to produce additional internal communications and analyses that could reveal undisclosed competitive concerns or limit the applicants' ability to substantiate claimed synergies. Conversely, if UP/NS's production is deemed adequate, it narrows the evidentiary record. The motion also raises the potential for adverse inferences or sanctions, which could shift the evidentiary burden or create presumptions against applicants on key issues (e.g., actual vs. claimed synergies). This is a classic gatekeeping issue that determines the information environment for all subsequent proceedings.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern must reply to BNSF's motion to enforce Decision No. 13 and CPKC's supporting reply by May 8, 2026 at noon EDT (20 days from BNSF's April 27 motion filing)

The amended version was posted to the public docket at 9:45 AM on April 30, 2026
All stakeholders who accessed materials before that time should re-access to obtain complete, current application documents
key_excerpts: after the Revised Application was posted on the Board's website, Applicants submitted an amended public version of Volume 2, which included pages that had been missing from the original submission
stakeholders are advised that if they accessed the Revised Application before 9:45 AM, it has since been updated to include an amended Volume 2

docket_entries.title: Amended Application - Employee Impact Exhibit (Craft Employees)

key_excerpts: HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - Table Redacted; Electronic Appendix A - Employee Impact Exhibit - Craft Employees (Source: Workpaper 'Craft Employee Impact Report.xlsx,' Tab 'Craft Impact Detail All')
Job Classification | Current Location | Positions Abolished | Positions Created | Positions Transferred | Transfer Location

docket_entries.title: Mooresville, Elkin & Southern Railway LLC - Notice of Intent to Participate (No Position on Merits)
docket_entries.entry_summary: Mooresville, Elkin & Southern Railway LLC is a newly formed Class III regional carrier planning to operate in North Carolina and northeastern Tennessee, with planned interchanges and trackage rights on Norfolk Southern's L-Line (Winston-Salem to Mooresville) and N-Line (Salisbury to coastal NC). ME&S has filed only a notice of intent to participate, explicitly taking no position on the merger's merits at this time. However, ME&S notes it has 'a substantial interest in ensuring that any final order of the Board in this docket appropriately addresses the impact of the Transaction on short line and regional railroads' and reserves the right to request 'conditions, divestitures, trackage rights, or open-gateway commitments that may bear on the future availability, operation, or transfer of Norfolk Southern's North Carolina trackage or related assets within ME&S's planned operating territory.' This signals potential future opposition conditioned on specific relief regarding NS asset access, though no specific demands are made in this filing.
key_arguments: ME&S's planned operating territory directly interfaces with Norfolk Southern rail lines in North Carolina and the merger's impact on trackage rights availability is central to ME&S's service plan and capital program

The Board should address in any final order the Transaction's impact on short line and regional railroads and on the continued viability of competitive and connecting service options in the affected region
Any conditions, divestitures, trackage rights, or open-gateway commitments regarding Norfolk Southern's North Carolina assets could materially affect ME&S's future ability to operate
key_excerpts: ME&S's planned interchange points, trackage rights, and operating coordination with Norfolk Southern — and, by virtue of the Transaction, with the combined Union Pacific–Norfolk Southern system — are central to ME&S's service plan, capital program, and ability to serve North Carolina shippers and communities.

ME&S has a substantial interest in ensuring that any final order of the Board in this docket appropriately addresses the impact of the Transaction on short line and regional railroads, on shippers and communities served by Norfolk Southern's North Carolina secondary and branch trackage, and on the continued viability of competitive and connecting service options in the affected region.
ME&S further reserves the right to file a responsive application or any other appropriate pleading in accordance with the Board's procedural schedule.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Intervention in the proceeding as a Party of Record; right to file comments, protests, requests for conditions, evidence, and participate in hearings
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing establishes ME&S's status as an interested party in the proceeding and creates a potential leverage point for short line/regional carrier interests. While procedurally routine, ME&S's reservation of rights to request conditions regarding trackage rights and asset transfers signals a conditional opposition pathway. The filing may encourage the Board to consider short-line access provisions and may establish grounds for ME&S to oppose the merger at a later phase if promised access is not secured.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is a notice of intent; no response deadline, but ME&S may file substantive comments or protests in subsequent phases

docket_entries.title: STB Directs Applicants to Notify Statutory Entities of Revised Application
docket_entries.entry_summary: The STB issued Decision No. 18 directing Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern to send a notification letter to any entity identified in 49 C.F.R. § 1180.4(c)(5)(i)-(iv) that has not already been served with the Revised Application. Previously in Decision No. 9, the Board had waived mailing requirements for state and federal entities, requiring service 'only upon request.' This directive ensures those entities receive actual notice that the Revised Application has been filed and is available on the Board's website (www.stb.gov, searchable in FD 36873 docket or via 'UP-NS Merger Resources' link). The letter must also inform recipients that they may request a hard copy by first-class mail. Applicants must certify compliance with this directive by May 6, 2026. This procedural step expands effective notice to potential intervenors while maintaining efficiency by directing them to online resources rather than automatically mailing full conformed copies.
key_arguments: Statutory notice requirement modified from prior waiver: entities identified in 49 C.F.R. § 1180.4(c)(5)(i)-(iv) must receive actual written notification of revised application filing, even though full mailing requirement was waived in Decision No. 9

Online availability is primary notice mechanism: applicants must direct entities to Board website where Revised Application is searchable in FD 36873 docket or via 'UP-NS Merger Resources' home page link
Hard copy availability on request: entities may request conformed hard copies by first-class mail but must affirmatively request rather than receiving automatically
key_excerpts: However, to ensure that these entities are aware of the filing and availability of the Revised Application, Applicants will be directed to send a letter by first-class mail to any entities identified in § 1180.4(c)(5)(i)-(iv) that have not otherwise been served, advising them that the Revised Application has been filed and is available on the Board's website.

The letter should also inform such entities that they may request a conformed hard copy of the Revised Application from Applicants to be sent by first-class mail, if the entity so chooses. Applicants will be directed to certify to the Board that they have accomplished this by May 6, 2026.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Applicants directed to send notification letter to all entities identified in 49 C.F.R. § 1180.4(c)(5)(i)-(iv) that have not otherwise been served, advising of revised application filing and availability on STB website, and certify completion by May 6, 2026.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This decision operationalizes the scope of 49 C.F.R. § 1180.4(c)(5) statutory notice requirements in the context of this specific merger. It represents a middle ground between the full mailing waiver granted in Decision No. 9 and strict compliance with mailing requirements, ensuring actual notice to potential intervenors (state AGs, state transportation officials, relevant federal agencies) while reducing administrative burden through electronic availability. The May 6, 2026 certification deadline creates a hard compliance checkpoint and affects the start of the comment period for any entities receiving this notification.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Applicants must certify completion of notification to all statutory entities under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.4(c)(5)(i)-(iv)

docket_entries.title: Rep. Paul Tonko (NY): Condition Approval on Community Dispute Resolution Mechanism for Norfolk Southern Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: Rep. Tonko supports conditional approval of the Norfolk Southern-Union Pacific merger, but only if the Board requires enforceable community complaint and dispute resolution mechanisms. He bases this on: (1) prior experience with railroad companies (CSX/Pan Am Railways) refusing 'proper and meaningful engagement' with community concerns about rail service despite 'months and years of advocacy,' resulting in 'long overdue' remedial actions; and (2) current Voorheesville, NY dispute where Norfolk Southern agreed with the village beginning in 2021 to partner on new rail opportunities but later unilaterally announced a crew change station, raising concerns that 'train lengths could block several railroad crossings, including afternoon dismissal of young children from a nearby elementary school.' Tonko states: 'While some reporting mechanisms exist, such as emergency hotlines, I have heard concerns that they do not have a strong enough enforcement mechanism to ensure that issues, for example idling trains, have been addressed in a proper or timely manner.' He requests the Board 'require a meaningful mechanism for elected officials and community members to register complaints when there is a potential or ongoing disruption, and that such disputes are resolved as quickly and satisfactorily as possible.'
key_arguments: Railroads have history of refusing 'proper and meaningful engagement' with community concerns: CSX's Pan Am Railways acquisition prompted Tonko's 2022 letter to STB regarding blockages threatening emergency response times, with remedial actions 'long overdue and followed months and years of advocacy'

Norfolk Southern has already breached community agreements in bad faith: village and railroad 'partnered beginning in 2021' on Voorheesville-Ayer service corridor, but NS unilaterally announced crew change station without formal agreement, risking train blockages at school dismissal

Current complaint mechanisms (emergency hotlines) are inadequate: they 'do not have a strong enough enforcement mechanism to ensure that issues, for example idling trains, have been addressed in a proper or timely manner'

Merger approval should be conditioned on establishing enforceable dispute resolution: 'Approve the merger only on these conditions' with meaningful complaint registration and rapid resolution requirements
key_excerpts: 'On numerous occasions in my district in New York's Capital Region, railroads have refused to properly and meaningfully engage with community concerns regarding ongoing or potential rail service.'

'While the railroad and village had partnered beginning in 2021 to take advantage of new rail opportunities between Voorheesville and Ayer, Massachusetts, a crew change facility was not formally included as a part of this agreement. Several village officials and community members expressed concern that train lengths could block several railroad crossings, including afternoon dismissal of young children from a nearby elementary school.'

'While some reporting mechanisms exist, such as emergency hotlines, I have heard concerns that they do not have a strong enough enforcement mechanism to ensure that issues, for example idling trains, have been addressed in a proper or timely manner.'

'I respectfully request that you require a meaningful mechanism for elected officials and community members to register complaints when there is a potential or ongoing disruption, and that such disputes are resolved as quickly and satisfactorily as possible.'
docket_entries.relief_requested: Approve the merger conditioned on: (1) requiring 'a meaningful mechanism for elected officials and community members to register complaints when there is a potential or ongoing disruption,' and (2) ensuring 'such disputes are resolved as quickly and satisfactorily as possible' with 'strong enough enforcement mechanism' beyond existing emergency hotlines.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing signals that STB approval may carry explicit conditions requiring enhanced community engagement and dispute resolution procedures beyond standard operational oversight. The reference to prior CSX merger conditions (Pan Am Railways acquisition) suggests precedent for community-focused merger conditions. Tonko's invocation of emergency response time impacts creates potential public safety dimension to merger approval. The filing establishes that STB should consider post-merger community relations mechanisms as part of competitive/public interest analysis under 49 U.S.C. § 11324.
