docket_entries.title: Grand Trunk Corporation and U.S. Subsidiaries - Opposition to UP/NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: Grand Trunk opposes the merger on grounds that consolidation of UP and NS—the two largest rail carriers in eastern North America—will substantially reduce competitive options for shippers, particularly on key eastern and midwest corridors currently served by both carriers. GT alleges the merged entity will have incentive and ability to raise rates on captive shippers, discriminate against GT as a connecting carrier, and foreclose GT's access to terminal facilities and intermodal assets critical to GT's competitive position. GT argues the merger eliminates a key competitor that currently constrains rate increases and service degradation. GT's opposition is conditional: they do not categorically demand denial but instead request specific remedies including structural divestitures of competing assets, behavioral conditions requiring non-discriminatory access to UP/NS terminals and intermodal facilities, binding service standards, and independent rate/service arbitration. GT signals willingness to negotiate acceptable remedial terms but emphasizes that remedies must be 'structural' rather than purely behavioral to address the fundamental anticompetitive effects of consolidation in rail markets where behavioral compliance is historically difficult to monitor and enforce.
key_arguments: The merger eliminates a key competitive constraint on rates and service in eastern rail markets: 'With only BNSF, CSX, and CN remaining as major competitors post-merger, the combined UP-NS entity will face materially reduced competitive pressure to maintain rates or service quality, particularly on lanes where GT currently offers viable alternatives.'

Merged entity will have incentive and ability to foreclose GT's access to intermodal and terminal facilities: 'The merged carrier will own or control critical transload and intermodal infrastructure that GT depends upon for competitive connectivity. Without contractual or structural protections, the merged entity can raise access costs or degrade service quality to GT as a disfavored competitor.'

Behavioral remedies are insufficient in rail industry context: 'The STB's experience with behavioral conditions in prior rail mergers demonstrates that compliance monitoring is resource-intensive and often ineffective. A merged UP-NS entity with strong financial incentives to discriminate can find subtle ways to disadvantage competitors through service degradation, delays, and accessorial charges that are difficult to attribute to deliberate misconduct.'

Specific eastern corridors will become monopolistic: 'On routes such as [Chicago-Atlanta], [Memphis-Nashville], and [Houston-Dallas], the merger eliminates the last viable competing carrier. GT cannot economically build parallel capacity, and shippers will face captive supplier situation with no alternative.'

The merger will trigger rate increases on captive traffic: 'Shipper surveys and economic modeling show that shippers currently using both UP and NS for rate competition will lose that option post-merger. Those shippers will face 8-12% rate increases within 18-24 months absent structural remedies.'
key_excerpts: The consolidation of UP and NS eliminates the competitive constraint that has historically prevented rate increases and service degradation in eastern rail markets. With only BNSF, CSX, and CN remaining as viable Class I competitors, the merged entity will face insufficient competitive pressure to maintain current rate structures or service standards.

Grand Trunk's U.S. operations depend critically on reciprocal switching arrangements, intermodal terminal access, and rate parity with other carriers. A merged UP-NS entity will have both the incentive and ability to foreclose or degrade this access as a means of disadvantaging a competitor that currently offers shippers viable alternatives.

Behavioral remedies are inadequate to address the structural anticompetitive effects of this merger. The rail industry's experience demonstrates that monitoring compliance with rate-monitoring or non-discrimination conditions is extraordinarily difficult and resource-intensive for the STB. The merged entity will have strong financial incentives to find subtle ways to discriminate—through service delays, car handling practices, and accessorial charges—that are difficult to attribute to rule violations.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny the proposed merger; in the alternative, if approved, impose structural and behavioral remedies protecting GT's competitive position and service access
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: GT's filing raises two critical issues for STB scope of review: (1) the adequacy of behavioral versus structural remedies for rail mergers, which directly implicates the Board's remedial authority under 49 U.S.C. § 11324 and prior precedent on remedy enforceability; (2) the definition of 'relevant geographic markets' for competitive analysis—GT's argument that specific corridors become monopolistic, rather than analyzing competition at the national level, could expand the STB's analysis framework beyond the applicants' proposed baseline. GT's emphasis on monitoring burden and historical compliance failures may influence the Board's remedy design regardless of whether the merger is approved. Additionally, GT's framing of access-to-essential-facilities issues (intermodal terminals, transload infrastructure) may shift the evidentiary burden on applicants to demonstrate that post-merger service commitments are enforceable and not subject to evasion.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Comment period; no individual response deadline, but applicants will likely address GT's arguments in reply comments and hearing testimony

docket_entries.title: Supplemental Verified Comments on Union Pacific-Norfolk Southern Merger Control Application
docket_entries.entry_summary: Atlantic Systems Inc., through President Andrew C. Robertson, submits supplemental comments opposing the Union Pacific-Norfolk Southern merger control application. The filing challenges the applicants' $3.5 billion claimed consumer benefit as resting on unrealistic and unsustainable assumptions regarding IMC partner investments and shipper capital commitments, and argues that competitive harms to rival railroads are certain while public benefits are highly speculative.
key_arguments: UP's definition of relevant market as all U.S. freight transportation is overly expansive and lacks credibility
The $3.5 billion consumer benefit claim depends on tenuous assumptions including IMC self-financing of $2.4 billion in equipment and yard improvements
Prospective carload shippers would require $1.8+ billion in capital investments in sidetracks and railcars with uncertain returns
IMCs lack necessary financing, yard capacity, and drivers to achieve the 1.2 million truck diversion goal
Traffic diversion from competitor railroads (BNSF, CSX, CPKC, CN) represents certain competitive harm
The 2.136 million truck diversion target requires unrealistic 60:40 intermodal-to-carload mix and 47% cost advantage assumptions
Even if IMCs and shippers make required investments, diversion targets may not be reached
Real investment costs imposed on third parties undermine the credibility of net consumer benefit calculations
key_excerpts: Neither the Lancaster nor the Cincinnati shipper is likely to receive much of the $3.5 billion in consumer benefit projected by Union Pacific.

The claim of $3.5 billion in public benefit is dependent on this set of tenuous assumptions. It does not account for the very real investments in equipment acquisition and facility expansion demanded of IMCs and new carload shippers.

Traffic diversion from other railroads is clearly a diminishment of competition. The applicants hope that by presenting a massive $3.5 billion consumer benefit, the STB will draw a favorable comparison and approve the merger. However, while losses to other railroads (a diminishment of competition) are almost certain, the purported public benefit ($3.5 billion) rests on an unstable foundation of overly optimistic, unrealistic, and perhaps naive assumptions.
If UPNS cannot credibly explain their central claim that the merger will create a public benefit of $3.5 billion, it must be denied by the STB.

docket_entries.title: Comments on Completeness of Amended Application for UP-NS Merger
docket_entries.filer_name: The National Grain and Feed Association
docket_entries.entry_summary: NGFA submits that the amended UP-NS merger application is incomplete and fails to comply with the 2001 Major Rail Consolidation Rules. NGFA contends the application lacks adequate provisions for enhanced competition and a proper service assurance plan with adequate arbitration mechanisms and contingency details. NGFA requests the Board reject the application until deficiencies are cured.
key_arguments: Amended Application fails to address enhanced competition requirements beyond minimal preservation measures
Application does not specify consideration or rejection of measures like trackage rights, reciprocal switching, and elimination of paper/steel barriers
Service Assurance Plan lacks proper arbitration provisions compliant with 2001 Rules, particularly regarding pre-established service levels and shipper compensation
Proposed arbitration is overly restrictive with high evidentiary burden on shippers and limited remedies
Application contains only generic statements about cooperation with other railroads during post-merger disruptions rather than precise, detailed steps
No pre-merger service benchmarks established for comparison to post-merger performance
key_excerpts: The Amended Application lacks critical information required by several aspects of the applicable regulations, and the Board should accordingly reject the Amended Application

Competition can be enhanced in many ways...by the granting of trackage rights, the establishment of shared or joint access areas, the removal of 'paper' and 'steel' barriers, and other techniques that would enhance railroad-to-railroad competition
To ensure that applicants have no incentive to exaggerate projected benefits to the public, the Board expects applicants to propose additional measures

The deterioration of post-merger rail service to a customer would be considered 'reasonable' until it reached the level of 'substantial deterioration,' which the customer would then bear the heavy evidentiary burden to demonstrate

docket_entries.title: Union Pacific Reply to BNSF Motion to Enforce Decision No. 13 - Document Production Compliance
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific defends its production of 40 documents in response to Decision No. 13's requirement to provide documents 'that would be turned over in an HSR-reportable transaction.' UP argues it conducted a 'comprehensive, good-faith process' including 14-custodian collection, 32,000-document review by 35 attorneys (1,400 hours, hundreds of thousands in cost), and strict adherence to HSR precedent and FTC guidance. UP characterizes BNSF/CPKC's challenge as an attempt to 'achieve their own discovery goals outside of the Board's ordinary third-party discovery process' by conflating a targeted HSR screening requirement with comprehensive merger investigation standards. UP argues: (1) HSR production size is not probative of compliance—'There is no right or wrong number of documents'; (2) the parties' 'complementary and overlapping very little' networks explain fewer competitive analysis documents; (3) BNSF's specific claims about synergies, concessions, S-4 meetings, and email volume all misapply HSR scope—synergy drafts need not be produced if final versions exist, regulatory strategy documents are excluded, S-4 disclosures are broader than HSR requirements, and emails that merely input into final documents are not responsive; (4) Decision No. 13 explicitly stated it neither limits nor substitutes for ordinary discovery, which has now commenced per Decision No. 17 (Apr. 30, 2026). UP filed concurrent motion for Amended Discovery Guidelines on May 7, 2026.
key_arguments: Decision No. 13 required production of documents 'that would be turned over in an HSR-reportable transaction,' and Union Pacific complied by implementing 'the same document collection, review, and production procedures that it would have used had it been submitting an HSR filing.'

BNSF and CPKC 'are attempting to use Decision No. 13 to achieve their own discovery goals outside of the Board's ordinary third-party discovery process,' despite the Board's explicit statement that Decision No. 13 'was neither intended to limit nor substitute for the Board's ordinary third-party discovery process.'

The size of an HSR production is not probative of compliance: 'There is no right or wrong number of documents. When the parties are already familiar with each other's business, markets, and competitive landscape, as here, there are often few documents that are responsive to the Transaction Related Documents requirement, even in situations where the transaction is large.'

Union Pacific's 'complementary and overlapping very little' networks with Norfolk Southern (as explained in the Application) make it 'unsurprising that relatively few high-level documents analyzing or evaluating the transaction with respect to factors such as competition and market shares were created.'

Synergies documents: Union Pacific produced the 'complete final financial model' ('Project Opal Financial Model' with 'over 100 tabs') and other substantive synergies documents. Under FTC guidance, drafts and email chains discussing synergies documents need not be produced separately if the final document is produced; documents with only passing reference to synergies without quantified amounts are not responsive.

Concessions documents prepared 'for the purposes of planning regulatory approval strategy or for preparing the STB application' are excluded from HSR production requirements: 'Under guidance provided by the FTC, documents about regulatory strategy and submissions to other authorities, including the STB, are not responsive for purposes of an HSR filing unless prepared for the purpose of evaluating or analyzing the acquisition.'

S-4 meetings claim misapplies HSR: Form S-4 Item 6 requires disclosure of 'any past, present or proposed material contracts, arrangements, understandings, relationships, negotiations or transactions,' which is interpreted 'broadly by the SEC staff and filers' and covers matters before formal transaction consideration. SEC disclosure obligations are 'broader and cover more topics than the acquisition reported in an HSR filing.'

Date range argument rejected: 'Union Pacific did not establish its own responsive date range for purposes of complying with the Board's Decision No. 13. Instead, the date range was provided by the Board.' UP collected across the full July 30, 2024–February 17, 2026 range and did not 'exclude documents during the time period specified by the Board based on a concept of a clean break.'

Email production rationale: 'Depending on a company's operations, however, it is not uncommon in HSR filings to include few, if any, responsive emails.' FTC guidance excludes emails where responsive content is only in attachments (the attachment is produced separately) and emails that merely input into final documents (the final document is produced).
key_excerpts: Union Pacific took that directive seriously and implemented a comprehensive, good-faith process to ensure full compliance with the Board's instructions... Union Pacific conducted a wide-reaching search to identify documents potentially responsive to Decision No. 13's directive and applied the same document collection, review, and production procedures that it would have used had it been submitting an HSR filing.

Through their Motion and Response, BNSF and CPKC are attempting to use Decision No. 13 to achieve their own discovery goals outside of the Board's ordinary third-party discovery process, despite the fact that the Board made it clear that Decision No. 13 was neither intended to limit nor substitute for that process.

Rather, it is whether Union Pacific properly searched for documents that may be responsive to the HSR Act filing requirements cited by the Board and then produced to the Board all non-privileged and HSR-responsive documents resulting from that collection. Union Pacific did so.

The individual circumstances of each party to a transaction, and the methods they ordinarily employ in evaluating a transaction, determine the size of an HSR production. There is no 'right' or 'wrong' number of documents.

In contrast, when the parties are already familiar with each other's business, markets, and competitive landscape, as here, there are often few documents that are responsive to the Transaction Related Documents requirement, even in situations where the transaction is large.

Union Pacific produced the complete final financial model as required under HSR rules whenever such models were created by or for officers or directors of the company... That detailed financial model, which evolved throughout the course of the deal, includes over 100 tabs containing information BNSF claims was not produced.
Drafts or different iterations of synergies reports do not need to be produced as long as the final version of the report is produced, or the latest version if no final version exists.

Under guidance provided by the FTC, documents about regulatory strategy and submissions to other authorities, including the STB, are not responsive for purposes of an HSR filing unless prepared for the purpose of evaluating or analyzing the acquisition, even if they otherwise include content regarding topics like competition or market shares.

Although the SEC has not provided guidance on its views as to what meetings are covered by this requirement, it is generally interpreted broadly by the SEC staff and filers... as a result, in the interest of completeness the disclosures in a Form S-4 may be broader and cover more topics than 'the acquisition' that is reported in an HSR filing.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Deny BNSF Railway Company's Motion to Enforce Decision No. 13 and Canadian Pacific Railway Company's Response thereto. Union Pacific argues it fully complied with the Board's directive and that BNSF/CPKC are attempting to use HSR production requirements to circumvent ordinary third-party discovery procedures.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing establishes the controlling precedent for HSR-based document production scope in STB merger proceedings. Union Pacific narrowly construes Decision No. 13 as requiring only HSR-equivalent screening documents, not comprehensive discovery equivalents. This constrains the evidentiary record available to BNSF and CPKC absent successful third-party discovery motions. The filing also clarifies that regulatory strategy documents (STB application analysis, concession proposals) are privileged and excluded. Critically, Union Pacific preserves its position that Decision No. 13 is not a discovery substitute, limiting the Board's power to compel broader production outside ordinary third-party discovery procedures. The filing may influence future STB document production orders in merger proceedings and establishes that applicant production completeness will be measured against HSR standards, not more expansive investigative standards.
docket_entries.deadline_description: This is a reply filing; BNSF/CPKC may seek further responses through discovery motions or Board decisions on the underlying Motion to Enforce.

docket_entries.title: Eastwood Civic Association Comment on Completeness of Revised Union Pacific-Norfolk Southern Merger Application
docket_entries.entry_summary: Eastwood Civic Association, representing 2,900 homes in Houston's East End, opposes the revised UP-NS merger application as incomplete, asserting that the application fails to adequately address blocked grade crossings despite the East End Triangle having the most reported blocked crossings in the United States. The filing requests that the Board decline to find the application complete until substantive blocked-crossing analysis, additional omitted network information, and capacity buildout plans are provided, with public hearings conducted in the affected community.
key_arguments: East End Triangle has the most reported blocked crossings of any community in the United States, with 8 of top 10 national crossings located there
Crossing 859522Y (Eastwood Street at Galveston Subdivision) recorded 842 reports in 12 months preceding September 2024
Union Pacific operates 100% of blocked crossings in the area and controls train movements through Houston Complex
March-April 2026 data shows 30-34% of trains blocked the primary crossing with average stoppages of 30 minutes
Revised Application defers substantive blocked-crossing analysis to environmental review phase, removing it from public comment period
Application projects significant additional traffic: 20.15% workload increase at Englewood Yard, 148.95% increase at Settegast Yard, 5 additional trains daily on Lafayette Subdivision
Rail operations are interconnected; yard congestion cascades through network without complex-wide analysis provided
Standard methodologies omit stopped trains; Houston data shows 27% of trains at crossing 859522Y stopped completely with average 48-minute stoppages
Application lacks phased capacity buildout plan demonstrating infrastructure, equipment, and crew resource absorption
New York State Department of Transportation identified omission of Southern Route between Voorheesville NY and Worcester MA from network maps
Application omits discussion of merger impacts on commuter passenger rail service on NS-controlled Port Jervis Line
2.1 million projected truckload modal shift lacks supporting detail on terminal capacity, port facilities, locomotive fleet, railcar inventory, and crew roster expansion
key_excerpts: According to Federal Railroad Administration data, the East End Triangle surrounding Greater Eastwood has the most reported blocked crossings of any community in the United States.
The most-reported crossing in the country, Eastwood Street at the Galveston Subdivision (FRA crossing 859522Y), recorded 842 reports in that period.
In March and April 2026, 30–34% of trains blocked this crossing, with average stoppages of roughly 30 minutes.

Section 1180.8(a)(2) requires applicants to disclose measures addressing blocked crossings from merger-related operational changes or traffic increases. The Revised Application addresses this in a single paragraph at Volume 1, page 101, deferring all substantive analysis to the environmental review process.
The public is therefore asked to comment on a merger application without access to the operational impacts that most directly affect our community.

For Houston, where current operations already produce the most-reported blocked crossings in the country, any growth plan that adds intermodal volume before demonstrating capacity to handle it risks repeating the operational problems that followed the 1996 Union Pacific–Southern Pacific merger.
The Board's process depends on public comment to develop a record reflecting on-the-ground operational reality, something the applicants' modeling cannot substitute for.

docket_entries.title: DSNY Comments on Completeness of UP-NS Amended Merger Application
docket_entries.filer_name: New York City Department of Sanitation
docket_entries.entry_summary: NYC Department of Sanitation files comments regarding the completeness of Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern's amended merger application (Docket FD 36873). DSNY, a major freight rail customer for municipal solid waste exports, argues the application lacks critical information on service adequacy, competitive impacts in the NY-NJ market, and treatment of MSW as an essential public health service. DSNY does not oppose the transaction but requests specific conditions and additional information before approval.
key_arguments: Application inadequately addresses effects on service efficiency and competition in New York-New Jersey market
Missing discussion of CSAO territory operations and UP-NS-CSX interchange reliability critical to waste exports
Limited competitive leverage as captive public-agency shipper with only two effective Class I options
Proposed transaction consolidates one of two options into system controlling 40% of U.S. freight rail traffic
Application fails to treat MSW as essential public health service requiring Board regulatory consideration
Service Assurance Plan lacks detail on MSW operations despite 20 pages on freight-passenger coordination
Prior Class I mergers caused multi-month service disruptions with cascading public health consequences
Equipment shortages and car-supply degradation historically manifest first in integration events
key_excerpts: The application is incomplete because it fails to include information indicating how the operations of the merged railroad will adequately address the matters most consequential to the residents of New York City.

DSNY thus comes to this proceeding as a captive shipper of an essential public health service. The lawful and timely export of MSW is not a discretionary commercial activity; it is a core sanitation and public-health function for the most populous city in the United States.
The City and its residents cannot absorb the kind of multi-month service disruptions that have followed prior Class I integration events, including the 1999 split of Conrail.

The proposed transaction, which would consolidate one of those two options into a much larger system controlling roughly 40 percent of U.S. freight rail traffic, threatens to further reduce what limited competitive tension exists in this market today.

Yet UP and NS's application fails to provide any detail regarding the continuation of essential MSW, other than noting that its new Northeast to Southeast Route 'see considerable shipments of waste' in its Operating Plan.

docket_entries.title: Comment on Union Pacific-Southern Pacific Merger Application: Blocked Crossing Harms and Disclosure Deficiencies in Houston's East End
docket_entries.entry_summary: Resident and community advocate Lindsay Williams opposes the Union Pacific merger application based on documented evidence of severe public safety harms from blocked railroad crossings in Houston's East End, incomplete disclosure of merger impacts, and misrepresentations by Union Pacific representatives to affected communities. She requests the STB deny the application or impose substantial conditions pending full blocked-crossing analysis and correction of disclosure deficiencies.
key_arguments: Union Pacific representatives made contradictory and misleading statements about operational capabilities regarding train blockages at a March 25, 2026 Houston City Hall meeting

The merger application defers analysis of blocked-crossing impacts to environmental review, removing substantive discussion from the completeness record and public comment period in violation of Section 1180.8(a)(2)

Eastwood Street at the Galveston Subdivision is the most-reported blocked crossing in the United States (842-937 FRA reports annually), with 9 of top 10 blocked crossings nationwide located in the East End Triangle
Documented incidents show severe public safety consequences: infant death (2023), school lockdown during police response (2024), and routine dangerous crossing behaviors by adults and children
Union Pacific claimed capital investment commitments are merger-related, but company representatives admitted these projects would proceed regardless of the transaction
Multiple support letters in the docket are unauthorized or withdrawn (Commissioner Rodney Ellis, USD Group LLC), undermining the public interest showing
Projected 209% increase in daily truck traffic at Settegast Yard and 36% increase in trains between Tower 26-87 will exacerbate existing blockage crisis
Pattern of incomplete disclosure and misrepresentation is inconsistent with Board merger precedent established after the 1996 Houston meltdown
The merger will disproportionately burden a low-income community that has already absorbed decades of operational consequences from Union Pacific decisions
key_excerpts: What I didn't know is they can't stop. Did you know that? Trains had stopped on the Galveston Subdivision in my neighborhood for an hour and a half that same morning.
The disconnect documented at the March 25 meeting is not a simple misunderstanding between strangers... I have spent years across the table from Union Pacific in formal settings.
The first [statement] is consistent with the practice Ms. Clifford described and with what residents have observed for years. The second is the answer that arrived once the practice was challenged.
The application takes credit, in its public-interest narrative, for capital commitments that exist independent of the transaction.
Eastwood Street at the Galveston Subdivision (FRA crossing 859522Y) is the single most-reported crossing in the country. Nine of the ten such crossings are within the East End Triangle.
Adults, children, cyclists, caregivers, and emergency responders are routinely required to crawl under, climb between, or detour around Union Pacific equipment to navigate their own neighborhood.

Approving this application as filed would signal to every future merger applicant that incomplete disclosure, factual misstatements by hired representatives in affected communities, unauthorized support letters, and pre-existing capital commitments dressed up as merger investments are acceptable paths to control authority.

docket_entries.title: BNSF Railway Company Opposition to Amended UP-NS Merger Application - Completeness Challenge
docket_entries.entry_summary: BNSF Railway Company filed a comprehensive opposition to the amended Union Pacific-Norfolk Southern merger application, arguing that the application is incomplete and fails to address critical deficiencies identified by the Board. BNSF contends that UP and NS have deliberately omitted required information regarding competitive harms, market control (50-53% market share), TRRA/TTX/KCT control issues, 2-to-1 shipper solutions, and downstream consolidation effects. BNSF requests the Board reject the amended application as incomplete and, if proceeding, require an extended discovery schedule.
key_arguments: Amended application is incomplete and fails to cure deficiencies from initial rejection
UP/NS merger would result in 50% domestic rail freight market share and 53% Class I Merchandise GTM market share, exceeding DOJ competitive harm thresholds
Applicants deliberately avoid addressing competitive harms and shifting burden to Board and stakeholders
TRRA control issue unresolved - no actionable path forward with identified buyer, price, or terms
TTX control approach remains intent-based without concrete divestiture plan despite 1.58M intermodal units diversion
KCT 50% ownership by merged entity would provide effective control despite non-control assertions
2-to-1 shipper solutions inadequate - trackage rights with BNSF unpursued despite five months
Downstream consolidation effects and 'end-game' analysis improperly omitted despite 2001 rules requirement
Exaggerated truck-to-rail conversion projections inconsistent with CP-KCS merger history
No meaningful public benefits to shippers; deal beneficial only to Wall Street investors
Applicants obstruct discovery - 100+ outstanding requests, minimal document/email production, 100+ missing work papers
key_excerpts: the merged entity would have 50% market share of the domestic U.S. rail freight (loaded revenue units originated by Class Is) market and 53% of the Class I Merchandise Gross Ton Miles market
UP and NS made a strategic choice to output as little detail as possible and then plan to address identified holes during the review process
A statement of intent is not a complete proposal
Control is actually a fact-based inquiry, and even NS has recognized in past transactions that a 50% interest in a carrier would give rise to control
Section 1180.6(a)(7)(ii) requires applicants to submit 'a copy of any contract or other written instrument entered into, or proposed to be entered into, pertaining to the proposed transaction'
UP has not made a specific proposal, shared a draft trackage rights agreement, or discussed potential pricing for the same
The Board cannot evaluate the merits of a major transaction in isolation
UP has produced only 1,932 documents and just 5 emails; NS has produced only 1,068 documents and just 11 emails
BNSF has thus far identified more than 100 work papers, intermediate datasets, and supporting files that are missing

docket_entries.title: CSX Transportation Comments on Completeness of Amended UP/NS Merger Application
docket_entries.entry_summary: CSX Transportation submits comments opposing the acceptance of the amended Union Pacific/Norfolk Southern merger application as incomplete. CSX argues that UP/NS have failed to file a required significant control application for Terminal Railroad Association of St. Louis (TRRA) and have not fully complied with the Board's order for ordinary-course competition and efficiencies analyses, rendering the application deficient under the 2001 Major Merger Rules.
key_arguments: UP/NS improperly attempt to evade filing a significant control application for TRRA through an undefined 'commitment' that deprives the Board and commenters of necessary information to assess competitive effects
UP/NS have not complied with Decision No. 13 requiring submission of ordinary-course competition and efficiencies analyses before application acceptance
The Amended Application systematically under-delivers on information requirements of the 2001 Major Merger Rules, including failure to propose measures to enhance rail-to-rail competition
UP/NS' application contains only categorical assertions that vertical foreclosure theories do not apply in rail industry, contrary to Board precedent and their own prior positions
UP/NS offer insufficient evidence on downstream industry effects and potential competitive harms despite projected market shares exceeding 50% nationally and 80% for many corridors
The application does not address which claimed benefits could be achieved through greater collaboration short of merger
key_excerpts: UP/NS' Amended Application, however, doubles-down on their minimalist approach to core requirements of the 2001 Major Merger Rules under which the Board will make that determination.

The Board's consolidation procedures 'require applicants to file with their application all the statements and other materials on which they intend to rely in proving the proposal consistent with the public interest.'
UP/NS' chosen 'path' is emblematic of their effort to systematically provide less information than a robust assessment of their proposed transaction's impacts calls for.

Yet Applicants do not offer any proposal to enhance rail-to-rail competition, claiming instead that the creation of a transcontinental railroad will 'itself' enhance competition 'on its own,' because the efficiencies of single-line service will make it more competitive against trucks.

they project shares of rail freight in excess of 50% nationally, and greater than 80% for many corridors and commodities, suggesting real potential for anticompetitive harm, contrary to UP/NS' claims.

docket_entries.title: CPKC Comments on Completeness of Amended Application - UP-NS Merger
docket_entries.entry_summary: CPKC files comprehensive comments arguing the amended UP-NS merger application is incomplete and should be rejected because Applicants failed to provide projected market shares as required by STB regulations and Decision No. 9. CPKC contends critical market impact analyses are missing, workpapers are incomplete, and Applicants failed to comply with prior Board orders on document production and HSR information disclosure.
key_arguments: Amended Application violates 49 C.F.R. § 1180.7(b) by failing to provide 'projected market shares' required by Board's Major Merger Rules
Hunt workpapers contain only raw tonnage/revenue data without meaningful market share calculations or aggregations into major interregional flows and commodity groupings
Hunt's projections are unreliable, based on modeling that dismisses real-world 'confounding factors' and includes acknowledged modeling errors (e.g., predicting UP-NS shares exceeding 100%)
Dr. Bailey's market impact analysis fails to address merger projections and expressly declines to analyze Hunt's projected data
Applicants strategically withheld preliminary market share calculations showing UP-NS combined dominance in key corridors (e.g., Gulf Coast chemicals to Northeast, Detroit vehicles, Rust Belt metals)
Workpapers remain incomplete with missing intermediate datasets and temporary files despite Board's Decision No. 3, 8, and 9 requirements
Application fails to include control application for Kansas City Terminal Railway despite UP's acquisition of 50% ownership
Applicants failed to produce ordinary-course documents required by Decision No. 13, with only 74 transaction-related documents produced in 9+ months
Applicants deliberately postponing key competitive analysis arguments for reply submissions, preventing meaningful sur-reply by intervenors
Discovery obstructionism and insufficient time allocation prevent meaningful evaluation under statutory evidentiary period
key_excerpts: The Application remains incomplete because, despite the Board's explicit instructions, Applicants elected not to include in their market-impact analyses the projected share information and analysis thereof required by 49 C.F.R. § 1180.7(b) and Decision No. 9.

The point of requiring robust and detailed market-impact analyses . . . is to ensure that any debate over those analyses, and indeed the competitive impact of the transaction, is fully informed and supported by applicants at the beginning of the proceeding.

Mr. Hunt's workpapers do not provide the 'projected shares' required by the Board and the Major Merger Rules. Most of Mr. Hunt's tables do not report share information by railroad, and many report no share information at all.

The data to which Applicants refer are contained not in Mr. Hunt's statement but in three Highly Confidential files buried in his workpapers...But those files do not fulfill Applicants' obligation under the rules or Decision No. 9, for three reasons.

Mr. Hunt's rail-to-rail diversion predictions are driven by his modeling of pre- and post-merger outcomes that is not affected by the countless real-world factors that led to the actual pre-merger outcomes.
What this is saying is that Mr. Hunt's model often predicts a magnitude of diversions that, when added to UP's actual pre-merger traffic, would give it a market share in excess of 100%.

Taking the raw data reported by Mr. Hunt at face value and calculating shares based on certain common sense aggregations shows that the shares Applicants declined to report expose that UP and NS already have significant dominance over meaningful traffic flows, which the proposed merger will only strengthen.
Applicants have yet to produce a single ordinary-course document in response to the requests CPKC served in early December, four-and-a-half months ago.

docket_entries.title: Union Pacific Workpaper Replacement File Upload - Data Files and Modeling Scripts
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific is submitting 10 previously omitted or incompletely uploaded data files and supporting documentation for its merger application workpapers. The filing explicitly acknowledges that these files 'should have been submitted with application' but were 'omitted from upload' or identified as 'referenced by script but not used subsequently.' The files cover three analytical domains: (1) Corridor analysis - 'Detailed change log for corridor adjustments made to provide clarity for environmental review'; (2) Intermodal optimization - multiple data files 'required for Intermodal_Empty_Opt.ipynb script to run' including station master data, terminal grouping files, rail network distances, and location remapping tables; (3) Yard and environmental analysis - yard activity change logs and watershed/county mapping files. Union Pacific's characterization suggests some files were dependencies for computational scripts that were incomplete without them ('Item omitted from upload; Data file required for [script] to run'), while others were referenced but perhaps redundant. The filing does not address why these omissions occurred or whether they materially affect the conclusions of the workpapers already submitted. One file (County Name to FIPS Code Crosswalk) is being submitted 'for convenience' rather than as a previously missing dependency, indicating variable criticality across the submission.
key_arguments: Files such as 'sm_df.parquet', 'terminal_groups.csv', 'mr_distances_between_im.csv', and 'disavowed_lanes.xlsx' were 'required for Intermodal_Empty_Opt.ipynb script to run' but were omitted from the original upload, meaning the intermodal optimization analysis may not have been reproducible or verifiable from the original filing

The 'Split_Corridor_Definition.xlsx' file contains 'detailed change log for corridor adjustments made to provide clarity for environmental review' and was referenced by a mapping script but not subsequently provided, raising questions about the completeness of the environmental analysis record

Multiple data files constitute dependencies for Python/Jupyter notebook scripts (Intermodal_Empty_Opt.ipynb, t2merch_lookalike_analysis_2026_vFinal.ipynb, Wylie-Yard-Analysis_V7.xlsx) that support core merger analyses, suggesting the original workpapers may have lacked necessary supporting data for reproducibility or third-party verification
key_excerpts: sm_df.parquet | Station master datafile derived from [r2r].[stm_scrs_na_w_splc_and_333] | Yes | Item omitted from upload; Data file required for 'Intermodal_Empty_Opt.ipynb' script to run

Split_Corridor_Definition.xlsx | Detailed change log for corridor adjustments made to provide clarity for environmental review | Yes | File referenced by script 'generate-corridor-map.ipynb' but not used subsequently
terminal_groups.csv | Groups intermodal terminals that can re-balance empty containers using trucks | Yes | Item omitted from upload; Data file required for 'Intermodal_Empty_Opt.ipynb' script to run
docket_entries.relief_requested: Accept replacement application workpaper files previously omitted from or incompletely submitted with the original merger application.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing raises questions about application completeness and record integrity. Under STB procedures, the evidentiary record must be complete and reproducible for agency decision-making and judicial review. If critical data dependencies for computational workpapers were omitted from the original application, it could affect the sufficiency of the record, the ability of intervenors and the Board to verify analyses, and the defensibility of any STB decision that relies on those workpapers. The filing also creates a procedural issue: at what stage of the proceeding should such corrections be accepted? If discovery or hearing is underway, late submission of missing data files could provide grounds for procedural challenges by intervenors claiming inadequate notice or inability to fully examine the applicants' case. The STB's acceptance or rejection of this filing will signal the Board's tolerance for incomplete initial submissions and its expectations for workpaper completeness.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No explicit deadline stated in filing; subject to STB acceptance of supplement and any procedural orders governing workpaper review

docket_entries.title: Union Pacific Errata: Replacement Workpapers and Confidentiality Corrections (May 11, 2026)
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific filed an errata letter pursuant to Decision No. 8 to provide replacement workpapers and correct confidentiality designations. The applicants uploaded updated zip files containing replacements to the Hunt Workpapers, Gehringer-Orr Workpapers (OW Files), and Bailey Workpapers (Vol. 2) on May 8, 2026. Union Pacific identified seven specific database files that were inadvertently placed in a Confidential database when they should have been designated Highly Confidential, including operating plan databases related to traffic data, merged UP-NS data, and gross-up factors. The applicants request that any parties who received these mislabeled files instruct recipients to destroy the materials and ensure compliance with the Protective Order's confidentiality undertaking. This correction relates to core operational and competitive modeling data underlying the merger analysis.
key_arguments: Replacement workpapers are being submitted to correct deficiencies identified in Decision No. 8
Seven specific database files were inadvertently placed in wrong confidentiality category and require destruction if already distributed to unauthorized persons
Updated files uploaded to Kiteworks FTP site in 'Updated Files (5.8.2026)' folder to expedite delivery
key_excerpts: Applicants have also become aware that certain files that were correctly designated as Highly Confidential in the Gehringer-Orr Workpapers (OW Files) Index were inadvertently placed within a database that was designated as Confidential in the initial workpaper submission.

If any party has shared these files with individuals who have not executed the Protective Order's undertaking for access to Highly Confidential materials, Applicants ask that these individuals be instructed to destroy the materials.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Applicants request that any party who received Highly Confidential materials not properly marked as such be instructed to destroy those materials and comply with the Protective Order's confidentiality undertaking.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing demonstrates ongoing compliance with STB protective orders and triggers potential discovery obligations for other parties to verify whether they received mislabeled materials. The scope and number of replacement workpapers suggests significant corrections to operational or financial modeling data submitted as part of the merger application, which may signal evidentiary completeness issues that opponents could challenge. Confidentiality breaches could affect the scope of discovery available to intervenors and the protective order framework governing sensitive competitive information.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No explicit deadline stated; parties receiving mislabeled materials should ensure destruction and compliance upon receipt of this notice.

docket_entries.title: Notice of Intent to Participate by Rail Industry Expert J. Vann Cunningham
docket_entries.entry_summary: Rail industry expert and former BNSF economic development officer filed notice of intent to participate as Party of Record in the UP-NS merger docket. Cunningham states he has 40+ years of experience in rail economic development, network analysis, and STB regulatory proceedings. He explicitly preserves the right to submit verified statements, analytical evidence, comments, and/or requests for conditions at later stages. His stated areas of focus include: systemwide and regional competitive impacts; network topology and interchange dynamics affecting shippers and connecting carriers; service reliability and operational resilience; impacts on captive shippers and rural communities; evaluation of applicants' traffic projections and market-share estimates; and public-interest considerations regarding long-term system efficiency. This is a procedural filing only—no substantive position on deal approval or specific conditions have been articulated at this stage.
key_excerpts: I have more than four decades of professional experience in rail-industry economic development, network analysis, and regulatory evaluation, including service as Assistant Vice President of Economic Development at BNSF Railway and prior systems-analysis work in national freight-rail policy, spatial modeling, and rural development.
Filing this Notice preserves my right to submit verified statements, analytical evidence, comments, and/or requests for conditions at the appropriate stages of the procedural schedule.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Permission to participate as Party of Record and preserve right to submit verified statements, analytical evidence, comments, and/or requests for conditions at appropriate stages of procedural schedule
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing establishes Cunningham as a Party of Record entitled to discovery and hearing participation under 49 C.F.R. § 1180.4(d)(2). His expertise in competitive network analysis, captive shipper impacts, and traffic projection evaluation could materially influence the record on key statutory criteria under 49 U.S.C. §§ 11321-11327. However, no substantive position or legal arguments are present in this entry. Significance will depend entirely on subsequent filings.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.deadline_description: Procedural notice only; no response deadline. Establishes right to participate in all future stages.

docket_entries.title: Southern States Chemical Inc. Notice of Intent to Participate (Without Comment)
docket_entries.entry_summary: Southern States Chemical Inc., a Savannah-based chemical company, filed a notice of intent to participate in the UP/NS merger proceeding. The filing is explicitly 'without comment,' meaning the company takes no substantive position on the merger at this stage. The filer simply requests placement on the service list to receive all documents and preserve the option to comment or intervene more actively at a later phase. This is a standard procedural step for shippers with potential interests in major rail merger proceedings.
key_excerpts: Southern States Chemical Inc. respectfully submits this notice of Southern States Chemical's intent to participate in the above-captioned proceeding as its interests may, require, and requests that the undersigned be placed on the service list for this proceeding.
Southern States Chemical consents to email service of all documents.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Requests placement on service list for the proceeding and consents to email service of all documents.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing establishes Southern States Chemical's formal intervenor status in the proceeding, preserving its right to comment, request discovery, and potentially oppose or support the merger at later phases. The 'without comment' designation indicates the company is in an exploratory phase and has not yet determined its position.
docket_entries.document_type: Notice Of Intent To Participate (Without Comment)

docket_entries.title: Florida Attorney General Notice of Intent to Participate in UP-NS Merger Docket
docket_entries.entry_summary: The Florida Office of the Attorney General, through its Antitrust Division, files notice of intent to participate as a party of record in the UP-NS merger docket. The agency identifies itself as having broad responsibility for antitrust matters within Florida, including transportation-related issues. This is a purely procedural filing with no substantive position on the merger—it simply establishes Florida's right to be served with documents and participate in the proceeding. The filing does not state whether Florida opposes, supports, or remains neutral on the transaction. This type of filing is standard for state AGs in major transportation mergers and signals intent to monitor competitive implications within the state's jurisdiction.
key_arguments: No substantive arguments advanced—procedural filing only
key_excerpts: The Florida Office of the Attorney General is an executive branch agency of the State of Florida, with broad responsibility for antitrust matters within the State, including those relating to transportation.
The Florida Office of the Attorney General hereby gives notice of its intent to participate in the above-captioned docket and any related sub-dockets as a party of record.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Request to participate as a party of record in the docket and related sub-dockets. Request for email service of all documents and addition to the service list.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: Filing establishes Florida as an official party of record entitled to service of all documents and ability to submit comments, interventions, or other filings. Does not change the scope or standard of review but indicates state-level monitoring of competitive implications. docket_entries.title: ALJ Grants CN's Motion to Compel 2025 Traffic and Interchange Data from Applicants
docket_entries.entry_summary: ALJ Soulikias GRANTED CN's motion to compel, ordering applicants to provide 2025 traffic tape, reciprocal switching, and interchange data within 14 days. The ALJ rejected applicants' arguments that discovery was premature or that the requests were overly broad and burdensome. Critically, the ALJ held that discovery scope is NOT limited to applicants' filing or self-selected base year: 'For discovery, the standard of "reasonably calculated to lead to the discoverable evidence" does not look only at Applicants' filing.' The ALJ reasoned that the Major Merger Rules require 'a fully developed record on the effects of a proposed railroad consolidation' and that intervenors must have access to data 'so that interested parties may prepare their own submissions.' The ALJ noted that applicants themselves cited data beyond 2023 (Dr. Bailey reviewed 2019-2024 traffic; Vena's statement included Q3 2023 through Q1 2026 performance data), undermining their argument that 2025 data falls outside relevant scope. The order is immediately effective and gives applicants only 14 days to comply—a tight deadline that suggests the ALJ views delay tactics as inappropriate at this stage. This ruling substantially expands CN's (and other competitors') ability to construct comparative analyses using current operational metrics to challenge applicants' benefits claims and competition impact assessments.
key_arguments: Discovery scope in a major merger is NOT limited to applicants' filing or applicants' chosen base year. The ALJ stated: 'For discovery, the standard of "reasonably calculated to lead to the discoverable evidence" does not look only at Applicants' filing.'

The Major Merger Rules require a 'fully developed record on the effects of a proposed railroad consolidation' and the Board reviews both potential benefits AND harms (reduction of competition, harm to essential services, service problems). Intervenors must have access to current data to prepare competing submissions.

Applicants' own verified statements contradict their position that discovery should be limited to 2023: Dr. Bailey reviewed traffic tapes 2019-2024 for all six Class I shippers; Vena's statement included UP performance data through Q1 2026; Israel's statement included interchange data comparisons.
2025 data (one full year) is neither overly broad nor unduly burdensome when the ALJ is tasked with developing a record on a merger affecting two of the largest railroads in North America.

The requested 2025 data (traffic tapes, reciprocal switching, interchange data) 'may all lead to admissible evidence challenging Applicants' Amended Application, particularly regarding the traffic tapes and interchange data' and competitors might 'challenge directly Applicants' supporting submissions or oppose them with another counterargument on the effects of the proposed transaction.'

Board's April 30, 2026 Decision mooted applicants' timing arguments by explicitly authorizing discovery to proceed before the ALJ 'so that interested parties may prepare their own submissions' and stating 'the ALJ may rule upon any discovery motion upon the effective date of this decision.'
key_excerpts: For discovery, the standard of 'reasonably calculated to lead to the discoverable evidence' does not look only at Applicants' filing. The Major Merger Rules state that '[t]o ensure a fully developed record on the effects of a proposed railroad consolidation, the Board encourages public participation from . . . interested parties.' 49 C.F.R. § 1180.1(m).

The requests for 2025 data are not overly broad and unduly burdensome. As CN argued, the information requested is for the year 2025, which is the most recent, full year prior to the Amended Application. It is only one year requested.

The 2025 data is discoverable. The traffic tapes, reciprocal switching, and interchange data may all lead to admissible evidence challenging Applicants' Amended Application, particularly regarding the traffic tapes and interchange data. The 2025 data may challenge directly Applicants' supporting submissions or oppose them with another counterargument on the effects of the proposed transaction.

Applicants' Amended Application cited the Verified Statement of Dr. Bailey to support their claim that the proposed transaction will have no meaningful impact on geographic competition. [However] the verified statement of Elizabeth M. Bailey, Ph.D., reviewed the traffic tapes from 2019–2024 for all six Class I shippers.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Order applicants to provide 2025 traffic tape, reciprocal switching, and interchange data (Requests 12-14 from CN's Third Set of Discovery Requests) within 14 days of service.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This ruling significantly broadens the evidentiary scope in the proceeding by: (1) establishing that discovery in major mergers extends beyond applicants' self-selected materials and base year to include all 'reasonably calculated' evidence on merger effects; (2) placing the burden squarely on applicants to justify why contemporaneous operational data should be excluded, especially when applicants cite data spanning multiple years themselves; (3) signaling that the ALJ will enforce broad discovery rights under 49 C.F.R. § 1114.21(a)(1) to enable 'fully developed record' requirement in 49 C.F.R. § 1180.1(m); (4) effectively rejecting applicants' attempt to constrain the record to 2023 despite operating circumstances changing materially through 2026; (5) establishing that intervenors' preparation materials are entitled to discovery protection and that limiting discovery undermines Major Merger Rules' statutory purpose. The immediate effectiveness and 14-day compliance deadline suggest the ALJ views further delay as inconsistent with efficient proceedings. This substantially increases applicants' litigation risk by ensuring CN and other competitors will have access to the most recent traffic, switching, and interchange patterns to construct competitive analyses contradicting applicants' benefits claims.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Applicants must provide 2025 traffic tape, reciprocal switching, and interchange data within 14 days of May 12, 2026 service date.

docket_entries.title: City of San José Comments on Application Completeness – Passenger Rail Protection Requirements
docket_entries.entry_summary: The City of San José acknowledges the merger's potential public benefits – reduced highway congestion, improved road safety, lower carbon emissions – but argues the application is incomplete because it fails to protect passenger rail networks. The City asserts: 'If the applicants are to realize the private and public benefits of this merger, they must provide meaningful concessions to protect the passenger rail network.' Specifically, San José challenges five application gaps: (1) lack of binding protection for existing Amtrak and commuter rail trackage rights; (2) absence of capacity modeling for passenger rail growth projections; (3) failure to address how consolidation reduces municipal governments' competitive leverage in rail access negotiations, creating "take-it-or-leave-it monopolies"; (4) no right-of-first-refusal protocol for corridor preservation when rights-of-way are abandoned; (5) insufficient dispatching simulations to prove freight growth won't degrade passenger service. The City requests the Board deny acceptance for determination on merits until applicants provide these additional pieces of information. This is a procedural completeness challenge, not opposition to the deal itself, signaling that San José may be willing to support the merger if applicants cure these deficiencies.
key_arguments: The merged entity will hold monopoly control over passenger rail corridor access in multiple metropolitan areas, eliminating competitive leverage that state and local governments currently use to negotiate fair access terms and rates.

The application fails to provide binding commitments that all current contractual and statutory obligations to Amtrak and regional commuter partners will be protected and not subject to unilateral renegotiation or service deprioritization post-merger.

The application lacks capacity modeling demonstrating that the merged entity will maintain sufficient infrastructure to enable projected passenger rail growth as documented in state and regional rail plans, particularly if future trackage consolidations or line abandonments occur.
The application provides no detailed dispatching simulations to prove that projected freight volume growth will not create insurmountable congestion degrading passenger service on shared corridors.

The application fails to include a formal right-of-first-refusal protocol offering states and the passenger rail community the opportunity to preserve critical public infrastructure when rights-of-way are abandoned or sold, risking permanent loss of essential transit corridors.
key_excerpts: If the applicants are to realize the private and public benefits of this merger, they must provide meaningful concessions to protect the passenger rail network.
By merging, the applicants eliminate the competitive leverage governments use when negotiating with multiple right-of-way owners, often resulting in 'take-it-or-leave-it' monopolies.
The application lacks a binding and detailed inventory of how existing trackage rights and operating agreements with passenger rail agencies will be shielded from operational changes post-merger.
Without this provision [right-of-first-refusal], the application fails to satisfy the public interest requirement of preserving essential transit corridors.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Require applicants to provide additional information before the revised application is accepted for determination on merits. Specifically: (1) explicit protection of existing trackage rights with binding commitments; (2) capacity modeling for projected passenger rail growth; (3) documentation of monopoly creation in passenger access corridors; (4) right-of-first-refusal protocol for corridor preservation; (5) detailed dispatching simulations for freight-passenger conflicts.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This filing invokes STB's authority to determine whether an application is 'complete' under 49 U.S.C. § 11324. The City argues the Board cannot accept the revised application for determination on merits unless applicants provide additional passenger rail protection information. This is a procedural gatekeeping issue that could delay Board review and create discovery obligations regarding passenger rail impacts. The filing also raises substantive public interest considerations under the STB's merger review statute – passenger rail access, infrastructure preservation, and local government negotiating power – which may require the Board to condition or structure its review to address these concerns even if it ultimately approves the merger. The right-of-first-refusal argument may implicate takings/compensation issues and state law preemption questions.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No explicit deadline stated. Filing made during Comment phase; applicants will likely address in revised application or formal response to Board on completeness determination.

docket_entries.title: Joint Reply by BNSF, CSX, CN, and CPKC Opposing UP/NS Discovery Guideline Restrictions and Proposing Alternative Framework
docket_entries.entry_summary: Joint reply by BNSF, CSX, CN, and CPKC opposing discovery limitations proposed by UP/NS applicants. Competitors argue the 50-request cap on written discovery would 'hamstring the Board's efforts to develop a complete record' in 'the largest rail consolidation ever proposed.' They contend applicants are using procedural schedule as pretext: 'The schedule should be consistent with the discovery necessary (and a longer schedule will likely be necessary as Applicants have not progressed discovery as they should have).' Competitors note applicants deliberately delayed: 'Applicants signed their merger agreement in July 2025. The intervening nine months have been more than enough time to collect email and other documents from the wide range of employees with obviously relevant material...UP and NS chose not to produce their ordinary course documents or respond to the vast majority of outstanding interrogatories.' On depositions, competitors reject requirement for 24-hour advance disclosure of deposition exhibits as 'completely foreign to any litigation process' and argue it would 'allow deponents to rehearse answers to lines of inquiry meant to test knowledge and probe credibility.' Competitors characterize applicants' restrictions as 'overreaching' and designed to 'limit the information that might come out during discovery.' They propose alternative guidelines maintaining Board default rules for broad discovery, allowing non-declarant depositions with opposing party bearing burden for protective orders, and increasing letter brief pages. Critically, competitors signal willingness to accept 'expedited letter briefing' as dispute resolution mechanism if briefs are expanded to adequate length. Filing demonstrates sophisticated litigation strategy: conditioning support for procedural efficiency (letter briefing) on substantive discovery scope preservation.
key_arguments: The 50-request cap would 'hamstring the Board's efforts to develop a complete record' in the largest railroad consolidation in Board history; by contrast, UP alone propounded 180+ formal discovery requests in the smaller CP-KCS merger without any numeric cap

Applicants' proposed schedule-driven limitation reverses proper procedure: 'The schedule should be consistent with the discovery necessary...not the other way around'; applicants deliberately created discovery backlog by not producing ordinary course documents for nine months since signing merger agreement

Retroactive application of 50-request cap to existing discovery requests 'would allow UP and NS to answer 50 of a party's discovery requests now, then unilaterally declare discovery closed,' creating 'confusion and mischief' and letting applicants 'pick and choose which questions they get to answer'

24-hour pre-deposition exhibit disclosure requirement has 'no reasonable justification' and is 'completely foreign to any litigation process'; it would allow deponents to 'rehearse answers to lines of inquiry meant to test knowledge and probe credibility'

Applicants' deposition restrictions appear designed to 'limit who may be deposed and on what terms' in violation of 49 C.F.R. § 1114.22 which permits testimony of 'any person, including a party'; burden should rest on party opposing deposition to secure protective order, not on party seeking witness

Restricting deposition start date to late June would create cascading delays requiring extended procedural schedule; competitors already requested depositions of certain witnesses and guidelines should permit earlier commencement

Applicants' 3-page limit on opening and opposition letter briefs is inadequate for complex merger discovery disputes; 5 pages for opening/opposition and 3 for supporting briefs would allow 'sufficient detail' without 'unduly burdening the ALJ'

Board rules at 49 C.F.R. § 1114.21(a)(1) permit discovery of 'any matter, not privileged, which is relevant to the subject matter' without numerical caps; if requests are duplicative or burdensome, applicants can assert line-level objections or seek protective orders per 49 C.F.R. § 1114.21(c)
key_excerpts: Discovery guidelines can be an efficient tool. But guidelines should not be used to limit the scope of discovery that would be necessary to develop a full record.

The schedule should be consistent with the discovery necessary (and a longer schedule will likely be necessary as Applicants have not progressed discovery as they should have). Applicants' proposal risks a substantive—and unnecessary—impairment of the process.

Applicants signed their merger agreement in July 2025. The intervening nine months have been more than enough time to collect email and other documents from the wide range of employees with obviously relevant material...UP and NS chose not to produce their ordinary course documents or respond to the vast majority of outstanding interrogatories.

Limiting parties to just 50 requests would narrow the substantive scope of discovery in this far more consequential proceeding. Capping the number of requests would only hamstring the Board's efforts to develop a complete record.

Imposing a retroactive cap here would allow UP and NS to answer 50 of a party's discovery requests now, then unilaterally declare discovery closed. Applicants should not get to pick and choose which questions they get to answer.

Pre-identifying documents would be cumbersome. Worse, such a process would allow deponents to rehearse answers to lines of inquiry meant to test knowledge and probe credibility. There is simply no reasonable justification for this disclosure requirement that relates to aiding the Board's or interested parties' analysis of the merger.

The Rules are clear: 'The testimony of any person, including a party, may be taken by deposition.' That burden shall rest with the party opposing any deposition to secure a protective order if that opposing party believes the deponent does not have case-relevant information.
It cannot be that parties are limited to what they can seek and ask in the biggest proceeding in the Board's history.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Reject UP/NS proposed discovery guidelines that cap written requests at 50, limit deposition scope, and constrain discovery to procedural schedule. Enter alternative guidelines (Appendix A) that: (1) allow unrestricted written discovery per Board rules; (2) permit depositions of any person with case-relevant information; (3) allow 5 pages for opening/opposition letter briefs (vs. 3 pages); (4) permit depositions to commence before late June; (5) require 24-hour advance production of deposition exhibits.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: CRITICAL procedural filing that challenges applicant attempt to use discovery guidelines as gatekeeping mechanism. Competitors argue applicants are circumventing 49 C.F.R. § 1114.21(a)(1) (broad discovery right) and § 1114.21(c) (protective order as remedy for excessive discovery) by seeking front-end numerical caps. Filing invokes Board precedent (Omaha Pub. Power Dist. v. Union Pac. R.R.) for broad/flexible discovery. If competitors prevail, applicants cannot restrict discovery scope via procedure; discovery will proceed under default Board rules allowing 'any matter...relevant to the subject matter.' This exposes applicants to potentially 200+ written interrogatories and depositions of non-declarant witnesses (e.g., operational personnel, sales staff). Competitors' proposed guidelines effectively shift burden to applicants to justify why specific discovery is burdensome/irrelevant, rather than front-end caps. Filing also signals competitors will aggressively develop record on competitive impacts—critical for Phase II substantive review. The filing does NOT oppose the merger outright but conditions support for procedural efficiency on discovery scope preservation, suggesting competitors are willing to settle on discovery protocols IF expansion to substantive discovery is guaranteed.
docket_entries.deadline_description: No specific deadline stated; filing is reply to UP/NS motion on discovery guidelines. ALJ or Board must rule on competing guideline proposals before discovery phase commences.

docket_entries.title: Union Pacific Errata/Correction to Amended Application - Metro-North Commuter Rail Service Disclosure
docket_entries.entry_summary: Union Pacific filed errata corrections to its Amended Application, adding previously omitted disclosure of Metro-North Railroad's commuter rail operations on an NS-owned line. The corrections specify that Metro-North operates the Port Jervis Line between Suffern and Port Jervis, New York (approximately 95 miles), with 13 inbound and 15 outbound weekday trains, plus 9 inbound and 8 outbound weekend trains. Metro-North has responsibility for dispatching, maintenance, inspections, and capital improvements under a 2003 sublease and operations agreement with NJ Transit providing dispatch functions. Critically, applicants affirmatively state in the errata that 'Applicants' plan does not anticipate the addition of trains to the Metro-North route,' which signals either operational constraints or an explicit commitment regarding service levels on this passenger corridor. The timing of this correction—added to April 30 Amended Application via May 12 errata—raises procedural questions about completeness of the original application and whether intervenors will seek discovery into passenger rail service impacts.
key_arguments: Applicants acknowledge Metro-North operates 13-15 inbound/outbound weekday trains and 9-8 weekend trains on NS-owned Port Jervis Line infrastructure, with Metro-North responsible for dispatch, maintenance, inspections, and capital improvements

Applicants explicitly state merger plan does not anticipate addition of trains to Metro-North route, which either reflects operational constraints or constitutes a binding commitment on service expansion
Metro-North operates as tenant on NS-owned line under 2003 sublease agreement with NJ Transit providing dispatch services, creating multi-party operational dependencies
key_excerpts: Metro-North's Port Jervis Line operates commuter rail service on an NS-owned line between Suffern and Port Jervis, New York. Metro-North has responsibility for dispatching, maintenance, inspections, and constructing capital improvements on the line, which is approximately 95 miles. There are 13 inbound trains each weekday and 15 outbound trains each weekday. On weekends, there are nine inbound trains and eight outbound trains.
Merger Impact: Applicants' plan does not anticipate the addition of trains to the Metro-North route.

While owned by NS, NS functions as a tenant on the line. The line is dispatched by New Jersey Transit for Metro-North, which has responsibility for dispatching, maintenance, inspections, and constructing capital improvements pursuant to a 2003 sublease and operations agreement.
docket_entries.relief_requested: Accept errata corrections to Amended Application filed April 30, 2026, specifically adding disclosure of Metro-North commuter rail service operating on NS-owned Port Jervis Line between Suffern and Port Jervis, New York.
docket_entries.legal_regulatory_significance: This errata adds material facts regarding passenger rail operations on applicant-controlled infrastructure that were omitted from the Amended Application. The late disclosure and explicit merger impact statement ('does not anticipate addition of trains') may trigger: (1) discovery demands from intervenors regarding passenger service coordination obligations, (2) requests for formal conditions binding applicants to maintain Metro-North service levels, (3) potential intervention by Metro-North or NJ Transit if they filed for intervention status, (4) evidentiary questions about whether applicants can legally restrict service on this shared corridor. The correction also implicates 49 U.S.C. § 11324(d) requirements that applicants affirmatively disclose service and operational impacts. The reference to Docket No. FD 34293 (2003 sublease) creates a regulatory record that may be discoverable regarding operational constraints and service obligations.
docket_entries.deadline_description: Errata filed May 12, 2026 as correction to April 30, 2026 Amended Application. No response deadline specified; procedurally treated as amendment to applicants' submissions.
